# Clarion Call

## Abortion and the Vedic Viewpoint

*No-Choice No-Life*

The Eastern, and typically the ancient Indian or Vedic world view on life, advocates that consciousness, not matter, moves the world. Therefore in this world view life in the womb is not a material development resulting from the combination of the male sperm and the female ovum. Rather life, or consciousness makes possible the combining of the these two which in turn produce a karmic material body for the soul to take birth in. The consciousness of the man and woman in general and particularly at the time of conception, attracts a particular soul with karma that in most instances corresponds with the consciousness of the parents.

In the Vedic view human life is meant for self-realization and the act of sexual intercourse is to be embraced, as is every other human experience, in such a way as to promote spiritual consciousness. The fleeting pleasures of the senses are reactionary. That is, they bring with them, along with momentary pleasure, a karmic reaction that keeps us in the cycle of birth and death, reincarnation. If our human life is spent in the culture of God consciousness, we can transcend the cycle of birth and death and thus never have to see another womb.

From the Vedic viewpoint, those who are being aborted in this life may very well have performed abortions in their past lives. So the choice is ours, and so are the consequences. If we choose a life of self- realization and higher spiritual values, then when we also choose to indulge in sexual intercourse, we do so full knowing the natural result will be children. It is meaningless to insist that sex is natural and at the same time advocate contraception and abortion which are human attempts to enjoy the pleasure of sex while avoiding natural the consequences. Animals also have a sex drive but they do not indulge in it at times which are not conducive to procreation. Humans are intended to conduct themselves similarly, and then raise their children in a life directed towards self-realization. Unfortunately we have distorted life so much that many artificial desires seem "natural." Thus many people are sexually agitated most of the time.

Therefore the Vedic view is both pro-life and pro-choice at the same time. Women have the right to choose whether to conceive or not. That's where the choice comes in. If men and women choose not to conceive they have no business indulging in sex, that is, if they are interested in a life of self realization.

## Agricide

An Interview with Dr. Michael Fox  
By Jay Wagner

Dr. Michael Fox is the director of the Humane Society of the United States and author of several books including Agricide. What is the future of our planets agriculture? What are the far reaching side effects of our high tech approach to farming? In this interview Dr. Fox addresses these and other issues with deep insight.

\[NOTE: Some text may be out of place\]

Clarion Call: In your book Agricide, you mentioned that unless there is a turnabout in the way that agricultural industry is being conducted, the next generation will face inevitable "agricide." What does that mean, and what is the next generation actually facing?

Dr. Fox: We are pretty much in the middle of it even now. It's a crisis that has been growing, and my definition of agricide is essentially the failure of the agricultural food production system to be sustainable— ecologically, economically, and in terms of contributing positively to our health. The food production system has become increasingly toxic with pesticides and other agrichemical residues, and together with the hazards of the various antibiotics and other drugs that are given to farm animals to help them cope with the stresses of intensive confinement and husbandry systems and to boost productivity—such as the synthetic hormones—all of these certainly pose a question in terms of human health. Then we have the spectre of depletion of our agricultural soils through soil erosion , and even more insidious is the depletion of our central trace minerals, so the crops that are produced are nutritionally deficient because the proper fertilizers are not being used; and this again has an adverse effect on human health and on the health of the farm animals that are being fed some of these crops. So this in my mind is agricide. We're stealing from future generations basically because we have a chemically dependent agriculture that is primarily meat-based, and the meat-based food production system is wasteful of non-renewable natural resources.

Clarion Call: It was Cesar Chavez who told me that when the crop becomes dependent upon chemical fertilizers, it also becomes more susceptible to insect attack, and therefore requires more insecticides. Is that something that your scientific findings have unearthed?

Dr. Fox: Yes, this is well documented now. It's precisely the same phenomena analogous to the farm animals too: the more we force them to grow rapidly, to produce a lot of milk or a lot of eggs, the more their system becomes stressed and more susceptible to disease, just like the super-fertilized agricultural crops become more vulnerable to various pests. So the crops will need more pesticides and the farm animals will need more antibiotics and other disease-controlling drugs.

Clarion Call:  To my understanding , this is unique in human history. Do you care to speak about how all of this has evolved?

Dr. Fox: It evolved, I believe, way back in the time of Francis Bacon and Rene Descartes. Descartes reckoned that animals are unfeeling machines and he evoked religious authority that animals can be exploited for whatever purposes we choose— which goes back to Thomas Aquinas, the Augustinian tradition— while Francis Bacon gave religious sanction to having what he called a commerce with nature— that we can improve upon nature through instrumental power of scientific knowledge; and this gave birth to today's technocracy that uses knowledge as power rather than empathetic knowledge to work co-creatively with the forces of nature.

Clarion Call: So what you're saying is that there's a need to change the philosophical view, the world view, of food production....

Dr. Fox: Yes, the whole world view. We need a paradigm shift away from hard medicine, away from hard agriculture and linear thinking. By hard I mean using potentially harmful drugs and interventive procedures. We think we have some new innovation and then we have problems, so we then apply a new technological fix. For example, we try to boost the crops with artificial fertilizers and we use super-fast growing hybrids that are more susceptible to diseases, so we then use chemicals as the next technological fix. We have a residual problem with the chemicals— one extreme example being genetic damage in human beings because many of these chemicals are mutogenes— so the next technological fix is genetic engineering to correct these problems in human beings. Or we can have a bureaucratic fix— which we call government oversight—to regulate the residues and the use of these chemicals, which of course is silly. We just get into a vicious circle or a treadmill effect. The primary beneficiaries, of course, are the peddlers of these new technological fixes — petrochemical companies or other companies that are investing heavily in biotechnology— or the government bureaucrats themselves who benefit from "regulating" that which cannot be regulated. So I see it basically as a state-of-mind problem that is having a negative impact on the state of the environment.

Clarion Call: Can you talk about what we are to expect if things don't change?

Dr. Fox: We can expect a continuing deterioration of the farming industry, the extinction of the family farm, and the shift towards factory farms. If we don't have a paradigm shift towards a regenerative and healthful agriculture, we will have a worsening health condition in the populous. Many of these chemicals have been linked with genetic damage, sterility, cancer, and birth defects. These are going to increase. The loss of the family farm is a great tragedy because we are losing the wisdom of generations acquired in particular by regions of people who know best how to farm. Plus the small family farming network is a diversified form of agriculture, and when we lose agricultural diversity, as in any ecosystem , we have increasing instability, and that does not speak well for economic sustainability. And another concern is that our agricultural system will become much more vulnerable to pests, blight, drought , and so on.

Clarion Call: Are the problems which the farmers have been recently experiencing all part of this agricultural system's incorrect evolution?

Dr. Fox: Yes it is, and the government has essentially aided and abetted the demise of the family farm, as have many of our land-grant colleges which, as in California, have developed the Tomato Harvester and the Agribusiness Tomato. The best place for these tomatoes is probably on the fenders of cars; they're very hard to store and pack, and the land-grant colleges have not fulfilled their original mandate to help role communities improve their agriculture. They've aided and abetted the demise of rural communities.

We have a tax structure that favors the factory farm. However, we also have consumer power, and as I suggested in my Agricide book, the consumers can support local producers and farmers' markets and develop their own co-ops, ideally buying food that has been properly raised without chemicals, and on regenerated soils too, so the products themselves are more nutritious.

Clarion Call: You mentioned that in one sense the government is partially responsible for these developments, and it's certainly not the first time that the government has made a mistake, but I'm curious— under what pressures is the government encouraging this direction of things?

Dr. Fox: Well, I think it's the ideology that bigness is best, but there are limits to the economy's scale. The government, and especially the U.S. Department of Agribusiness— as I refer to the U.S.D.A.— should get out of the marketplace and allow a free market economy to blossom. The best role that the government could play would be to provide advice and encouragement in the way of tax incentives to farmers who get away from chemically dependent farming, but they have an ideological mind set that the use of pesticides and other chemicals is the best and most efficient way to produce food, and the bigger the farm the better; but we have evidence to the contrary. However the government also is essentially a puppet strung by some of the large corporate interests and their lobbyists, notably the petrochemical and the pharmaceutical companies, both of which profit royally from the kind of agriculture that is practiced today. The primary beneficiaries are these large companies— the multinationals and their investors— and not the public, not the rural communities, and this needs to be changed.

You know, although agribusiness claims that our food is probably the cheapest in the world, there are many hidden costs, and one of them this last year was $9 billion that has come out of the taxpayers' pockets to subsidize farms, to give them price supports, and to actually pay them not to produce, which is ridiculous. Predictions for next year is $13 billion, and this is insane. The government needs to get out of the marketplace and selectively assist those farmers who are not producing food that is contaminated with various chemicals.

There is another problem where the super farms are not actually owned by the farmers, but are owned by off-farm investors who can use it as a tax shelter. There is a problem when they employ managers of their operations who don't have the feeling for the land or for the animals because their children's children are not going to inherit the land, and they don't have the same kind of empathy that is so important and is an integral aspect of sound agricultural practices and humane animal husbandry.

Clarion Call: What kind of erosion and other practices are taking place that are actually causing the destruction of lands?

Dr. Fox:  One of the problems is that the farmers have been encouraged by the government and by the banks not to produce crops for export to feed the hungry world, but to raise corn and soybeans to feed farm animals in more affluent countries so people there can maintain the meat habit. This increasing production pressure has meant that farmers have not engaged in such practices as crop rotation and letting the land rest or fallow, and along with improper plowing practices, this has led to increasing problems of soil erosion, especially where farmers have engaged in what is called "sodbusting" and opened up land which is very prone to soil erosion anyway, and we are now losing about six billion tons of topsoil a year. The government's response has been to encourage farmers not to plow in order to control weeds, but instead to spray herbicides on the ground to control the weeds, which causes further poisoning of our water. It's unnecessary, because there are many other ways to control weeds and to prevent soil erosion.

Another problem is that we are running out of water. A lot of deep aquifers are now running dry, and many like the Ogalala are also poisoned by agricultural chemicals, and the main reason for this incredible exploitation of our water reserves has been to irrigate crops not to feed people, but primarily to feed farm animals so we can enjoy more meat. So it's back to what we discussed earlier— that the great weakness in U.S. agriculture is not only the use of harmful chemicals, but the fact that it is meat-based. You can produce 280 pounds of high-quality soy protein per acre, and from that same acre you can only produce 15 to 20 pounds of beef. So it's very silly to maintain the present structure of agriculture that is meat-based. A lot of people who claim to care for wildlife sit down and eat their steak or their chicken, not realizing that the production of livestock and poultry has meant the expansion of agriculture, the opening up of more land, and the displacement, poisoning, and extinction of many wildlife species in this country.

So we need to help restore nature and cut back on our meat consumption and production if we are really concerned about the rights of wild animals, and a number of studies have shown that this will also improve our health, that we need to get away from a high meat and saturated fat diet and shift towards a high fiber, grain, bean, and vegetable diet.We also have to be careful, as I mentioned in the book, about eating fruits and vegetables that are out of season or those that have been imported from other countries, because many pesticides now banned for use in this country are still manufactured in this country and exported, so we are poisoning ourselves as well as contributing to the poisoning of people in other countries. The estimated death rate is at least 40,000 a year, which is ridiculous.

Clarion Call: Is this part of what you referred to in your book as eating humanely?

Dr. Fox:  Eating with conscience, eating humanely. I think of tofu as a humane alternative to meat. Generally I would say that the most inhumane product is veal. Veal calves are kept in crates in which they cannot walk or turn around for 16 weeks. And when you look at how on these large factory farms the mother sows are kept either chained to the ground with a tether around their shoulders their entire lives or kept in narrow pens in which they cannot walk or turn around, then you would see how eating pork and bacon from the piglets who are the offspring of these sows is also contributing to animal cruelty.

So we can wipe off pork, bacon, ham, veal, and then you think, "Well, how about lamb? The sheep have a nice, happy life, generally." Well, there is a move now to raise sheep in confinement, and those that are kept on the open range are generally not cared for properly, and there is indiscriminate poisoning of coyotes and other predators.So it's ultimately an enlightened decision, I think, to move towards vegetarianism. It's the ultimate answer as I see it.

Clarion Call: There's one very strong statement in your book Agricide to the effect that the industrialization of American agriculture is emerging as a threat to the nation's security. Can you explain what that means?

Dr. Fox: Well, I think the security of a nation is based primarily upon a sound economy, and a sound agricultural economy has to have a sound ecological base, and we have an ecologically unsound agriculture, and therefore it's a threat to our long-term economy, especially when we are running out of topsoil and irrigation water. It's also a threat to the national security because it jeopardizes our health and is contributing to the demise of rural communities, which is analogous to the disenfranchisement of peasants in the third world by colonial agribusiness; and there is more unemployment, and what happens to the farmers who are unemployed? Suicide, depression, emigration to the cities, loss of rural wisdom— I think that, too, is a threat to national security.

Clarion Call: Is the best way to change all this just to educate the consumers and try to get them to change their tastes, so to speak?

Dr. Fox: I think consumer education is a vital ingredient of any social revolution. Another one is to educate the legislators, and we are endeavoring to do that too. We're not alone; there are many other farming groups and consumer advocacy groups endeavoring to do this, to bring about a paradigm shift or a change in the world view. We need to move toward a more holistic, more empathetic, and basically more spiritual way of relating to the creation. When we abuse the creation, when we abuse factory farm animals, when we abuse the land by poisoning it with chemicals, we ultimately abuse ourselves, because everything is interconnected. We need to develop a reverence for the creation, and that's an important element of good farming practices.

Clarion Call: Dr. Fox, could you briefly outline the goals of the International Network for Religion and Animals?

Dr. Fox: We are actively pursuing a dialogue with various religious leaders and religious communities, bringing to their awareness the plight of the animal kingdom, and it is quite evident when you start reading the basic scriptures of all the major religions of the world that they all recognize the importance of treating God's creation with reverence. The crises that humanity faces today are primarily ideological, spiritual, and ethical, and I feel we need to make choices that resonate with enlightened self-interest and contribute to the greater good, and in my bag vegetarianism is certainly one. Another is endeavoring to change our lifestyle so that we live more gently. If we want a new piece of furniture, are we going to buy new teak or mahogany and contribute to further deforestation of the tropical rain forests, or buy some older piece of furniture that somebody else had years ago and is simply being recycled? There are many, many ways of living humanely, living with conscience, that to me is a spiritual and an ethical imperative. The Hopis have a term for our condition. The Hopi Indians call life out of balance koyaanisqatsi, and we have an imbalanced agriculture and generally a society that is living out of balance with the rest of creation; and more technological fixes are not going to restore that balance until we have a mental fix, a change in heart and mind. Reverend James Morton from New York, for example, says that ecology is the science of the body of Christ, through which we learn our sacred connections. Now this is a new kind of thinking that is appearing today, and there are very similar quotes from Taoism, from Buddhism, and from Hinduism that are leading us toward a humane planetary stewardship. "Tea de Chada," the great Jesuit priest and paleontologist, said in the fifties that "We are rapidly approaching the point where we will have the final choice between suicide or adoration," and I believe that we've reached that point now. The suicidal path is in tide with agricide, with the technocratic imperialism of using power over nature, power over the creation, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. We have to find the way to live gently. Let us use knowledge not for our own selfish gain but to further the greater good.

Clarion Call: Thank you.

Jay Wagner is the founder of Cultural Media Services and an assistant editor for Clarion Call  
For more information readers can write to The Humane Society of the United States 2100 L Street, NW Washington, D.C. 20037

## "Animals' Rights - Humans' Wrongs"

Interview with Tom Regan by Jay Wagner

Clarion Call: Professor Regan, you are widely accepted as a founder and prominent leader in the animal rights movement. Could you describe what is meant by animal rights and what do you mean when you speak of the "rights view"?

Professor Regan: There are many people who feel that we have an obligation to be kind to animals, and not to be cruel to them. But this view doesn't make it a matter of justice that we treat animals in a certain way—just that it is nice if we are kind and not very good if we are cruel. Many people think that we should be nice to animals because if we are not nice to animals we will not be nice people, and then we will end up beating up our children and our neighbors and so on. The problem is, these views don't focus on our duty to animals but only on the effects our treatment of animals has on us. The rights view says, "We owe it as a matter of strict justice to treat animals in a certain way." In particular we owe it to these animals not to eat them, for example, or not to put them in cages for our entertainment, or not Lo use them in education or in surgery, which Is so anachronistic and yet characteristic of modern medical education in the United States. The current view is, "These animals are ours, we may do with them as we wish." The rights view says, "No you may not. They cannot claim their rights, they cannot understand their rights, and in this way they are very much like mentally enfeebled human beings. But they have them none the less."

The important thing to see is that the animal rights position, properly understood, is the human rights position. It's not that we are saying that non-human animals have a right to be treated with respect but human animals don't. We're dealing with the rights of all animals, and since we humans are animals, it follows that we have the same basic kinds of rights as they do.

Clarion Call: Your fate, you have said, is to help others see animals in a different way—as creatures who do not belong in cages or skillets. How would you have people see animals?

Professor Regan: It's a very difficult thing. It's something we all struggle towards and I'm not sure that I have perfected it myself. To quote from Dustin, "... see them as other nations, see them as sharing the earth with us, co-inhabitants with us," but essentially having the capacity, as in the case of wild animals, of living quite separately from us. In the case of domestic animals the great challenge is to figure out how to live in a mutually respectful symbiotic relationship. It is very difficult to do that.

Clarion Call: What were some of your main reasons or motives for writing The Case For Animal Rights? And do you feel these objectives are being accomplished?

Professor Regan: T think the main reason I wrote the book was to finally say in a very disciplined, rigorous, and in some ways an emotionally detached style that animals in fact do have rights and are entitled to he treated accordingly because of strict justice. Many people talked about animal rights and it had become a slogan—part of the political rhetoric of America and its talk of rights. But no one had set out to make the case for animal rights in a very disciplined, sustained way. So I thought it was important to do that. Certainly it is not a popular book, one that you can race through. It is a book to be studied rather than to be read. But I also think of it as a weapon. Frequently thofee of us who advocate animal rights are considered uninformed, illogical, sloppy, sentimental and so on. And I take the book to be a philosophical tool for ramming those accusations down the throats of those uninformed, emotional, illogical and sloppy thinkers who make these accusations.

Clarion Call: I understand that the Vietnam War, Gandhi and, believe it or not, the death of your own pet dog all became impetuses to your involvement in the animal rights movement. Can you fill in the missing parts?

Professor Regan: Regarding the Vietnam War, it occurred to me that if I was going to be an effective activist in the streets, I'd have to combine my activism with scholarship. So I began to research the fields of nonviolent conflict resolution, pacifism, aggression, war, and so forth, and in the course of doing that it was inevitable that I read Gandhi. Gandhi was obviously very relevant to the question of violence and war and so on. He was the first one who challenged me to think about what I call the invisible violence in our life, in particular the food that we eat. We normally don't think of the violence that goes into the production of animal products—meat and other byproducts. Gandhi was the first person who taught me that the fork is a weapon of violence. I was worried about napalm and M-17's and flame throwers, and here I was participating in violence myself and yet blind to it. So intellectually I derived the arguments for vegetarianism from Gandhi's influence. But what opened my heart to the issue was the death of our dog. It was before we had children, and as so often happens the dog was like a surrogate child for us. When we returned home one day the dog had been killed, which caused us tremendous grief. But I realized in the course of that experience that there was in me (although suppressed or repressed by society) a great caring for animals that wasn't considered appropriate for a man. This was part of the aculturization in our macho society in which men are not supposed to care about animals. Nonetheless I felt a deep love for this particular animal, but it was too great a love, too great a sense of compassion, to be reposed in just one creature; it was a more boundless compassion. I was very fortunate that my head and my heart came together at that particular time in my life. And from then on there was no turning back.

Clarion Call: Rene Decartes holds a very influential position in the history of Western philosophy. What were his views regarding animals and consciousness, and how has that influenced the modern world view?

Professor Regan: Decartes, a Catholic thinker, argued that animals are nature's machines. He thought of them as unthinking, unfeeling creatures who are not aware of anything, who are essentially like wind-up toys, except that you don't have to wind them up. It was an enormously influential view, because it happened to coincide with the development of experimental physiology. This was during the 17th century in France. The Cartesian scientists were intellectually given a license not to worry about how the animals responded, and of course this was before anesthesia. They literally nailed dogs up by all four paws, then simply opened up their stomaches and studied the circulation of their blood— on live, un-anestheticized animals who were screaming in agony. In many ways, I think that today's fields of research involving non-human animals were birthed by Decartes' ideas. And to this day there are many closet Cartesians out there who are still part of the scientific establishment, who still wonder whether animals feel pain. It was not only historically influential, it continues to be influential.

Clarion Call: In the realm of religion, I can see Christendom uniting against cruelty, but they haven't as yet seen the fork as a weapon of violence. What do you, and Judeo-Christian leaders you know, find in that tradition that would support animal rights and vegetarianism?

Professor Regan: It's going to be difficult to persuade the great masses of Christians to give up the meat on their plate. What we can do is to persuade them to give up supporting the factory farm. In effect this would be to give up eating meat, because it's very difficult to get any meat that has not been raised on a factory farm. So we may end up having defacto Christian vegetarians without their being de joure. In other words they will be vegetarians so long as the meat comes from a certain source, but otherwise not.

It is absolutely clear that in Eden our diet was vegetarian. So, Biblically speaking, what we have now is a fallen world; and one step back to Eden would be to stop eating meat. Biblically this is absolutely clear. When I speak to Christians and to Jews in those terms, then they at least begin to think, maybe it is not just factory-farmed veal that I should be saying no to, maybe there is something deeper here. After all, why remain alienated from God over a hamburger?

Clarion Call: In your interview in The Animals' Agenda magazine you stated, "There is no way out of our own bondage and current predicaments without helping animals." And you have also said, "There will be no peace in the world until there is peace at home." How would you support these statements?

Professor Regan: They may be more declarations of faith than they are hard core scientific claims. Most people are unaware of the invisible violence in their lives. They go and buy toothpaste and shampoos and deodorants and so on, unthinkingly. These are items that we need, and we bring them home and we use them, and when we are out of them we go and replenish them. People must begin to realize that these products have a history of violence to them in which animals have been used in testing them in excruciatingly painful ways, like eye irritancy tests, skin irritancy tests and other sorts of tests. All the products in our home have been tested in these ways, unless we go to the trouble to find products that have not been tested in those ways and buy them. I have got to believe that supporting that kind of thing in ignorance is a terrible human failing. We are just fooling ourselves if we think we can bring peace to the world, and change the opinions and the visions and the desires and the ideals of people all throughout the world, if we can't even say to ourselves, "By God, I've got to get rid of this stuff in my house." I mean, whom are we fooling?

My view is that those over whom we have control are ourselves. That's where we should start. Peace begins at home. Nonviolence begins at home. Progress begins at home. I'm not saying not to work as a political activist. Of course, I do that myself. But I think we have to work to clean up our own act, to get our own house in order. But then people say, "We will lose so much. You are asking us to give up so much." And my view is, "No, you don't lose, you gain." What you gain is control of your life—through the knowledge of what you are doing with a dollar bill. Take those ideals of harmony and justice and nonviolence and caring and compassion and express them in the marketplace. That's where it begins.

Clarion Call: You have described that animals are used in the field of science nowadays in three subcatego ries: education, toxicology or poisons testing, and research. What are your views on the age old argument about stopping progress if we don't use animals in these ways?

Professor Regan: Let's go through them: education, toxicology testing and research. In the field of education the United States is an anachronism. We normally require our young people, sometimes from grade school up, to dissect and vivisect animals, and if a young person says, "No, I have an objection to doing this," then they are ridiculed, they are punished, or something happens. In fact there is a recent case in California of a fourteen year old girl standing up and saying, "I'm not going to dissect this frog," and she was hassled. So the school board says, "Okay, you don't have to dissect the frog, but we are going to put a little note on your permanent record that says you didn't do all the work that was required of you." Well, I hope that all the young people and their parents reading this say, "Enough is enough!" We should not brutalize our children in this way by forcing them to do something which, if they did on their own in a public place, they would be arrested for. If you take a frog into a shopping mall and prepare to dissect it, you are going to get arrested. But you take that same situation and put it in a school and require somebody to do that and punish them if they don't. Now that kind of schizophrenia is unfathomable to me!

In medical education in Great Britain, both in human medicine and in veterinary medicine, no student is ever required to dissect or vivisect an animal. In seventeen British universities, including Cambridge and Oxford, it is a written policy that if you have a conscientious objection to doing any dissection or vivisection you need not do it. Now, are we in America seriously going to say that this fourteen year old girl, or all those for whom she speaks, can't get a decent education in the life sciences without dissecting and vivisecting? Heavens no. Gandhi, my hero, says, "You can judge the character and greatness of a society by how it treats its animals." There are always two victims in a laboratory situation. One is the non-human animal and the other is the student. And sometimes I think it's the instructor too who has been victimized.

Now let's consider product testing, toxicity testing. First I would like to mention that there are nonviolent, cruelty-free cosmetics and household items that are available. (If people write to me I will send them a list of cruelty-free products,) Very often people say, "If we don't do these toxicity tests on animals then it is a great risk for public health." That is just propaganda produced by the animal exploiters. In the November 1986 issue of Nature magazine it was shown that if you do a battery of ten non-animal tests (such as cell and tissue culture and mathematical modeling tests), you can get results that are superior to all the animal tests regarding carcinogenic and other effects. Now, there are sixty thousand human-factured chemicals in the marketplace. Sixty thousand. And only two thousand have been tested on animals. If we started right now and tried to test on animals the other fifty-eight thousand that are out there—that we are breathing, eating, inhaling and getting exposed to through our skin and so on—it would take us a hundred years and it would cost between two and four million dollars for each test. We neither have the time, nor the will, nor the financial ability to do this. But if we do the battery of non-animal tests we can do it in two to four days for two hundred dollars per chemical. Now, anyone who says, "You are against progress, you are going to set back science, you are against public health, you really hate human beings, you just love animals," and so on, this is, I think, ridiculous.

The only people who are going to say that with a straight face are the people who are in the business of making money from the sale and use of animals. And my view is, don't believe them, don't taist them. They always say, "We love animals; we wouldn't use them if we didn't have to." Well, that's just rhetoric. I have never known a research scientist who said that who went to the trouble to buy cruelty-free cosmetics. And those alternatives already exist. If they really loved animals they wouldn't buy products of pain. I've never known a research scientist who said, "I wouldn't use animals unless I had to; I love animals," who is a vegetarian. But if they really did love animals the way they say they do, they wouldn't eat them, because there is an alternative there, and a healthier alternative as well. So don't believe these people for a minute. They use animals because they have been trained to use animals, because they have a career tied up in using animals, and because if they didn't use animals they wouldn't have a job any more!

In a very important book called Alternatives to Pain For Experiments on Animals Dallas Pratt reports on a hundred or so cases that he investigated in which scientists used animals in painful experiments when valid nonviolent scientific alternatives already existed. In terms of research, there is every reason to believe that animal experimentation is actually retarding the progress of science rather than helping it go forward. All we have to do is look at cancer research as a case in point. They have put twenty billion dollars into cancer research. And as the recent report from the Office of Technology Assessment states, they have really made no significant progress in twenty years of research. Why? Because they give cancer to mice and rats—that's their methodology. Then they try to extrapolate that to human beings. I think that the future of- all advances in medicine and research is at the cell and tissue level, which doesn't have anything to do with whole animal model testing.

I think the thing that people need to realize also is that science is just big business, an enormous business. In fact, I refer to the medical-industrial complex, which is much larger and more sinister than the military-industrial complex because it gets away with more. It's not in the business to keep people well. It's in the business to have people sick, and this is a great failing, a social failing. So, what we need to do is not only change laws and change attitudes and so on, but also to change the whole complexion of science and medicine as practiced in this country.

Clarion Call: In the epilogue of your book, The Case For Animal Rights, you stated that the rights view is not anti-business, nor anti-science, nor anti-freedom of the individual, and yet those whose business it is to use animals in research and in trade might disagree. How would you defend your statement?

Professor Regan: To say that a i certain business should end is not, in / and of itself, anti-business. There was a business in the trade of slaves, and when we said, "Look, you can't do this anymore, you can't buy and sell slaves as pieces of property," that wasn't anti-business. We were just saying that there are some things that are not to be bought or sold. So similarly, if we arrive at the point where animals are not bought and sold for scientific purposes or for gustatory delight, that will not be anti-business. People will still be encouraged to make a fiving. There is nothing in the animal rights movement or philosophy that follows any particular party line or economic line, i It is not conservative or liberal, Repub-1 lican or Democrat. It is not against the 1 free market. It just says, if you do have a free market then you are going to i have to make a living without exploit -) ing animals. And that's not anti-business. In fact, what it does is create all kinds of new businesses, alternatives like tofuburgers for example. So, it's not anti-business and it's certainly not anti-freedom of the individual. No one 1 has the freedom to violate the rights of anybody else. That's not one of our f freedoms. If we agree that animals have rights, then no one has that free-t dom. So it's not against human freedom, it's against the excess of human t freedom.

Animal rights could hardly be char-t acterized as anti-science. In fact. I think r the animal experimentation methodology that characterizes Western science is anti-science—stagecoach methodology, something that fits the 19th century. Here we are almost in the 21st century and people are still dissecting rats and pithing frogs. What does that tell us? It tells us that rather than animal rights being anti-scientific it is very pro-scientific. We want to see science outgrow its past; grown-up science is what we want. I think of Galileo's contemporaries when he said, "I want you to look through this telescope to see what's out there.'' And of course they all said, "No. No. We have no need. We know what's out there. We don't have to look." When contemporary scientists say, "There are no alternatives," that is like Galileo's contemporaries saying, "We already know, we are not going to look." Again, almost to a person, when the scientists that I have dealt with say there are no alternatives, they have never made the slightest conscientious effort to find them.

Clarion Call: There is a rise of interest in preventive medicine, and a growing acknowledgement that indeed diet has something to do with health. Gandhi influenced you dietar-ily. If you will, talk about your dietary convictions and practices-Professor Regan: When I read Gandhi he challenged me to think about the violence that I was supporting by eating animals. That made a profound impact on me. So when I entered the animal rights movement my first step was at the dinner table, so to speak. Since that time I have learned a great deal about what others have to say about diet, its effect on the environment on the one hand, and its effect on the human body on the other. If we look just at the health aspect of it, the arguments against eating animals are so overwhelming. We are what we eat, and if we eat a lot of fat we are going to be fat—in the wrong ways, in the wrong places, and in the wrong times. It just makes sense not to eat meat.

When people say, I don't eat red meat, just chicken, that really cracks me up, because somehow they think that if they eat white meat they will minimize their health risks. In fact, back East the pork industry has a major campaign to convince people that pork is white meat.

We have recently seen the statistics about the effects of eating cnicKen. According to a report issued by the National Resource Council, there are millions of cases per year of people becoming sick from the Salmonella bacteria in chicken—mil-lions of cases of Americans having flu-like symptoms: diarrhea, vomiting, fever and so on. And people say, Oh, it's the flu. It's not the flu, it's Salmonella poisoning! There are people dying of this bacteria. So the idea that we can avoid serious health risks by eating white meat is just laughable.

The way to prevent illness most effectively is through our life style. If we stop smoking, stop drinking heavily, stop eating meat, and get enough exercise, we will become healthy— either to sustain our health or to recapture it if we have lost it. People say, "If you don't eat meat, look at what you are giving up." My message is always the same: Look at what you are gaining. Not only are you getting your health again, you are gaining your life again!

Clarion Call: I'm sure the animal rights movement has something to do with the fact that now as many as a hundred thousand philosophy students a year are discussing such issues as the moral basis of vegetarianism.

Professor Regan: That's true, there has been more written by philosophers in the past decade on animal rights than has been written in the previous two thousand years. What we have is an enormous outpouring of interest in this particular issue, and it has found its way into the classroom, into the textbooks. Typically, where students are taking courses about contemporary issues like abortion, euthanasia, nuclear war, famine and pollution, now animal rights is also on the agenda of moral concern. It is in these sorts of courses where animal rights is making its presence felt. It's not a fad. This is not going away. On the contrary, intellectual activity in this area is increasing all the time. People are writing their dissertations on animal rights. Now animal rights is part of mainstream academic intellectual life in the United States, in England, in Australia and in Europe. Throughout the ages we have had wonderful, important, articulate, influential people speaking for animal rights, but until now it never made it into the clas-sroom.

Clarion Call: To quote directly from your writings, you said, "There is another revolution coming and it is going to be a big one." At the same time, you see animal rights issues as a cause celebre on America's college campuses. Will this issue of animal rights supply the same intense motivation that, say, free speech, minority Continued on pg. 48 rights and other issues did to recent past generations?

Professor Regan: My hope is that the rising generation of students will see animal rights as their issue, and not just in terms of the laboratory animal issue, but a larger issue of the integrity of creation and respect for nature. It's going to be bigger and broader, but it's still going lo be their issue. It'll be for them to say, "Enough is enough. We .ire not going to continue to do what our parents did, what our grandparents did, and so on. We are going to take charge of something here." I am very hopeful that the revolution is coming, and the philosophy of youth—which ib question authority, question authority—wiil find its focus in the animal rights movement. Tn particular I encourage young people to see the connection between the animal rights movement and students' rights. I am a quaint person, I .suppose. I still think that students have rights. In the Sixties we thought we did and we certainly let the world know that. My guess is that in the Seventies and the Eighties the students forgot about that. They were like intoxicated yuppies thinking about BMWs and their latest Sony stereo. My hope is that they will he yuppied out. that we will see the pendulum swing the other way now and they will say. Wait a minute. Things...things are not the source of human fulfillment. Things are not whal satisfy a human's longing to make something good and creative and positive out of this mortal flesh. It's really what we do that matters, it's the testament of our life not the car in our garage that counts. I think that philosophy is going to be reborn and that is certainly what I am committed to. I am going to work very diligently to rai.se the consciousness of students to say, "I will not dissect this animal, I will not vivisect this animal, and you will not punish me. I have a right here." And even the students who don't want to say that, I want those students to say that thatstudent has that right and they will back that student's right. And I want to challenge the .system, every chance I get, in the public schools, in universities and so on, on the basis of the students' rights.

Clarion Call: How do people interested in the animal rights movement get more information and participate?

Professor Regan: I always tell people to investigate the organizations. There are a lot of good organizations out there. I never say join this

one rather than that one, although of course 1 would hope that people would be interested enough to support mine. The way to study it on one's own is to subscribe to a magazine called The Animals'Agenda, the magazine of the animal rights movement. It doesn't favor any one organization over any other. It just tries to report on what's going on in the movement. Write to: The Animals'Agenda, P. O. Box 5234, Westport, Connecticut 0688t. As I said before, if people are interested in a li.st of cruelty-free cosmetics and also in finding out more about what our foundation is doing, they can write to me at Eden Croft, Raleigh. North Carolina 27612.

Clarion Call: Thank you very much. Professor Regan.

Professor Regan: My pleasure, thank you.

## Animal Rights

The Spiritual Origin of Animal RightS  
By Steven Rosen

In recent years there has been quite a bit of talk about animal rights (and its concomitant vegetarianism) as a religious imperative. Animal rights activists with a religious bent say that concern for animals is indicative of a superior moral and ethical sensibility. This view is especially held by proponents of the vegetarian movement, of which there are over ten million in the United States alone. Some of these Ḍspiritual vegetariansÓ try to self-righteously shove their dietary preferences down other people's throats, so to speak, claiming that one cannot profess to be religious if he is supporting unnecessary cruelty to harmless creatures. Others quietly practice their culinary spirituality, without preaching to their neighbors. But one thing is certain: more and more people see the concern for animal rights as a religious way of life—a spiritual dynamic unto itself.

But this is clearly an extreme position. And it gets more extreme as the ranks of animal rights activists continue to grow. With groups like the Jewish Vegetarian Society and Christians Concerned for Animals, one wonders whether devotion for God is being replaced with devotion for the animal kingdom. True, Jesus said that if one does good Ḍto the least of these, he is then also doing good to me.Ó This points to an essential ḌonenessÓ between God and his creation. There is simultaneously a great difference between God and his creation, however, and one who places undo emphasis on the creation may thus inadvertantly neglect the creator. Such extreme, unbalanced perspectives, in which one's allegiance shifts from God to dog, are becoming more and more common. What one eats is becoming more important than to whom one prays. A noted example of this can be seen in a particular statement by Isaac Bashevis Singer, the 1978 Nobel Laureate, who has gone so far as to say: ḌIf a voice came from God and said to kill animals for meat, I would not listen to Him. I feel that strongly about it. Vegetarianism is my religion.Ó

Kindness to all creatures is, of course, a fundamental religious principle, and it has been endorsed by sages of all traditions. But kindness to all creatures is only *part of* religious practice—not the central focus. It is not an end in and of itself. At least not according to any of the major religious traditions. Most monkeys and pigeons are also vegetarian, but their spiritual insight may leave a great deal to be desired. Nonetheless, special interest groups have emerged, and animal rights, like so many other sub-religious concerns, has come to dominate the spiritual sensibility of many practitioners.

There is quite a history behind the infiltration of animal rights in the spiritual arena. More importantly, there is quite a history behind the abandonment of animal rights and the deletion of scriptural texts dealing with the equitable treatment of animals. Today, in the West, it is still the biblical ḌleftÓ that makes a case for animal rights as a plausible concern, what to speak of as a religious focus. The mainstream is quite comfortable with its meat-and-potatoes spirituality. But prominent voices from within the religious community are speaking on behalf of the animals, making a convincing case for at least considering their concern. Richard Schwartz's excellent book *Judaism and Vegetarianism* (New York, Exposition Press, 1982) and Andrew Linsey's *Christianity and the Rights of Animals* (New York, Crossroad Pub., 1987) were groundbreakers, showing that scripture and tradition are more than supportive of the animal rights concern from within the Western re-ligious milieu.

Why, then, do Western religious traditions seem, on the whole, to denounce animal rights and all that it stands for? One reason, perhaps, is the extreme view of religious animal rights activists, as we've noted. But Schwartz and Linsey point to more fundamental problems, showing how the scriptures have been adjusted, maligned, interpolated, and interpreted to suit the whims of political and relig-ious figures across the centuries.

Not so in the Eastern religious traditions. The Orient has managed to by and large maintain at least a healthy reverence for all of God's creation, often extending to the point of vegetarianism. Because the Eastern religions are ancient—especially the early Sanskrit and Pali texts—many a scholar has been led to research Eastern texts with a view to finding the source of the animal rights sensibility. Since the five major world religions—Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, and Hinduism—all originate in the East, academicians have especially considered Hinduism, the oldest of all Asian religions, to be an important starting place for their investigation of the spiritual origin of animal rights.

In fact, they found that Hinduism *is* among the earliest and strongest propounders of animal rights and all related issues. As far back as history can re-cord—before Hinduism came to be known by that foreign name (the word *hindu* was introduced by Persians, not by the ḌHindusÓ themselves)—the Hindus were advocating the equitable treatment of our four-footed, feathered, and scaly kin. All were considered brothers and sisters under God's fatherhood.

Ancient India's scriptural legacy, the Vedic literature, was originally emphatic in its support of monotheism and animal rights. God was seen as the ultimate father—much as he is in the Judaeo-Christian tradition—and all living entities (which the Vedas number at 8,400,000 species) were seen as his children. This sense of spiritual family was often taken to the point of vegetarianism. So deeply ingrained was the tradition of *ahimsa—*ḌharmlessnessÓ—that saints, sages, and prophets of the ancient Vedic tradition were particularly strong advocates of animal rights. Laymen and strict adherents were also loving and kind—to all creatures—as a matter of course, natural tendency, and religious obligation.

The principle of ethics which they followed was known in ancient Sanskrit as *sarva-bhuta-hita*, which means Ḍkindness to all creatures,Ó as opposed to the more limited vision of *loka-hita,* or Ḍkindness to one's own species.Ó The former ethical system, says the Vedas, includes the latter, and therefore it is to be embraced by those who are wise. Love of all creatures is a more inclusive ethic, and followers of the Vedic tradition were encouraged to develop this broad spiritual vision.

Even today, religious traditions that are based upon the Vedic revelation tend to support kindness to all creatures. For example, contemporary Hinduism, which bases its fundamental precepts on the Vedic canon, is a strong advocate of *ahimsa*, as we have noted, even though it has relaxed its mandate on vegetarianism and its support of monotheism. Despite the fact that many Hindus over the course of time have found scriptural rationalization for moving toward polytheistic religion, they have largely maintained their vegetarian ideal, with over 700 million Hindu vegetarians in the world today—this includes 83% of India's current population. Buddhism and Jainism are also strong in their support of universal kindness. In some cases, these two Hindu heterodoxies are more extreme in regard to animal rights than their parent faith.

This can be seen in the fact that the Vedic tradition was once a propounder of animal sacrifices, albeit in very specific situations. Such sacrifices are few and far between today, but they do exist. The scriptures themselves, however, denigrate these sacrifices as extreme measures meant to bring crude, irreligious people to the point of God consciousness, and then, the scriptures tell us, it was only meant for a previous age—not for our current age of Kali. By following rules and regulations in regard to the slaying and eating of animals, and by saying the appropriate prayers, one was at least able to gradually raise oneself from the mode of ignorance to passion and finally to goodness. But the scriptures warned that to attain the level of true transcendence—the goal of the religious pursuit—one would have to bid adieu to animal sacrifices in general and meat-eating in particular. In both the *Shiva* and *Padma Puranas*, it was emphasized that animal sacrifices were an inferior mode of worship.

In certain parts of the Vedic literature there are descriptions of rituals and ceremonies in which a horse is offered to God in a sacrificial arena. The purpose of these rituals, say the Puranas, was not to sanctify the eating of horse flesh. Rather, it was to prove the efficacy of Vedic *mantra* (mystical sound vibration). To this end, an old horse would be led into a fire of sacrifice, qualified brahmins (priests) would chant the sacred *mantra*, and the horse would then emerge in a rejuvenated body. The animal was never harmed, only rejuvenated. Today, of course, there are few qualified priests, if any, who could perform such sacrifices, and again, the Vedas themselves specify that these rituals were only intended for an earlier age.

Another type of animal sacrifice mentioned in the Vedas involved a goat which was to be killed in the presence of the goddess Kali, one of the celestial supervisors of the material world. The details for the procedure of her propitiation are described in an ancient work known as the *Markandeya Purana*, a scripture that prescribes rituals for the gradual elevation of the spiritually ignorant. In all, the Vedic canon recognizes eighteen Puranas—six for those in ignorance, six for those in passion, and six for those in goodness. The *Markandeya Purana* is one for those in ignorance. When this goat ritual is mentioned in the Puranas for those in the mode of goodness, it is said that one must appease the goddess with a facsimile of color—an offering of red flowers instead of a blood sacrifice. Nonetheless, in Calcutta today there is an unscrupulous class of men who, in the name of sacrificing goats to the goddess Kali, run quite lucrative slaughterhouse businesses.

But the original, ancient ritual was quite different. Worshippers of Kali were obliged to chant the Sanskrit word for meat (*mangsa*) into the goat's ear before killing it. The word carries deep meaning. Etymologically, *mangsa* is broken down into *mang* (me) and *sa* (he). According to traditional Indian philology, the implication is as follows: ḌAs I am eating him now, he will be eating me in the future.Ó This is an example of the famous Hindu law of karma: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. While the word *karma* literally means Ḍact,Ó it naturally implies causality as well.

This conception of *karma* reinforced for many practitioners of Eastern religion the importance of fair treatment between the species; what goes around comes around, cause and effect, action and reaction. The notion was so fundamental and so integrally connected with animal rights that it was to be found in many aspects of Sanskrit linguistics. The noun *pashughna* (Ḍhe who kills the bodyÓ), for example, can apply to both the Ḍmeat-eaterÓ and to Ḍone who commits suicide.Ó Again, Hindus take this dual meaning as an implicit indication that there is a severe reaction awaiting anyone who devours flesh-foods.

In the cream of all Vedic scriptures, known as *Srimad Bhagavatam*, the sage Narada instructs the great King Prachinabarhi about the karmic reaction to meat-eating: ḌO ruler of the citizens, my dear king, please see in the sky those animals which you have improperly sacrificed—without compassion and without mercy—in the sacrificial arena. All these animals are awaiting your death so that they can avenge the injuries you have inflicted upon them. After you die, they will angrily pierce your body with iron horns and then eat your fleshÓ (*Bhagavatam*, 4.25.7-8). This, again, is reminiscent of the Sanskrit word for Ḍmeat,Ó i.e. *mangsa*, and all of its subtle implications. Actually, as one reaches the later volumes of the *Bhagavatam*, it becomes even clearer: ḌThose sinful persons who are ignorant of actual religious principles, yet consider themselves to be completely pious, without compunction commit violence against innocent animals who are fully trusting in them. In their next lives, such sinful persons will be eaten by the same creatures they have killed in this worldÓ (*Bhagavatam*, 11.5.14).

Such Vedic prohibitions against the mistreatment of animals were considered especially meaningful when applied to the cow, the killing of which produced a particularly poignant reaction. According to Keith Akers in his comprehensive study *A Vegetarian Sourcebook*: ḌHindu vegetarianism got its greatest push from the Krishna cult, which originated the prominent position of the sacred cow in Hinduism, which persists to this day.Ó Akers's observations echo the findings of early explorers in India: Megasthenes, Hsuan-Tsang, Fah-Hian, and even Marco Polo, all of whom noted the connection between cow protection (i.e. animal rights) and the Vaishnavite worship of Krishna, who is depicted as a cowherd boy.

According to the most ancient Vedic traditions, the original cow, mother Surabhi, was one of the treasures churned from the cosmic ocean, and the Ḍfive products of the cowÓ (*pancha-gavya*)—milk, curd, ghee, urine, and dung—were all considered purifying. In fact, because of these five items, the cow continues to play a central role in the Vedic ideal for humanity: simple living and high thinking, a life close to nature and God. For example, cow dung serves as an inexpensive fertilizer. Stored in underground tanks, cow dung also generates methane gas that is used for heating and cooking. In addition, cow dung is an effective disinfectant and is used both as a poultice and a cleansing agent. Thus the cow plays a prominent role in India's practical life, in her economy and agriculture.

Despite the veneration bestowed upon the cow, however, it should be noted that, contrary to popular belief, there is no Ḍcow-goddess,Ó and no temples are ever constructed in her honor. Rather, the cow is respected in her own right as one of the seven mothers because she offers milk as does one's natural mother. (The other six mothers are the biological mother, the midwife, the wife of the *guru*, the wife of the brahmin, the wife of a genuine king, and the Earth. Sometimes the scriptures are also accepted as one of humankind's natural mothers, for we are nurtured on the knowledge contained therein).

It is the Vedic scriptures, in fact, that adamantly forbid the slaughter of mother cow, and the vast majority of India's population still comply with this scriptural mandate. The Vedic lexicon *Nighantu* offers nine names for the cow, three of which—*aghnya* (Ḍnot to be slainÓ), *ahi* (Ḍnot to be killedÓ) and *aditi* (Ḍnot to be cutÓ)—specifically decry slaughter. These Sanskrit synonyms for ḌcowÓ are found throughout the Vedic literature and are summarized in the epic work *Mahabharata*: ḌThe very name of the cow is *aghnya*, indicating that they should never be slaughtered. Who, then, could slay them? Surely, one who kills a cow or a bull commits the most heinous crimeÓ (*Shani-parva*, 262.47). It should be noted that while it is true that the cow is a central focus in the animal rights issue of the East, all animals are seen as our brothers and sisters, spirit-souls that are inhabiting various types of material bodies. According to the Vedic tradition, souls sometimes inhabit human bodies and sometimes they inhabit animal bodies—but the souls themselves are equal.

Although the treatment of the cow plays a prominent role in the animal rights sensibility of the East, certain underlying issues of the animal rights movement are hardly addressed. For example, some feel it betrays a certain hypocrisy to bestow such reverence on the cow and yet drink her milk without giving it a second thought. In the West, such issues hold much weight with the animal rights contingent, but in India the topic is barely even discussed. Milk always has and always will be a staple of the Indian diet. Since the majority of Indians do not consume meat, fish, or eggs, though, there is little worry of getting high cholesterol levels from milk products. And since cows roam freely and give their milk in the same way, the question of cruel factory farms does not become a factor. The Vedas describe that the cow, unlike her human counterpart, gives more milk than her offspring requires, and thus the excess is naturally meant for human society. This may seem like a simplistic understanding, but the entire Indian subcontinent has lived by this principle for millennia.

The Vedic ideals of cow protection and *ahimsa* do have their limitations, though, and this is experienced by many modern adherents. There are extreme but common situations that test the mettle of practicing Hindus. For example, Mahatma Gandhi himself noted that, at times, *ahimsa* was merely an ideal with no practical application. ḌI have come to see,Ó wrote Gandhi, Ḍwhat I did not see before: that there is sometimes nonviolence in violence.... I had not fully realized the duty of restraining a drunkard from doing evil, of killing a dog in agony or one infected with rabies. In all of these instances violence is in fact nonviolence.Ó Finding the appropriate middle ground has thus always been a great bane in the practice of conventional Hinduism, and it continues to instigate hot debates. Buddhism, it is said, originated as a reaction to this issue, and it is still known in India as Ḍthe middle path.Ó

In the Vedic tradition, then, nonviolence has to be practiced with common sense; but it is not always a black and white situation. Nonetheless, Indian philosophers have compiled literally hundreds of volumes in an attempt to clarify the grey areas. For instance, historian S. Dasgupta concludes that if a dangerous beast enters a cattle shed, one should kill the beast, for the principal objective is to maintain social order and the well-being of the people. Higher forms of nonviolence, he says, may include being ḌviolentÓ for a greater good. Hindus throughout history have no doubt taken diverse positions in regard to this question—Gandhi, for most of his career, not the least among them. But it should be noted that Dasgupta's view seems to be supported by the traditional texts such as *Bhagavad-gita*, which claims that unqualified nonviolence may result in more harm done than good. For example, if Arjuna, the hero of the *Gita*, would have avoided warfare, the whole world would have become overrun by demoniac elements, causing more harm than the entire battle of Kurukshetra. The *Gita* consequently recommends that one approach a genuine spiritual teacher to learn, first of all, just what genuine spirituality is, and then how to decipher when and where one may take liberties with fundamental spiritual teachings such as *ahimsa*.

Such a teacher will be able to explain to his students all of the variables and unique situations that may arise in the practical application of *dharma* (religious duty), and how to deal with each one in an appropriate manner. But the fundamental principle of all Vedic injunctions is that everything must be done in pursuit of God's will.

The principle of *ahimsa* received additional emphasis 2,500 years ago,when Buddhism manifested as a major force among the priestly class of India. In Tom Regan's *Animal Sacrifices*, theologian Christopher Chapple writes: ḌBuddhism, like Jainism, originated in India as a religious movement easily distinguishable from Hinduism in its nonallegiance to Vedic texts and in its disdain for animal sacrifices.Ó Since Buddhism and Jainism abhorred animal sacrifices, one may legitimately wonder why these two offshoot traditions did not embrace Vedic texts, which also forbid animal sacrifices for our current day and age. The plain fact is that in the time of Buddha's appearance in this world, Vedic texts were being misrepresented among the masses as supportive of animal sacrifice, and for this reason both Buddhism and Jainism arose as reactionary alternatives to the Vedic tradition.

Original Indian Buddhism was, consequently, fully given to the principle of nonviolence, which to this day is considered the first of Buddhism's nine major precepts. But as Buddhism traveled to other lands—such as China, Japan, Burma, Cambodia, Tibet, Thailand, and Vietnam, among other places—the essential teaching of animal rights and its concomitant principle of *ahimsa* was severely compromised. Of the two chief branches known today, Mahayana and the older Theravada, both are tolerant of meat-eating and have lost virtually all sight of animal rights, although in Mahayana Buddhism meat consumption is still somewhat frowned upon. Members of Zen Buddhist monasteries, of course, are more strict in regard to abstinence from flesh foods, but the followers of original Indian Buddhism are few and far between.

Contemporary Buddhist movements such as the Buddhists Concerned for Animal Rights are interested in reestablishing the roots of *ahimsa* sensibility. And certain Buddhist denominations such as the Cao Dai sect, which originated in South Vietnam, now boasts some two million followers, all of whom are vegetarian.

Among the less prominent Eastern religions that practice true *ahimsa* is Zoroastrianism (also known as Magianism, Mazdaism, or Parseeism). Originally a sect that flourished in ancient Persia, it is now centered primarily in Bombay. Zarathushtra (Zoroaster in Greek), who founded this religion, was an ardent and well-known advocate of animal rights in Persia around 600 B.C. Under Islamic rule, many Zoroastrians fled from Iran in the seventh century A.D., and their modern successors are the Parsees of India. Many of the 200,000 Zoroastrians in the world today seek to emulate their founder by practicing vegetarianism.

Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak (1469-1538), is an interesting blend of Hindu and Islamic beliefs. Because of Muslim influence, most branches of the Sikh religion are not supportive of animal rights, nor are they vegetarian. Still, the Hindu side of Sikhism's roots is a phenomenon to be reckoned with, and many adherents find much in their scriptures to support the doctrine of compassion for animals. For example, Sikh scholar Swaran Singh Sanehi of the Academy of Namdhari Culture had this to say: ḌSikh scriptures support vegetarianism fully. Sikhs from the period of Guru Nanak had adopted the Hindu tradition and way of living in many ways. Their disliking for flesh-foods was also part of the same tradition and way of living. Guru Nanak considered meat-eating improper—particularly for those who are trying to meditate.Ó Of the world's ten million Sikhs, the Namdhari sect and Yogi Bhajan's 3HO Golden Temple Movement are strictly in favor of animal rights and vegetarianism.

As far as animal rights in general and the doctrine of *ahimsa* in particular, the East has reached full evolution in the religion of the Jains. Originating with the great saint Mahavira (599-527 B.C.), Jainism has grown very powerful and today claims over four million followers, all of whom are strict vegetarians. In India, Jains are famous for their animal hospitals, and it was a Jain monk, Hiravijaya-Suri, who persuaded the Muslim emperor Akbar (1556-1605) to prohibit the killing of animals on certain days. Buddhist luminaries such as Emperor Ashoka (268-223 B.C.) and Harsha (fifth century A.D.), were also powerful supporters of animal rights in India, but the Jains have elevated animal rights to a religious principle. This then brings Eastern religious doctrine to a full circle, for the Puranas also strongly declared that *ahimsa paro dharmo*—Ḍnonviolence is the highest duty.Ó

Conclusion

Compassion for animals is an integral part of the Asian mindset and has been so throughout the annals of recorded history. This unique perspective is summarized by the well-known exiled leader of the Tibetan people, Tenzin Gyatso, the fourteenth Dalai Lama, who may well be considered one of the world's most important contemporary religious figures and an eloquent representative of all Eastern nations:

In our approach to life, be it pragmatic or otherwise, a basic fact that confronts us squarely and unmistakably is the desire for peace, security, and happiness. Different forms of life at different levels of existence make up the teeming denizens of this Earth of ours. And no matter whether they belong to the higher groups such as human beings or to the lower groups such as the animals, all beings primarily seek peace, comfort, and security. Life is as dear to a mute creature as it is to a man. Even the lowliest insect strives for protection against dangers that threaten its life. Just as each one of us wants happiness and fears pain, just as each one of us wants to live and not to die, so do all other creatures (Tenzin Gyatso, *Universal Responsibility and the Good Heart*, Dharmasala, India, Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, 1980, p. 78).

Western schools of thought are now echoing their parent faiths of the East. As is natural for an adolescent, the young traditions of the West are often extreme or overzealous in their support of newly-found causes. Animal rights and vegetarianism are not exceptions to the rule. Because we are unaccustomed to the sensibility of the *ahimsa* principle and because our own Western scriptures have been largely misinterpreted, it seems our safest course is to grab tightly to our parents' hands and be led gently down the road of truth.
