The Sushruta Samhita (a treatise on Ayurveda) calls the process of energetic activation vata. The activity of producing heat, light, energy, digestion, and transformation is called pitta. That process which manifests stability, solidity, and inertia is called kapha. Vata comes from the sanskrit va,to move; pitta comes from the sanskrit tap, to produce heat; and kapha comes from the sanskrit shlish, to join, embrace, or adhere.

The doshas manifest in a triplicity just as do the gunas. The three doshas work in a continuous dynamic harmony to maintain health in the body. They are pervasive in the body and, without adequate prevention, their working inevitably causes impurities to accumulate. Over a twenty-four hour period the doshas predominate in turn. Air (vata) is preponderant in late afternoon, fire (pita) at noon or midday, and water (kapha) in the morning. The cycle repeats itself during the evening, night and predawn hours. The doshas are distributed throughout the body:Vata below the navel, pitta between the navel and the heart, and kapha above the heart.

Each of the doshas represents a quality of force, a way of manifestation of the laws of nature. Though the Sanskrit word vata means "air", the correct conception of the term vata dosha is the process of movement or energetic activation. Kapha and pitta are said to be motionless and requirevata dosha for activation. Just as air is dry, vata is dry, cold, rough and moving. In the body vata can be thought of as nerve-force.

The term pitta dosha signifies the force that heats, lights, metabolizes, and transforms. In the body pitta is responsible for digestion and metabolism.

Kapha has been called the primal constituent of the human being, exhibiting a "healthy inert" quality. The force for which it is named is manifest in instinctive behavior, bodily endurance, growth, lubrication of the joints, courage, forgiveness, potency, and cohesion of bodily tissues. Kapha is cold, unctuous, and heavy; pitta is hot, fluid, and sharp; vata is cold, and dry. The eternal interplay among these forces accounts for all types of biological and physiological functions.

A summary of the three basic constitutional types shows them to be distinct and, after some practice, easy to identify. The following tridosha questionnaire will allow you to discover your unique individual body type of prakriti according to the tridosha theory

Tridosha Questionnaire  
Test Instructions

1\. For each category (one through twenty-five) on the questionnaire, select the one choice that most closely approximates your individual constitution, either:

\* Kapha (water-type)

\* Pitta (fire-type)

\* Vata (air-type)

Then put a check in the appropriate box. For example, if your response to the first question is endomorph, check box one, column K.

2\. When you have finished answering all twenty-five questions, add the number of check marks in each category and enter the sum in the subtotal boxes.

3\. To obtain a percentage ratio of the three elements in your personal constitution, multiply the number of answers in each subtotal box by four. If you answered all twenty-five questions, the three percentage figures should add up to one hundred and you will have an approximate picture of your unique constitutional type as determined at conception.

4\. Conclusion: Usually one element will predominate -that is, will be a larger percentage of the total. In Ayurvedic medicine, this is considered the main constitutional type for diagnosis and treatment of the individual.

Chart

Each constitutional type displays all three dosha qualities to some degree. At the time of conception our physical constitution reflects a unique combination of the tridosha. According to the Ayurvedic texts the properties of the kapha type are: pale, heavy, cold, smooth, polished, soft, majestic and slow; as well as sweet, delicate, and slippery. This constitutional type has soft, silky, oily, fine skin. The body is muscular, symmetrical, and fleshy. The kapha type person is fond of the sweet tastes and, since kapha is cold in action, the kapha type likes foods that are hot both in temperature and in seasoning. Kapha types should avoid fatty foods and oils, as well as dairy products. Kapha persons are slow to anger and slow to forget.

The properties of the vata type with some exceptions are opposite those of the kapha type. The vata person tends to act, and react, much more quickly. Movement is characteristic of the vata person. The physique is dry,light, mobile, cold and hard, and the body is uniformly slender. The constitution is dry because of the predominance of air. The personality is quick in all things: to love, to forget, to digest, and to move on. Often an excess of vata of air is associated with nervousness or neurological disorders. This constitutional type should avoid all drugs and use diet and other natural means to achieve maximum health and longevity.

In the pitta constitution the fire element predominates. Often artistic in temperament, this body type tends to think in creative ways. The person in whom the fire element predominates is moderate in build, neither short nor tall, neither heavy nor thin. The qualities of pitta are hot and slightly oily. This constitutional type often has problems with thinning hair or premature greyness. Freckles, moles, and skin disorders are also associated with an excess of pitta dosha.

The three constitutional tupes are partially recognized in America as the physiological types of endomorph, mesomorph and ectomorph, as designated by American psychologist William Sheldon. However, Ayurveda provides levels of classification more profound and sophisticated than Sheldon's system. The key to health and longevity is a constant balancing of the doshas according to individual body type. The constitutional makeup of all people contain all three doshas to some degree.

According to Ayurvedic theory, the six tastes found in all foods also have a significant effect on the balance of the doshas. Most foods have a variety of tastes, but one or two predominate. The sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent tastes affect the doshas, either balancing or aggravating them, depending on the body-type.

Because diet is a major means of affecting the balance of the doshas, it is suggested that when eating the atmosphere be peaceful and the food be balanced to include all six tastes. Very cold or iced beverages (and food) can interfere with digestion and are to be avoided. Eat only when the previous meal has been completely digested, and rest briefly after the meal. A small amount of liquid, except for milk, may be consumed with the meal. Milk can be drunk alone or with sweet foods or cereals. Large amounts of fluid before, during, or after meals is not recommended.

The doshas tend to be prominent or aggravated in their seasons. In the United States, the kapha season generally begins the first of spring (March through June), pitta season begins in summer (July to October), andvata season is fall and winter (November through February). Some Ayurvedists believe, however, that winter is kapha season and spring is the season in which kapha and pitta are combined. As a general rule, Ayurveda suggests that foods be taken seasonally to counter balance the seasonal effect on the doshas. Very generally speaking, this means that in winter, when vata is aggravated, fewer vata-increasing foods should be taken; in summer, fewer pitta-increasing foods; in spring, fewer kapha-increasing foods.

Suggested diet for Vata Dosha

This body type should eat breakfast and have small light meals throughout the day. Vata people do well to avoid foods that are dry or bitter. Sweet and hot foods are good for them. All dairy products are recommended; Ayurvedic herbs are available to correct milk allergies. Vata types need to add more oily and sweet foods and sour and salty tastes to the diet They should drink warm or hot water and use spices such as cinnamon, cardamom, cumin, ginger, salt, cloves, mustard, and licorice. Nuts and nut butters of all kinds are beneficial. Vata types should avoid foods suggested in kapha and pitta diets. Because Vata dosha is aggravated in fall and winter this type should increase warm milk, hot water, and oily foods during fall and winter seasons.

Suggested diet for Pitta Dosha

The Pitta constitutional type should eat breakfast, preferably grains, fruits and some dairy products. This body-type should avoid chilies, nuts, honey, hot spices, and very hot drinks. If indigestion occurs, lemon juice in water is a cooling drink. Pitta types should add cool foods and liquids, sweet, bitter, and astringent tastes. They should avoid honey and sour tasting foods, such as yoghurt, pickles and aged cheese. Avoid spices except cinnamon, lemon, coriander, cardamom, and black pepper.Pitta types should avoid foods suggested in kapha and vata diets. Because Pitta dosha is aggravated in summer, this type should be sure to increase cooling foods and drinks.

Suggested diet for Kapha Dosha

This body type should avoid eating before at least 10 A.M., should avoid sugar, fats, wheat, dairy products, salt, and add lighter, drier foods. Kapha types should not eat after the sun has set, especially moist foods such as watermelon and ice cream. The evening meal should be lighter and drier than lunch, which should be the largest meal of the day. Kapha types must avoid iced or cold drinks and substitute warm drinks. They should avoid large quantities of foods, and over indulgence in the sweet, salty, and sour tastes. Fasting one day a week as a means of weight control and health maintenance is recommended for healthy kapha types Kapha types should avoid foods suggested in vata and pita diet. Because Kapha dosha is aggravated in the spring, at that time this type should decrease the size of meals and increase low-fat, high-fiber foods.

Nutritionally, the Ayurvedic approach works through specific procedures for preventing the accumulation of bodily impurities, doshas , through appropriate diet and herbal food supplements for each individual body type. The Ayurvedic approach brings about balance through comprehensive instructions about nutrition, as well as daily and seasonal routines, and personal hygiene. The primary Ayurvedic approach to mental hygiene is through the daily practice of meditation or yoga. When looking at an individual, the Ayurvedic physician sees the whole person including the immortal self. This is very different from the traditional Western approach. The Ayurvedic phisician conceptualizes the individual as potentially in perfect balance and perfect health. Ayurveda is designed to prevent an imbalance before it can manisfest or, if there is an imbalance, to correct it. The modern medical approach usually concentrates on the disease only after it has manifested. Modern science has in the past defined health as "absence of disease." According to Ayurveda, health, is much more a state of perfect balance of the physical and mental, leading toward immortality. Ayurveda is really health oriented rather than disease oriented.

It is the patient, however, who must establish perfect health by actively participating in the healing process. Ayurveda recognizes one's own self as the ultimate healer, and the Ayurvedic physician becomes a partner with the patient to help the patient achieve perfect balance and develop an invincible immune system. The Ayurvedic preventive treatment, panchakarma, is one of several types of Ayurvedic treatment designed to rejuvenate the physiology and the entire immune system. In addition to panchakarma, another treatment that is a popular part of Ayurveda is herbal food supplements. Ayurvedic herbal supplements are known for their rejuvenative and curative powers.

The goal of all Ayurvedic physical and herbal treatments is to remove imbalances from the physiology so that digestion and elimination work perfectly. This ensures (1) that impurities are not produced in the body by incomplete digestion; (2) that any unsuitable substances which contact the physiology through the enviroment are eliminated properly; and (3) that digestion can produce the highest possible quality of nutrients to support the body.

In a healthy body, the process of food digestion goes through various levels of refinement until the finest essential part of the food (rasa) is produced. This rasa created by the initial phases of digestion is then transferred with its nutrients to the lymphatic system and then to the blood, muscle, fat, bone, bonemarrow nerve tissue, and then to the generative fluids, semen, and ovum. The very end product of the nutritional process is called ojas . Ojas is an ultra- refined substance known in Ayurveda as "vitalessence." Such a substance is so far almost unknown to Western science.

The rasa theory of Ayurveda describes the way in which nutritional material undergoes succeedingly finer states of transformation and separation into finer and more subtle nutrients until it reaches a final stage in human physiology as ojas, the ultimate nutrient.

According to Ayurveda, ojas is produced in humans in two different ways in small amounts in a fully-functioning digestive process; and in the practice of deep meditation, when subtle aspects of sound stimulate the physiology to produce ojas . It can take up to a month to produce ojas from food, but it is produced more quickly through meditation. In Ayurveda, ojas is synonymous with good health. (Ayurveda explains that health is latent in ojas as butter is latent in milk). In some translations of the Charaka Samhita, ojas is likened to the Chinese theory of 'chi'. In degenerative diseases the ojas (or chi) does not circulate in the body but is excreted through the kidneys and bladder. A lack of ojas causes premature aging and degeneration of the immune system.

All of the restorative methods of Ayurveda are aimed at creating and conserving ojas and strengthening the entire immune system through the proper application of the tridosha theory. The tridosha theory of Ayurveda represents the main Ayurvedic method for diagnosis and treatment of the individual and is universally applicable for all people at all times.

Ayurveda By Linda Treadway Ph.D.

## Ojas: The Secret Of Health

By Cynthia Copple

I wake up in the morning swimming in anxiety. Fear lives in every cell of my body, which feels cold, stiff, tense. I have a knot in my solar plexus; a sharp spasm grips my intestines. The feeling is of dread, like something bad is about to happen. I have to work hard to focus on what I am afraid of. It feels so overpowering and negative that all of my natural resources seem to be trying to avoid it. When I focus, I find old fears dressed up in the issues and events of the present: I will run out of money and have difficulty surviving; I will be abandoned by those I love and who love me; I will make a fool of myself or make some terrible mistake (or I have already made some terrible mistake, the consequences of which I have not yet experienced, but will soon).

It all boils down to the thought: “I’m not good enough,” the feeling of fear, and the bodily experience of the guts wrenching and muscular tension, all at once. It is a familiar feeling, an old friend. I want desperately to be rid of it forever.

This may not sound like a health issue, but it is, according to ayurveda. Because anxiety, as well as fear, grief, fury, poor diet, and excess sex, deplete *ojas*. And our health depends largely upon ojas, the physical countepart to the subtle energy that creates well-being throughout the entire body from the cellular level on up. Without ojas we would not be alive, and it is ojas which keeps us healthy.

Ojas is a concept that can greatly aid us in staying healthy in our modern stress-filled lives. Today, many of us feel the pressures of living life in the fast lane; we have stressful jobs, our relationships are stressful, we eat rich foods, we do not eat regularly, our sleep is not sound, we do not exercise regularly, and we struggle to achieve our goals and keep driving ourselves to succeed, forgetting to stop and smell the flowers, forgetting to pay attention to nature which surrounds us, forgetting to listen to our bodies. Our bodies are there only to take us where we’re so frantically going; our minds are in charge. It is as if our minds have enslaved our bodies.

Through stress, ojas is depleted. The knowledge of ojas can give us tools which enable us to take charge of our health, to use our body’s own natural healing capacities, and to restore the harmony of our mind and body and cease the mind’s ignorant domination over the body.

I first began to understand the concept of ojas in l982 when I was present during an examination conducted by my ayurvedic teacher, Dr. Trivedi. He was examining two newly-diagnosed AIDS patients and their partners. That summer he was teaching ayurveda for the first time in the U.S.; he had never traveled out of India before then and he was 66 years old. He was very conservative in his views on sex and was startled to find heterosexual couples living together, married couples choosing not to have children, women choosing abortion, young people choosing not to get married, the extent of divorce, and homosexuality. He never condemned anyone, however he did have strong views on what was “natural” and what was not. To him, “natural” meant harmonious with nature, promoting physical health, because he is an ayurvedic doctor, and ayurveda is the science of health.

After examining the four young men, doing a pulse diagnosis and asking them a number of questions, he spent some minutes lost in thought. The current Western understanding of the disease had been described to him by a medical doctor who was studying ayurveda, but Dr. Trivedi had said, “We do not see disease as occurring the same way in every person. Disease is as individual as the individuals are. We see everything in terms of vata \[air/ether\], pitta \[fire/water\], and kapha \[water/earth\].”

He thought again, then concluded: “Low ojas. This AIDS must be caused by low ojas.” At that time, AIDS was front page news, in the headline of the *San Francisco Chronicle* as a possible epidemic, with doctors and scientists unable to determine what caused it. It was not known whether it was a virus or how it was transmitted. It was thought to be associated with a weakened immune response like lupus and other so-called “auto-immune diseases,” but the exact connection was not clear.

In talking to these men, Dr. Trivedi found out that they had a few things in common besides being gay. A common factor in these men was the fact that at one time they had engaged in frequent sex—as many as six partners a night for several nights a week at the gay bathhouses. They also had not been concerned about their health, had not eaten regularly, and ate fast food frequently. According to ayurveda, one of the factors which depletes ojas is excessive sex, whether homosexual or heterosexual, and ojas depletion means the body is more vulnerable to disease. And since ojas is created in the body through digestion, poor dietary habits can also decrease ojas.

I began to take the concept of ojas more seriously at this point, wondering what “ojas” specifically is, and how to keep it at a high level in the body. I had a bad cold that summer and was becoming aware that I had more colds than many people. Perhaps this too was caused by ojas depletion? It became clear to me that if I was to stay healthy as I pass into middle age (which was fast approaching), I would need to pay attention to my ojas.

What is ojas? Ojas is the product of *Shukra Dhatu,* the seventh of seven tissues formed one after the other from food through digestion. *Shukra* contains the essense of all of the tissues; it contains the blueprint for the next generation. The quality of ojas is dependent on the strength and digestive abilities of the previous six tissues. If any tissue is deficient, ojas will be deficient. At the same time, if ojas is increased, the health of each tissue will be increased.

Charaka, who compiled the major text on Ayurveda around 50 A.D., explains that there are two types of ojas: *para* ojas and gross ojas. Each person has only eight drops of para ojas, which reside in the heart. If those 8 drops are depleted, death results. Everyone has about two handfuls of gross ojas, or normal ojas, which resides in the ten arteries originating from the heart, and from there circulates throughout the entire body.

According to *Sushruta Samhita*, one of the primary Ayurvedic texts dating from around the fifth century B.C., ojas is a physiological substance with the following characteristics: it is cooling (when there is less ojas, the coolness of the mind goes, the mind loses concentration, insanity may result); viscous, clear white, slimy and soft. It carries *prana*, the life force, to every part of the body. If ojas is absent, the cells and tissues will die.

Charaka has described ojas as sweet, like the taste of honey, with a distinct smell. Chakrapani, one commentator, has mentioned that “The chief function of ojas is *vyadhi ksamitva* (natural resistance against disease).”

There several possible parallels to ojas in Western terminology. Ojas is present in the reproductive force which underlies and is the essence of each tissue, and thus albumen, a blood plasma protein, could be related to ojas. A commentator on *Sushruta Samhita*, Dallana Mishra, defined ojas as a fatty substance completely combustable in character, which produces the softness and elegance of the body, especially in the female. Thus it could be a fatty acid.

Ojas may be related to the immune system and the lymph system; its characteristics sound like leukocytes, white blood cells which are formed in the lymph tissue or bone marrow and which circulate in the blood as well as in lymph fluid and intercellular spaces. They guard the tissues against invasion by foreign organisms or chemicals, and are important in antibody production. Ojas is said to be both energy and matter; the energy latent, manifesting matter when the body’s well-being is at stake, which does sound like the immune response.

Whatever it is, according to ayurveda, we can't do without it! *Sushruta Samhita* states that muscles have tone and move without hindrance due to ojas. A clear voice and a glowing face are due to ojas. The whole body works smoothly because of ojas. Thus ojas does more than fight disease—it creates positive health.

What are the signs of low or depleted ojas? The first sign is timidity: a person who is normally fearless becomes timid, begins to fear. Then, free- floating anxiety or weakness of an arm or body part. As ojas continues to deplete, the nervous system weakens, anxiety increases, the sense organs become defective, the complexion becomes grey, a person loses his normal thinking power, and has malice in his heart. A person with low ojas becomes highly irritable and reactive. Finally, a person loses weight.

These signs sound like Epstein-Barr virus or Fatigue Syndrome—the diseases of people under stress. Even Crohn’s disease and arthritis show signs of low ojas. According to ayurveda, every disease means ojas is low; otherwise the body would heal itself.

What are the causes of ojas depletion? Any shock, psychological or physical (accidents, injuries, surgery, trauma), dehydration or anemia, excessive fasting, eating only one kind of food, or diets which are excessively dry or without fat.

Fury, white-hot anger, depletes ojas. Losing ojas means losing patience, losing control. A person gets madder and madder and loses control—even to the point of paralysis. Parkinson’s Disease and other nervous system diseases seem to be due to ojas depletion, perhaps related to this emotion.

Another cause is grief. When someone close to us dies, and we experience sorrow, ojas is depleting and we are more vulnerable to disease. Ojas depletion is also caused by hunger and fatigue; without proper nutrition and rest, the body can’t keep up its ojas. And stress, anxiety, worrying, and mental depression cause ojas loss. If persons have more than one of these factors affecting them at the same time, the depletion of ojas is greater. Yet stress seems to be part of our modern lifestyle. What can we do to prevent ojas depletion, to build our ojas and stay healthy?

Ojas is created through the digestive process. Good digestion and assimilation of nutrients is one of the most important factors in maintaining our ojas. The ayurvedic view is not “you are what you eat,” but “you are what you digest.” Hunger is a sign of the digestive fire’s readiness; when hunger is present, food can be properly digested. Conversely, we should not eat when we are not hungry. Without a “hot” digestive fire complete with necessary digestive enzymes, the food will not be broken down into molecules which can pass through cell walls into the tissues or which can be excreted through normal channels. When this happens, the food turns into toxins, or *ama,* which circulates in the body, accumulating where there are weak spots and creating biochemical imbalances which may lead to disease.

When digestion is sluggish, an ayurvedic tonic like drachsha increases the body’s utilization of nutrients, tones the tissue, and increases ojas. When digestive problems of gas or no appetite occur, hingwastock churna, an ancient ayurvedic formula, is usually recommended. And for mild indigestion, triphala is the best traditional ayurvedic remedy. Yet prevention is the best medicine, and ayurveda has a very specific approach to diet which is tailored to the individual.

Since ancient times, ayurveda has promoted certain herbs as increasing ojas, including shataveri, licorice root, and amla. Amla is the Indian gooseberry fruit, and has the highest naturally occurring concentration of vitamin C. It is made into a sweet paste with about 20 herbs, honey, and ghee (clarified butter) called chavana prash, which is a pro-ojas tonic.

Almond milk is also pro-ojas. This is prepared by taking 20 raw almonds and soaking them in water overnight. (With 20 raisins if pitta is weak.) The next morning, peel the almonds and put them into a blender with a cup of fresh water. Add a pinch of cardamom and a peppercorn and blend for five to eight minutes. Since this is noisy, I recommend putting the blender into another room.

According to Dr. Trivedi, khir, a traditional Indian rice pudding, promotes ojas, and when there is energy loss after sex, khir should be taken before and after to increase strength. To make khir, put half a cup of rice, some raisins, and six cups of milk in a pan. Bring it to a boil, then reduce to a simmer until the rice is cooked. It should be soupy. Take it off the burner, add cinnamon, cardamon, cloves, pippli, and honey to taste.

Ojas can also be increased through lifestyle changes. A pro-ojas lifestyle, according to ayurveda, is one which does not increase vata. The tendencies of vata are to a large extent opposite those of kapha, and ojas is the subtle energy of kapha dosha. What is an ojas-depleting lifestyle? Anything which increases vata—excessive movement, dryness, irregularity in eating, sleeping, work—will decrease ojas. And anything which increases regularity, calm, and happiness will increase ojas. Dr. Trivedi says, “Love balances the doshas.” Love increases ojas. Negative emotions, especially when repeated as a pattern, decrease ojas. Irregularity decreases ojas. Getting enough sleep without interruption is very important; working the night shift will deplete ojas, as will a new baby’s sleep interruptions.

Regular meals, especially of hot, soupy foods and without excessive dry, gas-producing foods, will increase ojas. Eating sufficiently has to be a priority in a pro-ojas lifestyle; without adequate fuel at regular intervals, the body will not function properly. The ayurvedic weight-loss program involves herbs to balance the doshas and make the digestion more efficient, a special diet, and eating regularly. The “balanced meal” in ayurveda is one in which all six tastes are represented; to eliminate oils completely will decrease ojas, as will “mono-meals” of just one food.

Regular exercise increases ojas; excessive exercise, to the point of exhaustion, depletes ojas. Oil massage, especially with ayurvedic herbally medicated oils, increases ojas. (If one is overweight, dry massage or massage with herb packs is preferable to the use of oils, which increase kapha.) Oiling the feet at night with sesame oil also decreases vata, which increases ojas. The oil is absorbed into the capillaries, which nourish the nerve endings which reflex to many other parts of the body. Some people naturally have more ojas than others; it is inherited, along with vata, pitta, and kapha.

To have good ojas, one also needs a calm mind, and steady emotions. Yoga and meditation can increase ojas. According to yoga, peace and inner freedom come from the control of the senses and mind. When the mind, senses, and body are released from the survival patterns we have programmed into them since childhood, patterns which no longer suit the experiences we have—patterns of fear, worry, and anxiety which have no positive function and deplete our ojas—then our body is free to create its natural patterns of health and joy.

Through our lifestyle, our habits, and the patterns of our thoughts, emotions, and actions, we override the natural patterns of the body/mind/emotions. Today many of us hardly know what our natural patterns are: we are what we have created through our willpower, and how we would be otherwise is hard to imagine. If we remove these imposed patterns which are obstacles to our body’s natural processes, then, as ayurveda states, the body will heal itself.

Life is stress-filled, the only real solution to health problems is to eliminate the stress, which is decreasing our ojas. We can re-balance the doshas with herbs and dietary changes, but as long as the cause is there, we can’t expect radiant health. This means that to change one’s health situation often means that one must change one’s life. A little pill will not undo what a lifetime of patterns has created; we must undo the patterns.

## Ayurveda-Rasayana-Rejuvenation

*Fountain of Youth; The Science of Rejuvenation* By D. N. Das

Once a year, on a full moon day during the winter month of Magha, an ancient barefoot *rishi* climbs into a tree in the *amla* groves near his hermitage. He nestles himself in the crook of the tree, plucks a hard green fruit, holds it up to the sky and vibrates the mantra *om*. He waits as one drop of *amrita*, the nectar of immortality, drops into the fruit, changing the small bitter *amalaki* into a sweet golden tonic. He eats the fruit as he has done for thousands of years and peacefully returns to his penance, knowing that his body can last for eons if need be.

In another part of the Himalayas an aged *sadhu* prepares for the event of a lifetime, complete physical rejuvenation. After weeks of preparation which included rigorous internal cleansing, special yoga postures, and a complete retreat from all worldly affairs, he approaches the specially designed hut where he will abandon his age-encumbered body. Inside lies a specially covered wooden table. After filling his belly with the juice of several rare herbs, he undresses and climbs inside the table. The lid is closed. After six months asleep the sage will awaken. All of his hair and all of his teeth will have fallen out and been replaced anew. His complexion will be smooth and flushed. And his life-span will have increased 100 years.

Sound too fantastic to believe? Does this remind you of something more from the Age of Heroes than the *kali yuga*? These stories refer to rejuvenation and aphrodisiac therapy, two of the more esoteric forms of treatment found in the *Charaka Samhita.* Although in this day and age we may not experience the radical types of renewal described above, these treatments modified for our times, can radically improve our health and overall well-being.

Indian mythology has it that the science of rejuvenation and aphrodisiac therapy, were introduced to the human quarter by Indra, the king of the demigods. Toward the end of the previous *yuga*, or cosmic cycle, a great assembly of sages approached Indra for help. The *brahma rishis* and great yogis were suffering from a variety of physical ailments as well as old age because of having left their hermitages high in the inaccessible mountains in favor of dwelling among the common folk. Indra taught these sages these processes of mental and physical renewal so that they could regain their lost vitality and return to their penances high in the Himalayas.

Rejuvenation and aphropdisiac therapy are similar, yet distinct. While aphrodisiac therapy deals more specifically with revitalizing the reproductive organs, rejuvenation aims at the entire health of the participant.

The most fundamental ingregients in ayurvedic rejuvenation are*rasayanas.* A *rasayana* is any treatment or medicinal substance that replenishes and strengthens the vital fluids or *rasas* in the body. *Rasa* literally means "juice" or "sap," the "vital essence," "taste," or "relish" of a thing. It is often explained as the nutrient portion of food derived from the process of digestion. *Rasayanas* as a dietary supplement rather than a therapy are often meant to replace food altogether, and are usually taken in large quantities for limited periods of time, ideally in peaceful and temperate surroundings. Although *rasayanas* can be targeted to affect specific organs, they usually are used to strengthen and heal the entire psychosomatic system.

According to Charaka,“A person who uses *rasayanas* will get long life, memory, increased intelligence, good health, youthfulness, improved luster, complexion, and voice, optimum strength of body and the senses, humility, and attractiveness."

There are two types of rejuvenation therapy. In the first type the participent enters a specially constructed cabin and remains there for an extended period of time; one, three or even six months. The second and more common type is undergone while the participant continues with a light work schedule, follows a restricted diet and inges various *rasayanas*. I wish I could tell you about the exotic treatments I received in South India, or the special room I stayed in during my retreat in the Himalayas, But I can't. Everywhere I went I found the same thing: no one was doing rejuveation retreats. What I could find were plenty of practicing *vaidyas* offering *rasayanas* and treatments, interested post-graduate students to talk to, and plenty of references in the original ayurvedic texts about rejuvenation. So I have tried to piece together enough information in this article so that one can initiate a rejuvenation program for oneself. If you try it, you may not wake up in the morning with a new head of hair or the face of a twenty year old, but you may find that your thinning hair has thickened up a bit and that you don't need as many cups of coffee or ginseng cola to get you through the day.

To get the most out of rejuvenation therapy, cultivate the qualities of mercy, charity, tranquility, and purity, and generally immerse yourself in the *sattvic* (peaceful and regulated) mode of life. All this amounts to the mental, physical, and ethical purity necessary for rejuvenation. But before you decide to actually undergo therapy internal cleansing is necessary. For this, the ancient *pancha karma* sysyem is recommended.

*Pancha karma* deserves a more complete treatment than can be given here. However, we can discuss how these therapies are used in conjunction with rejuvenation \[see side bar\]. Internal cleansing through *pancha karma*  brings about "liquefaction" of the vitiated *doshas* through massage and oliation. In this altered state the imbalanced *doshas* flow into the central channels where they reside: *vata* in the colon, *pitta* in the large intestine, and *kapha* in the stomach and lungs. They are then removed along with the accumulated waste products from these internal channels. This serves to dramatically improve the overall efficiency of the bodily systems. Without *pancha karma* the *rasayana* formulas are less likely to reach the depleted tissues, and in the case of disturbed *doshas* and *ama* (toxins caused by faulty metabolism of food nutrients) the *rasayana* treatment done without *pancha karma* can actually aggravate the problem, rather than alleviate it. *Rasayanas*  increase the quantity and quality of *rasa* in much the same way as water used for gardening nourishes both weeds and flowers at the smae time. It is therefore necessary to cleanse the body and insure that the internal organs are in good health before undergoing rejuvenation. Under the guidence of trained health care professionals, rejuvenation therapy should be proceeded by at least one or two weeks of such internal cleansing.

Changing your diet is crucial to the success of your rejuvenation therapy. For optimum benefit you should avoid pungent, bitter, sour, and salty tastes, subsisting exclusively on milk or on milk, honey, and ghee. If this is not possible, you must be careful to avoid hot, pungent, and sour spices like chilis and tamarind, salt, pickles, potatoes, white flour, tapioca, white rice, all flesh foods, eggs, mushrooms, and members of the onion family, as well as coffee, tea, cigarettes, and alcohol. During rejuvenation you should also avoid too many sprouted grains and raw vegetables, which put a strain on the digestive system. You should eat *kichari* (equal part mung beans and basmati rice), bland, liquid foods, milk, beans, yogurt, brown rice, corn meal, whole wheat flour, gourds, bitter vegetables, bananas and plantains, ghee, butter, and fresh fruits. Although for the purposes of rejuvination your diet generaly should include more sweet, nourishing foods. But to choose the particular vegetables and fruits to use during rejuvination you should stictly follow the guidelines for your constitutional body type. These can be found in Dr. Vasant Lad's *Ayurveda: The Science of Self Healing* and Dr. David Frawley's new book *Ayurvedic Healing: A Comprehensive Guide.*

As a candidate for rejuvenation you should avoid sexual activity of any kind, physical labor, day sleep, aimless talk and activities, late hours, and strong emotions. Rise early, but get plenty of sleep, wear clean white clothes, bathe at least twice a day, and engage yourself in religious activities like *japa, puja,*reading the scriptures, and gentler forms of yoga.

Next one must choose where to undergo the rejuvenation program, and then careful consideration must also be given as to which formulas will be the most effective. Although it could be done at home, if you really want to enjoy the benefits of rejuvenation, implement this program as part of a yoga or 'back to nature' retreat. Get away and focus on your mental and physical health for a while, rather than on your business or personal affairs. Try a cabin or a tent in the Rocky mountains, a bed-and breakfast in Maine or New Hampshire, visit a yoga ashram in Hawaii, or a health clinic in New Mexico. And if you are really bold, you could go to the Himalayas where rejuvenation therapy was born.

Two ideal cities for regeneration of the body *and* soul are located on the banks of the Ganges River in the Himalayan foothills: Hardwar and Rishikesh. These two ancient cities, which have recently been rejuvenated themselves with an influx of Western disciples and money, are famous for their *rasayana salas* (centers that offer treatments and medicines for rejuvenation), and when we went there last winter it was easy to see why. The Himalayan foothills are beautiful and temperate. Even in the first week of December it had not gotten too cold and we could go out in the evening in a sweater and a shawl. Both banks of the Ganges in Rishikesh are lined with ayurvedic pharmacies maintained by the big ashrams there. And in Hardwar we visited two major ayurvedic colleges and saw several pharmaceutical works as well.

The Himalayas are rich in herbs like *amla, bibhitaki, haritaki, bhringaraj*a, *shatavari, kalmegha, aswaghanda,* and *vacha,* all of which are important ayurvedic rejuvenators, and are likewise rich in fresh honey, cow's milk, and ghee, which are essential for most *rasayanas*. The Himalayas are also a major source of the important mineral rejuvenators, *shilajit* and mercury. The big ashrams have created a flourishing cottage industry out of the collection of herbs and the production of medicines, and they maintain a certain spiritual air about the whole thing that only serves to improve the subtle qualities of the herbal formulas.

Although recent experiments in Bombay on two *rasayana* formulas, *gudhuchi* (*tinosporia cordifolia*) and *shatavari* (*asperagus racemosus*), showed that these two formulas have marked effects on the immune system (these immunostimulants proved extremely effective against candida albicans, stress-related stomach ulcers, and other disorders), the effects of *rasayanas* cannot wholly be reduced to the action of enzymes and alkalis. Dalhana, the famous ayurvedic botanist and medieval commentator on *Charaka* and *Sushruta*, states that the actions of the *rasayana*  formulas are inconceivable and beyond the grasp of reason (*achintya*).

The two most important of these formulas are *chyavana prash* and *brahmi rasayana*. Each contains about 42 different herbs and each is credited with remarkable powers of rejuvenation. Other important *rasayanas* include *haritaki rasayana,* which is another complex formula containing 35 different herbs, and *amla rasayana,* which is little more than *amla* and ghee but which is also a powerful rejuvenator. *Triphala* is also considered a *rasayana* and along with *chyavana prash* is the most commonly available of these formulas in the West.

For those who can afford it there are rejuvenation formulas using gold and precious stones as well. The most costly *rasayanas* available include the *brihat chintamani vat*, which by the time it reaches Chicago or Denver could easily cost as much as $2180.00 for ten grams, a two-week supply! *Suvarna vasanta malati* is another rejuvenator using gold and precious stones costing about $1454.00 for ten grams as is *Makaradwaja vati* made with alchemically humanized mercury, gold, and sulphur at about $900.00 for ten grams. The most expensive medicine we could find was *suvarna bhasma* (gold ash) at about $16,360.00 for ten grams, depending on who your supplier is. Of course if you go to India yourself you can save a lot of money, but beware—the market abounds with false *bhasmas* and gem elixirs.

Actually, as with all things, the simple *rasayanas* are the best \[see Appendix A\], and when administered in conjunction with *pancha karma* and followed up with *kaya kalpa,* aphrodisiac therapy, they can have the greatest effect. It may be that with the increasing popularity of ayurveda in the West a rejuvenation retreat may be available here in a few years. In the mean time you can undergo out patient rejuvination treatments at one of the ayurvedic clinics currently operating in this country, or you can design your own rejuvenation program. But the most important factor in successful rejuvenation is not some magical formula, or an exotic physical therapy, but the state of mind of the recipient.

In the words of Charaka: "Persons who are truthful, free from anger, who avoid intoxication, who are celibate, who practice nonviolence and are vegetarian, who are peaceful and pleasing in their speech and deeds, who practice *japa*, who are clean, sober-minded, charitable, and austere; who are prayerful, who worship God, the guru, and their elders, who are free from profane activities, who are compassionate, who keep regular hours and rise before the sun, who habitually take milk and ghee, who act appropriately according to time, place, and circumstance, who are rational, egoless, good, and broadminded; who possess a love for spiritual knowledge, who are self-controlled, and who regularly read the scriptures—these people get the most out of rejuvenation therapy."

Notes:

1\. The Western idea of an aphrodisiac is generally a substance that *irritates* the reproductive organs. But in the ayurveda the term “aphrodisiac” (*vaji karana*) is used to refer to any substance or treatment that *nourishes* the tissues in the reproductive system. Their value lies in the fact that not only does it take nutrients from all the tissues of the body to produce the reproductive fluids, but these same fluids when preserved and nourished can replenish the entire system. For those who practice celibacy but still desire the health benefits of *kaya kalpa*, the recommended dosage is usually cut in half to avoid the excessive sexual stimulation these formulas can cause.

2\. *Japa* is silent repetition of mantras on a rosary. *Puja* is the worship and care of sacred persons or objects and includes the offering of foods, flowers, incense, and the like.

Appendices

A. Simple *rasayana* formulas you can make at home:

1\. *Pippalivardhamana rasayana*

It is easier to follow than to say. All that is required are some whole pippali. Ten of the pippali peppercorns should be taken gradually, increasing the dose daily in increments of ten. After ten days this amount should gradually be decreased at the same rate. Strong persons can take the full dose, ground and boiled in milk. Persons of moderate strength should take only six pippalis in decoction. A decoction is formed when the herb is gently boiled in eight times its weight of water and the volume of water is reduced to one-fourth by the boiling. Weak persons should take only three pippalis in the form of a cold infusion. A cold infusion is formed when the drug is allowed to sit overnight in four times as much water. By the time you have taken the full dose you will have consumed 1000 pippalis. After they digest follow them with some rice, milk, and ghee.

2\. Three *triphala rasayanas*

a. Along with honey and ghee take one *haritaki* fruit early in the morning on an empty stomach. Before lunch eat two *bibhitaki* fruits followed by four *amalaki* fruits after lunch. By the use of this *rasayana* for one year, it is said that you will extend your lifespan to 100 disease-free years.

b. *Triphala* mixed with licorice powder, bamboo manna, pippali, honey, ghee, and sugar is an excellent formula for rejuvenation.

c. *Triphala* along with *sarvaloha* (fine powders of gold, zinc, tin, lead, iron, copper, and silver boiled in *myrabolan* juice), calamus root, *vidanga* (*embilia ribes*), pippali, garlic, honey, and ghee. Take daily with milk for one year. This is an excellent *rasayana* for going about one’s daily business.

3\. *Shilajatu rasayana*

*Shilajatu* (mineral pitch) should be immersed into a hot decoction of the herbs that have been prescribed for the alleviation of the patient's vitiated *doshas*. After it has absorbed the decoction it should be immersed again. This should be repeated for seven days. This *shilajatu* should be mixed with an equal amount of iron powder and taken with milk. It should be administered in doses of 48, 24, or 12 grams for seven weeks, three weeks, or one week, depending on the strength of the individual: strong, moderate, or weak. While taking this *rasayana* a person should live exclusively on milk.

B. Simple *kaya kalpas* for aphrodisiac therapy:

1\. Basmati rice with liberal quantities of milk and ghee, sugar and honey.

2\. Thirty pippalis made into a fine paste and fried in 1 to 1 1/2 ounces of ghee. To this add enough milk to make a thick drink. This should be taken according to the strength of the individual as pippali is a very strong herb. It should be followed with a meal of milk and basmati rice prepared with ghee.

3\. Ghee with *shatavari*, ten times as much milk along with sugar, pippali, and honey is an excellent formula.

4\. Equal quantities of licorice powder, ghee, and honey. This should be taken every day with milk.

Side Bar

*Pancha karma* and its role in rejuvenation therapy:

1\. Purgation, or *virechana,* is accomplished by the administration of herbs which are tonic laxatives and purgatives. This is especially useful in *pitta* disorders. It brings about clarity of mind, efficiency of the sense organs, vigor, and improved digestion. Purgation is an absolute prerequisite to rejuvenation as the intestines and colon must be thoroughly cleaned before the ingestion of the powerful tonic formulas that make up *rasayanas*. In addition, Charaka recommends a diet of barley gruel for one week prior to undergoing treatment to insure this optimum state of internal cleanliness.

2\. Enema, or *basti,* is next in importance in *rasayana.* Medicated enemas are useful in a wide variety of conditions; they can be nourishing, emollient, cleansing, and/or cooling depending on the substances used. Medicated enemas are the principal means of correcting internal *vata* disorders as *vata's* seat is in the colon.

3\. Emesis, or *vamana,* is induced vomiting by use of herbal decoctions and manual stimulation of the gagging reflex. It is especially useful for congestive disorders of the upper bodily region and treatment of vitiated *kapha*.

4\. Errhine, or *nasya,* is nasal administration of medicated oils or powders to throw out or mollify vitiated *doshas* from the neck up. *Nasya* has three varieties: purgative, nourishing or cooling, and sedative or alleviating. It has no direct connection with *rasayana* per se, but is often recommended as part of a daily routine and could certainly be added to a rejuvenation program with great effect. It should not be used after enemas, however, as this will disturb the upward and downward moving airs, leading to a vitiation of *vata.*

5\. Sudation, or *swedana,* is one of the most important therapeutic actions in the ayurveda. There are thirteen different types of *swedana,* including application of hot oils, herb packs, steam treatment, wrapping in blankets, exercise, and exposure to heat. Although *swedana* is not always considered one of the *pancha karma,* it often serves as a prelude to them. To prevent excessive depletion of the tissues, sweats must be preceded by *snehana*, or oleation. Oleation can be done by enemas as in *basti,* or by massage. Sweating and oleation serve both to cleanse and nourish the tissues, and so play an important role in rejuvenation therapy.\*

About the "bloodletting": You yourself said that it is often not included in *panca karma*. So why not leave it out?

## Banaras

On Death and Dying

"The City of Light by Swami B G Narasingha

Long before the days of the American settler, or before Europe had a place on the world map, Banaras, on the western bank of the Ganges, had become a legend in her own time. In fact, Banaras may very well be the oldest living city in the world. In the words of the late Reverend M.A. Sherring, "Twenty-five centuries ago, at least, Banaras was famous. When Babylon was struggling with Nineveh for supremacy, when Tyre was planting her colonies, when Athens was growing in strength, before Rome had become known, or Greece had contended with Persia, or Cyrus had added luster to the Persian monarchy, or Nebuchadnezzar had captured Jerusalem, and the inhabitants of Judaea had been carried into captivity, she had already risen to greatness, if not glory."

I have visited Banaras on several occasions during my travels in India. The view of the city by boat from the Ganges is outstanding. The city extends for three miles along the banks of the River Ganges. There are more than seventy magnificent ghats (large stone staircases descending to the river) where numerous temples, shrines, yoga ashrams, and pavilions overlook the sacred river. When the rays of the morning sun fall upon Banaras, everything takes on a gorgeous golden hue, as if the city were self-effulgent. From the pre-dawn hours until after dusk the sacred life of the Hindus centers about the river. Bathing, worshiping, praying, meditating, even cremation, are all happening simultaneously at the ghats. The dramatic impression left in the mind, having seen Banaras even once, is not easily forgotten.

In the old part of the city there are many narrow streets filled with shops and stores of every description. Silver and gold merchants, expert craftsmen at work making brass and copper vessels, cloth merchants and tailors, fruit and vegetable sellers and fresh juice stalls fill the narrow lanes. Bare-chested men, perched on small wooden platforms in open air restaurants, sit cross-legged cooking puris (deep fried flat bread) and vegetables on open wood fires—-the aroma of which attracts hungry passers-by. Women in colorful saris and men clad in all white cotton shirts and pants move to and fro through the busy thoroughfares while large white brahma bulls wander freely about. Banaras is typically Indian.

The most famous street in Banaras is Vishwanatha Lane. Entering the lane from the vicinity of Dashashwamedha Ghat and continuing north, one soon comes to the entrance of the principle place of worship the ancient Vishwanatha Temple. Marble floors worn by the constant influx of barefoot pilgrims, beautiful silver altars decorated with flowers, the sent of burning oils and incense, arched doorways, and finely sculpted stone pillars all combine with the ringing of bells and the sounds of gongs to create an enchanting atmosphere. The upper portion of the inner Sanctom is crowned with a golden dome which can be seen from the street. One hundred thousand pilgrims come to the Vishwanatha temple every day, and on festival days the attendance increases many fold.

Vishwanatha is a name for Shiva, the predominating deity of Banaras, who is considered an incarnation of the destructive quality of Godhead. While talking to a brahman priest at the Vishwanatha temple, I learned that the Hindus not only credit God with the creation but with the destruction of the universe also. The priest showed me a passage in one of his old, handwritten palm leaf scrolls:

"Just as milk is transformed into yogurt by the action of acids, yet the effect 'yogurt' is neither the same as nor different from its cause, namely milk, so I worship the primeval Lord, of whom the state of Shiva is a transformation for the performance of the work of destruction." (Brahma-samhita)

Banaras is a very special place for Hindus—it is said to be the place where liberation is easily achieved "Kashyam maranam muktih, "In Kashi \[Banaras\] one easily attains liberation or freedom fromsamsara, the cycle of birth and death." There are seven ancient holy cities, such as Banaras, mentioned in the Hindu scriptures. "Ayodhya, Mathura, Hardwar, Dwaraka, Kanchi, Ujjain, and the city of Kashi." Of these, Kashi, "the City of Light" refers to Banaras. The Hindus call Kashi the city of light because it illuminates truth and reveals reality. Hindu philosophers have always believed that reality is transcendental to the plane of mundane existence. The body, they say, and the world around us are always changing due to the influence of time. Due to the time factor the world has no permanent existence and therefore can not be the ultimate reality. Hence, for a Hindu, reality does not exist within the jurisdiction of time, the great force which turns the cycle of birth and death, moving the world from beginning to end. The Hindus call it Kala Chakra, "the wheel of time," but Banaras, they say, is its hub, where movement or time has no influence. Indeed, in Banaras, time goes by as if having no influence at all: Banaras remains as she is, as she always was, and the soul of man is said to be set free under her divine influence.

India's holy places are known as tirthas or "crossing places" between heaven and earth. Tirthas are not to be confused with high energy centers, like mountain tops or areas where the forces of nature are present with overwhelming proportions. They are points where the marriage between transcendence and the mundane take place. These crossing places are compared to shallow water in the raging river of birth and death—shallow water, that is, in the sense that mundane influence is at a minimum. This makes it easier for the seekers of eternal truth to make the journey to the other side—to the side where birth and death have no jurisdiction. A tirtha not only provides a crossing place for the "upward" journey of the soul, but it also provides for the "downward" crossing—for the crossing ofdevas and other higher entities who sometimes descend to this world for the good of mankind.

The residents of Banaras are called "Kashivasis," meaning those who live in Kashi. A Kashivasi lives a good life, following the path of religiosity, economic development, and material enjoyment. Hindus consider these the first three goals of life: dharma, artha, and kama, respectively. However, a Kashivasi is said to automatically achieve the fourth goal of life, moksha or liberation. To achieve liberation usually takes many, many lifetimes of severe penance, austerity, meditation, and yoga practice. But the Kashivasis are said to achieve liberation in only one life. They believe that if one lives and dies in Banaras he will immediately be freed from the cycle of birth and death.

There are more than a million people living in Banaras—Bengalis, Marwaris, Maharastrians, Nepalis, and so on. But above these national designations they share a common identity—they are all Kashivasis. The spiritual benefit of living in Banaras is why they are there. For them, occupation and employment are secondary concerns. Slogans of liberation, moksha, are written on walls and billboards throughout the city in the same manner that one would expect to see political propaganda or cinema advertisements. One frequently used and well-known slogan goes like this:

"This we know for certain: Where the River Ganges flows, in the place know as Kashi, moksha, liberation, is guaranteed."

In addition to the resident Kashivasis there are those who come to Banaras at the eleventh hour. They come to Banaras on death's notice to spend their last days in the sacred city before leaving this mortal world. They come for Kashi Labh—"The benefit of Kashi." Throughout the city there are innumerable hospices that open their doors to accomodate the dying, providing them the psychological and spiritual support they need to face death fearlessly. A hospice usually consists of a compound with thirty to forty rooms set around an open courtyard. There are trees and flowering plants in the courtyard which make a park-like enviroment. The rooms are well ventilated with plenty of sunlight.

Checking into a hospice, a dying person is given a room, humbly furnished with one cot, where he may remain with his family or friends until the end. Often the dying prefer to lie on the floor where they will be in contact with the earth, for Hindus consider the earth to be our "Mother."

Each hospice has a special room set aside called the puja room where sacred hymns and the names of God are chanted around the clock. The first rule of a hospice is that only those who are dying and who believe in liberation in Kashi, and have come especially for "Kashi Labh," may stay there. Those who wish to get well by taking medicine should stay elsewhere in a hospital. Written on the wall at the entrance of a hospice is an encouragement for the dying: "Where else does a person obtain liberation as he does in Kashi, simply by giving up the body, with very little effort at all!"

The Hindus believe that when one is dying he should prepare his mind and consciousness for departing from this world and entering into the next. It is as important for a Hindu to have a good death as it is for him to have a good life. Along with the art of living, they say, one must also master the art of dying.

The Hindus believe that what the mind thinks about at the time of death will determine the state of being in their next life. Therefore, they say that one should fix his mind on God. In some cases, though, the old and infirmed can not utter the names of God at the time of death, so the family members chant the names for them.

Upon visiting a hospice I found that it was not a morbid atmosphere as the Western mind might imagine. Rather there was a solemn air about the hospice, an air of profound expectation. There was occasional singing of devotional songs, and meditative music was played for the benefit of the patients.

After death, before the body is cremated, the deceased is kept in state for a few hours in the home or hospice while friends and relatives come to offer flowers and a few parting words. Then the deceased's\`remains are carried through the streets on a decorated palanquin, followed by well-wishers who chant repeatedly,"Rama nama satya hai! Rama nama satya hai!" "God's name is Truth! God's name is Truth!" Then the body is taken to the cremation ghat and purified with the sacred waters of the Ganges. Finally the body comes to rest on the funeral pyre. The body is then surrounded with burning incense, sprinkled with sandalwood oil and covered in flowers—all in the midst of friends, relatives and priests, who utter sacred hymns. Finally the eldest male member of the family ignites the pyre with the sacred flame.

During these ceremonies for the dead more emphasis is given to the departed soul of the deceased than to the body he has left behind. After the cremation is completed the ashes of the deceased are reverently placed in the Ganges. His family members then perform the sraddha ceremony for eleven days—consisting of fasting and reading from holy books, reciting prayers and offering specially prepared foodstuff to help the departed soul through the transition period to his next life. The sraddha ceremony is not a period of mourning but a period of purification—both for the deceased and for his family.

Hindus believe that until the body of the deceased is destroyed by the cremation fire, the soul remains in this world in a subtle form due to attachment. But when the body of the deceased is cremated the soul is then freed of lingering attachments to bodily ego. Thus cremation is thought to expedite the soul's passing to his next life. Furthermore, since it is believed that liberation is achieved by one who dies in the sacred city of Banaras, or on the banks of the river Ganges, or where the names of God are being chanted, the Hindus say there is no need for lamentation for the dead. But if a Hindu can not die with at least one of these three benefits, then there is certainly cause for grief.

Banaras has recently become very popular among the many European and American tourists who come to India each year—though they have a different fascination with this ancient city than do the Hindus. Most Westerners come to Banaras in search of fine hand-woven silk dresses and woolen carpets. Some come to photograph the yogis and snake charmers who live along the banks of the river, to enjoy a holiday and discover a culture different than their own. Inevitably, though, after hearing about the cremation sites, everyone is drawn to this strange spectacle which sometimes proves to be more than they bargained for. In fact, the sight of a body burning in the funeral fire can sometimes be so overpowering that many visitors have to return to their hotel rooms to recuperate.

Death is an undeniable fact of everyday living. Hundreds of people die every day in Banaras and are taken to the ghats for cremation. At any given moment one might see a body being carried through the streets in route to one of three main cremation sites. Trucks loaded with wood for burning the dead arrive in the city every day. Stretchers for carrying the dead are sold at road side shops along many of the main bazaars. It is also not uncommon to see a crowded bus entering the city from the countryside filled with people and carrying a dead body wrapped in white linen on the roof. The Hindus have been known to bring the body of a deceased relative from as far away as five hundred miles just to be cremated at Banaras. At the cremation ghats sometimes as many as a dozen cremations take place at once—each on a separate pyre. The burning ghats are in operation twenty-four hours a day, 365 days a year. Although death is always present, they say one never really becomes callous to it. Rather it is a constant reminder of the temporary nature of this world.

Although Banaras is known to Hindus as "the city of light," it has been dubbed by many Western visitors as "the city of death." One American lady commented on her visit to Manikarnika, the city's busiest cremation ghat, "It was horrifying! Death was everywhere. Dead bodies were being thrown into blazing fires. The smell was sickening. Have they no respect for their dead?" Coming face to face with the reality of death and the total destruction of the body can be an unnerving experience. Not everyone is ready to accept that reality.

In India cremation is also the only logical means to dispose of the body. As opposed to the burial system widely practiced elsewhere in the world. India simply doesn't have enough land to bury her dead, India is a country literally thousands of years old and there are more than 750 million people living there. Therefore burying the dead becomes impractical. If India buried her dead then in the centuries to come there would eventually be a shortage of land.

Death and dying in Banaras, like many Indian traditions, is often misrepresented to the Western public by sensational journalism and inaccurate reporting. An impression often given in the West is that Banaras is under the grip of death—bodies are burned as a savage ritual without respect for the dead and an atmosphere of darkness and despair hover above the city. But nothing could be farther from the truth.

In contrast to our "death denying" culture in the West where death is hidden from view—forestalled as long as possible and often feared as the end of everything—the Hindus are comfortable with the fact of death. Death is considered natural, unavoidable, and the most certain of human realities. Death is something that everyone has to face regardless of religion, culture or nationality. Therefore the Hindus say, "Why not learn to accept it and deal with it in a dignified manner?"

Banaras has been described as India in a microcosm. In Banaras all that is Indian comes before us in an instant. She is ever so peaceful and charming, yet Banaras challenges the very concepts and values of Western civilization. But if that challenge is met with an open mind we may learn something for our eternal benefit. I have several times seen a body burned on a funeral pyre at Banaras, and it has given me a desire to end my body in the same way. Everything is over at once. The body is dead and the spirit has departed. The purifying fire destroys in a few hours all that remains behind, casting it to the wind, turning it into smoke and ashes. As the ancient texts of India say,

"Let this temporary body be burned to ashes, and let the air of life be merged with the totality of air." (Isopanisad)

While death is one of the most prominent features of Banaras, the city itself lives on. I don't think that in all of my travels there is anyone place that brings to mind the importance of life as Banaras does. A visit to this holy city is a wise investment for anyone interested in gaining deeper insight into the mysteries of our life here and hereafter.

Banaras is like the soul itself. Although she is ancient, she is young as well. As the soul lives forever yet remains ever youthful so Banaras seems untouched by time. Another traveler, Mark Twain has described her thus: "Banaras is older than history, older than tradition, older even than legend, and looks twice as old as all of them put together!" Indeed, Banaras is more than old— Banaras is practically eternal.

## The Gita As It Was

Rediscovering the Original Bhagavad Gita  
Phulgenda Sinha, Open Court, 1987, 268pp. paperback.

The Bhagavad Gita is one of the most important texts to come out of India. Although widely published and read as a separate text, Bhagavad-gita originally appears as an episode in the Mahabharata, a great historical epic consisting of some 100,000 couplets (the epic was recently popularized by Peter Brooks' nine-hour dramatization on stages around the world).

The Gita occupies chapters twenty-five through forty-two in the Bhisma-parva section of the Mahabharata. As it begins, Krishna is standing in the midst of a battlefield—as a charioteer—for his friend and devotee Arjuna. The dialogue that ensues is the gita, or "song," of bhagavan, God. He sings the song because Arjuna is in need of instruction. Bewildered by the mandate to fight, Arjuna hesitates to engage in the fratricidal war before him. Krishna, however, elucidates the implications of Arjuna's reluctance. He points out that, as a warrior, Arjuna's specific duty is indeed to fight on behalf of the righteous. And his hesitation, Krishna adds, though superficially noble, is actually based on illusion, a misidentification of the body with the self. The opposing party is, after all, guilty of many atrocities and already doomed, even if many of them are Arjuna's relatives. God has sealed their fate or, rather, they have sealed their own fate, and Krishna is encouraging Arjuna to act as an instrument in meting out the appropriate reaction. The Gita's seven hundred verses embody Krishna's arguments in this regard and Arjuna's ultimate acquiescence.

What does this overview of the Gita have to do with Phulgenda Sinha's book? It appears that Arjuna's work was left unfinished. While he definitely did Krishna's work on the battlefield, there is a new enemy of his Lord's Gita—but this time the battlefield is academia and the weapon is independent research. To be sure, the Gita has been represented in speculative commentaries many times in the past, the earliest being the great Shankara commentary in the eighth century A.D (not to be confused with his devotional prayer/poem praising the Gita) While important in its own right, it missed the essentially theistic nature of the Gita's overall message. Shankara's forced interpretation opened up a new school of scriptural hermeneutics for the Gita, and less worthy renditions soon flooded the market. Sinha lists them in his own work and doubtless refers to them as authorities: Huxley, Hartmann, Steiner, Tagore, Schroder, to name a few. While these men may enjoy a certain distinction in their respective fields, they are hardly authorities on Bhagavad Gita.

The more important commentaries are scarcely even mentioned by Sinha, but they should be known to our readers: The Anugita, The Gitamahatmyas, Jayatirtha's commentary, the work of Vedanta Deshika, and even the more or less monistic interpretation of Bhaskara. More important still are the commentaries of Ramanujacharya, Madhvacharya, Vishvanath Chakravarti Thakur, and Baladeva Vidyabhushana; Sinha refers to them only superficially, for they do not support his view. Interestingly, Sinha mentions every contemporary and popular edition of the Gita—save and except the Bhagavad-gita As It Is of Bhaktivedanta Swami. And it is this definitive edition, it may be noted, that is ridiculed in the title of Sinha's work.

The premise of Sinha's book is not new. His obvious lack of respect for the traditional Gita (shown in the fact that he is ready to change its contents) is due to the influence of foreign invaders in India-- Muslim fundamentalists and Christian missionaries who denigrated the sacred scriptures of Indian antiquity. They had for centuries misled the Indian people.The British, for instance, had convinced nearly the entire Indian subcontinent that they were illiterate because they could not read the Bible. These ill-informed foreigners had no idea of the highly sophisticated Sanskrit language or the comprehensive Vedic scriptural tradition. Due to ignorance and cultural isolation, they felt that Vedic culture was backward and even barbaric. Many scholars were and are weaned on this sort of misinformation. Sinha is clearly one of them.

His discovery of "the original Gita" is presented like a detailed detective mystery. Unfortunately, Sinha more resembles a bumbling Inspector Clouseau than a more competent Sherlock Holmes. He cites authorities that were discredited years before his birth. As if to add insult to injury, he further cites Richard Garbe and Eve Weber, originators of "the Borrowing Theory," which states that all theistic notions found in the worship of Krishna are attributable to, or "borrowed" from, Christianity. Sinha takes this notion even further, saying that there was no concept of a "One Almighty God" in India prior to the ninth century A.D.

What Sinha doesn't mention, however, is that these scholars who propounded the borrowing theory were eventually made the victims of their own misconceptions when the evidence of Megasthenes was brought in. This evidence engendered undeniable archaelogical conlclusions, proving once and for all that Krishna worship is not only not derived from Christianity but that possibly it was the other way around. Moreover, the Megasthenes evidence made clear that the worship of "One Almighty God," as Sinha states it, was indeed accepted by early worshippers of Krishna—before the Christian Era (what to speak of the "ninth century A. D." !).

Now let us get to the heart of Sinha's erroneous contention: All of the great commentators and the time-honored Vedic tradition are wrong. The Gita does not include seven hundred verses as is normally supposed. Rather, says Sinha, the original Gita is composed of a mere eighty-four, and he kindly enumerates these carefully chosen verses in his book. But the problem is this: After going through his 250-page work more than four times, I still could not see exactly how he came to his conclusions. His evidence is poor; his clues are lacking. For anyone even moderately aware of Vedic culture and theology, Sinha's detective mystery falls short of even a grade B movie.

Sinha's method is not unlike the dubious techniques of Western scholars. He compares language, writing style, and Sanskrit phonetics. Then, in a more or less arbitrary manner, he decides which of the Gita verses are authentic and which are interpolations. Although highly speculative, Sinha seems to swear by his conclusions. He replaces caution with carelessness, and substance with wishful thinking.

In fact, his book lacks so much substance that a discerning reader might naturally question if Sinha had possibly embarked upon his project to receive financial backing. Using ancient religious texts to obtain a grant for further research is not uncommon. According to a recent article in India Abroad, scholar Vedavyas (not to be confused with the compiler of the Vedic literature, who has the same name) discovered forty-five "missing" Bhagavad-gita verses. "The original text of the Gita," says Dr. Vedavyas, "had 745 verses, and now I will reveal the missing forty-five." Hailed as a big scholarly breakthrough, Vedavyas' claim won him a grant and notoriety—for about two weeks. Then, in the same newpaper that acclaimed his discovery, came the startling counter-claim from another scholar, nullifying the forty-five verse theory. And so it goes...

Almost as if in anticipation of such deviant interpretations, the Gita itself gives information as to how one can know the truths contained in its very pages. The fourth chapter sings loudly: evam parampara praptam, imam rajashayo vidhu. This is the original Sanskrit, and it says, in essence, that one must approach a spiritual master in disciplic succession (parampara) to know the truth of the Gita; it will not suffice to approach an academic research scholar. The mysteries of religious literature are best left to religious mystics, and scriptural hermeneutics are best left to those whose lives embody the scriptures. In this regard, the Gita's message is crystal clear: approach a self-realized soul. He can give you knowledge because he has seen the truth. By contrast, a mental speculator, however adept he may be, can only teach one how to speculate. One who studies the Bhagavad-gita clinically—from a distance—can never enter into its deeper understanding. One who lives the Gita, however, can resolve all philosophical, historical, and hermeneutical problems, both for himself and for those he teaches.

Sinha is in the former category. His approach is academic, speculative. And it is a poor academic and speculative approach at that. Sinha's publishers, Open Court, have published other, more worthy Gita-type books for scholars and lay persons alike. The Universal Gita by Eric J. Sharpe was Open Court's first attempt in this area. This delightful book gives an accurate overview of the story behind the Gita and documents its journey West. The reader is introduced to important Western transcendentalists who found more that a little merit in the Gita's teaching: T. S. Eliot, R. W. Emerson, H. D. Thoreau, Walt Whitman, and even Albert Einstein are included.

After the success of The Universal Gita in 1985, Open Court released an even more ambitious work: Arvind Sharma's The Hindu Gita. This scholarly book picked up where Sharpe's book left off, detailing the traditional Indian commentaries from Shankara to Madhva. Sinha could have greatly benefited from reading these two books.

Since The Hindu Gita did as well for Open Court in 1986 as The Universal Gita did the year before, the logical conclusion was to keep the Gita material coming. Unfortunately, they took too big a risk with Sinha's work. Scholars reject it as untraditional and lacking evidence. Believers denounce it as sacrilegious. I just felt it was a waste of paper.

Steven Rosen

## Caste System - Social Paradigm

*For the Synthesis of Material Difference and Spiritual Oneness*

*I remember my seventh grade teacher telling me about India’s horrific caste system. She taught that India’s caste system was the height of social injustice. Yet somehow I could not agree with her, although at the time I did not have a logical response to the contrary. All that India meant to me was the tall, slender Indian lady draped in a silken sari with bangles on her arms, a ring in her nose, and a red dot on her forehead, who I would see from time to time with her young son, walking through the corridor at lunch hour. She would bring a special lunch for her son, and to me she represented something mysterious that was somehow deeper and richer than all the “facts” I was gathering in school. It was hard for me to believe that the great social evil, the caste system, as described in my seventh grade world history class, was an accurate portrayal of the culture of India. Later I came to find that my skepticism was warranted*.

Progressive, socially conscious zealots, especially in the land of “rights”—Hometown, USA—are quick to point out social inequalities, both at home and abroad. Today the outcry for human rights is one that is hard for even the world’s most oppressive regimes to ignore. Following the Reagan administration, conservative President Bush won the election by condemning liberalism, calling it the “L” word; ironically, however, historian Albert Schlesinger recently pointed out that Bush’s call for a “kinder and more gentle nation” exemplified those in power yielding to the rising force of liberalism.
