Liberalism that leads to kinder and more gentle nations is certainly desirable. If this kind of liberalism is on the rise, it is encouraging, because it indicates progress in the spiritual direction. We want equality for all, and, after all, we have heard that “all men (and women) are created equal.” So a social system that determines a person’s social status and rights by the family in which he or she is born would seem—to be generous—outdated. And India’s caste system appears to do just that. Four orders of occupation are outlined: the intellectual, the martial, the mercantile, and the laboring class, and in whichever family one is born in, the dye is cast, and one’s life’s status is fixed. It is thought that one’s social status can change only by achieving a higher birth in the next life. This social system seems contradictory to the spiritual values of ancient India, which hearken us to see the equality of all living beings. How could a spiritual culture have a repressive social system?

Obviously, it can’t. In reality, the repressive caste system is not representative of spiritual India, but of modern India. India’s spirituality does not foster the caste system, but it does, however, recognize a natural fourfold social structure. The division of society determined by birthright (the caste system) is but a vitiated form of another social system that recognizes a social structure that undeniably exists not only in India but throughout the entire world.

This social structure is called *varnashram.* The Sanskrit word *varna* literally means “color,” but it refers to the “color” of the mind, or one’s temperament, and not to the body. It therefore implies a standard of conduct or mode of occupation that naturally corresponds with one’s mental disposition or karmic tendency. The *varnashram* social system divides human effort into four classes of occupation by determining one’s karmic leaning, not by what family one takes birth in. It first takes into consideration one’s spiritual status and then determines one’s material propensity.

In India today the outer structure of the *varnashram* system is acknowledged, but the spiritual substance behind it is severely lacking. Because of this, India’s social system may appear at a glance more dehumanizing than both capitalism and communism, but history reveals that both of these modern forms of government are corruptions of the *varnashram* institution.

How strict observance of one’s birth lines came to determine one’s status in India is somewhat understandable inasmuch as birth in a particular family dictates considerably how we will think. Especially in a society where the family unit is strong, children tend to be molded in accordance with their parent’s views: sons often take up the family business, for example. Moreover, following a spiritual worldview, souls tend to be born into material families whose values mirror their stage of spiritual evolution. All of this is relative, however, and there are many exceptions. Sometimes children seem to have been born into the wrong family in that they differ so much from the interests of their parents. Almost every family has a “black sheep,” not in the sense of an evil son or daughter, but a child who does not identify the family’s values. Thus, India’s overemphasis on the importance of birth rather than on each individual’s qualities and inner attitude has corrupted her social system.

To appreciate how both the communist and capitalist ideologies are but the *varnashram* system in decay, a more detailed explanation of what the *varnashram* system is and how it works will be helpful. As we will see, *varnashram* is sometimes manifest and sometimes not, but its influence nonetheless continues to exist throughout all societies.

Manifest *varnashram* consists of recognizing material inequalities and taking advantage of them to derive our inherent spiritual equality. Unlike materially-based social systems, *varnashram* does not artificially attempt to find equality through material adjustment. Rather, it finds beauty and higher truth in our material inequality. Because in this system success is not determined by material advancement, material inequality is not indicative of one person being inferior to another, any more than an apple is inferior to a banana. Both are valuable in their own right. Unlike the modern democratic ideology, which attempts to reduce everyone to the same set of basically material values, equating happiness with material advancement, *varnashram* recognizes the uniqueness of all people and directs them toward spiritual values.

The *varnashram* system views all living beings as spiritual entities within material bodies, and progress in this system is spiritual development that leads in the direction of transcending birth, death, and all material inequality. Ultimately, *varnashram* culminates in the development of love of Godhead. Since the soul or consciousness is the very basis for experience, it is most practical to have a social arrangement that is designed to foster experience of the soul, by which all other material experience can be accurately understood. We may observe that material, goal-oriented social systems do just the opposite: they either obscure the soul altogether or leave room for the half-baked conception of a soul composed of both spirit and matter.

The division of labor (*varna*) and station of direct spiritual culture (*ashram*) in the *varnashram* social body can be compared to the division of our bodies: head, arms, torso, and legs. The intellectual class is the head of society. Although smaller than any other class, its detached influence permeates the entire society. The intellectual class writes the books of the society and conducts research for the advancement of knowledge. The arms of society are the martial class. Those who belong to the martial class engage in “hands-on” management; they are the government administrators and valorous leaders who organize while taking advice from the intellectual class. They too are highly intellectual but possess a passion for administration. The mercantile class, synonymous with the agriculturists, is the torso of society and is profit-oriented. The laboring class, as the legs of society, assists others and provides necessary forms of relaxation, such as arts and entertainment.

All societies are made up of people with these dispositions. By examining the basic values of any society, we can also find four basic domains: knowledge, status, wealth, and pleasure. All human effort is aimed at these values. Thus these values also create the four *varnas*. For example, if wealth-seeking is our goal, we will be confined within the commercial perspective and experience everything in light of profiteering. The ancient Vedic culture, in which *varnashram* was fully operational, recognized these different mentalities to be manifestations of material nature’s karmic influence. These influences or modes of material nature were perceived to pervade every aspect of material life.

The forces of creation, maintenance, and destruction, which are operative in all spheres of life governed by time and space, are considered to constitute our mental makeup. Our goals and values are determined by that makeup, and regardless of any other external conditions, that innate karmic disposition will determine our working propensity. When we are engaged in accordance with our karmic tendency, we can be productive, and when the governing worldview does not cause us to feel that we are in any way inferior to another, regardless of our material social status (by way of promoting spiritual development), we can be peaceful.

To safeguard against corruption and exploitation, the institution of *ashram* is essential. This side of *varnashram* is especially important for the intellectual and administrative classes because they lead the society. Society’s leaders and intellectuals must pass through all four stations of spiritual culture. This begins with student life (*brahmacharya*), in which celibacy is mandatory, as is austerity and the practice of meditation under the guidance of a spiritual mentor. For most, this is followed by married life (*grihasta*) until the children are prepared to raise families of their own. Married life is the time for “worldliness” tempered by one’s earlier education in spiritual values and one’s meditative experience. After married life, men and women enter into retired life (*vanaprasta*) and prepare themselves ultimately for a life of renunciation (*sannyasa*), in which they free themselves from all attachment to that which is temporary. In this way, *ashram* helps insure that the leaders of society are free from false possessiveness and the tendency to exploit others.

When the most influential sections of society advocate spiritual values and exemplify a high standard of spiritual pursuit, all sections of society experience a unity in diversity. While all people are variously engaged in accordance with their diverse material natures, and thus form subcultures within the larger culture, they are unified in spiritual pursuit. *Varnashram* synthesizes material difference with spiritual oneness, making God the center of society and offering the fruits of labor unto Godhead. All labor, although different, is seen as one—devotion.

Far from being a primitive or foreign social structure, *varnashram* is a highly sophisticated arrangement for harmonious living, both materially and spiritually, which involves organizing society from a spiritual perspective. Western governments have emphasized the separation of spiritual pursuit and the affairs of the state in the name of protecting spiritual liberty; but, in effect, they have made our spiritual interest a secondary concern. If we want to “believe,” we can, but the state is not about to investigate the nature of reality enough to understand the spiritual nature of consciousness and organize society based on such findings. By contrast, the v*arnashram* system organizes our material efforts in such a way that all of its members can experience the real self.

*Varnashram’s* external classification of people may remind us of what we learned about medieval Europe’s feudal system, as does the idea of any God-centered society. Indeed the similarities between these two social systems strongly suggests ties between Europe and India. The feudal system could very well be seen as Europe’s version of *varnashram,* while the breakdown of the feudal system has given rise to our present-day Western social systems. Although our modern social systems are usually viewed as improvements from feudal times, they may also be viewed along with the feudal system as the breakdown of *varnashram*.

Medieval Europe’s corrupt form of government with its “divine kings,” “holy wars,” and exploitation of the masses, causes us to shy away from the idea of a spiritual God-centered form of government. Even today, religious fundamentalists stand out as beacons of totalitarianism, threatening our freedom of thought. We must remember that mere belief in religious dogma is far from self-realization. Full-fledged *varnashram* does not advocate fanatical religious belief but actual transcendental experience and God consciousness for which there are objective symptoms. *Varnashrama’s* successful implementation depends on experience of the spiritual self, an experience that can be accessed through genuine traditions.

The Protestant Reformation of 1529 c.e. was a reactionary movement that overthrew the spiritually corrupt feudal system with its four classes of pontiffs, overlords, vassals, and serfs. The feudal system was only a primitive approximation of actual *varnashram:* when its intellectual priestly class became polluted with worldly ambition, their power—a moral and spiritual force—was lost. In this condition their preeminence appeared no longer justifiable in the eyes of the administrative martial class of kings. When the administrators sever themselves from spiritual guidance, they become tyrants who only mouth religious dogma, using it to justify anything and everything. What follows, as history has shown, is such a mercantile/agriculturist uprising as the French Revolution (1789 c.e.). People who are money-minded and clever in business build industry and trade, and in their unquenchable thirst for wealth, they exploit the laboring class, which in turn leads to further revolt, the likes of which was seen in the Russian Revolution of 1917 c.e.

Thus *varnashram* is quite relevant to us today. As the concept of *varnashram* moved west from ancient India to medieval Europe, it became polluted. From that corrupted form of *varnashram,* our present sociopolitical systems have appeared. What we are now experiencing is the decline of *varnashram*. Both capitalism, the mercantile government, and communism, the government of the laboring class, are forms of government in which wealth and material fulfillment are the predominant values. Communism is openly atheistic, and thus in pursuit of material values. Although God is allowed in the capitalist society, capitalists pray to God for the same material wealth that the atheists find without acknowledging God. *Varnashram,* on the other hand, is led by unswerving righteousness and genuine spiritual understanding. Today’s social systems consist of merely varying degrees of decay in manifest *varnashram*—although all of the four classes continue to exist, their status is either not admitted or not properly implemented.

If we objectively view the present-day struggle between the political left and right as a decay of the superior social system of ancient India, we can conclude that the modern ideologies of socialism and capitalism do not have the potential to create a truly just and merciful society. The problem that we are faced with in advocating the superiority of the *varnashram* system is that those in power are not about to move aside. Nonetheless, the rising interest in genuine spiritual experience cannot be denied or legislated away; it is a subtle yet powerful force, and in time it will prevail.

The West’s reemerging interest in the transcendent is a natural and ultimately unavoidable development. We have almost reached the bottom of social decay in the forms of the exploitation known as capitalism, which thrives on greed; and communism, which inevitably leads to brutality. From here there is only one way to go—up. In his insightful article “Blueprint for Social Harmony,” printed in *Sri Mayapur* magazine, Dr. William Deadwyler has summed up the hopelessness of our world’s two most prominent social systems: “Both are rooted in the past and are expressions of social putrefaction. Certainly, European and American society in the twentieth century has become fatally infected by *vaishya* \[mercantile\] values run amok. But *shudra* \[labor\] values run amok are no improvement. As a totally materialistic philosophy, communism fosters rather than eliminates the seeds of exploitation and conflict, encouraging the very conditions it seeks to ameliorate. Consequently, under communism there will never be a society free from the domination of one group by another, of the many by the few, and that domination will be carried on by the most brutal means possible. Both capitalist and communist ideologies are products of exploitation and envy, and neither therefore can hope to eliminate them. They cannot offer release from the process of social degeneration because they are created by it. . . .”

The upliftment of human society rests in the hands of those yearning for and those already experiencing what is most natural—the spiritual dimension. A new society must have at its head a class of people free from material attachment, who can actually do good for others, being free themselves from the very causes of human suffering: lust, avarice, envy, and the like. A truly intelligent ruling class sees intelligence as subordinate to the soul and sees the soul as assisting consciousness in carrying out its healthy intuitive spiritual purpose.

Only people of integrity who can distinguish themselves from their mind and senses’ “call of the wild” can lead us to real civilization. This is a call for a radical change in society, but in the face of our present situation of spiritual decay, there is no more noble an alternative. The respiritualization of society is essential, and ancient India’s Vedic *varnashram* system serves as a blueprint for the work at hand.

## Chanakya’s Maxims: Politicians and Their Qualities

Adopted From The Sanskrit

1\. In the happiness of the people lies the politician's happiness. Their welfare is his welfare. A politician should not consider what pleasures and benefits can be derived for himself. A politician should only consider what will be pleasing and beneficial for the people.

2\. Many politicians have been destroyed who were controlled by lust, anger, greed, infatuation, arrogance and envy.

3\. A mad elephant tramples everything in its path. Likewise is the potitician who is devoid of proper learning about the goal of life and advised by unwise councel.

4\. A politician, disciplined by spiritual knowledge, will be interested in disciplining his people. Being devoted to the welfare of all beings his state will thrive and prosper.

5\. Because of cooperation from his supporters a successful politician accomplishes all that he sets out to achieve. A potitician without the support of the people meets with utter failure and frustration.

6\. The worst politician is he whose character is untrustworthy. He can neither help himself or his people.

7\. The role of the perfect politician is to always work for the benefit of all living beings. This is also to include the birds, beasts and even trees and creepers.

8\. A politician who performs his duty properly and protects the citizens surely goes to heaven. One who neglects his duty and cheats the citizen will have to stay in this world and suffer the reaction.

9\. One who has no knowledge of the difference between matter and spirit should not cheat himself and others by posing as a politician.

10\. A politician should introduce righteous activities within the state, like chanting of the holy names of God. A politician should never support unrighteous activities like the opening of slaughterhouses.

Chanakya Pandit, whose writings are renowned throughout India, lived during the 3rd century B.C.. During the reign of King Chandra Gupta, the saintly Chanakya served as an adviser to the king. Chanakya's deep learning and realization of the Veda have made him immortal in the minds of men as one of the greatest wise men ever to have lived.

The uniqueness of the Maxims of Chanakya is that all though this wisdom was spoken over two-thousand years ago in an age with a culture long past, the essence of the truths of Chanakya are still relevant in our modern civilization.

## Chanelling - Doshas or Demons?

By David Frawley

Channeling has become a very widespread phenomena in this country. For many it is becoming the preferred source of spiritual knowledge. As an explaining mechanism, some hold that nearly all scriptural, prophetic, or revealed knowledge is essentially "channeled." It is appropriate, then to inquire about the role and status of channeling in yoga and Ayurveda.

Channeling was well known in ancient India and China and occasionally mentioned in their literature. These literatures suggest that we may allow other entities, either the disincarnate or beings in subtle worlds, to work through us in various ways, for good or ill. One Upanishad tells of people going to visit a woman possessed by such a being to obtain knowledge. More often, however, channeling was looked upon as a very doubtful activity, or simply ignored. As yogis developed their own direct perception of truth, channeled information became less important. Since the tradition focuses on developing self-realization, it tends to be critical of practices which culminate in a loss of consciousness or personal control.

General "channeled" experiences were classified by both Hindus and Buddhists as being vikalpa or false imagination. Such phenomena were thought to be caused by the yogic energy (kundalini) moving out of the space of personal awareness. Impurities that work through peripheral channels into the outlying astral worlds are proposed as the mechanism of vikalpa. Such phenomena are counted among meditative disorders. Buddhist scriptures such as the Sdurangama contain long lists of entities and visions which one may encounter along the path, and recommend merging them back into one's own mind and not following them in any way.

By way of contrast, Ayurveda classifies much of channeling-like experience under various types of possession. A whole series of psycho-physical disorders caused by possession are traced to the activity of various entities. Included among sources of possession are ghosts and other lower entities, lesser celestials, demigods, and gandharvas. Such beings may possess humans for purposes of play. They often impart certain knowledge or display unusual creative or psychic abilities in the beings they inhabit. While their hosts may find them inspiring, or may even acquire genius or other psychic gifts from them, yoga maintains that any form of possession involves some weakening of the grip of the soul through a disruption in the vibratory field of the astral body or aura.

There are, in addition, a whole series of negative beings endowed with the powers of darkness called asuras or rakshasas. These entities are said to often take the form of spiritual teachers or "holy men" in order to get access to the human consciousness. In the great epic The Ramayana, the demon Ravana is able to take Rama's wife Sita when he appears to her in the form of a brahman priest. Such beings appear as false teachers using spiritual truth for their own aggrandizement. They may also appear as false inner guides. In this form, their powers may range from creating mild disturbance to promoting evil in historic proportions.

In the traditions of yoga, the mere display of occult power or mimicry of spiritual wisdom does not automatically confer trust on such entities. Their capacity to lie, trick, cause irrational ideation, and provoke with false imagination must always be cause for prudence and caution.

Generally, vata (air) types of persons will express an affinity to become channelers, though channeling generally aggravates vata. Jane Roberts, for example, who popularized channeling with her series of "Seth" books, also succumbed to rheumatoid arthritis, a vata disorder, at age 57. According to Ayurveda, channeling-like activities may result in damage to the nervous system when done for a prolonged period or, as with other practices, when performed in an addictive manner. In the yoga teachings, the astral weakening may affect one's personal karma and predispose its reincarnated subject to a major nervous disorder or congenital defect.

Some kapha (water) types may also be inclined to the practice of channeling. Attributes of greater stamina and endurance may complement this inclination. The ability of the kapha type to receive impressions and passively absorb them shows an obvious relation to these activities. Persons with pitta (fire) constitutions, on the other hand, tend to have attributes of pride and personal control and are less likely to yield to the presence of a channeled entity.

Frequently, the types of beings channeled reflect the constitution of the channeler. Kapha types may be likely to channel loving, kind, or gentle entities from their higher nature; from their lower nature, however, may come those entities dominated by greed and lust. Pitta types would be inclined to powerful, critical, and perceptive beings. Vata types may more often manifest erratic, stimulating, but unstable forces.

The yogic experience with channeling-like states of consciousness is not entirely negative. Some yogis have used astral beings as helpers and allies. Certain types of knowledge or capability could be facilitated by these beings. Yogananda relates a story of one such being who was subdued and used by a yogi after it had tricked him. However, we do not find much evidence of such entities being used as teachers or guides. Their general unreliability and limitations render them rather doubtful for such purposes.

Perhaps, for all their potential for benefit or entertainment, Ramana Maharishi's reminder about the matter of channeled entities serves as a good foundation for subsequent thought. It was his opinion that the attribute of a true guru was his ability to impart the techniques that would bring peace to his students; power, diversion, and even knowledge are of lesser importance.

In yoga, great emphasis is placed upon the unfolding of consciousness and self-realization. Its aim is to free the mind from all external illusions and influences (maya). Though the power derived from yoga may permit communication with other beings, the caution of yoga greatly favors being wary of such communications. This is especially true where such possessions are accompanied by a loss of personal consciousness or other effects which may reduce our ability to reflect and apply our active understanding to the task of gaining self-realization.

## Continence

The Case for Continence

As conscious beings we have the capacity to create life through our sexual energy. This is, of course, in a relative sense only. Creators we may be yet only as instruments, for on the macrocosmic scale, life’s origins can be traced to an ultimate spiritual cause. If we consider the origin of all life divine, it is natural to think of our own microcosmic part in creation as a sampling of the work of divinity. Therefore, it follows that the sexual fluids of procreation are an extremely valuable commodity.

The emergence of a new ethic, “the preservation of the planet,” has caused many to adopt the paradox of “freedom through restraint.” For example, recent legislation curtailing smoking in public suggests that people are becoming more conscious that the freedom to breathe fresh air requires that we refrain from smoking. Many of us now refrain from ingesting highly processed foods jam packed with preservatives that are good tasting but life taking. Similarly, it may be time to consider retaining the sexual fluids within us that are life giving. This will require tremendous restraint, yet may result in an unprecedented sense of freedom. Perhaps it is time to reconsider continence, a long-forgotten virtue of days gone by.

The concept of continence presented herein is not a wholesale advocacy of complete abstinence from sexual indulgence. Rather, it is a well-rounded approach to sexual freedom. The first wave of the sexual revolution promoted only a one-dimensional view of sexual expression—genitally-centered, orgasmic sexuality. The case for continence promotes a heightened regard for the sexual energy that lies within us. It draws attention to the multidimensional nature of sexual energy. Not only is our sexual energy the source of the highest sensual experience (its most limited aspect), but it is the source of procreation, optimum health, increased mental and intellectual capacity, and mystic experiences. Moreover, complete understanding of sexual energy leads to the ultimate spiritual experience.

Progress requires acceptance and elimination. Life is like a great ladder consisting of many steps. We have to be more concerned with reaching the top than with any particular step. At one point acceptance of a particular idea may constitute progress. Later that same idea may have to be eliminated in order that we remain progressive. To let go of the first step enables us to ascend on the ladder of life. Yet for many the ascent beyond one-dimensional sexuality may seem nearly impossible and perhaps unnecessary. I will raise some very practical points that show how, by changing some of our habits and the way we think of ourselves, continence (the impossible) becomes plausible. I will also discuss the advantages of embracing continence, either in relationship with our life’s partner or as a single person, for continence can help us in our progress in the physical, intellectual, and spiritual dimensions.

The gross sexual urge is both natural and formidable. The urge is so strong that we seldom entertain the thought of curtailing it. Yet in keeping in harmony with nature there are several points to consider. Although it is obviously true that the sexual urge is natural, the extent to which we are one-dimensionally absorbed with it is unnatural. Bypassing the broader scope of the emotional need for relationship and dealing only with the gross act of sex itself, it is apparent that we *can* live without it. In comparison, other natural biological needs, such as eating and evacuating, can never be given up. By nature’s arrangement, there is no scope for sexual indulgence during childhood or old age.

There are cycles for all species during which the sexual urge heats up, and it is at this time that the female is most fertile. By nature’s arrangement, sex and reproduction go hand in hand. In consideration of this, contraception, an invention of humanity, appears rather unnatural. We proclaim ourselves animals of reason. But it is questionable just how rational an animal we really are, when sexual indulgence outside of procreation seems to be our norm. Of course, animals also indulge in masturbation, and other sexual acts outside of procreation (although rarely). But they are, after all, animals without reason. Reason dictates that our sexual preoccupation is unnatural. Although it may *feel* natural enough, such feelings may be largely prompted by external influences.

Although Freudian psychology attempted to present a nonmechanistic explanation of the sexual urge, its explanation grossly neglects certain physical considerations. If we examine some physical causes for sexual desire, we will find a natural way of decreasing gross sexual activity. For example, there is considerable evidence to support the idea that diet influences sexual desire. The diet that people keep is often unnatural—determined by the demands of the fastidious tongue rather than nutrition.

In *The Better Way,* Issac Newton makes the following statement: “They who have ever carefully noted the effects on themselves of most kinds of alcoholic stimulants, of coffee, oysters, eggs, spices, and excess of animal food of most any kind . . . cannot surely with justice charge upon ‘nature’ the exuberance of their amatory desires.”

Many civilizations of the past, such as the Orphics, Pythagoreans, Essenes, Gnostics, neo-Platonists, and Manichaeans, practiced continence with a view to achieve optimum health and spiritual regeneration. All of them held that for the practice of continence to be successful, one must maintain a vegetarian diet. Pythagorus, Plato, Aristotle, St. Theresa, St. Francis of Assisi, Spinoza, Newton, and later Gandhi and Tolstoy, to name a few, all practiced continence with the help of vegetarianism.

Today of course there are an increasing number of people becoming vegetarians. The arguments in support of this diet are overwhelming. They include medical, ethical, economical, and spiritual considerations. On all fronts the vegetarian movement is going forward, held off only by obstinacy and the need of a proper vehicle to make its ideals known everywhere. Vegetarianism is a giant step in the direction of world transformation. Such a vegetarian worldview could also provide impetus for a continent lifestyle to catch on.

Of all foods meat, and beef in particular, is the most potent aphrodisiac. Along with meat, fish and eggs produce a similar effect—sexual excitement. The testes, when well filled with sperm, stimulate the sexual sensory centers. The heads of the sperm consist chiefly of nucleoproteins. Foods rich in protein, when absorbed in the diet, influence the sperm to cause sexual excitement. Of course people accustomed to a diet consisting of these kinds of foods will not be able to identify them as the source of their sexual arousal. Yet if they refrain from meat eating for a short time, they will notice that their sex desire decreases.

A high protein diet of meat, fowl, fish, and eggs is also high in uric acid. Coffee, tea, and chocolate also contain uric acid, as well as caffeine and other toxic alkaloids that are sexually stimulating. Caffeine increases the heartbeat, raises the blood pressure, and thus serves as an aphrodisiac, while uric acid causes inflammation of the genital mucus membrane that is the seat of sexual sensitivity. In women an acid-forming diet causes inflammation of the uterine mucus membrane and tends to promote the occurrence of leucorrhea and increased menstruation.

Tobacco is another powerful aphrodisiac. Men who work in tobacco factories often experience increased nocturnal emissions. This is the result of tobacco’s irritating effect on the genital mucous membrane. Tobacco can also create havoc in the female reproductive system, producing sterility and cancer of these organs.

All the above-mentioned stimulants have a strong influence on the blood. Toxic blood caused by stimulants coupled with the toxic effect of poorly digested food irritates the nervous system and especially the extremely delicate nerves that govern reproduction. Through the nervous system, with the help of the brain, passions are aroused.

Adopting a vegetarian diet and eating alkaline rather than acid producing foods will counteract uric acid formation and reduce sexual inclinations. The secret to sexual control for men lies in maintaining the blood and urine in as alkaline a state as possible so as not to irritate the sexual centers in the mucus lining of the prostatic utricle. This state is best achieved through a low protein diet. Vegetables that contain large quantities of fiber and water, such as cabbage, turnips, beets, and carrots, and fruits like melons are helpful in this connection. Potatoes are very alkaline and among grains rice is lowest in uric acid content. In general, a low protein diet is the best diet for pursuing continence.

Thus by the mere changing of our diet we may find that the impossible becomes plausible. We have to remember that most Americans thrive on meat, fish, and eggs, and between meals pay considerable attention to other stimulants, such as coffee, tea, and cigarettes. Along with our sexually stimulating habits, we are constantly bombarded with sexually explicit advertising, in which men and women are often depicted as nothing more than sexual objects. Sex is on our minds, to say the least. Naturally, the average person will cringe at the thought of sexual abstinence, but have they stopped to consider the fact that they are practically *living* on sexual stimulants?

A healthier diet and freedom from smoking and intoxication are positive in of themselves and are also integral parts of a continent lifestyle, yet there are still other positive benefits that result from recycling our sexual energy. Hearing about these benefits makes continence even more plausible. While improving our overall health, continence may also be a solution to major social dilemmas that threaten humanity. A continent lifestyle also aids intellectual growth and contributes indirectly to spiritual development, without which true continence is not possible.

In light of continence and the emerging ethic of planetary preservation, there are several modern day dilemmas worth mentioning. The AIDS epidemic, the threat of overpopulation, and the seemingly endless debate surrounding abortion are all issues that could be practically solved by continence.

While I write, the headline in the San Francisco *Chronicle* reads, “AIDS State of Emergency Sought.” If there is a state of emergency, we should be prepared to consider any positive proposal aimed at bringing about a solution. A public education program is already in place with government funding. This is the most complete remedy at hand. Education generally takes precedence as the optimum long-range solution to any problem. I am suggesting this education focus on continence because over the centuries the ancients and the wise have extolled the virtues of a continent lifestyle. Courses on continence would revolutionize our present one-dimensional sex education. The present program has no scope for penetrating to a deeper understanding of the nature of our sexuality. Such limited, one-dimensional education may prove to be counterproductive. To a large extent (through advocacy of contraception) it serves to *promote* genital, orgasmic sexuality, which, ironically, may lead to the breakdown of our overall health, including the immune system!

With the development of sexual energy in youth comes maturation, which includes physical maturation. Modern-day Western psychosexual theories consider only the physical body however. This model is a closed system, which doesn’t take into account the subtle body or consciousness. For example, this model suggests that periodic discharge of semen is necessary after one reaches maturity. On reaching maturity, in this model, there is no longer an internal need for the semen. Although this is a popular conception that promotes genital sex, it is by no means the unanimous opinion within the scientific community.

In another model, which considers higher realities, an alternative use for sexual energy arises. The popular Western model is in line with the “throw-away society” we live in. Our second model, a spiritual one, calls for a recycling of the sexual energy, which creates a greater balance in body ecology. This results in increased mental and physical vitality. In this model there is also scope for transmutation of sexual energy, which is necessary for higher psychic development.

Sexual fluids when retained increase overall vitality. Any male athlete is afraid of untimely nocturnal emission the night before a match. Sexual contact is often prohibited for women and men alike during athletic training. Overall, it is reasonable to propose that semen, which is instrumental in cell reproduction, when retained will serve to produce and generate vitality within.

Gandhi wrote, “The horror with which ancient literature regarded the fruitless loss of the vital fluid was not a superstition born of ignorance . . . Surely it is criminal for a man to allow his most precious possession to run to waste.”

Pythagoras, the founding father of geometry, taught that there was a direct connection between semen and the brain. He cautioned that the loss of semen weakens the brain, while its conservation serves to nourish it. This idea was also very prominent in ancient Indian society among the *rishis*. Pythagoras lived a century-long life and such longevity was common among generations of people who adhered to the Pythagorean doctrine. The *rishis* and yogis of India’s spiritual culture developed extraordinary mental powers and lived long and healthy lives.

In *Taoist Secrets of Love*, contemporary Taoist teacher Mantak Chia writes, “Because a single drop of semen houses such prodigious life energies, frequent loss of fluid depletes the body systems of their most precious nutrients and speeds the inevitable physical decline into old age. Retaining the seed within the body is the first step in reversing this cycle.” About brain nourishment, Omraam Mikhael Aivanhov writes in his *Sexual Force of the Winged Dragon*, “Men and women must use this \[sexual\] tension to feed and water the cells of their brains.”

Lecithin, an organic phosphorized fat, which is the chief constituent of both brain and nerve tissue, is an essential component of semen. The semen consists of a highly concentrated form of blood—the cream of the milk of blood. Besides containing lecithin, semen is rich in calcium, phosphorous, iron, vitamin E, and hormones. With the loss of semen comes the loss of lecithin from the blood and brain when new semen needs to be produced. Conservation of semen through continence leads naturally to increased brain nutrition and increased intellectual energy.

Monastic spiritual culture often involves years of study of philosophy, which requires nourishing the pituitary and pineal glands. The pineal gland is richer in lecithin than any other part of the body. Continence preserves lecithin, which is then used by the body to nourish the pineal glands. Thus it is understandable why religious orders often recommend continence for those who wish to live a life of spiritual practice.

Scientific studies on senility conducted a century past by the father of endocrinology, Dr. Brown-Sequard, lend support to the theories of the *rishis* who maintained that retaining vital fluids increases longevity and improves overall health. Professor Brown-Sequard was a prominent physiologist well known for his research work at Harvard. His interest in senility found him engaged in various experiments. These experiments showed a connection between senility and a deficiency of internal secretions from the reproductive glands. Excessive sexual activity can greatly diminish the supply of sperm, which otherwise would be internally secreted. The internal secretions are reabsorbed into the blood and, after passing through the bloodstream, accumulate chiefly in the tissue of the central nervous system. This in turn nourishes the brain. These secretions seem to have a selective affinity for the tissue of the central nervous system based on their similarity in chemical composition, both being rich in phosphates and lecithin. Indeed, no two constituents of the body are so remarkably similar in composition than the sperm and tissue of the central nervous system.

Although he did not discover the cure for senility, which results from the autointoxication of the entire endocrine system and not merely the gonads, Brown-Sequard’s work is important and relevant to our discussion. His experiments, in which he found that hormonal injections prepared from the tissue of animals had amazing regenerative effects, serve to substantiate the theories of wise men of the past: that the sexual fluid, the source of regeneration, can if retained increase vitality, including mental powers. His conclusions were verified much later by several research doctors, one of whom, Dr. K. S. Guthrie, in his work *Regeneration* remarked: “But if the human sperma is as good if not better \[than animals\], why should not each man preserve his own, instead of wasting this and then procuring other by repulsive and brutal means? . . . Should man inject into himself the testicular secretions of animals when he could preserve his own and keep his body continually at the highest point of vitality?”

Optimum health, increased mental and intellectual power, a solution to overpopulation and venereal disease, and instilling humanity with an increased sense of reverence for the process of creation are all compelling reasons for moving in the direction of a continent lifestyle. But most compelling is the way in which continence assists in the development of spiritual consciousness. To find the spiritual source of our sexual energy will be the most we can do for ourselves and our planet.

The mystics of both East and West have been practitioners of continence for centuries. The East, however, has provided us with more information as to how the sexual energy when controlled and transformed can produce mystical experience.

The Eastern idea of continence is known as *brahmacarya.* It is mandatory for student life within the *ashram* (living place of the guru). Those who leave student life for marriage on the advice of their guide also live a continent life, engaging in sex only for procreation rather than sensual pleasure. Those who forego marriage throughout life accept the renounced order of *sannyasa* on completing their student life, as do those in married life after their children leave home. It is generally in the renounced order, after many years of spiritual practice, that the heightened effects of continent life begin to show themselves as the fruits of dedication in the form of *brahma tejas*, spiritual power.

Uninformed persons are more or less controlled by their sexual energy and thus they remain within the world of sensual experience. Others by controlling the same gross sexual energy can, at will, produce good progeny and keep optimum health and sound mind. The *sannyasin*, however, masters the sexual energy at the subtle level. *Sannyasis* are also thereby free from the subtle forms of worldly sexual involvement such as the desires for distinction, adoration, and profit. They are free from these desires because they are self-satisfied due to experiencing their higher nature. The real *sannyasis* transform the coal of sexual sensuality into the diamond of self-realization. They live in the world, but are not of it. They have no greed, lust, or envy, which are all painful conditions that inhibit us from giving fully of ourselves to others.

*Ojas* is the subtle form of sexual energy*.* Stuart Sovatsky, author of *Tantric Celibacy*, describes *ojas* as “a powerful alchemical distillate of the hormones of sexual motivation.” It develops in the body as sexual energy is sublimated during a month-long bodily process. Food is transformed into blood and blood into bodily tissue, bodily tissue is then transformed into mental energy, or *ojas*. If sexual orgasm is indulged in more than once in thirty days, this bodily cycle is thrown off. Thus overharvesting of sexual fluid through frequent orgasm depletes *ojas*, while continence and meditation increase its supply. This energy creates a subtle force (*virya*) that enables one to work in wonderful ways sometimes unseen by the physical eye. The much higher spiritual experience of love of God involves tracing out the infinitely more subtle source of *ojas*. This is done through the culture of a willingness to be again controlled, this time by the source of conscious energy in a divine life, rather than by the material expression of sexual energy as we are in material life. This is an exercise of the inner heart, the transformation of lust into love and the death of the material ego. To come under the influence of the divine energy is to become forever free from the constraints of material illusion. It is the antithesis of illusory life in which we are *used by* the gross sexual energy as slaves of matter, while all the time thinking ourselves the master.

Although it is true that we are masters, it is more as caretakers. The “power” that we derive from dominating matter for our sensual titillation is illusory. It is better to be in harmony with the powers that be. We must rise above the false sense of power and proprietorship derived from material identification and sensuality to understand our proper connection with divinity.

There is much at stake in human life and it is important that we use our valuable human energy for the optimum result. Ultimately we are pleasure seekers by nature. There is pleasure in continence. The pleasure derived from using our sexual energy conscientiously for higher achievement does not involve taking from others under the guise of giving. Anyone who seriously considers the case for continence lays a foundation for ultimate happiness.

Human life is for more than sophisticated animality. We are the caretakers of our planet and its creatures. It is time we develop the courage to do this work, God’s work, and bring love and life to all creation. Seeing ourselves as part of an organic whole, we must adopt the thinking of, “What is in it for the whole?” and give up thinking, “What is in it for me?” The personal sacrifice involved in our evolution toward wholeness may seem very great, but it in no way can compare to the greatness of achieving the goal. The virtues of a continent lifestyle have been heralded for ages by some of the world’s greatest men and women—the kind our present world needs more of.

## Cookbooks - Reviews

"If one has a strong desire for meat, he may make an animal out of ghee and flour, and eat that. But never let him slay a living being for the sake of something to eat...." —*The Codes of Manu*

"And behold, I have given you every plant-yielding seed which is upon the face of all the Earth, and every tree with fruit; to you it shall be as meat...." —*The Holy Bible*

"All bodies subsist on food grains which are produced by rain. Rain is called forth by sacrifice. Sacrifice is the purpose of work." —*Bhagavad Gita*

With the increasing popularity of vegetarianism in the past few years there has been a corresponding rise in interest in Indian cooking, which survives as the world's oldest vegetarian culture. It is only natural that as the West becomes more interested in humane and healthy dietary lifestyles, that India's millennial-old traditions of cooking based on principles of compassion, nonviolence, and physical and mental hygiene will become increasingly popular. Besides that, the food tastes great!

I had the opportunity to cook in an ashram for several years. In the ashram kitchen we closely followed the tradition of ayurvedic Indian vegetarian cooking taught by our guru. I still have the opportunity upon occasion to cook for others, which I find tremendously satisfying. Struck by the richness of flavors created by using only fresh vegetables, grains, milk products, and a few spices, guests often ask, "Do you eat this way every day?", as if to say that food so good should be reserved for special occasions. But what I think they are tasting, besides clean food made with fresh ingredients, is the love and devotion that goes into the cooking. With the help of a few sound principles of cooking, a good list of raw ingredients, and maybe a good cookbook or two, every day can be a festive celebration in the kitchen that will overflow into every room of your house. Here's a few new cookbooks.

*Great Vegetarian Dishes* by Kurma dasa, Bhaktivedanta Book Trust, 1990. simply put, is a great vegetarian cookbook. Kurma das has given us a beautiful and well written cookbook full of exquisite recipes and full-color photographs. The photographs are an amazing feature of this book. You'll put on a few pounds just browsing through it!

In the first chapter he gives us a few simple recipes for such important ingredients as yogurt, curd cheese, ghee, and vegetable stocks. Then he sets before us page after page of mouth-watering delights. He describes over 200 recipes from every corner of the globe, like Bengali *pushpanna* rice, Gujarati yogurt soup, Italian *polenta*, *gado gado* salad from Indonesia, cheesecake, mango ice cream, and the king of desserts, *gulab jamuns* (deep-fried milk balls in rose syrup).

The balance of recipes is tipped a little in favor of ethnic Indian cuisines, but it’s easy to forgive Kurma das this indulgence when we remember that not only was cooking considered a fine art in the ancient Vedic culture of India, but served as a practical demonstration of the four goals of human life: religion, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. Cooking was seen as duty, support of family and clan, something to be enjoyed, and finally, offered to God, it became the door to salvation.

Kurma's book is not for the day-to-day, unless you're an emperor or perhaps an avatar. Opulent and exotic dishes fill the book, making it wonderful for festivals, special occasions, and holiday cooking. Want to convert your family to vegetarianism? This Thanksgiving take one recipe from each of Kurma's chapters: one rice dish, one soup, one vegetable main dish, a chutney or two, a couple of savories, a nice salad, a couple of his fantastic desserts, and one of his marvelous drinks, and your relatives may never go home. (Then again, maybe that's not such a good idea after all!)

*The Ayurvedic Cookbook* *by Amadea Morningstar and Urmila Desai, Lotus Press, 1990, $16.95.*

This is much more than a cookbook. It is an ayurvedic text on health as well. The first chapter goes into the subject of ayurvedic nutrition in some depth. The authors describe the concepts of the doshas (*vata, pitta and kapha*) and *rasa* (taste) in ayurveda. They help us to define our constitutional type and explain the effects that the different *rasas* have on our health. Areas that have been glossed over in other ayurvedic books are given thorough treatment, including a description of the workings of the fire of digestion, the *chakras* as they relate to diet, and dietary regime. Seasonal changes in diet are also described. I especially enjoyed this well-written and informative section of the book.

Next the authors enter into the actual recipes themselves. What makes this book different from other cookbooks is not an emphasis on cooking for variety in the kitchen, but cooking for health. Each recipe is coded for the seasons and how it affects the doshas, so that at a glance you can see how a given recipe is going to affect yourself and those you cook for.

Most of the recipes are vegetable dishes and are cooked the same way. The slight variations of spice and combinations of vegetables is authentic to Indian cooking. Whenever someone asks me how I cooked a particular preparation, I almost always tell them that I cook everything the same way. In a wok or large skillet, heat ghee, add spices, as soon as the seeds start to pop add the ingredients and some water or other fluids, cover, and cook. This is the basic formula for Indian cooking and is followed in three-quarters of the recipes in this book.

Page after page of marvelous recipes follow. Not exclusively Indian, there are some Mexican recipes and some non-traditional vegetarian foods like tofu and soy milk find their way into here as well. The recipes are all simple, healthy, and pleasant. In fact, simplicity stands out as a hallmark of these recipes. From that viewpoint alone, anyone interested in authentic Indian cooking will really enjoy this book.

The one major fault of*The Ayurvedic Cookbook,* however, is its inclusion of eggs in the recipes. Eggs are not a part of the traditional diet of India. For reasons of cleanliness and compassion, the *Bhagavad Gita,* the *Atharva Veda*, and other ancient texts forbid the eating of any food composed of blood and semina. The civilized people of India have only been introduced to egg-eating recently, by the British. Unfortunately, this unhygienic dietary habit is now widespread in India due to the strength of the Western medical presence on the sub-continent.

Aside from this, with a working knowledge of the principles learned in a thorough study of this book, a person could adopt the ayurvedic diet completely. For those less committed, it’s still a wonderful vegetarian cookbook that transcends both East and West.

*Amazing Grains by Joanne Saltzman, H. J. Kramer Inc. 1990, $12.95.*

Neither is *Amazing Grains* an ordinary cookbook. Joanne Saltzman, founder of the School of Natural Cookery and great fan of whole grains, has presented us with a simple guide to the preparation of whole grains as side dishes, main courses, salads, and desserts. She has done this in a clever and instructive manner. First she teaches us about the different grains available to us, then describes how they can be prepared. She then gives the recipes and accompaniments to the grain dishes like sauces and marinades. The way in which she presents the simple recipes for this simple food is such that we see how the recipe was formulated and how it can be varied upon. She suggests alternatives in each recipe so that a relatively small number of recipes become the springboard for all kinds of creative cookery with grains.

Here's a nice meal for Autumn entertaining: savory Cantonese fried rice is a simple but satisfying preparation; the sweet potato halva serves as a nice, warm, and filling dish perfect as the nights begin to cool down; and the salad is light and a little astringent, while the pineapple and coconut punch serves as both a beverage and a dessert. If you’re watching your weight, replace the Sweet Potato Halva with a baked potato or green salad and eat less. Enjoy!

Savory Cantonese Fried Rice  
(from *Great Vegetarian Dishes*)

Preparation time: 30 minutes

4 tablespoons sesame oil

1 teaspoon minced fresh ginger

1/2 teaspoon asafoetida powder

1 small carrot julienne cut

1/4 cup finely slivered celery

1/4 cup finely diced cabbage

1/4 cup unpeeled cucumber cut matchstick size

2 tablespoons bamboo shoots cut matchstick size

2 tablespoons diced red peppers

1/4 cup cooked green peas

1/4 cup mung bean shoots

1/4 cup crumbled firm tofu

3 tablespoons soy sauce

2 teaspoons Chinese chili oil

1 teaspoon salt

1/4 teaspoon black pepper

2 cups long grain rice cooked without salt chilled over night

Heat 1 tablespoon of the sesame oil in a wok over moderate heat. Saute the minced ginger for one minute. Add the asafoetida, and increase the heat to full. Add the carrots, celery, and cabbage and saute for another 2 or 3 minutes. Add the cucumber, bamboo shoots, red peppers, green peas, and bean shoots, and saute for one minute; then add the tofu, soy sauce, chili oil, salt, and pepper. Saute for one minute.

Empty the contents of the wok into a bowl, cover with a lid, and rinse the wok.

Heat the wok until dry and hot, add the remaining sesame oil, and saute the chilled rice over full heat. Add the vegetables and serve immediately.

Sweet Potato Halva  
(from *The Ayurvedic Cookbook*)

Preparation time: 1 hour (most of it unattended)

5 cups grated sweet potato (3 or 4 large sweet potatoes)

4 cups whole milk

1 cup raisins

1 cup blanched almonds or pecans

8 or 9 tablespoons of ghee

2 teaspoons ground cardamom

1/4 teaspoon saffron

Preheat oven to 400 degrees.

Grind nuts into a powder. Wash and grate sweet potatoes and saute in half of the ghee just enough to coat it. Stir in the milk and raisins.

Spread a little ghee on a covered 8"x 8" baking dish or iron skillet and transfer the mixture to it. Cover and bake for 40 to 55 minutes or until all of the milk is absorbed. If you need to, uncover the dish for the last 10 minutes to allow the milk to dry.

When all of the milk is absorbed, stir in the rest of the ghee, nuts, cardamom and saffron. Press into a flattened shape. Add sweetener as desired.

Quinoa Salad With Grapes and Roasted Cashews

(from *Amazing Grains*)

3 tablespoons raspberry vinegar

1 1/2 tablespoons mirin

1/4 teaspoon sea salt

3 teaspoons dill

1 or 2 celery ribs diagonally sliced

3/4 cup red seedless grapes cut in half

3 cups cooked quinoa, well drained

1/2 cup tamari roasted cashew nuts

In a large bowl mix in all the ingredients one at a time in order. Let marinate for one hour, serve chilled.

Pineapple and Coconut Punch  
(from *Great Vegetarian Dishes)*

2 cups canned coconut milk

4 cups chilled unsweetened pineapple juice, fresh if possible

2 tablespoons raw sugar

1 cup crushed ice

1/4 teaspoon coconut essence

Blend the coconut milk, pineapple juice, sugar, and ice in a blender at high speed until very smooth.

Strain the mixture through a fine sieve into a clean bowl and add coconut essence.

Chill and serve in chilled glasses.

## Cruelty Free Products

by P.J. Birosik

Spiritual India has has always been opposed to cruelty to any living creature. Today most people are as well. Yet in today’s world the average consumer, unwittingly, is often implicated in some of the most extreme forms of animal cruelty. The average person, while engaged in basic bodily upkeep and body beautification (we’re not all rishis, and ashes and matted locks are little difficult to relate to), uses “medically approved” products that have been tested on animals, or that include animal products as ingredients. With good packaging and advertising, why would one think to stop and read the label? Think again! Read the label! More than that, investigate the entire process involved in bringing the product to the shelf; lest you be out of sink with at least the world view of the saints of yore, one that envisioned a balance in nature and a compassionate consumer.

As Mark Egide, President of Genesis Inc. says: "In the '90s it will be hip to be aware—aware of the planet we inhabit. This awareness will touch many things. . . including kindness to animals, because after all, its their planet too."

Consumers have already created a huge demand for top quality, reasonably priced, all-natural health and beauty products. Now this holistic consciousness is extending to products and items that are tested without cruelty to animals. This is due in part to recent media coverage of industry practices and the efforts of many professional organizations demanding the elimination of inhumane research methods.

This article serves as a round-up and exciting introduction to some of the cruelty-free products available today. Tested by a two-man, two-woman panel, as well as myself, these items were selected for their superior performance, natural ingredients, responsible packaging/disclosure, long shelf-life and overall quality. At the end of this piece is a list of organizations and corporations that offer useful information regarding animal testing and other pertinent information.

A forerunner in this area is Rachel Perry, Inc. whose titular Founder refused to do animal testing ''from day one.'' For almost 20 years, her Natural Skin Care System and other items in her 105-product line have been considered some of the very best available, rivaling the most expensive department store lines in terms of product quality and packaging.

Both male and female members of the test team unanimously praise Perry products, citing the ''delicious" natural fragrance in such products as Sea Kelp Herbal Facial Scrub (the first Rachel Perry product, and its still my favorite), Violet Rose Skin Toner, and Spearmint Leaf Revitalizing Body Wash. Using the suggestions in Perry's book, *"Reverse the Aging Process of Your Face,"* the team and myself strictly followed a cleansing regime for a week. The result? Amazingly smooth, supple and younger-looking skin with less visible surface wrinkles.

High marks go to the pairing of the creamy, lubricating French Massage Formula, which aids in the breakdown of unsightly cellulite, and Spearmint Leaf Body Scrub. The latter's mildly granulated texture exfoliates the dermis, leaving one's body gleaming and extremely clean. For a milder but just as effective cleanser, Aloe Vera All-over Body Wash is an acceptable soap substitute.

Rachel Perry has an extensive line of creams specifically pH- balanced for numerous skin types; all have distinctive, natural scents and superior absorption rates. The eight-piece Trial & Traveler Kit offers an excellent introduction to many Perry products in a handy zipper case.

Aubrey Hampton's innovative Aubrey Organics has been introducing unusually effective, all-natural beauty products for 21 years, such as the brand new 'Out of the Leaf Aloe Vera Fillet.' "Pretty is as pretty does"reads the ad. This paper thin slice of a real aloe vera plant (plus a little of Aubrey's natural preservative with grapefruit seed extract and vitamins A,C and E) may not look like the usual cream, ointment or lotion, but it sure works to cool, soothe and refresh one's face and neck. It's also good for kitchen burns. Remember to store it in the fridge!

While we couldn't sample all the 100+ products in the line, the special blend of Chinese herbals for hair and skin care in its Mandarin Magic products did impress all test team members. Exotic ingredients such as "earth smoke, " morus root bark and ginkgo biloba leaf are combined with ginseng root, chrysanthemum and angelica flowers, and other ingredients to "create products. . .that are in balance—in harmony with the earth, with ourselves, with all nature,"

The shampoo has a gel-like consistency and is very concentrated, while the hair-moisturizing jelly is applied to towel-dried hair and left on for extra conditioning and easier styling. Having avoided most mousses and gels, I was pleasantly surprised that the jelly did not weigh down my long hair; instead, it added shine, increased comb-ability, and reduced fly-away strands.

The Mandarin Orange-Cucumber facial cleanser smells delicious and has a light, milky consistency that does not leave a soap film or make skin feel dry or itchy. Instead, the pure natural cream base with aloe vera gel leaves skin clean and soft. When followed by the brand new Mandarin Magic Moisturizer, skin remains supple and moist for hours.

Aura Cacia has relied on the benefits of aromatherapy to make their line of massage oils, mineral baths and bath soaps "a joy to give, a pleasure to use" since 1981. They emphasize the use of true botanical fragrances rather than the common synthetic scents that "dominate even the natural foods industry." One percent of the Company's sales on the little green oval - Aromatherapy Bath Soap - goes to Rainforest Action Network. In addition, one percent of the profits are donated to "One percent for Peace."

Packed in air-tight pouches, the 3 ounce size of Sand Castle Mineral Baths last for three full, luxurious baths and are safe for whirlpool equipment. My jacuzzi smelled wonderful, and after adding a packet to the non-chlorinated tub water, the water was much softer. Other testers enjoyed the thick lather and long-lasting scent of the cocoa butter Bath Soaps, as well as the follow-up Massage Oil, which blends essential oils with almond and vitamin E oils, and can be easily diluted for quick absorption.

Earth Science believes there is no such thing as problem skin, only skin out of balance with nature. Their broad line of skin and hair care products is eco-friendly. They use no heavy metals or toxins in any products or processes. They have created a manufacturing process that does not discharge chemical waste. They use only recyclable plastics, and even shred their "junk mail" to use instead of Styrofoam packing peanuts for shipping.

These products are all formulated without soaps, animal products, mineral oil, artificial colors, petroleum products, formaldehyde or other possible irritants.

Earth Science's Herbal Plasma Skin Rejuvenating Mist is an ultra-pure herbal extract blend that immediately freshens, cools and calms the skin; it's permanently stationed by my computer, so I can just close my eyes and spray whenever I need a quick lift. The bright blue Azulene Desensitizing Eye Cream is not only fun to apply, but is also a very concentrated wrinkle-fighting formula.

Virtually all commercial and some "natural" toothpastes utilize ground animal bone, sand, stone or chalk to facilitate cleansing; these harsh abrasives can wear away delicate tooth enamel. Also, fluoridated tooth-pastes are under attack from the National Toxicology Program which released a report earlier this year, linking fluoride and a rare bone cancer. So, is it back to baking soda for clean teeth and fresh breath?

Peelu Products offers a safer, all natural alternative. For centuries, Third World peoples have chewed branches of the peelu tree as a remedy for bleeding gums, sensitive teeth, and to clean and whiten teeth; resins in the plant matter cover the teeth in a protective coating. Now available in extract, tooth powder, toothpaste and authentic chewing stick forms, Peelu is available to everyone. The taste is naturally mild, no artificial flavors, colors or sweeteners are included.

Auromere has been introducing the finest Ayurvedic products to the U.S. for fifteen years through its popular Auromere Pure Herbal Toothpaste, Chandrika Ayurveda Soap and Ayurvedic Massage and Sports Oils. Now the Company is introducing a new Herbal Toothpaste, one that features both Neem and Peelu, in combination with twenty-four cold-extracted (more potent than boiling) herbal extracts for optimum care of teeth and gums. Its natural licorice flavor is not heightened with saccharin or refined sweeteners, harsh chemicals or abrasives.

An interesting note: Auromere is wholly owned and operated by sadahkas of the Atmaniketan Ashram, a non-profit spiritual community dedicated to the practice of Sri Aurobindo's yoga of integral perfection.

Owned and run by vegetarians, Beauty without Cruelty has been creating elegantly packaged products for the worldwide market for twenty-seven years; now Genesis Inc. has brought the English-based line to the U.S. . Drug stores and supermarkets will not be offered the BWC line, so ask your natural food and specialty retailer for it. BWC also has national make-up artists touring the nation to demonstrate products and present in-store clinics. Most products are fragrance-free, a rarity in this market. Harmlessly obtained substances such as beeswax and lanolin derivatives from wool are employed in a few products, according to BWC, so read labels.

The cosmetics line for women is extensive: eye colors come in pressed shadows, pencils, crayons and sticks; face powders choices include loose and pressed; lip liners, sticks and glosses coordinate with nail colors. I found the soft, creamy texture of the Eye Colour Crayon much preferable to the usual hard, dry points, while the water-based Make-up Base is suitably sheer and contains avocado oil which helps moisturize skin.

BWC Skin Care uses a unique herbal formula, rich in vitamins and plant proteins, to provide necessary emollients and nourishment to skin. Both male and female test panelists reported good results from Purifying Clay and Rye Flour Mask, followed by Preventive Age Creme. BWC's oil-free Shampoo and Conditioner leave hair full and are environmentally safe. Incredibly useful is BWC's ingredient list, which not only demystifies ingredient names but also explains how each works. Did you know that ergocalciferol is just another name for vitamin D?

In an age of impurities, synthetics and pollutants, Aveda's natural aromatherapy cosmetics, hair and skin care products strive to balance the need for beauty with environmental concerns. To that end, the company recently opened a European-style spa complex in Wisconsin, with charming guest accommodations, an organic gourmet kitchen and more, on eighty acres of wooded grounds; the luxury retreat operates as a live-in or day-only spa. Aveda's product line is featured exclusively.

Owner Horst Rechelbacher began Aveda in 1978; last year it was one of several companies chosen to be an official sponsor of Earth Day 1990. His book, *Rejuvenation*  is a practical wellness and beauty guide for men and women. The company donates a percentage of its proceeds towards a national tree planting campaign, and has implemented a national recycling program through its product distributors.

Mainly available through salons, the products include the first Aromatherapy Lip Colour with breath-freshing essential oils in a completely natural base with a wide variety of colors that glide on moist, stay moist and do not feather; a patented Aromatherapy Permanent Wave that replaces high levels of chemicals with pure flower and plant essences to add curl and body without stripping away shine or softness; and gently cleansing, nourishing shampoos, clarifying gels, conditioners and revitalizers for hair. With approximately one hundred products available, what's next?—New technology in hair coloring.

Nature's Gate is a familiar name in most health food stores; their extensive line of products for hair, facial, body, oral and pet care are all environmentally sound, cruelty-free, "pure and uncompromising," produced with no animal by-products. I have tried most of their shampoos/ conditioners, and found each formula to naturally cleanse, nourish and beautify hair and scalp. Favorites include the Original Herbal Shampoo, a unique blend of ten herbal extracts; the luscious-smelling Rainwater Awapuhi Conditioner which uses Hawaiian ginger flower extract in a special body-building formula that add thickness to hair; and Rainwater Tea Tree Oil Shampoo for herbal non-medicated dandruff control.

In toothcare, the Company introduces three new flavors: wintergreen. mint and cherry- to its line of popular cream pastes. Also, Nature's Gate Herbal Moisturizing Lotion has a new formula with PABA-free natural sunscreen to shield skin from harmful UVA and UVB rays in a lush, moisture rich formula. Skin Therapy for dry, chapped or cracked skin is a heavy duty moisturizing lotion with golden seal, calendula, aloe vera, comfrey and other soothing, oil-based ingredients that are organic and pH-balanced for fast acting results.

Reviva Labs was started by one of the first licensed aesteticians in the U. S., and asserts itself as a leading innovator in skin care product development. Its new seven-product Hawaiian seaweed line utilizes natural negative ions to attract positive ions from the lower layer of skin cells, creating a new energy that results in fresher, brighter, younger-looking skin and hair. Seaweed is rich in vitamins, minerals and amino acids.

Natural Seaweed soap has a gentle scrub-action that leaves the body tingling fresh. The non-chemical Light Skin Peel has a peppery scent and uses crushed almonds to lift off dried skin cells. Reviva's Lipstick ingredients include: castor oil, a well-respected emollient and healing agent to help keep lips soft and smooth. A favored product among test team members is Ahhhloe Ice, a soothing message gel for sore muscles and joints which works better than more expensive drugstore balms, has no long lasting "medicine smell" and did not stain our clothes.

Let's not forget the animals themselves. . .Wow Bow Distributors is deeply committed to providing a healthy alternative towards a cruelty-free world by introducing "the best treat for your best friend" - a vegetarian dog biscuit! Jan's Wow Bow Health Biscuits are made from organically grown whole wheat flour, bulgur, cornmeal, fresh garlic and parsley, yeast, vegetable broth, without eggs if you prefer. Lovely to look at and smell, my parrot pronounces these a crunchy delight, even if they are marketed for dogs.

Many mail order services now offer all natural, cruelty-free products. Heartland Products requests that you "be kind to animals - don't wear them," and offers a line of non-leather shoes, cross trainers and boots for work and play. Ecco Bella offers their "catalog with a conscience" packed with cruelty-free products that do not contain animal or milk by-products. They have minimal impact on the environment, emphasize all-natural ingredients and recyclable packaging. In addition they donate twenty percent of the profits from the catalog to animal and environmental protection organizations.

Products include fragrances, household cleansers, pet care, cosmetics, personal care, aromatherapy, hair care, recycled paper products and natural gourmet foods. Also featured are useful and entertaining bits of information about product ingredients, EPA studies, even menu planning!

Vegan Street also offers a catalog of cruelty-free and environmentally safe products. Their products include: household products, natural cosmetics for both men and women, and recycled paper products for the home and office.

Other companies that manufacture cruelty-free products include: Bare Essentials, Larkspur, Rainbow, Jason and Sleepy Hollow Botanicals. Look for these products in your natural food stores.
