Within the Vedic tradition, the Vedas and the Upanisads and their corollaries such as the Puranas are considered much like law books in our present-day legal system. When two lawyers go to court they do so with a view to establish exactly what the law is in any given case. They both attempt to establish their case by citing from the standard books of law, as well as from those books which contain case histories of how the law was interpreted in similar instances. The Vedas and their corollaries can be compared law books case histories. Thus when we speak of the philosophical debates of Madhva we are discussing debates much like those that are held by lawyers today—or more accurately like those of scientists—due to the nature of the topics. They discussed reality and its nature in all states of perception, and each party theoretically was prepared, should he be defeated, to give up his previous conception, accepting the victor as his spiritual mentor.

Before writing his Vedanta Sutra commentary, Madhva travelled for several years. It was during this period that he realized that he should write a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita. Writing this, he decided to go to the Himalayas to pay his respects to Vedavyasa (said to be the original author of the Vedic literature who is still living in the Himalayas) and obtain from him his blessings for his new devotional philosophical system (sampradaya). Accompanied by his disciple Satya Tirtha he arrived at Badari and stayed at the Ananda ashram to prepare for the final part of the journey.

That night after presenting his Gita commentary as an offering to the deity, Madhva began to read the first line. Just then a celestial voice came from the deity asking Madhva to make a small correction. Where Madhva had written "I shall explain the meaning of the Gita according to my capacity" the deity interjected, "You can explain the full meaning, but you shall explain only a little in accordance with the capacity of your students to understand." Thus it was indicated that the unfolding of the fully theistic understanding of the Gita was to come through yet another great teacher at some future date.

Madhva then felt the desire to journey into the higher Himalayas to the hidden Badrinath, or place of Vyasa. He prepared for the journey by observing forty-eight days of fasting and silent meditation. Before his final departure he wrote to his disciples, "This place is holy. Vishnu is the supreme. My word is meant for the good of all. I leave to pay respects to Vyasa. I may or may not return. May God bless you." Ending his arduous journey, Madhva slowly moved to the sacred area where Vedavyasa was sitting surrounded by rishis. There, from the mouth of Vyasa, he received the blessings to write his commentary on the Vedanta Sutra. His mission accomplished, Madhva came back to the Ananda ashrama where Satya Tirtha took down Madhva's commentary and prepared for advance copies to be sent out.

Then, traveling towards the east, Madhva eventually came to the Godavari River (east-central India). There on the bank of the Godavari, at the town of Ganjam, he met a group of pandits and discussed philosophy. He defeated Buddhists, Jains, Charvakas and followers of Shankara. He converted the two great pandits, Sri Sobhana Bhatta and Sri Rama Sastri, who became his disciples and received the names Padmanabha Tirtha and Narahari Tirtha respectively. Accompanied by Sobhana Bhatta and other disciples he returned to Udupi, his spiritual position now undefeated and unchallenged. He initiated many devotees and convinced thousands of people to take shelter of his dvaita vada philosophy.

Udupi was to become the seat of Madhva's transcendental ontology of dvaita vada. It was in this town that one of the most significant events of his life occurred. While bathing in the sea Madhva noticed a merchant seaman in distress. High winds had made his approach to the shore hazardous and he had run aground on a sandbar. From the shore Madhva, waving his cloth, directed the sailor safely to shore. Upon arriving safely the captain felt greatly indebted to Madhva and expressed his desire to offer him a gift. Madhva consented and asked for a large piece of clay, the value of which was insignificant. But much to the astonishment of everyone, inside the clay was a large deity of Krishna. The news spread throughout Udupi and the deity was installed in the temple. Thus Madhva's school became firmly established in Udupi and to this day the deity is worshiped by the numerous followers of Madhvacharya.

Madhva then decided to visit Badrinath for the second time, no easy task even today. His travels met with much success and the reputation as a great scholar and devotee followed him wherever he went. Upon his return news of his influence came to Sringeri, the headquarters of the followers of Shankaracharya. Indeed the main topic in Sringeri was the increasing fame and influence of Madhvacarya. Padma Tirtha, the leader of the Sringeri ashrama, felt the necessity to meet the challenge thus he and Pundarika Puri came to Udupi to meet Madhva in a philosophical debate. Since Madhvacarya would never refuse any opportunity to discuss and prove the superiority of his philosophy, he consented.

The chosen text from which to debate was the Rig Veda. Pundarika Puri started to explain his view on the first hymn, but no sooner had he started when Madhva challenged him with questions that he was unable to answer. Padma Tirtha tried to save the situation, but he too became implicated in a humiliating defeat at the hands of Madhva.

That night, driven by envy, Padma Tirtha and his men stole Madhva's library consisting of many rare books. When the librarian reported this news to Madhva he started in immediate pursuit of the thieves catching up to Padma Tirtha's party about twenty miles southeast of Mangalore. As soon as Madhva reached there he sent a messenger to Jaya Simha, the ruling king of the area. The king in reply informed Madhva that the books had been given by Padma Tirtha as a gift on the full moon night, an ancient Vedic tradition.

Madhvacarya thus proceeded to meet the king in the town of Visnumangalam Tirtha. The procession was magnificent. Crowds of cheering people had gathered there to greet the attractive mendicant. Bands of musicians were playing melodious songs, brahmins were chanting Vedic mantras and many parties were singing the names of God. Madhvacarya walked through the center of town at a slow, majestic pace, his face beaming, his body effulgent. A garland of fragrant tulasi leaves was hanging from his neck all the way down to his knees. A beautiful pearl-white silk umbrella was held over his head, and great crowds were gathering on each side to have a glimpse of the renowned teacher.

As the procession continued the king came to greet him. He got down from his palanquin and bowed to the lotus feet of Madhvacarya. The king then proceeded on foot with Madhva until they reached the temple where a gorgeous reception was arranged in which the inhabitants of twenty-five villages had gathered together to welcome him. Madhva and the king entered the big hall and everyone sat down to listen to the recitation of Srimad Bhagavatam and Madhva's commentary. Among the listeners was the erudite pandit Trivikramacharya. Although he was ready to find fault and challenge Madhva, Madhva's explanations were so sharp and brilliant that there was no possibility of finding any fault with the discourse.

After recovering his library at Visnumangalam, Madhva departed and established his camp at Amaralaya. It was while delivering lectures on his commentary of the Vedanta Sutra that he was challenged by Trivikramacharya. During the time that Madhva's books had been stolen, Trivikrama had the opportunity to study the commentaries of Madhva and was thus at an advantage over everyone who had debated with him thus far. Furthermore, Trivikrama was so learned that it is said his command of Sanskrit enabled him to convey through explanation of any text any meaning that suited his purpose. However, after fifteen days Madhva finally defeated the pandit and Trivikrama became Madhva's disciple.

In due course Madhvacarya established eight temples in Udupi appointing eight of his principle disciples as head priests in charge of ancient deities. He lived for seventy-nine years and wrote thirty-seven books.

His philosophy at one point was thought by Western scholars to have been influenced by Christianity. Nothing could be further from the truth. Madhva has clearly supported his thesis with evidence from Vedic literature and his teachings can better be seen as a development in theistic thought from what was offered earlier by Ramanuja.

It is widely accepted that Madhva was an incarnation of the Hindu demigod Vayu, said to be in charge of controlling the wind. The idea that he descended for a particular mission and was thus greatly empowered to perform many uncommon deeds is offered as an explanation for the extraordinary events that surrounded his life. Uncommon feats of strength, flying in the sky, causing on two separate occasions plants to sprout from seeds by singing a particular melody (thus proving long ago that plants respond to music), eating four thousand bananas and one hundred pots of milk at one sitting, using small amounts of food to feed hundreds, meeting Vyasadeva at Badrinath, etc. are only a few of the wonderful feats of Madhvacarya. Many more have not been mentioned here. We have instead tried to emphasize his most outstanding contribution in the realm of philosophy and devotion, and even in this connection space will not allow us present in any detail his philosophical treatise of dvaita vada. Those who are inclined can study for themselves Madhva's in his treatise on the Vedanta Sutra. A comparative study of the Vedanta commentaries of Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva will prove very revealing for the sincere inquirer into the nature of the absolute truth as described in Vedic literature.

References:

1\. Kapoor, O. B. L., Philosophy and Religion of Sri Chaitanya, Munshiram Manoharlal Pub. 1977.

2\. Bhaktivedanta Swami, Chaitanya Charitamrita ( English translation and commentary), Bhaktivedanta Book Trust, Los Angeles, 1975.

3\. Sharma Phd., Reign of Realism in Indian Philosophy

4\. Sharma Phd., History of Dvaita Literature

5\. Sri Madhva Vijay

## Mantra and the Energetics of Sound

By David Frawley

Language is our medium of expression. We all depend upon it for most of what we do in life, whether in the ordinary or the spiritual life. Yet language is not a passive or objective medium. It has a certain form or bias to it relative to the culture that produces it. For this reason, it is not enough just to use words; we have to understand the nature and the limitations of the language in which they are cast. Otherwise, no matter what we may say, our language may distort it and cause it to have results other than what we may have intended.

There are two main factors in our usage of language: the first is the meaning of words; the second is their sound. Words have both an abstract meaning and an energetic sound quality. Generally, the meaning of words is determined by convention, not by sound. The sound is just a peg on which the meaning is placed. It is not the "b" sound that causes us to call a boat a boat, but the sense established by common usage. Similar sound patterns, like boat and boot, can refer to quite different things. The same sound patterns in different languages usually have very different meanings. The sound "go" in Chinese does not refer to what it does in English. On the other hand, different sound patterns in the same language may have the same meaning, like such synonyms as boat and ship. Normally, we are not conscious of any direct relationship between sound and sense. For this reason we have many languages in the world.

We learn the meaning of words through education and can look them up in the dictionary. While we find that some words have related roots that aid in determining their meaning, most of the time we have no way other than convention for knowing what a word may mean. We seldom look beyond what we are told words are supposed to signify.

Yet in the higher uses of speech we always strive for an integration of sound and sense. The most evident form of this is in poetry wherein such literary devices as rhyme, alliteration, or assonance are used to make the sound more appropriate and important; to allow sound to reflect and magnify the meaning of words. Most great writers and thinkers employ methods of connecting words both in sound and sense. Our higher intelligence naturally functions in this way as it tries to bring more power and creativity into our speech and to integrate the meanings we are trying to convey into an organized whole.

For language to have its best effect, it is not enough if the meanings are good; the words must flow and sound well together. Sentences with the same meaning can have quite a different effect upon the mind. We can compare such sentences that have similar meanings as, "The ship sailed into the shore," with "The boat blew into the bay." There is a proven aesthetic factor in language that cannot be dismissed.

If we examine the origins of language, we find that sound and sense become progressively related the further back we look. As our culture has become more complex and artificial, more out of harmony with nature, so has our language. Even in English, we have many related root sounds that reflect this earlier stage of language. The most evident are "st" sounds that reflect a root meaning "to stand, stop, or be still," all of which have an initial "st" sound. Note how many such words there are: to step (take a stand), to stare (to fix one's gaze), to stall, to be stagnant, a stake or a staff (things that stand), to be stiff, to get stuck, to be stupid (unable to move one's mind) and style (how our words stand together). The "st" sound even occurs in the middle of words, giving them their meaning, as in establish (to make stand) and system (how something stands together).

Such a language is much easier to learn and can be used to create much more subtlety in speech and expression. The further we trace our language back—in fact, as we trace all Indo—European languages back—the more they come to resemble Sanskrit, the ancient and spiritual language of India. Sanskrit has maintained this consistency of sound and sense through the preservation of its roots. For this reason, we often go back to such languages as Greek or Latin, which also have a greater etymological consistency, for creating new, meaningful terms in our language.

The great scriptures of the world are written in languages with a strong connection of sound and sense. In fact, the more we take language back in time, the more it moves toward mantra, scripture, or the Word of God as the probable origin of human speech. This reflects the ancient Hindu or Vedic view wherein language was envisioned by the seers in meditation from their union with the cosmic sound and Divine Mind. In terms of language, it is easier to speak of the development of human civilization as a progressive fall from the Word of God, not as a positive development.

Mantra is a yet more developed usage of language than poetry, where sounds take up and direct spiritual energies; wherein the word becomes a channel for the powers of consciousness. The Sanskrit language, the language of mantra, is based upon the right relationship between sound and sense. The entire language is poetic and spiritual. As such it can provide us with a foundation for reintegrating sound and sense and reestablishing a spiritual language, a language of truth— consciousness in the world. It best preserves the ancient spiritual language that we find intimated in the unity of all ancient languages.

One of the traditional paths of yoga is concerned with language, mantra, and the right use of sound. It is called *shabda brahma mantra yoga*, the mantra yoga of the Divine Word. Its most specific proponent was the great medieval Hindu writer Bhartrihari. This path often began with the learning of Sanskrit, even a spiritual study of grammar, and the writing of poetry, and moved into the use of mantra and meditation. Its basic proposition is that if we cannot integrate our language, we cannot integrate our minds. It sees that the key to integrating our minds is integrating sound and sense in the cosmic language of unity, where each thing becomes a symbol for the whole.

Sound does affect the mind, as we well know. The sound of the words must, therefore, affect us independently of their meaning. A true or spiritual language must keep the sound and meaning of words in harmony to maintain the right vibration in the mind. The effect of a word or statement may vary by its sound quality, though the meaning may be the same. The English word "peace" and the Sanskrit word "*shanti*" have the same meaning. But if we repeat them, we find that *shanti* has a much more peaceful effect upon the mind according to its sound quality. The "sh" sound is peaceful, quieting, and balancing. The word "peace," however, has a harsher "p" sound. Its connotation is more like someone asking for peace when being attacked, whereas *shanti* vibrates with the essence and enduring quality of tranquility. Sound thus creates meaning, and the energy of sound underlies our language, either supporting its conventional meanings or detracting from them.

The mantra Om can be defined in various ways; whole philosophical books have been written about it, but it can be used without knowing its meaning. The sound conveys and connotes these meanings to the subconscious mind, and gradually makes us aware of them: chant Om for several minutes, with attention and sensitivity, and observe its effect. It will be that of clearing, opening and calming, and directing the mind toward meditation.

Chant "*Om shanti*" for a period of time and then chant "Peace amen" for a similar period. Though the defined meanings are about the same, we will see, if we are not attached to one set of these words or the other, that *Om shanti* will have a more spiritualizing effect, will bring more peace, and will make us feel more balanced. This is simply owing to the more harmonious connection of sound and sense. Of course, if we are attached to the outer forms of words, then we will not be able to benefit from the vibrations of *Om shanti* because we will color it with our opinions rather than perceive its objective energetic quality.

It is our attachment to mere words that is responsible for most of the violence and evil that goes on in the world. We go to war to protect names and titles, or the boundaries and privileges they have been invested with. We want to preserve the name American, Communist, Christian, etc., and the power of those who identify with such names. But have we ever considered what the objective quality of these names is in terms of both sound and sense? The name, like a package, can be filled with anything. Names can be made into superficial and deceptive commodities. They can be filled with hate, prejudices, or self—interest —even the name of God can be spoken with such attitudes. The word God can be an excuse for projecting the prejudices of the individual or collective ego. Usually the name has become a way of masking the thing it is supposed to stand for so that we don't have to really deal with it. It allows us to even turn it into something else more comfortable for us and our prejudices. Often, as soon as we name something, we cease to see it. We all know of the word God, but do we ever stop and think as to the experiential reality it may be referring to? We can use it as casually as we would speak of weather or politics.

Hence, we must learn to reflect upon what we are energizing our words with; not just what their superficial meanings are supposed to be. The true meaning of words is not found in the dictionary, but in the intention with which we use them. This can be an intention to further truth, which is unity, or to establish barriers, which is ignorance. Words are the most basic weapons of war that serve to divide people. Without creating a division through name, we cannot look upon another as the enemy. We cannot kill another human being unless we have dehumanized them through a label by which they become something foreign, alien, or threatening.

We must consider if our words bring us into a real relationship with the thing they represent, or if they become a barrier to seeing the thing itself. To do this it is helpful to consider the sound quality of words and to reflect upon how our minds and their prejudices color our words. We must inquire into what is behind our words, rather than just following whatever unconscious or collective forces that might be mindlessly driving them.

Naturally, meaning is more important than sound quality in both words and thoughts. It’s more important that we speak the truth than that we speak poetically or mantrically. We only become shallow if we make sound more important to us than sense; that is, to make form more important than content. If we speak the truth, our words also will gain a certain refinement, a rhythm, and a clarity. Not only will we not shout, scream, or curse, we will not gravitate toward words with harsh or agitated sound qualities.

Poetic or mantric speech does facilitate the unfoldment of the higher levels of the mind. While it cannot do so by itself, it is a useful aid we should consider employing. Most of the time, there is a constant background noise in our minds. This reflects the kind of impressions we expose ourselves to during the day, and the kind of thought and speech that is habitual to us. If we listen to the radio a lot, we may have old songs reverberating in our minds. If we engage in a lot of gossip, it will repeat itself in our subconscious. If we are in conflict with another person, that emotional pattern will continue reverberating in our thoughts. Such background static keeps our minds at a certain level, and makes it harder to tune in to higher influences. From this level of agitation it may be very difficult, if not impossible, to still the mind and enter into meditation.

If we repeat a mantra or do various forms of chanting, a more refined and subtle vibration develops and can come to serve as the background pattern of our minds. If we continually go back to a chant like Om, Rama, or Hare Krishna each time our mind's static emerges, this will serve to bring a vibration of harmony and aspiration into the mind. It should be beneath our dignity as divine souls to allow our minds to dwell on negative thoughts and emotions, or to be controlled and distracted by external influences. Through the mantra, we have a tool for redirecting the energy of the mind inward. From this it is easier to have access to silence or clarity. A mantra can even help us break up deep—seated mental and emotional patterns and conditioning, as from childhood, or various traumas we may have had in life.

The spiritual life usually has two stages: the first is to develop *sattva* or purity of mind. The second is to still the mind, to go beyond the material mind. Generally, we cannot do the second if we have not done the first. Many of the problems in spiritual practices in this country today arise from trying to do the second step when the first has not been done. (In some cases, it may not have even been attempted). If our minds are noisy, disturbed, agitated, hyper—sensitive, reactive, critical, constantly busy, etc., we cannot just directly silence them. If we are addicted to external and sensory sources of stimulation and entertainment, we are not even in control of our minds and so cannot expect to be able to focus them.

First, we must set in motion forces to take the mind from its disturbed (*rajasic*) or dull (*tamasic*) quality to its natural clear quality (*sattvic*). The best and easiest method is the mantra. Yet purity of mind requires purity of lifestyle. We cannot bring clarity to the mind if we are living a confused or self—indulgent lifestyle, even if we do occasional chanting of mantras.

Sanskrit mantras have an objective connection between sound and sense. Even if we do not know what they mean, we can benefit from their energetic quality if we chant them with an open mind. Their meaning will become clear to us in time. Such meanings are not dictionary meanings, but connections to the cosmic energy and to the Divine Word.

Naturally, if someone chants a Sanskrit mantra with a greedy or power—seeking mind, it may not do any good. The mantra does not work mechanically. It requires a force of consciousness on our part, some devotion or real seeking of truth. It can magnify our aspiration, and if we are at all open, the mantra will have a positive effect that we can feel in time; not as a form of personal pleasure or mental satisfaction, but as a sense of the greater divine presence both within and around us.

The dissociation between sound and sense in our language is not a healthy sign. It is part of our dissociation in life generally, including the split between ourself and others, between humankind and nature, between humankind and God, and the division within us between our outer and inner being. Our thoughts and actions do not usually correspond. We say one thing and do another, or we say one thing but mean something else. Nor do our positions in life and our inner worth usually relate. Our political leaders are seldom men of honor, our religious leaders seldom men of divine wisdom, our cultural guides seldom possessed of any real truth—consciousness.

The dissociation of sound and sense causes us to be insensitive to the actual quality or nature of things but to take them for their conventional meaning. In this regard, our culture is filled with slogans and propaganda, false mantras like "buy and save" and "spend and gain," to condition our minds to various artificial desires and appetites. The advertising world is quite aware of the strength and the subconscious appeal of such catering to wishful thinking or self—indulgence. By this pattern of thinking, we see the package or the form, but do not perceive the content or the meaning. We are led to believe we need things that we don't, or that we can find happiness in some mere novelty. In this way, we can be manipulated, controlled, and driven by unnatural and unnecessary impulses. We become victims of the external world of consumption, and eventually we ourselves, like our commodities, are consumed and wasted, and can be thrown away like an old newspaper.

In our modern materialistic language, we try to make our words as specific in meaning as possible. Each different branch of knowledge and each profession has its particular specialized terminology. We have made our words precise, but has this served to give us more truth or to make us more narrow in our vision? In this way, we learn more and more about less and less, and are less able to communicate with each other. In mantric and spiritual language, however, there is seen to be only one real meaning in all words, which is truth or the Divine. In the ancient Vedic languages, apart from whatever else a word may mean, it usually also means God. How many of our words suggest such a spiritual reality to us? Different meanings are only possible because there is an underlying meaning or significance to being itself. This is the unity of life and truth which is consciousness as the necessary ground of all meaning. In our materialistic language, this essence of meaning, which is eternal and infinite, is broken up and divided into the compartments of words according to the divisive desires and fears of the ego. To put the world back together, we must restore the unity of the Word. This is to recognize that behind all superficial meanings is a unity of existence and consciousness. It is the truth of meaning we need to discover, not what a particular thing “means.”

Out of the ocean of consciousness the bubbles of words arise, on which our minds ride the waves of the world. When the truth of this is perceived we will realize that meaning comes from within. It does not belong to the things of the outer world.

*David Frawley is director of the American Institute of Vedic Studies in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and author of the book* Ayurvedic Healing.

## Medicine – The Second Medical Revolution

From Biomedicine to Infomedicine

An Interview with Larry Foss and Kenneth Rothenberg  
By Thomas Beaudry

If ever the time were ripe for revolution in the field of medicine it is now, at least in this sense: If one doesn't start soon it may be too late: It's a matter of life and death. Since the turn of the century "chronic" disease has replaced "infectious" disease as number one in disease-factored death. And after forty years of costly cancer research prestigious medical journals have reported the results in one word, "failure."

Biomedicine, tied to a physicalist world view, the result of the 17th century scientific revolution (the first medical revolution), seems firmly in place. Yet biomedicine is at an impass: the biomedical physicalist world view can not account for an overwhelming amount of data appearing in recent years that strongly suggests the role of mindfulness in the disease/cure equation.

Doctors Lawrence Foss and Kenneth Rothenberg, authors of The Second Medical Revolution, have vigorously attacked the very foundation of the biomedical approach to medicine in a language that biomedical advocates speak, that of modern and postmodern science. In this interview a new infomedical medical model, involving in the Khunian sense a paradigm shift, emerges giving birth to infomedicine: an almost spiritual approach to health care and disease cure that in the very least recognizes the social and psychic dimensions of our reality, and makes for a much more accommodating world in which the truly spiritually minded can live.

How did the two of you get involved in attempting to revolutionize medical practice?

Larry: Speaking for myself, my background is in the philosophy of science, which, perhaps over-ambitiously, undertakes to examine the foundations of different sciences. In this case it seemed somewhat overdue to look at the foundations of an applied science like medicine. Because of some experience in systems theory I was asked to contribute to a rationale statement for reinstituting a graduate school of nursing at a West Coast university. What piqued my curiosity was the reason for denying the request: nursing didn't require the high-powered technical resources of a medical research center. This was odd because it seemed to me that nursing was optimally situated to look at both the biomedical realms of disease as well as the psychosocial elements and yet it was being written off by the medical school community. So I became interested in examining the underlying premises of today's Western medicine, the biomedical model.

Ken: My formal background is in economics, quantitative analysis, and education. My interest in philosophy evolved after my formal years of education. Larry and I worked as colleagues together in an educational setting for a number of years. As a result of a very good working relationship, and his initial interest in the philosophical issues in medicine, I began looking at his efforts and commenting on them, and it just evolved. We've spent approximately seven years on this task. We began with the excitement of the philosophical issues at stake. These are issues that are potentially matters of life and death. The Second Medical Revolution was a result of a long-term examination of these issues crystallized in medicine.

Your's is an infomedical model as oposed to the present day biomedical model. Exactly what do you mean by the term "new medical model"? It's more than just a new therapy, isn't it?

Ken: Yes. We're talking about a multilevel integrated paradigm which offers not just healing techniques at the applied level but also basic sciences which rationalize alternative therapies. We are also offering a world view which is consistent with those basic sciences and which is reinforced by success at the applied and basic tiers. So when we speak in terms of a medical model, we're talking about three levels as opposed to merely therapeutic alternatives.

Larry: We regard the biomedical model, which is currently prevelant, to be based on the natural science paradigm of the 17th century which brought about the industrial revolution. This biomedical model views disease as the interactive product of two parameters, one environmental and one biological or genetic. This means that any data, any findings in medical research have ultimately to be subsumed under these two headings. Thus the impasse: over the past several decades, a number of findings have appeared in medical research which constitute circumstantial evidence for the role of mindfulness in the disease equation, while the biomedical model affords no formal place for it. So in keeping with the biomedical model either mindfulness has to be ignored— placebo effect phenomena, conversion symptoms, psychosomatic disorders, etc.—or it has to be reduced and explained in terms of one of the other two biomedically recognized parameters. Neither of these two options is satisfactory, thus the search for a new medical model.

People may not be so aware of the far-reaching and practically all-pervading influence of this mechanistic Cartesian/Newtonian world view of the seventeenth century from which the biomedical model logically follows. Can you shed some light on how deeply the philosophers of medicine or science are logically entrenched in the classical paradigm and how it causes them to think?

Ken: Members of the medical enterprise, as it is presently institutionalized, share certain categories of thought. These categories of thought derive from the natural science paradigm which sees the world as physical, measurable, and reducible. These categories have a tremendous impact on the way in which medical research is conducted and on the way in which the patient is conceptualized. As a result of these institutionalized thought commitments—what we would call a medical thought-world—disease is seen as a biological puzzle and the mind as separate from the body. To get some sense of the impact of this way of thinking, we can cite instances whre physical-reductionist assumptions lead to "structural amnesia." For example, mainstream medical research consistantly forgets that the patient is a biocultural being. Rather, in medical research the patient is seen as a series of systems—the endocrine system, the nervous system, the immune system—and these are further looked at in terms of organs, cells, and the search continues at smaller levels wherein ultimately persons are reduced to the atomic level. At these levels, the person as a social being is forgotten, the person as a cultural being is forgotten. So the classical view reflected in the biomedical model has a tremendous impact on the way medicine is conducted. Just take the language of medicine, for example. A patient goes in for a physical examination administered by a physician. The very notion of cause and cure are all interpreted in physical terms.

People in general think along these terms. While we may complain about medicine, or see that there are some shortcomings in the biomedical model, without even defining it as such, I think that unconsciously we all speak in the same language coming from this world view and don't realize how deeply we are implicated in it.

KEN: Exactly. It's systematically entrenched in our language and the way we think. It's largely the result of the exciting scientific gains in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, which offered the promise of greater knowledge and increased understanding in which to exercise control along with the optimism that, at least in the medical sector, cures could be found and the mechanisms of disease could be untangled. As you say, much of our current thinking reflects this sense that understanding leads to control. But as the research efforts for achieving this understanding are increasingly focused on a narrower and narrower physical base, many of the multilevel interactions that we're coming to see exist, are left out of the equation.

In order for the edifice of the natural science paradigm and the biomedical model to reign, the then prevailing world view had to be overturned. This is what you refer to as the "first medical revolution." Were the vanguards of the first medical revolution facing as formidable a task as you are today.

LARRY: I think, in fact, that the first revolution rebels did face as formidable a structure as we do today. The reigning paradigm was the neo-Aristotlean paradigm which certainly had its own enduring strengths. Its weakness was that it tended to be too metaphysical. The effort of the first revolution rebels was to secure a method which was experimentally testable. They were successful and the experimental method they established constituted a singal triumph over the ad hoc procedures of the time, which tended to be subjective, commonsensical and non-falsifiable. This is why so much of our vocabulary that you were speaking of is physically oriented. The scientific method is credited with an impressive series of successes in medicine for which in some ways the Western world is justly esteemed. One could then look at what we are trying to do today as a counterpoint to an excess.

To go back to the metaphysical to some extent?

Larry: No, really more dialectically to move toward a third position which incorporates the strengths of both. The vocabulary that we've selected as a synthetic alchemical stone to replace the natural-science-model explanation (which is top-downward, reductionistic, analytical) is "self organizational" (which is both top-downward and bottom-upward). This explanation is based on the findings of postmodern sciences, such as non-equilibrium thermodynamics, evolutionary biology and quantum mechanics.

In the biomedical model, if you discover a mental phenomenon that seems to contribute to the disease state, the task is to explain it in biological terms. This implies a second task of explaining biological phenomena in psychochemical terms. Again, we see the impasse in medicine today as, how on one hand to account for the evident successes of therapies which are predicated on the role of mindfulness as a co-causal factor of disease and cure, and on the other hand, how to do it scientifically. Since the prevailing paradigm doesn't allow for that mental parameter, if you are going to have a medicine that is at once scientific and bio-psycho-social you have a lot of explaining to do.

Can you talk about the vested interest that the scientific community has in the present mechanistic world view that inhibits them from changing?

Ken: The investment is pervasive: everything from large numbers of experts who have been schooled, tested, and given their credentials in the biomedical thought-world, to university curricula based on pre-med. requirements in physics, chemistry, and anatomy. Then there is the medical school curriculum and medical research which are increasingly focused on molecular biology and genetic factors. Pharmaceutical companies have a large investment in therapies based on chemically altering the diseased biological state and hospitals are set up to administer physical therapies—surgery, radiation, transplants, etc.—the whole institution is oriented towards alopathic medicine.

Larry: As in the case of any institutionalized paradigm there is an infrastructure in place. If you were to take a look at any scholarly medical journal you might be scandalized by the commercial ads touting the products of the pharmaceutical companies. The economy, the legal system and federal policies all reflect the biomedical model. So to dislodge a model it is not pretentious to speak of revolution.

In the past it would seem that other schools of thought, such as theology, psychology and sociology, have abdicated responsibility for explaining disease and perhaps unwittingly accepted a single-level material reality disease causation concept— the biomedical model. You must have a good sense for how that's changing now.

Larry: First of all, even within biomedicine, in the field for example of psychoneuroimmunology, we can hear a "cry in the wilderness" for a new model. As a case in point we cite a psychoneuroimmunologist who says, "We know that the mind plays a significant role in effecting the immune system but we can't rationalize that role." It reflects the plight of the current medical enterprise. Practioners themselves are up against evidence which seems to exceed the explanatory capacity of their instruments, in this case conceptual instruments. So the data just sit there unused or inadequately rationalized in terms of the existing conceptualization. That is to say it's denied, and mental/ emotional states become simply their neuro-physiological correlates, a draconian way of dealing with the evidence.

Ken: I think the alternative therapies that we see are a reaction to the narrowness of the biomedical disease concept. It's interesting to see the extent to which these alternatives are surfacing from many schools of thought. People are mobilizing, mimeographing, distributing information. There is increased attention in the media to issues like nutrition and exercise. I think the world is catching on a bit. However, from our point of view the efforts are not systematic.While at the applied level solutions are being offered, at the foundations level the conceptual shortcomings of the biomedical model are not being addressed. The dissatisfaction is out there but it is not sufficiently focused to offer an alternative model—it's mobilized but not rationalized.

Not in terms of Western scientific thinking anyway.

Ken: Correct.

That brings us to what you call the "failure of detente." Can you explain that?

Ken: When scanning the medical landscape, a number of alternative medical attitudes, strategies, research programs and therapies present themselves. Most notable among these are efforts like holistic health, environmental and behavioral medicine to name just a few. We have labelled such alternatives as "insurgents" given that the impetus for their origins is at least partly due to the narroness of biomedicine. Close examination of the claims made by such insurgents reveals considerable conceptual confusion. Typically it takes this form: the insurgent medical group will argue (often quite persuasively) that the patient is a bio-psycho-social being and as such is inadequately diagnosed and trreated by biomedicine, which treats the patient as a biological entity.

The soulution that most insurgents ultimately reach is that the triumphs of biomedical "cure" should be joined to the promising potential of holistic "care" and that, in tandem, the two approaches offer the patient a more comprehensive health care model. As intuitively attractive as this "cure plus care" combination might appear, it is conceptually weak—what we have termed the "failure of detente." From a foundations perspective, two widely divergent concepts of the patient—what the insurgents accept, biomedicine rejects— are simultaneously embraced. This conflict crystalizes over such basic differences as the insurgents' suggestions that mental/emotional factors can cause disease. Detente fails because you can't have it both ways. If the insurgents were to take seriously the foundations implications of their argument—what we would call taking the foundations initiatve—then this would be pointing to a new medical model—one that offers a research program which would rationalize their efforts. Until such an alternative stucture is in place, we can only anticipatethat even their successes will have little impact on biomedicine.

We argue that the infomedical model offers scientific foundations upon which to rationalize both the success of biomedicine as well as much of the literature that suggests a mindful component in causing and curing disease. Infomedicine recognizes the patient as a biocultural being and so offers a disease equation that subsumes within its expalnatory framework interacting levels of complexity—biological, psychological and socio-cultural.

Larry: Without a new foundation today's medicine is schizophrenic, an embodiment of what the French call deformation. The physician has a family, goes to the theater, prays, etc. and then when he or she goes to work suddenly she is only a physiological organism—period— in terms of the pathogenic influences that can affect her. And there's a melancholy side to the whole situation: there's a first-person perspective and there's a third-person perspective, and if you're going to be a scientist in today's Western currency then you've got to adopt a first-person perspective on the weekends and a third-person perspective during the week, and they are mutually inconsistent. Alternative health care advocates want to change this, but without a foundations change the alternative movement, while a reaction to the biomedical model, is unwhittingly an affirmation of it.

I noticed that in your book you did not address Eastern medicine, like India's ancient ayurveda or Chinese medicine.

Ken: I think the Eastern medical task is perhaps different from the Western medical task in the sense that each of us have inherited different vocabularies and sets of procedures. Those of the West have included the idea that in order for an explanation to be ultimately satisfying it has to justify itself by its scientific researchability.

Yes, in Eastern thought Western scientific researchability and verification are not the criteria for reasonableness. The ancient medical model of India, ayurveda, is based on a different paradigm than that of biomedicine as well as the one you are offering in the infomedical model. It's a truly spiritual world view wherein consciousness is foundational, mindstuff, consciousness, organizes matter.

Larry: In the West since the time of Decartes and Galileo the legitimate domain of what is "scientific" has meant the material world of extended objects (res extensa), as distinct from the conceptual world of mental objects—thoughts, feelings, beliefs (res cognitas). Insofar as these latter objects have shown themselves capable of mesuarably impacting patient disease state, the Western task has been to articulate a vocabulary that bridges this antimony. Infomedicine is such a vocabulary. It both derives from the findings of the natural (postmodern) science, and its ligitimate domain in the evolutionary world of self-organizing objects.

Ken: Interestingly the Western way of approaching a synthesis between East and West is often to show how these Eastern insights are consistent or coherent with the frontiers of Western science. That suggests the bias that the co-mingling of two cultures is achieved by subsuming one within the other—East within West. So efforts like the Tao of Physics and Dancing Wu Li Masters are, as I interpret them, attempts to incorporate or to invite Eastern metaphysics to fit in a way that is consistent with Western science.

Larry: Tactically, we believed that the only way we were ever going to reach an audience in the mainstream medical community was to do so in a language which that community speaks. We had just enough experience to know that it would be an instant shut-off if we didn't.

So yours is a material model in the sense that you maintain, in keeping with postmodern science, that "simple" matter comes first, it's foundational, and mind and consciousness come later as matter organizes itself into greater complexity. "Spiritual" in your model is man's psycho-component, a development of matter.

Ken: I mentioned earlier that biomedicine embraces a world view that is physical, measurable and reducible. In the info-medical model the world is seen in terms of interconnected levels of organization that reach both up and down. There's one world, and thoughts and actions in one sphere can have an impact on an individual's physical-mental state in another sphere. They could have an impact on the planet. They could have an impact on the universe. If you would allow that that's a kind of spirituality then in that sense there is a spiritual parameter to the infomedical model. In a more concise sense I think you're correct. If you look at the prefixes we chose, bio-psycho-socio, the "spiritual" dimension is included in the psycho-component.

Larry: To put that graphically you can visualize the biomedical pathogenic grid as composed of two axes, the physical and the biological. The patient is a biophysical system, and that's a researchable affirmation. What the second medical revolution attempts to show is that a third axes is scientifically feasible in terms of which the patient becomes a psychobiophysical system. The way that it does that is to invoke the post-modern scientific idea that matter is not ultimately reducible to sub-atomic particles, but rather is self-organizing. Just as in the theory of natural evolution, matter is continually complexifying itself. In an open universe like ours it's seen as self-normalizing, self-transcending. So we see from atoms and rocks we get trees and primates, and subsequently we get such interesting complex systems as you and I. These are developmental organizational levels which are both researchable and interconnectable. There's no reason, either conceptually or within natural evolution, why a self-organizational level could not be transpsychological or spiritual. So what we're talking about now is an open-ended patient who is at least psychobiophysical, that is, intentionally not just autonomically self-referential, and the explanatory procedure admits of an on-going complexification. So if someone can point to circumstantial evidence for spiritual phenomena having a role in a person's health state, there is now an explanatory framework in which that can be accommodated.

The exciting thing about the post-modern scientific finding or insight is that it really lends itself very easily (we hesitate in other contexts to invoke this parallel but here we feel perfectly free to talk about it), for example, to Teilhard de Chardin's omega point. Put in his terms, the postmodern science insight is that matter is successively evolutionary. So psychology or spirituality is a function of matter self-organizing developmentally. We're not talking about matter interacting with non-matter when we talk about mind or spirit interacting with body. We're talking about one level of material organization interacting with another developmentally successor level of material organization. For the Eastern metaphysician this is not necessarily a breakthrough formula but for the Western scientific mindset it is. It's a breakthrough formula because it permits just the kind of interaction that is prohibited on the methodological grounds of a mechanistic world view.

Again, I think the Eastern spiritual world view is that everything is consciousness rather than matter. Matter is but a distortion of consciousness. That which is conceived lies within the power of conception, not vice versa. I can appreciate that in the biomedical model such things a mental what to speak of spiritual influences are but superstition. Whereas, in the infomedical model they are at the very least given equal consideration as potential etiological factors. Your model is part of a world view that is, relatively speaking, more accommodating for a transcendentalist to live in. Not wanting to take away from the important work that you are doing, perhaps what I ultimately look forward to is a third scientific revolution.

Ken: Fair enough.

What is the post-dated check or logical-possibility argument of the biomedical advocates?

Larry: The logical-possibility argument is simply a reaffirmation that any findings can ultimately be converted to the chemical/physical explanation. Nobody has effected the reduction from genetics to chemistry or subatomic particles but a promissory note is offered. Since the scientific revolution was based on the methodological assumption that you could do so, and since there have been substantial gains over the past three hundred years by using this methodology, we have reason to assume that we can continue along the same path and in due course solutions to unsolved problems of the day will be found.

The significance of the postmodern science revolution is that we don't have to wait around anymore for something that may or may not happen. The logical-possibility argument is flanked. Now there is another methodology in which one does not have to proceed reductionistically but can proceed self-organizationally. Which means that one ought not seek to see genetics reduced to a nuclear physics explanation. Rather genetics itself is redefined. Biology is redefined as biophysics, and psychology is redefined as psychobiology, and these are each studies of material systems which have self-organized developmentally to higher and higher states of being or ecologicl niches.

I realize that you want to give some credit to the prevailing paradigm. But couldn't we say that the very world view resulting from the natural science paradigm was potentially the cause of many of the diseases that the subsequent biomedical model has found cures for—cures which are now being offered as evidence that we are on the right path?

Ken : It could very well be that a world view that incorporates the notion that the individual can come to understand the world in an impersonal ,detatched manner, is, in a planet-wide sense, pathology inducing. Embracing the idea that our thoughts are seperate from the material world and don't have an impact on that worldcan be said to have contributed to a host of evironmental maladies from the killing of Lake Erie to the depletion of the ozone layer. It is a myth that our scientific understanding has led to control. We are constantly surprised by the unanticipated consequences of our actions.

Larry: We are increasingly the architects of the world we live in. If God created the world at least we are evidently charged with re-creating it, and we are likely to be judged in terms of how we discharge that responsibility. The first scientific revolution occured at a time when we were still living in a world whose capital was essentially given to us. The second scientific revolution is occuring at a time when the world we inherited is running out of inherited capital.

Ken: In the broadest sense health today constitutes adapting to an environment that we co-create.

The successor model that emerges from a foundation of postmodern science is described by you as self-organizing. You've called it a cybernetic approach as opposed to the engineering approach found in the biomedical model. Can you explain the difference between a cybernetic approach and an engineering one?

Ken: In the biomedical model the pathogenic agent is something like a virus invading from without or the presence of too much or too little of some substance within. In that model the therapeutic way to address that would be some form of physical/chemical alteration like a transplant, an operation or pharmacceutical. The unit of pathogenesis is physical and the therapy is physical. A cybernetic or self-organizing approach would recognize that the unit of pathogenesis is not a reducible physical entity but rather a patient-in-a-certain state. That state can be characterized in terms that are biological, psychological, sociological cultural, spiritual, emotional, etc.

Cybernetics involves systems whose structures are composed of mutual causal processes as opposed to reducible physical properties. Cybernetic systems are systems in which the state of being is determined by positive or negative loops. The state of the system is not, therefore, determined by outside forces, but rather reflects the character of the system itself. Negative feedback refers to the renormalization of the system to offset some perturbation. Positive feedback would be a system reorganizing to another regime based on a combination of an outside influence and rule-governed behavior within the system itself. An engineering approach to disease focuses on a cause-effect relationships so that in a medical context the therapies assume that there is a simple cause for which there is a simple cure. A cybernetic approach recognizes that unidirectional causality with respect to a multilevel being is naive.

How does this fit with Marguli's and Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis?

Ken: The Gaia hypothesis suggests that planet-wide behavior writ large is self-organizing behavior. That is, we can note instances when environmental paramaters as well as biotic communities exhibit both renormalization or homeostatic behavior and self transcendent or evolutionary behavior. Gaia offers the important insight that life creates the conditions which contribute to life on earth. Thus life doesn't simply survive an implaccable enviornment, rather, life modulates the enviornemt in favor of its further survival. As for the medical implications: we not only must adapt to, but we also have some influence over the physical, psychological and socio-cultural environments that we occupy. Our responses to these circumstances are a result of both evolutionarily evolved as well as learned "programs" or responses. The extent to which we can gain knowledge of about these programs, which are part of our complexity, contributes to how we might modify our behavior and beliefs in such a way that we can maintain or return to health.

Larry: The Gaia hypothesis implies that the atmosphere is a caldron the dynamics of which we are increasingly responsible for. Analogously, placebo-effect phenomena illustrate the extent to which through changing our mental/emotional/spiritual state we can self-consciously activate neurochemicals which in turn alter the interior environment in which disease grows. To use a cliche, it's acase of mind over matter. But our paradigm protects us against the hurricane force of thiscliche. So, we have an intentionally self-referental system which is capable of leveraging its own mental/ emotional/spiritual states to affect the environment in which the disease grows, yet it's a therapeutic modality which remains clinically untapped. Biofeedback experiments offer further examples of this capacity. So continually we are referring back to the fact that foundational issues have clinical consequences and to speak only of the clinical consequences disengaged from the foundational issue is to advocate ad hoc medicine—detente.

There is no doubt that we are living in an information age but what exactly do you mean by "information" and thus infomedicine.

Ken: If you go back to the original meaning of the word inform, it is not just the transfer of an idea but its also an impact. To inform is to have an impact. What information means in the infomedical model is that information from a variety of levels can have an impact on the state of an individual. So while the biomedical model has spent a great deal of effort in understanding the messages at the physical level they have excluded other dimensions of information, such as psychological, social and cultural mesages.

Larry: Each organizational level communicates with respect to the complexity of that level. Just as biophysical system inter-communicates through genes, and genetic malfunction can disease the system, so a psychobiophysical system can inter-communicate through memes, which can likewise disease the system. So we can talk about dysfunctional memes like we can talk about dysfunctional genes.

What is the role of the physician in the infomedical model as opposed to his role in the biomedical model?

Larry: In a word it is to practice not at the Center of Molecular and Genetic Medicine but to practice at the center of Molecular and Memetic Medicine as well.

Ken: The biomedical doctor exercises control. The patient comes with a problem, the doctor addresses it. The doctor is the sole source of information and there is an assumed cause and effect relationship between the illness of the patient during exam and the response of the the doctor. The infomedical model on the other hand recognizes the cybernetic insight that control is a very ilusive concept. This is especially true in systems which are dominated by mutual causal feedback processes. Here, there is no control, rather there is participation. In the infomedical setting the doctor shares with the patient information in his/her examination of the kinds of social, psychological and biological responses of the patient. These responses might be thought of as rule governed behavior which is a result of our complexity as people. Understanding the relationship of these responses provides the kind of self knowledge that allows the patient to participate in the healing process, so that both patient and doctor are participants as opposed to the doctor as a spectator controlling the sequence of events.

What are the symptoms of disease and what does the diagnosis involve in the infomedical model?

Ken: In a sense your question suggests the power of the prevailing paradigm. Whenever someone says symptoms, immediately one thinks of headaches, pains here, pains there. We're certainly well aware of the kinds of symptoms of physical disease. The benefit of the infomedical model would be that along with the tremendous effort that has gone into understanding the biological basis of disease, also unpacked would be the kind of psychological and social programs that we as humans bring to circumstances. So the range of symptoms is expanded to include, say, an unhealthy attitude, a distorted world view or a misplaced value. As the concept of the symptom is expanded so is the concept of disease.

What are the economics of the infomedical model?

Larry: As far as acquiring federal funding for research in alternative therapies, the prejudice towards the biomedical model is so much a factor that without conforming to the prevailing paradigm don't expect funding. We are involved in model talk and that is something for which there is at present no institutionslized forum in medicine.

Once the infomedical model is in place what are the economics of that model? What should we look for in terms of doctor's bills?

Ken: Potentially the overall health care system could cost less and deliver more. In the infomedical model the doctor and patient would interact much more in discussion at the same level. In this setting many of the expensive health care remedies might be used much less. The expensive technology of the biomedical model might for the most part be reserved for emergencies. We would be looking at a totally different health care delivery system.

Your book has been called a seminal work and that is significant, but can you say anything about the resistance to this model from biomedicine?

Ken: Full knowing the strength of the biomedical model—it is alive and well—our greatest fear was that we might be ignored. That has not been the case. There is resistance to the idea of delving into other levels in search of disease causation, which may appear to unnecessarily dilute research efforts. Interestingly however, John Locke, who is often referred to as the father of empiricism, resisted the notion of using the microscope. His feeling was that it would introduce complications that would defray human speculation and introduce confusion into research. In the future I think that today's resistance to examining multiple factors in disease causation will look as the John Locke example looks today.

On that I couldn't agree with you more.

## Milk - Care of the Cow - Frawley

Dairy products for health or disease  
By Dr. David Frawley

“The mother of the cosmic powers, the daughter of the beings of light, the sister of the sun gods, the navel center of truth. I speak to those who are aware: do not harm the cow, the Earth.”—Rig Veda VIII.101.15

There is much debate in the natural food movement about the place of dairy products and their nutritional value. Some individuals file dairy products along with meat under the heading of bad food for humans and harmful to animals. Many vegans, or “pure” vegetarians, are in this category. Vegans will not use anything derived from an animal source. Many claim that dairy is an unfit food for human beings and causes many diseases from cancer to heart attacks. While there is a certain amount of validity to these statements, and we must take them seriously and with sensitivity, it is essential that we also understand the salient point which qualifies the vegans’ indictment: it is not dairy itself that is at fault but our methods of raising dairy animals and using dairy products. The spiritual and healing traditions of India, both Hindu and Buddhist, support dairy as an excellent and important food for human beings, particularly for those on the spiritual path. While dairy may not be recommended for certain physical or psychological types, it has an important, perhaps crucial use for most of us, not only for maintaining health but for promoting longevity and improving the quality of life as well.

Much of Vedic civilization revolved around the cow and her protection. The cow set the outer standard of diet and medicine with milk, cream, butter, ghee and yogurt. She also set the inner standard of spiritual practice by the gentle spirit she manifested. The outer care of the cow reflects the inner care of the self: the cultivation of divine awareness, which yields the “milk” of truth and pure perception.

Throughout the history of India, dairy products have been the favorite food of yogis and brahmins. In the ancient Vedas a greater variety of dairy products is mentioned than that of grains, fruits, and vegetables put together. Buddha, Shankara, and many other great saints and sages used dairy products. Favorite stories about Krishna relate the times he spent as a cowherd and butter thief. Dairy products are still used by the great yogis of India in modern times. Surely such men of wisdom were not insensitive to animals, nor were dairy products harmful to their health or intelligence. These sages explored all the domains of nature and all the planes of consciousness, and understood the intrinsic nature of things. Surely they could not fail to see the properties of dairy and its right usage.

Ayurvedic medicine, the traditional medicine of India, also uses many dairy preparations, particularly for improving resistance to disease, for promoting longevity, and for convalescence and regeneration. These include milk decoctions, medicated butters and ghees, and other special preparations. Dairy is not only recommended for the young but also for the old, and for those who are weak or debilitated.

**The sacred cow, the symbol of Brahman**

The cow is the most sacred animal in India and has been so since the most ancient Vedic times. This is partly because of the great abundance it provides. It naturally produces more milk than its calf needs and is quite happy to share the extra amount with human beings. The cow is a symbol of the Divine Mother. The cow is the incarnation of the Divine Mother in the animal kingdom. The greatest Vedic chant, the Gayatri mantra—to Om and the seven planes of existence—is visualized on a cow; as a mystic symbol, the universe itself is seen in the Vedic scriptures as a cosmic cow and the Mother of the Vedas.

We can tell how a people treats the Earth by how they treat their cows. Indeed in Greek, *Gaia* and in Sanskrit, *Gau* mean both Earth and cow. The Gaia principle that there is an organic intelligence pervading and regulating life on Earth is a modern recognition of the immanent Divine Mother. The Earth as the mystic cow yields the milk of life if we care for her with love and respect. Moreover, how we treat our cows also reflects how we treat ourselves as souls. Today the exploitation of these gentle animals reflects our spiritual suicide: our fast, reckless, consumer-oriented sensate culture— wherein the true refinement, innocence, and gentleness of humanity is thrown by the wayside—is polluting and destroying the very globe on which we live. Such carelessness is not very becoming of an age that claims great advancement in knowledge and communication. This exploitation is based on the misperception of cows as soul-less, devoid of any real feelings—as having been created by God for man’s convenience.

We have quite obviously forgotten how to read the cosmic language of nature. We do not perceive the voice of God in nature but see only raw material for our commercial desires. Yet even on this level it is not useful in the long run to pollute or burn down the house in which we are living.

In the great scriptures of ancient India we are advised that the cow should be given to the sages and brahmins, and she should not be given to kings and merchants, i.e. she should not be exploited for commercial or political ends. The meaning of this is that we should give our receptivity (our soul) to those persons who are spiritually developed. If we give it to worldly people they will simply slaughter it. Humankind is meant to take care of the innocent and gentle in order to develop ourselves spiritually. When we exploit them for our selfish ends we become demoniac and fall from grace.

The right care of the cow and the right use of dairy products is thus in harmony with a spirit of nonviolence. Raising a cow and learning how to milk it was an important duty for brahmin children in Vedic times. This was not to encourage them to profit from cattle; it was to teach them innocence and receptivity of mind from the cow to guide them in their meditations. We have to cultivate our wisdom with gentleness and receptivity in much the same way as we have to care for cows. In the New Testament also we read that the meek shall inherit the Earth, the humble will be exalted, and the innocent will see God. In modern culture, however, it seems that the meek and the gentle will be trampled underfoot, and we will live off of what they can provide us until there is nothing left.

**The use of dairy products**

There are a number of health issues relating to dairy products that must be understood to use them correctly. Some people lack the enzymes to digest dairy products, often because the ethnic group they were born into has no history of taking dairy products. Yet most of the problems we experience in digesting dairy are not from the dairy products themselves but from their wrong usage. Taken correctly, even those who may have previously had difficulty with dairy products may find them to be helpful; many have no difficulty with raw dairy products taken with the appropriate spices and in the right combinations.

Just as we cannot blame potatoes for the difficulties caused by eating fast-food french fries, so we cannot blame dairy for the way it is commonly being used today. Just as raw sugarcane juice is radically different in its effects from white sugar, just as whole wheat flour is quite a different substance from bleached white flour, so are raw and naturally prepared dairy products quite distinct from the artificial, mass-produced dairy products generally found today. Our pasteurized, treated dairy products are the equivalent of artificially prepared and processed foods.

In India the cow is allowed to give her first milk to her calf. It is only the extra, which is often considerable, that goes to human beings. If the calf is taken away from its mother, naturally the milk given by the cow loses much of its nourishing property. Let us consider: not only are the calves taken away from their mothers, they are slaughtered. The mother’s child is killed, and then we approach the mother for her milk. Can that be deemed humane? How would a human mother feel under such circumstances? Cows also have emotions and their grief and anger enter into the milk. It is well known that when a mother cow hears the call of her calf that she immediately begins to secrete milk. The mother cow knows when her calf is taken away and also knows that it is going to be killed; this causes emotions that in turn activate secretions of toxic hormones into the milk.

Cows are mistreated in many other ways including being confined in pens and milked by machines. They are mainly hybrid animals produced through artificial insemination, virtually “milk-machines” designed to produce five times more milk than in their natural state. They are fed hormones, antibiotics, and a diet of inorganically-grown grains. Various residues of pesticides are also absorbed into their tissues and the milk is one of the main places where these concentrations are highest.

Traditional ayurveda explains in great detail the properties of various dairy products, including not only those of cows, but of goats, buffalos, and other animals. However, there is nothing in the classical texts to tell us the effects of these modern methods of raising and preparing dairy. We do read in ayurvedic texts that the quality of dairy products from animals who are tethered or confined is much lower than from those who are able to roam and graze freely. Ayurveda also clearly states that we should avoid chemical residues and artificial drugs as they accumulate as toxins in our tissues and breed disease. It also speaks of how damaging our air, water, or soils causes epidemics. It is clear that many of the methods we are using to produce dairy products have a damaging effect on its quality as a food, and similar methods are damaging not only the other foods we are eating, but in fact our whole environment.

This gives rise to several questions. To what degree are our dairy products damaged? At what point do they cease to be helpful foods? To what extent can we counter these conditions without giving up dairy? What can we do to improve the dairy products we have and to encourage their right production?

Certainly I cannot claim here to have all the answers to these questions. We have to learn through our own experience. This requires that we take a very probing look at the subject. Yet to thereby form a crusade against a food that has a long history of positive usage is an overreaction and will prevent our genuinely understanding. While it is easier to make a blanket condemnation of something than to discriminate its wrong from right usage, such a one-sided mentality will lead to other errors. Though all the answers are not evident, we do know that our current methods of dairy production and usage have many negative impacts, a number of which we can counter.

**The Pitfalls Of Pasteurization**

According to the system of yoga, dairy as a whole is pure or *sattvic* in nature. It is born of love and increases our natural intelligence and sensitivity. Its beneficial properties are reduced not only by how we raise the animals but how we prepare dairy products, which starts with the process of pasteurization.

Pasteur was the father of the germ theory of disease. According to this theory, the best way to prevent disease which is caused by germs is to render our food and environment sterile. Nature is seen as unsafe and natural products are regarded with suspicion. From the standpoint of natural medicine, however, to sterilize something is to kill it. A sterile environment in fact becomes the best place for pathogens to develop in the long run, because the life-force and its natural factors of immunity has been destroyed.

Pasteurized milk is heated to kill any germs in it. This allows milk to last longer before spoiling; hence it makes it more commercially viable, but that does not make it a better food. In this process it is precooked, with much of its natural vitality thereby lost. While pasteurized milk is certainly a better food than mostof what most Americans eat— meat and junk food—we should not underemphasize how much better raw dairy products are.

Pasteurization was the first in a whole series of practices that has reduced the quality of our dairy products and progressively rendered them unhealthful and artificial. It began the mechanization of the production of dairy products and went along with the mechanized way of treating dairy animals. This is part of the false mentality which says that man can always improve upon what nature gives us and that natural products are safer if they are treated first—as if there were something inherently unsafe about them. We live in a culture that regards milk in its natural state as an unsafe food for human consumption. On the other hand, it considers that milk which is taken from animals who are literally tortured, raised in an artificial environment, fed artificial foods, and shot with drugs and hormones—and which is then processed artificially—to be a good and safe food. This reveals something fundamentally wrong with how we have defined ourselves as human beings.

Our dairy products are pasteurized, homogenized, refrigerated for long periods of time, and given additives including salt, white sugar, artificial flavors, or colors. The vitamins A and D added to milk come from fish and render it yet more inferior from the spiritual standpoint. The same insensitive mentality that abuses the animal also prepares the milk in a harmful manner. The natural pure properties of dairy are thereby rendered *tamasic* or impure by these different processes and hence such dairy products aggravate many diseases.

This is not to say that pasteurized dairy products are unfit for human consumption, but that we should use raw dairy if we can; and to really benefit from the healing properties of dairy, raw dairy may be essential. This is particularly important in health regimes aiming at rejuvenation or at improving the mind (*sattvic* and *rasayana* regimes). In many parts of this country raw dairy is illegal or severely restricted in sales, while pasteurized and treated dairy is available everywhere.

I have treated many patients who reacted adversely to regular milk, but when they switched to raw milk mixed with the right spices, found it to be an excellent food. After experiencing fresh dairy products from ayurvedic farms in India and from family farms here, what is sold in supermarkets here appears pitiful, like the difference between garden fresh and canned vegetables.

As we have discussed, the quality of dairy products is damaged by four primary factors, which are: (1) how dairy animals are treated and raised, (2) how dairy products are processed and stored, (3) how we combine dairy products with other foods, and (4) how we take and prepare dairy products.

Bad Food Combinations With Dairy Products:

Any dairy with yeast breads

Any dairy with sour fruit

Any dairy with nuts

Milk with yogurt

Milk with salt.

Good Food Combinations With Dairy Products:

Dairy with sweet fruit

Dairy with vegetables

Dairy with whole grains and whole grain flours.

Dairy with natural raw sugar or honey.

Milk should be taken warm or hot. The ayurveda says that milk taken warm cures diseases, but when taken cold can cause them. For instance, cold milk is said to cause arthritis. The best antidote for the mucus-producing qualities of milk is the right spices. Though cold milk is strengthening, it is generally not recommended.
