Dairy products used in cooking have a wider application. This is because their properties mix with the food. Using such things as milk, yogurt, cheese or sour cream in soups, curries, etc., can produce startlingly good results.

Ayurveda also notes that dairy products, like any food, if taken in excess—particularly if they are cold—become *tamasic*. (Overeating in itself is *tamasic* and can create serious physical and mental health problems.) The damp and heavy nature of dairy food, particularly cheese, can block and clog the channels of circulation. Hence the quantity of them which we take must be regulated.

**Dairy Products And How To Use Them**

**Milk**

Milk is considered to be an ideal rejuvenative food (*rasayana*) which nourishes the mind and heart. Milk is good for such conditions as bleeding from the lungs, dry cough, ulcers, infertility, and lack of vitality. Warm milk with ghee is a natural laxative. Pasteurized and homogenized milk, however, may be constipating.

Cardamom spicing is the best antidote for milk. Calamus is good also: though not pleasant to taste, it provides additional tonic effects for the brain. Ginger, cinnamon, and turmeric are also good. Many spicy herbs taken in milk not only make it more digestible, they also add medicinal effects to it. Warm milk with nutmeg before sleep is a good remedy for insomnia. Tonic herbs in milk decoctions become powerful rejuvenative foods. These include ashwagandha, shatavari, comfrey root , and ginseng. Milk is generally not recommended for *kapha* (heavy or watery) types, although milk fasts are recommended for all constitutions.

**Goat’s milk**

This is a good milk for *kapha* types, or for people who have mucus, congestion, or edema. Even so, it should be taken warm and with spices. It has a warm nature and should be avoided by those suffering from febrile or infectious diseases or hyperacidity (*pitta* types).

**Cream**

Cream is similar to milk but heavier; hence we have to be more careful with it when we are suffering from congestion or weak digestion. One good general rule about dairy, particularly in reference to its heavier products like cream or cheese, is to avoid it if you have a pronounced tongue coating, as this indicates congestion in the digestive system.

**Ice cream**

Ice cream is a potentially difficult food for the body to handle. Its cold nature suppresses the digestive fire, particularly if we take it after meals; therefore it is generally not recommended. However, the more natural forms of ice cream or frozen yogurt can be taken in moderation in warm weather if our digestion is good, if we are not overweight, and if we are careful how we combine it with other foods.

**Yogurt**

Americans have a number of illusions about yogurt. It is not a good food for weight reduction: it is sticky and heavy and in fact a good food for weight gain. While lowfat yogurt is better in this respect, it is still not good for weight loss. Yogurt is not always good in the morning as *kapha*, the biological water humor, is high at that time of day. There is more mucus and congestion in the system in the morning, so cold yogurt at that time can thereby aggravate mucus in the system. Taking it with fruit increases its cold and watery nature.

Yogurt combines very well with cucumber, which is light in nature and balances its heavy property. This is the basis of the Indian *raita* or yogurt salad served with most meals. It is best taken with spices like cilantro, cumin, coriander, or cayenne.

Yogurt is often the safest of the dairy products to take. Pasteurized yogurt is better than pasteurized milk, but the more sour the yogurt is, the more it can aggravate acidity in the body and make the blood toxic. Yogurt also becomes more acidic if taken with acid fruits or bananas. Yogurt is generally not recommended for *pitta* or *kapha* (fiery or watery) types, although sweet yogurt can often be handled easier by pittas.

A good way to take yogurt, particularly if we have diarrhea or malabsorption, is to mix it with equal parts of water in a blender and add some cardamom or nutmeg. This is called *takra* or Indian buttermilk. It is a very good food for convalescence.

**Buttermilk**

Our buttermilk often has large amounts of salt and is pasteurized, otherwise it is a good dairy product. It is more diuretic (water-removing) than other dairy products and less mucus-forming. It is better for *kapha* in this respect. It is also useful for weak digestion, malabsorption, and diarrhea.

**Kefir**

Kefir is another fermented dairy drink particularly useful for *vata* people, those of an airy or nervous constitution, although it has the same problems when combined with fruit as do milk and yogurt.

**Cheese**

Due to its heavy consistency, cheese is also potentially hard to digest and is not recommended where there is congestion, stagnation or channel blockage conditions. It can aggravate such conditions as arthritis, gout, infections, acne, colds, flus, and pulmonary disorders, and can increase cholesterol. Cheese is the least *sattvic* of dairy products. The more fermented and salty it is, the more its negative qualities. Still it is infinitely better than meat and fish. The rennet in cheese may be any one of four types, one of which comes from the lining of cows’ stomachs. (The other three types are vegetable, chemical, and microbial rennet.)

It is best to take cheeses that have no rennet, little salt, and are not strongly fermented. The milder, sweeter tasting cheeses are preferable to the sour, salty, and pungent types. Good antidotes for cheeses are spices like mustard, cayenne, black pepper, horseradish and cumin. It is helpful (and remarkably tasteful) to melt cheese over vegetables, particularly those like broccoli and cauliflower which are light in nature. In this way the properties of both the vegetables and the cheese are balanced.

Cottage cheese is probably the easiest cheese to digest and is light, cool, and nutritive. Cream cheese is a little more sticky but is also one of the better cheeses.

**Sour cream**

Sour cream is perhaps the most acidic of dairy products and can potentially aggravate many inflammatory (*pitta*) conditions including ulcers, heartburn, fevers, and infections. It is best for airy (*vata*) types.

**Butter**

Despite the additives in most butter which weaken its properties, such as coloring agents and large amounts of salt (or the pasteurizing process), butter is good for people with stronger digestion and more internal heat (*pitta* types). It should not be taken cold. It is better to melt it on the food it is taken with. Too much butter, like cheese, can clog the channels and elevate cholesterol.

Most of the problems people experience with butter are largely from its preparation. Ghee (clarified butter) made from raw butter is good for almost everyone. Compared to good ghee, much of our butter, margarine, and processed vegetable oils could also be called *tamasic* and are certainly not of any great quality. Externally, butter is good for burns and skin rashes, and it is said to improve the memory and functioning of the brain in general.

**Ghee (Clarified butter)**

Ghee is the best dairy product for human consumption. It gives strength, vitality, and intelligence. It counters fever and infection. It is easy for the liver to digest—perhaps the easiest of all the oils. It improves the immune system and promotes both longevity and awareness. It is an excellent food for mental work and meditation. It is best to take ghee with cooked vegetables or grains or in milk decoctions. (Taken directly, many oils may cause some nausea.)

Ghee is also the basis for many medicated oils like brahmi (gotu kola) ghee and calamus ghee. It can be used externally on the skin for inflammatory skin disease. It can be placed in the eyes (particularly triphala ghee) for improving vision. Turmeric ghee or turmeric cooked in ghee is one of the best foods for women and for building the blood. Ghee is useful as a lamp oil for meditation and *puja* (spiritual offerings), as its nourishing power feeds the *devas* (celestials). Ghee fires done on cow dung have a greatly purifying effect upon the environment and the mind. Ghee should preferably be made with raw, unsalted butter, and usually keeps for six months to a year.

**Buying dairy**

It is important that we exercise discrimination in our buying of dairy products. We should buy the best quality items we can find. We need to insist upon higher standards, but this does not mean that we have to reject dairy products altogether.

Try to get dairy products from companies that treat their animals well and feed them organically. Try to get raw dairy products if possible. Encourage legality of raw dairy products in your area, if they are not legal. Support your local farmers and encourage accessibility of raw dairy products in your area if they are inaccessible.

Given the sad state of most dairy products in this country, many of us may want to avoid them for this reason alone. This is certainly understandable. Still, many people, particularly those in debilitated conditions or of *vata* and *pitta* constitutions, will find regular milk useful, and it should certainly be taken before we resort to meat, fish, or other artificial foods.

Certainly the factory farm is a disaster for human health and the family farm must return. According to the Vedas, the farmers are the stomach through which vital energy is distributed throughout the entire society. On an empty stomach or one filled with toxins, society will not go very far, even with the help of computers.

We can only improve on nature if we work with nature. As it stands, our arrogance in dealing with nature, our commercial and exploitative attitude, is only going to harm us in the long run. Right now we are making money with our wrong attitudes, but this cannot profit us in the long run. We are also accumulating bad karma and wreaking havoc on the planet’s ecology. While money may rule the outer world for a time, karma is the fact we must ultimately face. In the world of truth, we must be prepared for the reaction to how we have treated the cow. We only cheat ourselves when we exploit nature; when we impose violence on nature, we only destroy our own inner peace, love, contentment and happiness. All abuse of nature is just a form of spiritual, and ultimately, collective suicide. It is not only compassion to nature that we must cultivate but concern for our own soul.

## Music - David Tame Interview

As In Music, So In Life  
An Interview With David Tame  
By Swami B V tripurari

If there is any modern conception of the nature of music, what can we say to describe it? Only that the tonal arts are thought to be based upon the intelligent generation of air vibrations, these air vibrations somehow serving to communicate various subjective moods or experiences. But if we look deeper, we realize that a society's very conception of the nature of music is itself conditioned by the general philosophical viewpoint upon which that society is based. This is most important, for it calls into question from the outset the twentieth century conception of what music is and what it does.

The modern notion (or lack of notion) of the phenomenon of music is, in short, the inevitable result of the current materialistic-reductionist world view. In this world view, music is inevitably described in terms of its most tangible, measurable aspect: that it consists of air vibrations. Also, according to this world view, human beings themselves—the very performers of and listeners to music—are merely biological machines evolved by luck, possessing no ultimate purpose for existence, and whose thoughts and emotions are nothing but biochemical processes automatically produced as conditioned reflexes to the world around them. To the materialist it naturally follows, therefore, that people only perform or listen to music in the first place because past experiences have "programmed" them to do so. At his most charitable, the materialist might grudgingly concede that these past experiences consisted of "pleasure-feelings"; that the first movement of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, in hitting this and that vibrational frequency, somehow releases stimulative chemicals into the listener's biomechanical brain. Putting it this bluntly, the materialist’s philosophy of music seems hardly sufficient. Yet the fact remains that the majority of contemporary musicians themselves do, ultimately, conceive of music in this way—as sound which entertains and gives pleasure to the brains of *homo sapiens*.

The result of this materialistic viewpoint on the music of today? A multitude of musical forms—but virtually all of them the music of, at best, materialistic humanism. A century in which, to a large degree, music has lost its way (for what direction can there possibly be to take when nothing in the universe possesses any ultimate meaning or purpose in any case?).

And yet, for perhaps two decades now there has occurred the beginning of a new awareness abroad in the world. Not only in music, but in many areas of life, among a certain minority of people there is to be found a resurgence of committed interest in matters of the spirit. Young and not so young people are frequently to be found rejecting the materialist world view outright. They seek instead to embrace a mystical outlook, and tend to do so with unswerving dedication. Some speak of a new age in which, it is said, religion will become more scientific in the best sense, and science will become more religious. Whatever the cause, that there is a new movement among some towards altruism, hope, brotherhood, and an interest in self-evolution is unmistakable.

Yet for all of our rejection of the philosophy of materialism, we have nevertheless failed to reject the music of materialism. Most forms of twentieth century music is utterly devoid of genuine regenerative spiritual value. The ancients may well have been correct in the belief that music patterns affect life patterns; and if so, then for a grassroots movement back towards spirituality to allow itself to continue to be subjected to the music of individuals who are of an entirely different frame of mind makes no logical sense. The minds of these performers are gross and coarse. To follow them while aspiring upward makes no more sense than to attempt to climb a mountain by rolling downhill. The nonmaterialist world view demands a nonmaterialist philosophy of music. And from such a philosophy, in its own good time, there will inevitably be born a new music of the spirit.

The alternative is too horrible to contemplate. From down through the decades there comes a warning to us on the dangers of wrong types of music—from none other than Henry David Thoreau, who wrote from his log cabin: “Even music can be intoxicating. Such apparently slight causes destroyed Greece and Rome, and will destroy England and America.” The modern man's reaction to Thoreau's warning is likely to be one of "Oh, but that's taking it a bit too far, isn't it?" *Yet it is precisely, absolutely at this point that twentieth century man departs from the viewpoint held by virtually every thinking person from ancient times right up to the nineteenth century (The Secret Power of Music).*

*David, you don't claim to be a musician, yet you have written a fascinating book about the power of music which has received rave reviews. What inspired you to tackle this vast subject, and to what do you attribute your success?*

Well believe it or not, I dabbled a bit in rock-and-roll in the past, but you're right, basically I'm not a musician. My goal was to adopt an interdisciplinary approach to study a number of subjects from an esoteric viewpoint, one of which was music. I thought music was the most important and it attracted me the most. In this book I brought together my knowledge of psychology, sociology, history, and astrology. I am not a musician adopting an esoteric approach to music, but an esotericist adopting a musical- and sound-oriented approach to esotericism.

After I wrote the book I sat back and waited for an onslaught of backlash. I expected that the reviewers would be very critical and uphold the idea that forms of music such as jazz and rock were good music. What amazed and encouraged me was that I got just the opposite. Although some musicians did complain, every review that I came to know about was positive or wildly enthusiastic.

It seemed that the book hit a chord within the hearts of the readers, which was a chord that I felt in myself when I first looked into the subject. It was something that I had known in my heart, but when I started to find out the facts, they reaffirmed what I had known intuitively. When I put all of the facts together and the book came out, it did the same thing for many people. It is something that we know in our hearts, but for many, needed to be put together and expressed.

*When you speak of music you are not referring to an abstract art or entertainment as most people today think of it, but as something much more profound.*

Right. It all goes back to the fact that sound itself is something far more profound than people of the twentieth century realize, and music is simply a specific use of that power which is sound. There are at least two aspects to the power of music that are verifiable in scientific terms. First, it has a profound influence upon our biological and chemical makeup, and there is considerable scientific data available to support this. Recently a Russian scientist named Aminev of Bashkir University released his findings after years of study on rock music. He found that rock-and-roll had a profound effect upon the chemistry of the body, creating a morphine-like imbalance which he called "rockamania." Once persons tune in to heavy metal, it is not just a simple decision to walk away from it, for it can be psychologically and chemically addictive. Our heartbeat, our nerves, our blood pressure, and our rate of respiration, as well as our emotions and intellect are all influenced by the music we hear.

Secondly, how music affects us psychologically, playing a major role in the formation of our character, is also observable. Psychology maintains that anything in our environment affects our character, and music is a very powerful influence within our environment. Moreover, because music affects the character of the individual, and because the individual is a unit of the society as a whole, it can be demonstrated with the help of sociology that music affects the direction of civilizations, as I have pointed out in my book.

It is the third power of music, however, that is most profound; one that as of yet may not be demonstratable. That is the power to move and even create, as the ancients believed that the world itself is a product of sound, and that through the right sounds one could transcend the world.

*How did ancient civilizations view music?*

The ancients believed that music and sound are an esoterically powerful creative and sacred force, and that with sound we can create, preserve, and destroy. In what you might call the classic ancient civilizations, such as India and China, music was used consciously to preserve and evolve the social structure. It was used not only to maintain the status quo, but to improve conditions, and as a means of evolving human consciousness. They believed that music is magic. You can't really separate sound from magic. Their idea was that through sound and music we could keep life on Earth below aligned with that which is above.

*While I think that most persons, if they stopped to think about it, would agree with what you’re saying—and many would even agree with the view of the sages of bygone days—they do not regard music as did the ancients in terms of practical day-to-day living. How have we arrived at our present-day regard for music principally as art and entertainment?*

After ancient times, after the life of Christ, there was not as deep an understanding of the power and purpose of music as there was in ancient times, but basically people realized that music was something sacred which affected the character of man. This continued right through medieval times and up to the time of the classical music of Bach and Beethoven. It was only really towards the end of the last century, just over 100 years ago, that materialism first began to rub off on musicians, and subsequently the materialism of the "new" musicians rubbed off on civilization.

What happened at that time was partly a forgetting of the higher divine purpose of music, and a change of intent on the part of new musicians. Although we don't think of Beethoven and Bach as saints but as great musicians, their actual intent in all of their composing was spiritual. The change was that music began to be appreciated in terms of its artistic or technical side regardless of its effect on society: "art for its own sake," something the ancients carefully guarded against.

Rather than being triangular in the sense of describing the relationship between humankind, nature, and God as did Beethoven's works, music became a description of the horizontal relationship between humankind and nature at best. Secular musician's "truth"—which is really only the expression of one's own self-centered outlook or personality—replaced music of the Self, or the expression of divinity. All of this has taken place gradually over the past century to the point that all sorts of rubbish sound combinations are considered artistically valid, and much of our music today is not even neutral in content, but negative "bad music." Again, good and bad here is not merely an artistic consideration, but a consideration of the influence of the music upon our consciousness.

*So you have evolved an objective criteria by which one can place value judgements upon music beyond what it sounds like to the outer ear?*

On the one hand you have the components of music such as style, rhythm, melody, and harmony, and on the other you have the intent behind it. Both things must be considered, but of the two the intent is more important. You can take a particular rhythm that is, in terms of its components, negative, such as heavy metal, and yet find that it may not always have a negative effect. What really determines the value of music is something that comes before the actual component of the music. It's the original birth of the feeling or emotion of the musician or composer, whether it’s conscious or simply an unconscious feeling.

I like Plato's criteria for art. He spoke of the three inseparable sisters: Beauty, Truth, and Goodness. Much of our modern music is an attempt to separate these three from one another. Thus we are invited to embrace a doctrine of aesthetics in which not only have morality and spirituality been discarded as unnecessary, but no firm standards of any form whatsoever remain; "do your own thing." The objective view—that music affects people and society—is not appreciated today because it demands of the artist a sense of moral responsibility. Plato was only one of the earliest of many commentators who have pointed out that the only freedom which is aesthetically viable in music is that which is married to self-discipline, otherwise freedom becomes a recipe for anarchy.

Truth we usually think of as being something intellectual, something we can prove. But if music is beautiful it has a quality of truth. It will be beautiful because it is aligned with the music of the seers and the harmony of the heavens. When music is ugly or bad it is an imperfect rendition of divine sound, and threfore it is "untruthful." We don't use the words “good” and “evil” so much these days. We would much rather say someone is misled rather than evil. But I would like to see these words reapplied to music. I would like to see the realization that if one's music is evil, then there must certainly be seeds of evil in the performer. At some level every musician knows his or her motives and surely the potential power of his or her music to influence others.

*So the physical sound one makes could be “good” while the intent behind it is “bad” or vice versa, and all of this must be considered.*

Yes. Addressing the subject of intent, experiments performed by Dorothy Retallack, who is probably the most well-known researcher on the study of the effect of music upon plants, are very interesting. In studying the effect of music upon plants you rule out any kind of psychological influence, so that the experiment is, in a sense, more objective. The effects are actual physical effects that can be monitored. Retallack found that playing similar melodies like heavy metal and a somewhat similar fast-paced oriental melody had opposite effects. She concluded that the subtle influence of intent within the music was the determining factor, although she could not isolate the intent.

Some time later in the ‘80s, Manford Clynes discovered a microstructure in music. The macrostructure is what you would write on the score, but the microstructure is something that we are not consciously aware of. It consists of the kind of wave shape of a note, the character of a sound, which he demonstrated was dependent on intent. Good music, while comprised of certain components, as is bad music, ultimately goes back to the character of the musician. His or her character will shape the kind of music he or she plays. It shapes the microstructure of the music and its objective effect upon the listener. Good music also generally involves a passing of the torch, so to speak. It has a spiritual background and hierarchy. In India for example, a disciple is trained by a teacher who is in effect a musical guru coming from a long-established lineage.

*So jazz, blues, and rock-and-roll are not part of the evolution of good music?*

Hardly. It has been well documented in my book that all three of these types of music have their roots in Africa's voodoo culture. "Jazz" is an African word for sex, and "rock-and-roll" is a translation of an African phrase for sex. From voodoo comes jazz and then comes blues. When you mix blues with country-western music you get rock. When I wrote *The Secret Power of Music*, originally I had a long treatment on rock. But I realized it would make the book too long, so I divided it into two, and the treatment on rock is coming out as a separate book entitled *Rock and Role* later this year.

*But nowadays there are many rock musicians who maintain that their message is a spiritual one.*

I can only reply in general because I don't know many of them personally. What I have found very often is that those who gravitate towards very avant-garde experimental music with heavy rhythms have a deficient view of what is spiritual. But I don't mean to say that there could not be someone who is generally spiritual who played some form of rock. One problem we have is that spiritually degenerate music is so widespread today. Most of us were raised on it rather than on classical music, what to speak of the music of the ancients. So it’s quite possible for someone who is highly spiritually developed to find himself in this musical genre.

My own experience, however, is that when I became interested in spiritual things, before I even really realized that music had any effect, I could no longer put up with heavy rhythms, and I found myself attracted to Gregorian chants and Indian music. For the most part rock, properly understood, is music warfare waged upon an unsuspecting society by guitar gunners who are frequently aware of their power to influence, and who do not have the best of intentions. I have dealt with this extensively in my upcoming book.

*What do you see as the basic difference between Eastern and Western classical music?*

The difference is basically the same as that between the two societies, Eastern and Western civilization. Western symphony music is linear in that it has a definite beginning, such as the overture, followed by a movement of tension towards an end, the climax. This parallels Western civilization, which tends to be moving towards certain evolutionary goals. Eastern classical music is *mantric* or circular and doesn't necessarily have features that are recognizable as a beginning or end. Tibetan or Indian music is more passive, more static, and the society that surrounds it is not so much goal-oriented or constantly seeking change as we do in the West.

*What do you consider "new age" music?*

I consider the work of the great classical composers such as Beethoven, Bach, and in the nineteenth century, Wagner, not to be old-fashioned, but music for a new age. There are some musicians in the twentieth century who are engaged in the musical expression of the capital "S" Self music, but the vast majority are not. Until the ‘70s, when some people began to desire to create a new age music, all forms of music have been at best what I call horizontal, or materialistic in an innocuous sense, if not vertical with an arrow pointing down rather than up, as did the music of the great classical composers and the ancients. Classical music did not change into the new electric avant-garde music; it simply ended.

In the latter part of the '80s what's called new age music did improve a lot. But the true music of the new age will have to be as artistically valid and perhaps even greater than the classical tradition of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. In other words, it must be real music. Most of the so-called new age musicians today know that their music is really just new age Muzak. There is nothing wrong with new age Muzak, but the point is to realize that that's all it is.

There is also negative new age music—the more electric science fiction sort of noises and things like that—but all of the recordings of piano, acoustic guitar, and gentle sounds of nature, etc. are fine, although they don't really go too far in the spiritual direction. What really happened during the birth of new age music was that there was a market gap. Rock had become too noisy for most of the baby boom generation and this Muzak helped to fill the gap. It’s a kind of practice music, the kind of thing that one usually didn't record, but people liked it and bought it. It's sometimes even a little uplifting, but it’s not going to bring about a real new age. It’s something to relax to, but spiritual life is not just a matter of relaxing. Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony is not really relaxing; it’s challenging and intense.

*What direction would you like to see things go in the near future?*

What I would like to see in the future is scientific research into the *objective* effects of different kinds of music, work such as Dorothy Retallack's research with plants. The other side of the coin is to find musicians who are spiritually advanced enough to know these things. I think people today need to better understand what life is really about in order to be able to appreciate what good music really is. If enough people understood the goal of life, that it is a spiritual goal, much of today's popular music would be out of business. Rock is still with us, but it fizzled out somewhat in the '80s. Nothing new really happened in rock in the '80s, and people are looking elsewhere.

It is often thought that the music we have available to us as recordings and on the radio are there according to market demand, but I don't believe that that is the whole story, and there are examples of how new record labels and new radio stations have *created* a market by introducing something new. So if morally and spiritually healthy forms of music can be produced and find outlets, there will definitely be a market for them, and we can begin to lift twentieth century music out of its present low point.

I don't believe the suppression of harmful or negative music is the answer. Humanity needs to exercise free will, even if it should bring about the downfall of our present society, which I truly believe rock might accomplish and has already accomplished to a large extent over the last 30 years. But the real answer is to offer sufficient higher alternatives, and this will be the real new age music.

As for what new age music will be, I think once people were waiting for and expecting entirely new musical forms, new sounds and timbers, the invention of new musical instruments and so forth. Well, all of that will probably happen, but new age music will really be distinguishable by its high mystical spirit. Given that high degree of spirituality, any form of music can be utilized to contain it: symphonic, folk, or something quite new. Ultimately new age music can only come forth when we have well-trained musicians who are also of very high spiritual caliber. Somehow along the line that caliber has for the most part been lost. When we get that genuine spirituality back, new age music will naturally follow.

*David Tame is an aspiring esotericist, author, and regular contributor to* Critique. *He presently resides in London.*

## Music - What the Musicians are Saying

## Robbie Gass

Although I am a musician, I have another life as well. My background in clinical psychology finds me teaching, lecturing, consulting, working with death and dying, establishing hospices, working with AIDS, and more. But music is my secret weapon. I find it has a power to tap into the layers of consciousness the way no other tool does. I find all types of clever ways to fit my music into almost all of my work, and I have found that it gives people I work with a greater sense of time and space, and often opens their hearts.

I was trained as a classical musician at Harvard, and later I got involved in rock professionally, and now I am a new age musician. New age music was originally conceived to have an esoteric and spiritual purpose, but to some degree now new age has become a marketing term rather than a philosophical one. Now, because there is a commercial market for new age music, many different things are being called new age music. I'm from the "old school" of new age music. My music with Wings of Song is in a sense too overtly spiritual to be too commercially viable, although it is selling quite well now.

Bach's music was also overtly spiritual. During his time practically all music was church music. Yet I think that to call his and the music of the other great classical musicians new age would be insulting. Their music is spiritual because it's sublime, and the level of its beauty reaches to a height that transports the listener to a spiritual state. New age music is much less ambitious musically. It tends to be relatively simple. It's not less musical, but it arises out of a different vision of music. The greatest classical composers like Beethoven and Bach, although different in style, wanted to go to the heights of musical depths and complexity and find a beauty and transcendence in that peak of musical expression. My recording of "Om Namo Shivaya" is at the other end of musical complexity. There was a time when I was a student of classical music that I would have dismissed this recording as a joke because of its lack of musical complexity. But classical music is designed to be an aesthetic experience which brings about uplifting spiritual sentiments, whereas good new age music is specifically *designed* to be a consciousness-uplifting experience, as well as an aesthetically appealing one. New age music aesthetically does not compare to classical music, but it's not supposed to.

Our chanting series is also not meant to be an authentic Eastern rendition of chanting mantras. It is more in line with a new American tradition of chanting that has developed. We take a traditional Eastern melody and then blend it with all sorts of other musical influences—say, twentieth-century Western folk accompaniment and harmonic interpretation—and in this way it becomes new age music. The blending of music that is going on in the world today is an example of cultures making love to one another. I think there is a lot of spirituality in this type of cultural exchange. And I don't think new age music has a monopoly on what's exciting that's happening in music.

I think that one of the most beautiful things about music is that it doesn't matter what the listener thinks or what their consciousness is; he or she will be influenced by the music they listen to. Music has been a bridge for me to spiritual life—it's "the singing of angels."

## Jonathan Goldman

Intent is what is most important in the creation of music. Wherever you are when you create a piece of music—physically, mentally, emotionally, and spiritually—that is all frozen in the piece of music and perceived by the listener on a very subtle level. It's important for musicians to understand this. There are only a few people in the field of commercial music who are conscious of music and sound as healing tools. A lot of the workshops that I've done demonstrated that often the people most reticent to find out about music's power to heal are musicians. This is because it means taking responsibility for the power and energy they are creating, and most do not want to do that. They are more interested in going for the big break and big bucks. What they don't realize, however, is that they *are* responsible; they *do* get a reaction for the musical influence they unleash.

I am a musician, but I consider myself a theacher who works with the transformative energies of sound and music, and I like to differentiate between the two. Sounds are singular tone frequencies that do not modulate with rhythm or frequency. Creating therapeutic music involves adding the muse to the type of sounds that bring about healing.

Today any sense of music's power to heal is reduced to the simple use of music for the release of endorphins, stress reduction, and relaxation, and its potential to entrain heartbeat, respiration and brain waves, but there is much more to music than that. The ancient civilizations maintained that every illness is a musical problem. Perhaps the only culture that has kept this sense intact is that of the Hindus, whose musical *ragas* are sensitive to the movements of the stars. Our task in music today lies in rediscovering what the ancient mystery schools knew long ago. Nowadays we need to validate what they've said in terms of modern scientific findings in order to get musical treatment into the places where it is really needed, such as hospitals and nursing homes.

What's an example of therapeutic music? All types of music may have *some* therapeutic potential. Michael Jackson may be therapeutic to kids suffering from a burn by way of taking their minds off the pain. Sometimes we need to hear fast music rather than relaxing new age music to be alert. Any form or genre of music has healing potential. We cannot stereotype "healing music" if we want to create a sonic prescription for the many different types of people in the world. Someone may wake well to German marching bands, while another to the sound of birds chirping. New age music deals mainly with water and air, while rock-and-roll deals principally with fire. Sometimes for proper balancing one who has an overactive water influence may need to hear fire music.

Of course there is also discordant sound. Sound which is discordant or disharmonic is detrimental to our health, and harmonically-created sounds are beneficial. The principle of resonant healing is at the basis of using sound as a therapeutic tool. Modern physics has verified that we are all vibrating atoms and subatomic particles. Every atom in the universe takes its characteristics from the pitch, patterns, and overtones of a particular frequency. Everything is a resonant frequency. Every part of our bodies have resonant frequencies. Illness is the body behaving out of tune; the application of harmonizing frequencies can bring the body back into tune. We are all wonderful symphonies of the self, although some of us are at present playing somewhat out of tune.

## Steven Halpern

Classically-oriented critics tend to put down "new age" music because it does not conform to the traditional Western compositional structures of tension, release, and resolution. By their myopic definition, Vedic music and much of the indigenous music from the rest of the world wouldn't qualify as "music." I love and appreciate the masters of Western classical music and see no need to ignore one form of music in order to enjoy another. Any ethnocentric attitude that excludes most of the world's music, or any evolutionary art forms like new age music, should be seen for what it is.

In a sense, we are only witnessing the continuation of a tradition that seeks to castigate a new art form. Beethoven and Brahms were the "new age musicians" of their time. Many other masters who we recognize today were severely criticized in their day. I wouldn't classify their music as "new age music" today, however. New age music would seem to be more appropriately applied to music that is new in terms of compositional structure, instrumental textures and timbres, and its expanded sense of space and time. Indeed, it is music that has been created as an artistic expression of the needs of our times.

Authentic new age music is created to bring the listener into greater attunement with his/her higher self and the universe. Much of the best new age music puts the brain into an *alpha* or *theta* brainwave state, whereas Beethoven puts most listeners into a *beta* brainwave. Whether it's better to be *beta* with Beethoven or *alpha* with Halpern is not the issue. The point is that they evoke different states, and the latter represents something new for our time (although quite ancient in Vedic contexts).

New age music may include a blend of classical elements along with either contemporary or ancient music, but it is more than that. Music is a carrier wave of consciousness. True new age music can only be played by a performer who is "in tune" himself. And this is why we have so much inferior "new age" music today: the economic opportunities have attracted artists and record labels with no inner experience to draw upon. They can play the notes, but there's nobody home. For them, using this label assures them of extra sales, but diminishes the integrity of the field and undermines the efforts of truly dedicated artists. For that matter though, let us not forget that there is a great deal of inferior classical, jazz, rock, and pop available today as well as the superior manifestations.

In the field of pop, rock, and certain sub-genres of new age, we are already seeing a blending of different elements into a “world music.” I know that that trend will continue to flourish and become even more interesting.

As for authentic (non-pop or neo-disco) new age music, I believe that its future lies in enabling us to more effectively fine tune our "human instruments" and enhance our feeling of well-being and atonement. Music has always been a wonderful tool for self-orchestrating on the spectrum of consciousness. In these days, as we seek legal non-drug alternatives, it seems self-evident that this form of music is here to serve us in a similar way that the ancient Vedic music served the Vedic civilization.

## Paul Horn

I don't consider myself to belong to any particular genre of music. I am just a musician. Record companies have to categorize musicians in order to evaluate them, but as far as I am concerned my music is always evolving, and I'm simply Paul Horn the musician. Throughout my career my music has been influenced largely by the spirituality of India and the sounds of Indian music. And because I have had the good fortune to travel all over the world, my music has been influenced by other cultures as well. Music is my life and spirituality is the basis of my life. My music is thus an extension of who I am, my values, my spirituality, my conception of God, etc.

Music is probably the most valuable commodity on the face of the Earth. I say that because it's the basis of all manifest creation. All manifestation comes from sound. According to Indian philosophy "Om" is the basic vibration from which everything emanates. We are vibrations; physically speaking, we are sound. Music is thus sacred, and it is only recently in the history of humanity that music has been used for secular purposes. Previously music was almost all devotional. It was only toward the end of Bach's life that secular music began to really take hold and people began to look to music for emotional satisfaction rather than spiritual upliftment. And of course today it has largely become just entertainment and has thus drifted very far away from the view of music as sacred and as a healing force. Not that music for entertainment is not also valid, but the idea that that's all that it is is very misleading. The sense of this was well known to the ancients, and we are perhaps just beginning to revive it. This is going on both inside and outside the realm of new age music—in all musical genres, among therapists, meditators, and others. It is the responsibility of a musician to become aware of this, and to make it the basis for his or her music. Personally I think music is again headed in the right direction. More and more musicians today around the world are beginning to view music in light of its higher purpose.

There used to be very strict laws as to what tones could be used and which ones could not. The Greeks *legislated* so that sounds that were dissonant would not be played. Of course we would be horrified at this today, our sense of freedom being what it is. "How dare you tell me what music I can play." But when you get right down to it, certain sounds *are* dissonant. When you use these sounds they affect the entire body, mind, and consciousness negatively. Of course I don't claim to have all the knowledge of the ancients, but I think these things are important to discuss.

When I play nowadays my ego isn't there, at least not in the way it used to be. I am not concerned with the reviews, I just play what comes through me. I am not consciously trying to preach or heal; I just play, and my spirituality comes through. I am playing to tune the main instrument which is me—to purify myself. I just came from a retreat. I meditate and perform spiritual practices and try to understand what are the important values in life and bring them into my music.

## Mystic Powers

## Demystifying Mystic Powers

*Is Power the Goal of Yoga?*

There was a time when answers to the majority of the questions about human nature and the world we live in were considered unknowable. Many of the workings of material nature that we understand today were at one time explained as miracles. In the field of medicine, *ad hoc* cures requiring "divine intervention" have today been replaced with routine medical procedures performed by practitioners of a different faith. Modern science has systematically demystified much of the world. But there are many mysteries yet to be explained. The supernatural powers possessed by advanced practitioners of yoga are one example.

The subject of mystic power always draws an audience. The recently published *Modern Miracles* of Erlendur Haraldsson, in which Dr. Haraldsson undertakes an investigative study of the psychic phenomena surrounding Sai Baba, an Indian mystic famous for displays of magical powers, was sold out almost everywhere I tried to purchase it.

In India, yogis have been exhibiting mystic feats for centuries and many of their accomplishments have been documented. The ancient literature of that country is filled with accounts of persons possessing supernatural powers. This information often fascinates Westerners, and even today anyone with sufficient interest can go to the Himalayan foothills and observe the wonderful prowess of India's yogis. Many people are doing just that in search of power through yoga.

The *siddhis* or mystic powers of yogis are many and of varying degrees. At a glance they are quite desirable. Would you like to be able to change your shape at will, appear in up to eight different places simultaneously or suddenly turn invisible? Who hasn't desired to know the future or read another's mind? What about attaining bodily strength like that of an elephant without having to look like Mr. America? Care to talk with other species? These are all only a few of the secondary yogic perfections. Shall I go on?

Unlike the above mentioned feats, which are also common to various indigenous cultures and shamanistic in nature, the yoga system speaks of eight mystic perfections (*asta siddhi*), which upon achieving one is often thought to have attained Godhood. In his *Yoga Sutras*, Patanjali Muni distinguishes these mystic perfections from the above mentioned lesser yogic perfections.

In India it is common for people who are only slightly accomplished in mystic yoga to advertise themselves as God. Aside from the fact that the idea of *becoming* God seems to contain inherently contradictory notions, these *siddhis* are indeed extraordinary, bordering Godliness, at least in the sense of God's power potential. However, God, it would seem, is much more than merely powerful. Perhaps his lovable aspect, his beauty and charm, is his better side, something not concomitant with the attainment of mystic power. Rather mystic power accompanies Godhead incidentally.

It is more accurate to say that accomplished yogis are merely tapping into their own mystic power rather than becoming God. After all, the living force is a mystery. How is it that a lemon tree can produce citric acid? Life producing chemicals; it is a mystery. So much so that scientists are trying to prove the opposite: life comes from chemicals. What is the ingredient that makes matter come to life? What is the power of the living force? Can anyone explain it? In this sense every soul has mystic power. The yoga system simply develops the mystic power already present in the practitioner. It doesn't turn the practitioner into God.

Before we discuss the eight *maha siddhis*, let's examine the dynamics of yogic attainment by which any of the above mentioned supernatural powers are acquired. The yogic model of the mind is different than that of modern science. In the scientific community the mind is really nothing more than neurological eruptions, another part of our biophysical makeup. Modern psychology is considered the study of the mind, but for the most part it seeks to cure mental disease by prescribing chemicals that affect the centers of the brain. In modern psychology, the mind is not an independent level of reality interacting with the body, rather it is a not yet very well understood aspect of our biology and ultimately our physiology. Parapsychologists and perhaps transpersonal psychologists are venturing on to what science would term thin ice—the study of the mind as an independent level of our reality, independent of our body.

While psychology explores the conscious mind in dream and waking states and the unconscious or subconscious aspect of the mind as well, yoga deals with still another dimension of the mind—the superconscious level. Yoga is the complete science of the mind (although when we use the term "science" it must be understood in terms of its etymology and not merely the severely limited notions it conjures up in our present day and age). The prevailing "scientific" outlook recognizes psychology due to psychology’s willingness to conform to the existing scientific framework, whereas parapsychology and now perhaps transpersonal psychology are seen as renegade quackery. And yoga, the complete science of the mind, is yet to be distinguished in some Western minds from its dietary associate, yogurt.

In yoga terminology *samyama* refers to mental exercise that awakens the superconscious and thus supernatural ability, which is only supernatural in terms of the popular conception of "natural," i.e. observable physical events. Seen otherwise (in terms of a broader conception of the nature of life) these powers are considerably demystified.

Before being able to perform *samyama,* the yoga practitioner must pass through five external processes: forming an ethical foundation (*yama and niyama*), mastering sitting postures (*asana*), controlling the breath (*pranayama*), and withdrawing attention from sense objects (*pratyahara*). *Samyama* refers to the last three aspects of the eightfold yoga system: *dharana, dhyana* and *samadhi*. These three stages are so similar that they overlap one another. Thus while practicing *dharana* (concentration) one slips into *dhyana* (meditation) and *samadhi,* or trance. Because these three are so similar, their threefold practice is addressed singularly as *samyama*.

When one’s conscious mind is peaceful (undisturbed by the senses and their objects) and one’s subconscious is subdued, one can perform *samyama.* The very nature of the mind is to penetrate an object, as this writer's mind is penetrating both the subject and the mind of the reader. By exercising *samyama* on a particular object, the object is penetrated in a heightened sense resulting in comprehension of the object *en toto*. Thus the essence of that object becomes known.

For example, when yogis perform *samyama* concentrating on hot coals, not only do they come to know the phenomenon of combustion, but they are able to identify the psychochemical process of combustion in the coals with that of the "fire" in the human body as well as that of the sun. The yogis thus penetrate the nature of fire on three levels, the astral (sun), the biological (human body), and the physical (the coals). They then reduce these three to a common denominator—material nature as the fire element. Their mental absorption on the material element of fire results in full *comprehension* or mastery of fire. Yogis therefore find no difficulty walking on fire.

The *Yoga Sutras* describe the relationships between various pairs of objects and what corresponding supernatural power one can attain by performing *samyama* on those objects. Thus by *samyama* on the relationship of body and space, one achieves levitation. By *samyama* on physical changes, changes in character, and changes of states of the world, one achieves knowledge of the past and future. By *samyama* on word analysis, one can understand the intentions of all species. By *samyama* on the psychic mechanism, one can read others' minds. By *samyama* on the form and color of the body, the yogi can disappear at will. By *samyama* on power, one achieves great strength, and by *samyama* on the sun, one gains knowledge of the universe.These are but a few examples outlined in the *Sutras*. Some discussion of these powers may reveal a practical side to them, thus demystifying them even in terms of the material conception of life. With regard to the *maha siddhis,* we will also attempt to see through the mystery of their mastery or at least examine their usefulness, thus putting them in proper perspective.

## Levitation

Within our bodies there are many electromagnetic forces, which are the same forces that govern other objects within space up to the stars and planets. The earth is said to move, despite its weight and massive size, at a rate of nineteen miles per second. It moves so, as do the other planets, on account of its being directly connected to gravitational and electromagnetic forces. Our bodies are indirectly connected with these forces. If we can directly connect our bodies with these forces through *samyama,* the power to travel in space is achieved.

Besides this physical levitation there is psychic levitation. Of the two, the latter is more important. If the psyche is in levitation (centered on elevating thoughts) this upward movement of the mind enables one to overcome physical attractions, which are the cause of suffering. When mental levitation slackens, one is maladjusted. When it is heightened one can function psychically at the speed of mind and travel faster than the speed of light. As the mind can go anywhere in a moment, so the yogi can mount the mental chariot and tangibly experience distant places.

## Knowledge of Past, Present and Future

The study of cause and effect is the infallible method of psychological analysis. The cause can be inferred from its effect while the effect can be understood from its cause. By studying the present, which is the effect of the past, one can know about one's past. Similarly, by knowing the present, which is the cause of the future effect, one can know what is yet to come. Through merging cause into effect and effect into cause, the yogi finds continuity, and thus time is transcended.

As the body can move in any direction in space, so the mind can move in any direction, not only in space but in time as well. The body can move forward in time as seen in the aging process, but it cannot move backward in time. The mind, however, can move backward in time, as it were, as in the case of mental regression wherein one "relives" one's childhood.

## Mind Reading

The mind is not bound by corporal laws. The psyche, which controls the movements of the body, also determines how the mind works. If one knows the laws that govern the mind, one can know others' minds in the same way that one knows one's own mind. People cannot read others' minds only because they cannot read their own.

Through deductive and inductive inference, one can also read minds to some extent. This is the method pursued by the psychoanalysts, who penetrate the minds of their patients. Again, it can be said that penetration is the very nature of the mind. Thus one who masters one’s own mental faculty can penetrate the minds of others.

## Invisibility

There are many things that we cannot see although they are all around us. Vision of anything depends on the eyes receiving the reflection of light from the object of sight. Without that reflection, objects remain invisible. The body is made up of atoms. It becomes visible to the eye of another because it possesses color, which is reflected in the presence of light. If one can check the perception of the color of the body by reducing the threshold of the perception of reflective light, one can in effect disappear.

## Maha Siddhis

The *maha siddhis* are also referred to as *asta siddhi* or eight mystic powers. These eight are particularly singled out from other lesser powers which are but partial manifestations of the same.

*Anima* is the power to make oneself small, so much so that one can enter into the atom or *anu* (smallest particle). *Laghima* is the power to make oneself lighter than air. Levitation is a partial development of this *siddhi*. *Mahima* or *garima* refers to the power to make oneself large, to expand in space, or to become heavy and immovable. *Prapti siddhi* refers to the ability to "touch the moon" or to acquire items from distant places. *Prapti* literally means "acquisition." Yogis are often known for their ability to "manifest" out-of-season fruits or small items of jewelry. This is really the power of acquisition rather than the power to manifest something from nothing. *Isita* is the power to create or destroy at will. *Vasita* is the power not only to penetrate and know others' minds but to control others’ minds as well. *Prakamya* is the ability to create wonderful effects within the scope of nature, and *kamavasayita* refers to the power to do things that contradict nature. All of these *siddhis* are indeed wonderful, yet on closer scrutiny it is apparent that they are not as desirable as one might think. This is in fact the statement of Patanjali Muni himself.These powers are really only side effects of the practice of yoga and not the goal. They are not something to be sought after, for if that is one's intention, the pursuit of God consciousness will be checked, and God consciousness is the very goal of yoga—union in love of God.

Modern science, our doubting Thomas, might consider that the accomplishments of the mystic yogis are the perfection of many of science's pursuits on the gross material plane. Most of the eight great *siddhis* have already been accomplished by modern technology to some extent. *Anima*, for example, the ability to enter into stone, has been achieved in the form excavating the earth through which man mines valuable minerals and creates subways (now homes for America's homeless, especially during the winter months).

*Laghima*, the power to walk on water and become lighter than air, has also been accomplished by modern technology, which can float huge ships across vast oceans and fly heavy machinery high in the sky. Similarly, in relation to acquisition (*prapti siddhi*), thanks to modern technology, what item from any distant place is not available for the person who has a sufficient bank balance? In America have we not become accustomed to enjoying fruits that not to speak of being out of season here, do not even grow in our country? Modern technology has made both the world smaller and our experience greater. Some see this as a kind of "spirituality." Actually, following this course leads to just the opposite—worldliness—as is the case with the pursuit of similar powers in the extended context of yoga.

The ability of the yogi to control the minds of others, *vasita*, by which many who are partially accomplished in the art speak nonsense and enamor the less intelligent with pseudo "yoga philosophy," has been perfected perhaps even more by modern man than any yogi. George Orwell's "1984" has come and gone leaving us with a sigh of relief. But Adulos Huxley's *Brave New World* has come to pass. The "medium is *more* than the message," and that's not such good news. Just turn on the television. Who's in charge? It would be prudent to suggest that we not underestimate the mystic power of the nightly newscast.

Practically there are parallels in the modern world of all the mystic accomplishments, although admittedly they are for the most part manifest in crude form. This observation, however, should serve to help demystify mystic powers, which amount to nothing more than the soul's inherent power to *subtly* manipulate matter. At the same time, exploring the potential subtle power of the soul may lead to a greater appreciation of the soul itself and from there to fulfillment. In light of this, it would be wise for modern men and women to reconsider the materialist conception of reality that they foolishly wave with the flag of empiricism.

The soul unfettered by the gross and subtle material coverings has immense power. Its full expression is not the power to control and manipulate matter and mind but the power to love. The power to love is achieved when one learns to love God—which is the very goal of yoga.

## New Age

Do we have the liberty to create new spiritual axioms in the name of enlightened Thinking?

In Search of the New Age  
By Swami B V Tripurari

By now the term "New Age" is part of the vocabulary of practically every American. A consistent definition of the term, however, is not as commonplace.

For the most part, the New Age—a recent name-tag given by the media—has meant a class of people of diverse interests united by common values. Marilyn Ferguson, social critic and author of The Aquarian Conspiracy, whose best-seller has been dubbed "The Handbook of the New Age" by USA Today, sees a New Age that has as its members those who espouse an underlying holistic philosophy. They attempt to see the interrelationship of problems instead of mechanistically viewing each problem separately. They emphasize decentralization of power with the view to promote the develop- ment of whole individuals and tend to view things globally by keeping the long-range interests of the planet in mind.

Ferguson sees many smaller movements and individuals as members of the much larger New Age social phenomenon. Although it is often thought of as a movement arising out of a spiritual foundation, many of the major influences have come from humanistic psychology. For example, the human potential movement of the '60s and '70s epitomized by psychologists like Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow are largely responsible for laying the foundation of the fundamental optimism which pervades New Age thought.

The movement's spiritual credentials are more directly questioned by Jonathon Adolph, senior editor of New Age Magazine. In a recent article written for the 1988 Guide to New Age Living, Adolph asserts that the claim that spirituality underlies the New Age phenomenon has been problematic and "a source of much confusion regarding the new age in general." He says, "The new age is not a religion," and he questions what is meant by spirituality by the many who loosely use the term.

However, the latest rising star on the New Age horizon—trance chan- nelers—have difficulty with the aforementioned concept of the New Age. They would like to deify it. Although the more down-to-earth humanistic New Age advocates recognize the "new spiritualists" to be members of the New Age family, more and more they are seeking to disassociate themselves from them, giving them a place on the fringe. Much to the embarrassment of long-standing members, the media recently has given more attention to this "fringe" element than it has to the entire New Age movement in the last decade.

A few weeks ago, Time magazine dedicated one of its covers to the New Age starring Shirley MacLaine. The thrust of the article dealt with the latest booming industry within the New Age—channeling—followed by crystals, surrounded by an aura of an old age said to have gone by. Many may have thought it unfair for Time to have characterized the entire New Age as a paranormal quasi-spiritual good way to make a fast buck, but the fact is that millions of people are becoming enamored by the prospect of quick-fix cosmic cures to the problems facing humanity.

What attracts people to the not-so-new spirituality is difficult to say. Channeling, for example, has been around since time immemorial. It has generally appealed to lower-class sections of society, and is prominent in many third world countries. In Brazil it is known as Macumba, and although most of the country is officially Catholic, unofficially Macumba is practically the national religion. While the poorer sections are open about it, the aristo- cratic class is equally involved behind closed doors. Haiti and many African nations are also heavily influenced by a type of spiritualism involving chan- neling, and one would be hard-pressed to find a culture where its influence was altogether absent.

Channeling was also spoken of by the Greek philosophers Plato, Aris- totle, and Socrates.1 Some say that those channeled insights had much to do with the shaping of the basic principles of Western law.2 President Lincoln invited the famous medium Andrew Jackson Davis to the White House and his channeled information inspired Lincoln to sign the Emancipation Proclamation.3

Channelers tell us that the popularity of channeling in America today is due to the new information that is being channeled to a people now ready for enlightenment, a people whose time has come.

Leaving aside the American way of marketing as another possibility of channeling's popularity, it is true that the information that New Age persons receive from channeled entities is different than the type of information sought after and received in many third world countries. Global prophecies, stock market predictions, and technological insights, for example, have replaced information about finding lost loves, catching unfaithful partners, and speaking with deceased relatives. Moreover, the new information is the news of a spiritual time to come and a new spirituality: a New Age. Just how accurate the new information is, however, is subject to suspicion, especially when it contradicts many of the spiritual truths held by persons of exemplary character for centuries.

Several popular channeled entities have labeled the traditional tran- scendentalists who have walked amongst us as members of the "old spiritual age." Although it is commonly understood that actions speak louder than words, these new New Age leaders, while speaking at considerable length, remain in such a state that their actions cannot be observed. In fact, those who channel the entities generally insist that they cannot even be held accountable for their own actions!

The "old spiritual age," however, has already spoken of channeling and the method by which the physically embodied can approach the disem- bodied, as well as what type of result such communication can be expected to produce. Throughout the entirety of revealed scripture in every major reli- gious tradition, channeling is referred to. The Old Testament considers chan- nelers as bad company. "Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, who practices divination or sorcery, interprets omens, engages in witchcraft or casts spells, or who is a medium or spiritu- alist or consults the dead" (Deuteronomy 18:10,11). And in the Bhagavad Gita we find: "Those who worship the demigods will take birth among the demi- gods; those who worship the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship ghosts and spirits will take birth among such beings; and those who worship Me will live with Me."(B.G. 9:25). From this sampling of verses it would appear that channeling is somewhat less than divine.

Of course channeling as it is known today is not to be confused with the inspired side of a saint through which revealed scripture is manifested. The willingness of God to move the pen of man depends on man's utter willingness to serve the will of God, devoid of any tinge of self-interest. The pens of the apostles of Christ, the inspired writings of Vyasadeva, the author of the Vedas, and Mohammed's Koran have left the world with timeless wisdom. Their inspired followers exemplify a wholesale dedication to the inspired word and its singular author whose message appears in various forms in accordance with time and circumstances. Possessed of that spirit, they are capable of shedding "new light" on the revealed truth; new light in the sense of not throwing out the words that have come before, but merely shining a brighter light on the same words. With the addition of the sun, the rose can be seen to bloom. That, however, is a far cry from suddenly replacing the rose with a dandelion. There is no doubt that God has spoken to man and so have ghosts. The two are not synonymous.

According to the Vedas, the mental world is the background of the physical realm. It is like a vast body of water, while the physical world can be compared to ice. Ice is a temporary transformation of water under certain conditions. The mental plane is far more accommodating than the physical. For example, if we look around the room we're in, we see so many objects. But how many of them can we physically take with us? By mental exercise, however, we can accommodate everything in the room and take it with us wherever we go. It is said that work is done in the mind. It is only later carried out through the senses. The mind is more subtle than the body, but more powerful. However, the mental world is not the divine world. God knows what evil lurks in the minds of men...(and most of us have some idea as well).

Above the mind is the intelligence, the power of discrimination. Although with the help of the mind I may determine that something is pleasing, with the help of the intelligence I may override that limited mental conception and determine that even though the mind says something is good, it may not really be good for me. The height of intellectual exercise is to discriminate between spirit and matter. That may give us a glimpse of the soul which is above the intellect. Intellect may lead us to the soul, but its capacity to guide is limited. Intellect is but a servant of the soul, and the soul is but a servant of God.

What kind of information can we get from the mental world? The only thing we can be sure of is that it will not be 100% accurate most of the time. It is certainly not absolute.

There are many types of inhabitants in the mental realm ranging from benevolent to demoniac, from progressive to regressive. It stands to reason that the type of entities which are most easy to get in touch with are those who are themselves attached to the physical plane. These would be entities who are possessed of physical material desires yet whose karma would not allow them to acquire a physical form. For example, suicide is said to produce the karmic reaction of having to take birth in the mental world where there are no physical bodies. These entities remain hovering in an ethereal form nearby, seeking opportunities to possess a body through which they can satisfy their desires. Similarly, those who do the work of channeling—the "gifted"—were most likely living in the mental world in their last life (there is a kind of death in the mental world); thus their consciousness is still attached to that plane.

There are others who derive pleasure from having their views heard and appreciated. Rather than being grossly materially attached, their connection with mundanity is more subtle. Philosophers and thinkers, speculators and the like who function on the mental plane, can easily acquire a large audience here. Their views are no more profound, however, than many of the thoughtful persons from this plane, although they generally have more knowledge of the physical world. Thus, most spirits can capture our attention by telling us about our past or something of the future.

In exchange for the satisfaction the spirits derive from our listening to them and taking their advice, those of an altruistic disposition often give practical help in many areas. In the fields of medicine, invention, science, investment, or in just helping one to feel good about themself, there is plenty of documented evidence that the disembodied can be helpful. Edgar Cayce provided consistently accurate medical data, although he knew little or nothing about medicine in his waking state. Lazaris of Concept Synergy currently gives a pretty good sermon about PMA (positive mental attitude). But that is about as far as it goes. After that, many spirit guides get in over their heads, especially when they contradict genuine spiritual traditions which have produced numerous saints on Earth.

An example of such contradiction is found in a popular theme of channeled guides, Westernized reincarnation. According to some new trance channelers, we can only progress. There is no question of falling back to a lower life-form. But the original literatures of ancient India, wherein the process of reincarnation is fully described, do not lend themselves to such interpretation. The idea that we can only progress does not match with our experience or common sense, nor give us license to freely choose our next incarnation. If a man is given a high and responsible position along with certain privileges and facilities, and misuses them as did, say, Richard Nixon, he will be hurled down or impeached.

Therefore, we must seriously consider that today's popular channeled entities may not be divine, but mental or astral, and cannot bring their audiences to the highest destination sought by genuine spiritual seekers since the beginning of recorded history.

If the more humanistic section of the new-agers are embarrassed by the many who have attempted to make divinity out of the paranormal, they have no one to blame but themselves. Humanism, after all, is nothing but the speculative attempt to equate humanity with divinity, and a man-made God is no God. Such a heretical idea of spirituality can never satisfy the soul of humanity. We should call a spade a spade, especially in this instance. Otherwise we become subject to potential contempt of the Supreme. This in turn may threaten our chances of ever achieving the harmonious life which, regardless of how much we herald its arrival, still continues to elude us. In the words of Plutarch, "It is better to have no opinion about God at all than such a one as is unworthy of Him: for the one is only unbelief—the other is contempt."

The license to speculate can be dangerous. Just as in mechanistic science there are certain axiomatic truths, so also in nonmechanistic science or spiritual science there are fundamental axiomatic truths. For example, that the platform of the soul lies beyond the limited conceptions of race, sex, nationality, and even the tradition of spiritual practice one may choose is an axiomatic truth. We are moved to raise questions, therefore, when our cultural orientation plays a prominent role in shaping our "spirituality." Do we have the liberty to create new spiritual axioms in the name of enlightened thinking? Until our own behavior is at least in accordance with the saints who have come before us in "traditional religion," a grain of caution may be in good taste.

Everyone has the inalienable right to pursue enlightenment at their own pace and of their own volition (necessarily), and there is tremendous scope for new revelation within our God-given traditional religious systems. From Shankara to Ramanuja to Madhva to Sri Caitanya, from Old Testament to New, there are many examples. We must look not to replace the law but to fulfill it. Too often speculative theories regarding the nature of spirituality expose themselves as uninformed opinions when they blame "shortcomings" in the "old age of spirituality" for their necessity to redefine divinity. In the words of Bernadette Roberts, author of The Experience of No Self, "The inclusiveness of the traditional paths is well attested to by the contemplatives who never went "outside" of their religion to see the divine in all that exists—or see all that exists as a manifestation of the divine. To overlook this fact is indicative of an out-of-hand rejection of traditional religion by those who have obviously never lived it. That some people choose not to go the traditional route is their prerogative, but to blame their choice on a deficit in traditional religion is contrary to the fact and totally absurd."

Our conjectures about the nature of Godhead must arise out of a strong foundation, one which has been laid down by saints and scriptures in previous times. Enlightened thinking requires that we are careful not to throw out the baby with the bath water. If we are truly interested in enlightened thinking, the planet is rich with examples from every religious tradition from which to draw inspiration. Is it enlightened thinking to feel that it is beneath our dignity to follow greater thinkers who have gone before us? Do not the greatest of thinkers advocate that we also think for ourselves? When so many saints have already come before us leading the way, perhaps it is only our lack of courage and utter attachment to this earthly plane that has forced us to come up with "new ideas" about spiritual life which may amount to no more than self-deception and relative improvements of character. No one can deny the noble character of Christ or the idea that a society of Christ- like men and women would undoubtedly be a New Age, but very, very few are courageous enough to follow such an example. Very few are thoroughly convinced of the dire necessity for a truly "new age."

Genuine spirituality remains above the mental and intellectual con- jectures of much of the New Age speculation, as something not to be known except by those to whom God so chooses to reveal Himself. After all, are we the subject or is He? This is not a discrimination on His part, but an invita- tion on His terms.
