At that time I thought that entrance into that state was largely a result of repudiating authority, as I had done relative to my parents, teachers, etc. I thought that gurus would definitely seduce me away from the existential integrity necessary to have an authentic experience. But then I realized after my initiation experience that there are so many levels of inner states, so many varieties of inner experience, that unless one had a secure relationship with one who was established in such a state, it was hopeless. There is no hope that you can reliably lead yourself into that state. Simply having an opening, an experience of a pale approximation of transcendence is not enough. The possibilities that open up to you in connection with a real guru are unlimited. If you have the fortune to encounter a real guru, this question will evaporate.

*How would you describe an authentic spiritual master? What does he do for the disciple?*

If I could answer that question perfectly, then we could throw away the rest of the questions. The simple answer is that an authentic spiritual master is at a level of development transcendental to selfish egotism. So his manner of interaction with all creatures is purely in the interest of their development. In practice the authentic master seems so close, so intimate, that he knows you perfectly, as if there is no gap between you and him. Simultaneously he seems incredibly elusive, as if you could never capture his essence, but that his essence is incredibly valuable, such that everything that you have ever cared about is a mere symbol for the reality which he seems to embody. So the interplay of that is that intimate side of the guru who seems like your best friend, a person who is so much like you that you and he are nondifferent, versus the elusive transcendent mysterious essence that you could never hope to understand. In that interplay, somehow you get led on in a certain direction pursuing the essence and comforted by the intimacy of the relationship.

The practice of this elusive game of hide-and-seek does not result in leaving one less capable of making competent and wise decisions in daily life. In that sense the relationship does not make one more dependent. People are afraid that they will become a slavish, obedient servant—a robot whose every move is controlled by someone else; but that is not the experience of those who have contact with a genuine guru. Rather, one becomes a servant, but a servant of truth, a slave of truth.

The relationship is anything but a process of slavish devotion to external commands. Sometimes there may be external commands. They may have a certain role to play in guiding us and breaking down a certain type of egotism. Thus we may be placed in certain situations where we have to confront our own inadequacies and gain some capacity to deal with situations that we otherwise couldn't have.

*How important is tradition and lineage in choosing a guru?*

The truth is one, and I would be very suspicious of anyone that was expressing a "truth" that was entirely new. My sense is that history is some kind of judge of these things, and there are certain personalities that shine down through the ages with an undiminished sense of spiritual integrity. If the doctrines associated with those great personalities have a certain kind of stature and reliability, and if persons associated with them have become enlightened,then that says a lot. And if the master has been pointed out by another recognized master, that is certainly a type of credential.

*What are some of the common misconceptions about spiritual life prevalent in contemporary spirituality?*

In *Spiritual Choices* I outlined five confusions common among spiritual groups that have appealed to people in the American context. The first is the confusion between spiritual perfection and worldly skill, which is very common. It seems to manifest in people who believe that by joining the right spiritual group they will become healthy, wealthy, and wise, with more emphasis on the healthy and wealthy. There is a good deal of emphasis on achieving physical health and material success by a certain approach to a spiritual teaching, and it is very puzzling why people believe these things. Great spiritual masters down through the ages have often been physically sick. Christ died on the cross: he certainly wasn't very good at managing circumstances. It seems that everything the great masters in history did was to teach us to be indifferent to such things, to teach us that the world of conventional perception is a world of ignorance and essentially a dream. It ultimately doesn't matter what happens to us in terms of the measure of our material success or health. In fact, all of those experiences are totally controlled by God. If God is perfectly benevolent and omnipotent, then nothing that happens in the world is without a purpose. It's all equally good for us and has to do with our awakening. So why would he come here and waste his time telling us how to manage our lives in such a way that we could encounter only pleasurable experiences? It doesn't compute. I think it is a mark of the decadence of the age, the degeneracy of the age from the spiritual point of view, that these assumptions have become so deeply embedded in the culture that they dominate our consciousness, even when we are relating to spiritual texts which essentially say the opposite.

The second confusion is between transcendent and ordinary types of non-rational experience, or between transcendence and regression. This point is so obvious that it is almost embarrassing to articulate it, but on the other hand it is so common a confusion that I feel I have to say something about it. Extremes of ordinary emotion or sensory stimulation can be confused with genuine transcendence of rationality. The human potential movement got involved in mixing Eastern spiritual teachings with psychology, and the masters who became most influential in that setting reinterpreted traditional Eastern teachings in a way that was very convergent with a vulgarized form of Freudian psychoanalysis. Their basic idea was that transcendence involves the repudiation of rational social controls, principally those governing sex and violence. So the expression of sexual and violent impulses and the emotional releases that follow are somehow equated with transcendence. It's both a misinterpretation of Freudian psychoanalysis and spiritual teachings. Transcendence is not correctly identified with one particular side of any mundane polarity with which we grapple—emotion versus reason. In this confusion, transcendence is not properly regarded as intrinsic, but as deriving from the desirability of its mundane consequences, such as emotional catharsis in which transformation is *supposed* to result. Ken Wilber calls this "pre-rationality" rather than "trans-rationality."

The third common confusion is that of mistakenly equating the mystics' actual transcendence of good and evil with antinomainism. Antinomainism means against norms. Today some spiritual seekers regard the repudiation of moral norms as a way of achieving monistic transcendence of the duality of good and evil. However, the mere rejection of moral norms is a false solution that amounts to a regressive avoidance of the issue, not transcendence of it. The unilevel fallacy here is in equating transcendence with what is really a psychological strategy within material consciousness.

In a sense all authentic masters transcend good and evil. They accept the saint and the sinner. They experience God's will in everyone, and they know that all action is either directly or indirectly an expression of God's will. Given that though, there is a process of development that all souls go through, an evolution of behavior in a less selfish, more generous and loving direction. The role of the master is to encourage that evolution in the people he encounters. It's all part of a perfectly orchestrated drama, and he is in harmony with every part of the drama. He is beyond good and evil and the play of duality and he helps people evolve out of duality. You can be a prisoner of good as well as a prisoner of evil. Often a master has to help one evolve out of the "prison of good" where we identify conventional morality with ultimate transcendence and are attached to a sense of ourself that is synonymous with good behavior. Good behavior isn't our essence. It's a minimum standard. Good behavior is often accompanied by motives that aren't good.

So an authentic master will not encourage you to physically perform immoral behavior, but he will get you in touch with your immoral motives. As Christ said, "Insofar as you look on a woman with lust in your heart, you are committing adultery." In some sense that's true. You have to transcend the desire to commit adultery as well as the act itself.

The fourth confusion—detachment with dissociation and repression—is also common, and in a way we've already touched upon that, only in another direction. In a way, being a prisoner of the good can be a form of dissociation and detachment, and it can seem as if you are detached from the consequences of your actions. But a person who seems to be indifferent to worldly attainments may only have succeeded in making himself believe that he is no longer concerned with worldly attainments because his external actions are not directed toward their achievement. In other words, let's say you become a monk, and because you are not actively seeking worldliness, you may fall into the illusion that you have actually transcended material desire. But in fact the psychological mechanisms of dissociation and repression could be at work, supporting your attachment to this false sense of yourself. A true master will always find ways to put you in touch with the relative desires that are still present within you.

And finally, the confusion of detachment with potent or effective attachment is also commonly found in the contemporary spirituality, particularly amongst groups that arose out of the human potential movement. Their idea is that you suspend the evaluative faculty, the faculty of judgement, and look at your emotions, desires, and beliefs about yourself with detachment. By doing so it is thought that you can come into harmony with all those secular forces and tendencies within yourself and gain the capacity to steer them and control them—to create your own reality. Although this may be a useful psychological technique for material gain, to confuse the goals of those techniques with transcendence of the self is ridiculous. To call it enlightenment is nonsense. To call the transcendence of desires the same thing as learning psychological techniques that enable you to satisfy your desires more effectively is so transparently contradictory that it's mind-boggling!

*Can you speak a little more on the relationship between mundane morality and transcendence?*

You have to somehow go beyond morality, but as far as I can understand, true saints never contradicted conventional morality. At the most they flouted social convention.

Every culture has a variety of social conventions that are arbitrary and historically contingent. They are usually in practice taken much more seriously in terms of determining one's conventional acceptance or exclusion from the mainstream of society. If you go to a party at a rich person's house at any time in history, you are much more likely to be kicked out for drinking your tea in the wrong style than you are if they know that you surreptitiously have a mistress on the side. Conventional morality is not the governing morality; it's arbitrary etiquette. So masters have often flouted simplistic rules of etiquette in a way that offended the expectations of their superficial disciples because they were trying to force their disciples to go to the heart of conventional morality in a purer sense and to become more indifferent to social conventions and social acceptance and rejection. But I cannot find any records of them breaking serious rules involving sexual immorality, or murdering people, or any similar serious violations of conventional morality, the likes of which you *can* encounter in contemporary spiritual groups in America.

*What about sex and spirituality—the tantric tradition?*

There are tantric scriptures in the East—in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Taoism—which advocate learning how to escape egoism by encountering the selfish, impulsive side of oneself, and somehow stealing away the energy that is attached to those desires or impulses, transferring them to higher spiritual goals. But in my reading of the tantric literature, one is never encouraged to directly act out those impulses. True tantrism does not involve the repudiation of conventional morality. And certainly the other traditions don't.

*What is your general feeling about the masters who have come to the West?*

I have been very discouraged regarding the masters who have come to the West. I have tried to develop my typology and flesh it out with multiple examples in each category, and I don't have any trouble at all finding examples in the unilevel categories, but I have had a very difficult time finding enduring examples in the multilevel categories. Teachers often enough seem to be accurately philosophically representing authentic spiritual traditions, but over a period of years I've found events occurring in their circles which in my mind are not consistent with what should be going on in the circle of a genuine master.

*What's actually taking place in history today in regards to enlightenment? It seems like such a rare thing to find a true master, yet so many people are talking about it.*

I think, to put it in Baba's terms, we are at present in an era in which reason is seen as most desirable, but we are moving in the direction of an era of intuition. We went through the transition from an era of sensation to one of reason, and now reason has become developed as much as it ever will for humanity at large. We're about to shift into an era in which the ideal norm will be seen to be intuition rather than reason.

Intuition, it seems to me, is a faculty that results from the balancing of emotion, intellect, and will, giving each of those faculties its appropriate place in the function of the organism, such that a new faculty emerges—the integrative faculty—which is intuition. Intuition knows what the truth is when it sees it in concrete circumstances. It doesn't have to separate out the different faculties—emotion, reason, willing, or action—but those faculties are blended so that the person knows what to do appropriately in the circumstances as they develop. I'm not saying that everybody will achieve the intuition which is characteristic of great masters. What I'm saying is that that faculty will be recognized as the desirable faculty, and mankind at large will come to try to embody it and point to it as an ideal.

In a sense, right now, we are simultaneously in both the best and worst of times.

## Interpretive Sensibilitiy Dimension

Anthony Typology

## Unilevel

"Definitive" mundande interpretations of spiritual themes, formal literalistic religion lacking the substance of genuine experience. Gives rise to false pride

Bluring of distinctions between levels of spirituql attainment;*Believing*, an element of speculative mundane consciousness, is confused with *knowing*, or direct spiritual knowledge, which occurs only in transcendent consciousness.

Expectation of rapid, dramatic spiritual advancement.

Self idolotry is promoted.

Transcendence is identified with the polarization of opposites. Aversion is erroeously identified with genuine detatchment.

## Multilevel

Strong sense of conviction is balanced with humility, resulting from the actual experience that one is dealing with that which is infinite.

Recognises distinctions between levels of spiritual attainment (actual realization, the teaching, its interpretation, etc.).

Spiritual attainment is seen as a something very rare, yet worth waiting for.

Attentuates preoccupation with self concept, whether positive or negative.

Dialectic interplay of opposities leading to the realization of a higher synthesis.

## Metaphysics Dimension

## Monism

The existence of seperate beings and things is illusory.

The true nature of all is formless.

All apparently seperate beings will eventually experience ultimate realization, in which the seperate self ilusion vanishes and consciousness realizes its infinite true nature.

## Dualism

The world is real.

Individuals have different final spiritual destinies.

Seperate selfhood persists even in ultimate spiritual gnosis.

One's final status depends on fulfilling moral and/or metaphysical criteria.

## Practice Dimension

## Technical

Reliance on techniques as the essential means of spiritual attainment. A technique is any well defined repetative mental or physical activity that is regarded as being instrumental to the achievement of transformation.

## Charismatic

Reliance on personal relationships to a spiritually realized person as the essential means of spiritual attainment.

## Sri Chaitanya

*Fulfillment of a Transcendental Dialectic*

By Swami B G Narasingha

Since ancient times India's ascetics and holy men have endeavored to realize the absolute truth by the culture of spiritual knowledge. Some of them followed in the footsteps of Buddha, practicing *ahimsa*, the path of nonviolence, seeking *prakriti nirvana* as the highest attainment. Later in history some, preferring to renounce work, followed Shankaracharya, and by the practice of sense control, they fixed their mind in meditation, merging the individual ego into *Brahman*, the ultimate state of oneness. In the development towards a transcendental theism, others, following Ramanuja and Madhva on the path of devotion, considered realization of the self as an eternal servant of Godhead—one in *purpose* with the Supreme—as the highest goal. But while Ramanuja and Madhva established theistic schools of thought based on Vedanta (as opposed to Shankara's ultimate monism), it was not until the advent of Sri Chaitanya that Vedantic theism's limits were unveiled.

Sri Chaitanya appeared in this world at Mayapur, Navadwip Dham, West Bengal on February 18, 1486 in the home of Jagannath Mishra, a scholarly *brahman* priest of the Vaishnava community. At the time of his appearance the moon was eclipsed, and thus all the noble residents of Navadwip Dham had gone to take their bath in the Ganges. Everyone was in a happy mood, and according to the customs of their time, everyone chanted Vedic mantras and the names of God as they bathed in the Ganges. Due to the chanting of these mantras the atmosphere became surcharged with spiritual vibrations, and at that auspicious moment, Sri Chaitanya advented.

The life history of Sri Chaitanya has been told by historians, scholars, and devotees alike. But there is an esoteric description of his appearance as well, and it is within this internal analysis that his teaching is based—a teaching that might well be considered the zenith of theism. Within this school of thought the prospect for an intimate relationship with a personal God beyond the duality of the world of time and space invites the devoted to participate in a labor of love which culminates in an eternal life of ecstatic rapture.

The Bengali classic *Chaitanya Charitamrita,* compiled in the sixteenth century by Krishnadas Kaviraja Goswami, reveals the inner identity of Sri Chaitanya which is accepted by all his followers. In this book the author describes Sri Chaitanya as Godhead himself, who in this incarnation disguises himself as his own devotee. Krishnadas emphasizes that Sri Chaitanya is the personal manifestation of the absolute truth in full, and he urges his readers to regard him in that way in order to enter into an understanding of the confidential nature of his life and precepts. According to Krishnadas, Sri Chaitanya is the *kali-yuga avatar* described throughout the Vedic literature.

The idea that *parambrahma* (the Absolute) is ultimately personal, making possible eternal devotion, and that Sri Chaitanya is that transcendental person, has also been explained in detail by his modern-day followers such as the eminent professor of Indian philosophy, Dr. O.B.L. Kapoor. Kapoor says that the appearance of Sri Chaitanya in this phenomenal world is the culmination of a transcendental dialectic which is inherent in the very nature of the Supreme Being. *Parabrahma*, says Kapoor, is *rasa* or concentrated bliss, which assumes a transcendental figure. The figure is that of Sri Krishna. Within *rasa* there must also be *rasika*, or the ability to taste transcendental bliss, says Kapoor. Thus in Krishna the unity of *rasa* and *rasika* bursts and blooms into the duality of Krishna and Radha. In that duality Krishna is *rasa*, the highest thing to be relished, and Radha is *rasika*, the greatest enjoyer of *rasa*. After reaching the highest state of divine love called *prema-vilasa-vivarta*, in which Radha and Krishna, the potent and the potency, are fully absorbed in one another's love, the transcendental duality of Krishna and Radha again combines.

According to Kapoor, "This union of love between Radha and Krishna, however, does not imply a monistic union, as does the *adwaitic* conception of formless Brahman or the Neo-Platonic concept of God as an experience, in which the loss of individuality of the devotee or the *sadhaka* is complete and irrevocable. It is...like the union between fire and a piece of iron. A piece of iron, when put for a long time in fire, becomes red-hot like the fire. Every part of it is animated by fire and acquires the characteristics of fire. Still, iron remains iron and fire remains fire. Similarly, both Krishna and Radha retain their identity. They are so absorbed in each other's love and lost in each other's thoughts that there is hardly any room in their hearts for the thought of anything else. Sri Chaitanya is the substantial or personalized form of this union." Thus the birth of Sri Chaitanya in this world at Mayapur was not like that of an ordinary child, but rather it was of the nature of divine descent.

After the birth of Sri Chaitanya, all the women of the village loved to see him every day. His uncle, who was a famous astrologer, foretold that the child would be recognized as a great personality in time, and he named him Vishvambhar (maintainer of the universe). The child's mother Sachidevi, however, preferred to call him Nimai since there was a neem tree near the place where he was born.

As a child Nimai liked to play with his friends on the banks of the Ganges, and as boys will be boys, Nimai and his friends would often get into mischief. Sometimes the boys would even splash water on the yogis who came to the banks of the river to meditate. However, when the adults came to chastise Nimai for his tricks, they became charmed by his cunning behavior. Everyone came to love Nimai as if he were their own son. In his fifth year Nimai was admitted into the school of Gangadas Pandit, where he mastered Bengali and Sanskrit in two short years. After that, Nimai studied at home, and by his tenth year he was already renowned as a great scholar, now known as Nimai Pandit. His scholarship was such that in his youth he defeated the greatest scholar of the time, Keshava Bhatt of Kashmir. In doing so he vanquished the pride that accompained the scholarship of the pundit. While Sri Chaitanya himself was a great scholar, he consistently deprecated the acquisition of knowledge for its own sake. In his view, learning was connected with reality only inasmuch as Godhead was served thereby.

Nimai had an older brother named Vishvarupa who left home to become a *sannyasi*, a member of the renounced order of life. This came as a tremendous shock to Jagannath Mishra and Sachidevi, but Nimai, in his usual way, consoled his parents in their grief and showered them with love. Shortly after the loss of their older son, Jagannath Mishra himself expired from this world, leaving his wife to widowhood with only Nimai to look after her.

On the request of his mother, Nimai married Lakshmipriya, a charming girl from a nearby village. But just after his fifteenth birthday, while Nimai was away from his village, Lakshmipriya died after being bitten by a snake. Although at the request of his mother he had accepted another wife, Vishnupriya, this marriage was also not to last for long, for shortly thereafter while visiting Gaya, Sri Chaitanya accepted initiation from his celebrated guru Ishwara Puri. This initiation marked a turning point in his life. When Nimai returned to Mayapur, he was no longer interested in scholastic achievement: his mind turned instead toward spiritual matters. Externally he appeared to have lost interest in conventional duties; from then on Nimai was a man transformed, as if God-inspired.

In the evenings Nimai would gather his intimate followers together in the house of Shrivas Thakur and perform *sankirtan*, the congregational chanting of the names of God. In those chanting sessions Nimai would sometimes exhibit ecstatic symptoms of love of God, and sometimes he would reveal his form to be the same as that of Sri Krishna. For almost eight years Sri Chaitanya continued to live at Mayapur.

In the daytime Sri Chaitanya used to send his followers from door to door to request every man, woman, and child to chant the names of God. He taught that simply by chanting the names of God one would easily realize his eternal relationship with God, whose name is nondifferent from Himself. In this way he taught the *yuga dharma* for the age of *kali.*

Sri Chaitanya instructed his followers that there are no hard and fast rules for chanting the names of God. Regardless of one's position in society, anyone and everyone was eligible to take part in this process. This, however, drew objection, and certain members of the priestly caste who "held a monopoly" on spiritual blessings opposed him. He had started the movement of chanting the names of God to uplift all classes of human society, announcing love of God to be the birthright of everyone, yet thinking him to be only an ordinary human being, foolish, self-motivated persons objected.

Contemplating in this way, Sri Chaitanya devised a plan. Knowing that a *sannyasi*, a member of the renounced order of life, was respected by everyone—even by the atheists—he decided to accept *sannyasa*. Thus even the nonbelievers would benefit by showing him respect. Once Sri Chaitanya had decided on his course of action, nothing could turn him back.

Early one morning in January, at the end of his 24th year, Sri Chaitanya bid farewell to hearth and home. Without the notice of anyone except his mother, he swam across the Ganges River and ran to Katwa, a distance of some 25 miles. At Katwa he went to the ashram of Keshava Bharati and requested him to kindly give him *sannyasa*. At that time he was given the name Sri Krishna Chaitanya. Now more than ever before, he was inspired to benedict the world with divine love. Taking a small group of followers with him, he immediately started for Jagannath Puri. Along the way, whoever saw him became absorbed in the mellows of ecstatic love, and whomever he met he requested to chant the holy names of God. Indeed, he was just like a great ocean that inundated everything and everyone with love of God.

At Jagannath Puri Sri Chaitanya converted Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya, who was at the time the greatest logician in all of India, into a follower of his movement of divine love. Sarvabhauma then became one of his principal associates. Sri Chaitanya remained at Jagannath Puri for some time, and then he decided to tour south India. For the next six years he traveled almost continuously and preached his doctrine of love.

On the banks of the river Godavari Sri Chaitanya met Ramananda Raya, the governor of Vidyanagar, and for several days had enlightening discussions with him on the topic of *prema bhakti,* devotional service in pure love of God. The followers of Sri Chaitanya maintain that the apex of theistic thought was revealed in those discussions. Ramananda Raya was a great devotee of Sri Krishna, and Sri Chaitanya solicited from him higher and higher truths regarding the nature of spirit at every moment of their conversation. The climax of their dialogue disclosed that the highest transcendental sentiments of love for God were those shown by the *gopis* (milkmaids) of Vrindavan during the advent of Sri Krishna. In their service to Sri Krishna, the *gopis* exhibited the topmost platform of surrender and unalloyed love in which even social conventions of mundane morality were transcended, thus showing that although the morally stout serve as a good example of religious life, there is yet a higher plane where adherence to law is overruled by love, and that pure love must ultimately be free from the type of calculation found in the theistic conclusions of Ramanuja and Madhva.

According to Dr. Kapoor, "...Never before was *bhakti* described as both the means and the end. Sri Chaitanya's characterization of love as the supreme goal is the most important landmark in the history of philosophy and religion. According to Sri Chaitanya, the center of reality is love, not Godhead. Love is the center not only for the devotee, but also for God. Love governs both. Though Godhead is the embodiment of love itself, he has an ever-growing desire for love. Love is a gravitational force that works at two ends: it draws the devotee to Godhead and Godhead to the devotee."

Continuing on his journey, Sri Chaitanya then visited all the important places of pilgrimage in south India and eventually returned to Jagannath Puri. After some time at Puri, he decided to visit Vrindavan, the land of Sri Krishna. Taking one servant named Balabhadra Bhattacharya with him, he traveled along the banks of the river Yamuna and through the Jarikhanda forest where, according to Balabhadra's diary, Sri Chaitanya caused wild beasts to chant and embrace, losing their natural enmity towards one another.

When he reached Vrindavan, Sri Chaitanya exhibited his ecstatic mood of dancing and chanting and many thousands of people came to see him every day. There, through his transcendental vision, he revealed the places of Sri Krishna's *lilas* (pastimes) which were otherwise lost for thousands of years. Later, under his direction his principal disciples excavated the whole area of Vrindavan with the help of wealthy patrons, establishing temples at those holy places of Sri Krishna's *lilas*. To date these temples are the principal places of worship in that holy land.

After leaving Vrindavan, on his return to Jagannath Puri, Sri Chaitanya stopped at Allahabad where he instructed Rupa Goswami about the process of devotional service, and after instructing him in the details of spirituality, he sent him to Vrindavan to write books on the science of *bhakti* and excavate the places of Sri Krishna's pastimes. From Allahabad he went to Banaras, where he met the brother of Rupa Goswami, Sanatana Goswami. On the banks of the Ganges he instructed Sanatana in confidential spiritual matters, and after one month he sent him to join his brother at Vrindavan. Later it was these two brothers and their nephew Jiva Goswami who, along with others, established the literary support for Sri Chaitanya's theology based on the Vedic literature.

Wherever Sri Chaitanya went, monists such as the highly renowned Prakashananda Saraswati of Banaras raised strong objections against him for his public dancing and chanting the names of God. They contended that he was a misguided sentimentalist without any real understanding of the *Vedanta-sutra,* which was at that time considered the single most important Vedic literature. They maintained that the sole duty of one in the renounced order was to study the *Vedanta-sutra* commentaries of Shankara. Unaware of the conception of transcendental emotion, they assumed that Sri Chaitanya's chanting and dancing were mere mundane sentimental outpourings.

Sri Chaitanya maintained that there was no need of any commentary on *Vedanta-sutra* since Vyasadeva, its author, had already written his own commentary in the form of *Shrimad-Bhagavatam.* He taught that the *Vedanta-sutra* propounded *achintya-bedabeda-tattva—*that the absolute truth in the ultimate issue is simultaneously and inconceivably one and variegated—the soul is part and parcel of God, but neither one nor any number of finite souls combined is equal to Godhead in full. Sri Chaitanya advocated that proper study of the *Bhagavatam* would culminate in God-realization and a state of transcendental emotion, as opposed to the dry, emotionless *adwaitic* monism.

In the words of Kapoor, Sri Chaitanya taught that the *ananda-brahman* of the monists "is the formless expansive glow \[aura\] of *Godhead*, just as moonlight is the formless expansive glow of the moon. In *ananda-brahman, rasa* is dormant, still and motionless. It is not *rasa* in the real sense....*Rasa-brahman* \[on the other hand\] is dynamic, restless, effulgent, ever-flowing, and ever-growing. It is astonishingly new and relishable—passing every moment beyond itself to new levels of *rasa*-consciousness."

After traveling and canvassing for several years, Sri Chaitanya finally returned to Jagannath Puri. There he stayed for the remaining 18 years of his life until his disappearance from the sight of mortal men during his 48th year. Sri Chaitanya's biographers have commented that during those last 18 years, he was surrounded by numerous followers, all of whom were on the highest level of devotion, distinguished from the common people by their character and learning, firm religious principles, and spiritual love for Radha and Krishna.

Historically, Sri Chaitanya has been regarded differently by different individuals. His immediate followers have accepted him as the supreme deity, Sri Krishna. Others have regarded him as a *bhakta-avatar,* a divine incarnation to distribute love of God. But that he was a noble and holy teacher is accepted by all who have come in contact with his life and teachings with an unbiased spirit. Sri Chaitanya did not appear in this world to deliver a certain section of human beings in India, but rather his purpose was to uplift all souls in all countries of the world to the pure and sublime platform of ecstatic love of God, the eternal religion of all souls.

It is my conclusion after having gone through the teachings of the spiritual masters of India chosen in this series to demonstrate a theistic development over thousands of years, that among Buddha, Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva, and Sri Chaitanya, there is no contradiction in that each represents a particular stage of enlightenment on the path of the ultimate truth. They all agree that our present egoistic preoccupation must be transcended, if we are at all to know any peace. There is visible in them a continuity of theistic evolution from one to the next, starting with the Buddha and culminating in Sri Chaitanya.

Buddha's "Four Noble Truths"—there is suffering, suffering has a cause, suffering can be surpassed, and there is a method by which one can attain freedom from suffering—have laid the foundation for the premise that there is a higher attainment, a higher goal in life than that which is generally accepted as reality. Buddha was then followed by Shankara who, improving on the premise of Buddha, established that eternal spirit (*atma*), and not simply negation of material existence, is an abstract positive reality. Ramanuja then developed the theistic conception found in Shankara from abstract monism to concrete monism, describing a *Brahman* with transcendental attributes. He founded a movement of *bhakti,* or devotion, based on the inherent nature of the living spirit. Madhva then continued the development from Ramanuja, emphasizing the eternal existence of both the soul (*atma*) and the Oversoul (*paramatma*) as necessary for the dynamics of *bhakti*. Finally Sri Chaitanya presented a love not of self-sacrifice, but one of self-forgetfulness, in which love itself, personified as Sri Radha, becomes the center for both Godhead and his devotee.

The late Bhaktivinode Thakur, a biographer and proponent of Sri Chaitanya's school of divine love, has given a valuable word of advice to all sincere souls who are hankering to know the absolute truth when he said, "Party spirit—that great enemy of truth—will always baffle the attempt of the inquirer who tries to gather truth from the religious works of his nation, and will make him believe that absolute truth is nowhere except in his old religious book." Therefore, the adherent of the path of self-realization should always have a comprehensive, gentle, generous, honest, sympathetic, and above all, an impartial approach, in order to acquire the greatest hope of attaining success on that path.

Notes:

1\. The Vedas describe four ages (*yugas*), the last of which in a continuous cycle is *kali-yuga*, the iron (industrial-technological) age of quarrel. For each age there is an *avatar* who teaches the recommended spiritual discipline for that particular age (yuga*dharma*).

References:

1\. Dr. O. B. L. Kapoor, *The Philosophy and Religion of Sri Chaitanya,* Munshiram Manoharlal Publishers, Delhi ,1976.

2\. Bhaktivinode Thakur, *Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu: His Life and Precepts*, Gaudiya Press, San Francisco, 1986.

3\. Bhaktivedanta Swami, *Sri Chaitanya-charitamrita* (English translation and commentary), Bhaktivedanta Book Trust, Los Angeles, 1975.

*This concludes the five- part series on the development of Vedantic theistic thought throughout the history of India.*

## Swami B.R. Shridhara, Remembering Him

The disappearance of dynamic spiritual leaders from the world is a great loss. At the same time, how can anything a truly great soul does be to our disadvantage? After all, they work only for our betterment. Having nothing to gain themselves, they are left only to give. Therefore the loss we suffer in their separation must be somehow for our good. Separation makes the heart grow fonder. For growth, trial is necessary. As the mother bird pushes the chicks from the nest that they may fly, great souls leave us behind, only that we might join them in their flight.

On August 12, 1988, at 5:28 A.M., while approaching his ninety-fourth year, Bhakti Raksahaka Sridhara Maharaja (Swami Sridhara) left this world, and in so doing left an emptiness in the hearts of the many who were touched by his kindness. Fourtunately that kindness was not the superficial cosmetic kindness we often offer one another, that serves to perpetuate our lives in bondage (karma). His kindness was that of a true sadhu or saint.

Another meaning for sadhu is "one who cuts." Real sadhus are those who speak the truth even though it may be unpalatable. They "cut" away at the material attachment that infests our hearts like a cancer keeping us from the wealth of our spiritual life. In the words of Thoreau: "A man is rich in proportion to the number of things he can afford to let alone." Those who have the company of a rich man, a sadhu, stand to inherit that same wealth themselves in due course. We need only qualify ourselves, and especially in the sadhu's absence that opportunity arises.

Swami Sridhara lived a long life of devotion. He appeared in Navadwipa Dhama of West Bengal in the year 1895. In 1927 he became a disciple of the founder of India's Gaudiya Math, Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakura. In 1936 he accepted the renounced order of life.

He domiciled in the holy land of Navadwipa for more than fifty years. He was familiar with the Western mind having been exposed to the philisophical thought of the West during the British occupation of India yet his vast knowledge of revealed scripture, which earned him the title shastra nipuna (scriptural genious), and his unique insights into their deep meaning were revealed to the West only recently (1981).

After the depature from the world of Bhaktivedanta Swami, founder of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness and foremost proponent of Vaishnavism in the modern world, several of his disciples sought further guidance from Swami Sridhara. Swami Sridhara and Bhaktivedanta Swami were "Godbrothers" (disciples of the the same guru). In this way the West knocked on Swami Sridhara's door although he himself never set foot outside of India.

His new found Western neices and nephews (the disciples of Bhaktivedanta Swami) in turn brought him more than one-thousand sons and daughters (disciples) in a few short years. This was principly done through the transcribing of Swami Sridhara's conversations and the forming of the Gaurdian of Devotion Press. The conversations of Swami Sridhara were intended to "polish" the disciples of Bhaktivedanta Swami as Swami Sridhara acknowledged Bhaktivedanta Swami had wanted.

The teachings of sudha bhakti (unalloyed devotion) are the essence of the rich spiritual tradition of Vaishnavism (Vaishnavism and Shaivism are two the principle schools of othodox Hindu thought). Swami Sridhara was also known as Bhakti Rakshaka, the gaurdian of devotion. Of all of his many achievements his safekeeping the conclusions of pure devotion from the many insugents wich arise in the material mind (especially Western minds) will perhaps be most remembered. After Bhaktivedanta Swami left the world, his spiritual children who lovingly annoyed the West for more than a decade, were in danger of loosing sight of the essence of a timeless spiritual tradition, which for the first time in history had appeared on American shores replete with customs, dress and top knott. In its transition from infancy to childhood its principle bearer had departed. The gaurdian of devotion, Swami Sridhara, became the not leagal but natural inheritor of the burden of that child, Gaudiya Vaishnavism in the West. Those who found his shelter both directly and indirectly he nurtured to adolecense boardering adulthood and thus the monumental task of transplanting an entire cultural spiritual tradition in forien soil begun by Bhaktivedanta Swami was kept on course although not without casualties.

He often described himself as a "backward pushing man" or one who had little if any ambition to be in the limelight. It was indeed apparent that he was not tainted by any desire for name and fame. As is the way in spiritual circles, one who gravitates towards the service of the center, rather than towards being the center, emerges as a natural leader. Thus Swami Sridhara became the natural leader of all devotional theists in the line of Sri Chaitanya for the last decade of his manifest appearance. Like the rising of the sun he needed no other lesser light of materialistic manuvering and propaganda to show himself. He was a self-effulgent personality who shed light in the dark night of Kali Yuga.

Although he was formally a member and substantially the leader of a particular devotional sect, his appreciation for divinity in all schools of thought was remarkable. He had an uncanny ability to trace out divinity even in the ordinary, the mundane. Even atheism was in his vision a manifestation of divinity, coming to keep away the insincere. He once described Judas of the Bible as the one who rendered the greatest service to the Christ by making possible his crucifixon and thereby his immortality. For Swami Sridhara not a blade of grass moved without the will of God. His vision: "The environment is friendly."

For the last five years of his life he was for all intents and purposes blind and deaf. Medical doctors failed to comprehend how he was still alive when three of the four main arteries to his heart had ceased to function. Despite this condition he waited patiently to leave the world, all the while preparing others for the same. His spiritual excitement to speak about Godhead in the company of earnest souls could not be contained in spite of "doctors' advice." He lived on another plane—an inviting one it was, beyond the struggle for existence

Swami Sridhara was featured twice in the last year in Clarion Call in "Sounds Sounds Sounds," and "Positive and Progressive Imortality." It is to our deepest regret that he no longer remains amongst us. Yet there is a beauty in his departure; he was not an ordinary man.

## Deity vs. Idolatry

"...those who see the spiritual form of the Deity in their soul's eyes, carry that impression as as far as possible to the mind, and then frame an emblem for the satisfaction of the material eye for continual study of the higher feeling, are by no means idolatrous."

By Bhaktivinoda Thakura

The attempt to confine Godhead to a limited form of finite constitution is certainly condemnable. Idol worship is but an imaginary idea of man regarding the form of God shaped within the limits of his relative experience.Yet the thought that Godhead is formless appears also to impose a limitation on divinity. Although form may limit it also has the capacity to enhance one's ability.

The conception of the unlimited form of divinity held by the Vaishnavas harmoizes the conception of form and formless and forever retires idolatry. Bhaktivinoda Thakura's essay from the late nineteenth century affords a unique insight into the conception of Srimurti, the deity.

There are some who object to the idea of worshiping Srimurti (the deity form of Godhead).They say, "It is idolatry to worship Srimurti. Srimurti is an idol formed by an artist and introduced by no one other than Satan himself. Worshiping such an object would arouse the jealousy of God and limit His omnipotence, omniscience and omnipresence!"

To this we reply, "Brethren! Candidly understand the question and do not allow yourself to be misled by sectarian dogmas. God is not jealous, as He is one without a second. Satan is no other than an object of the imagination or the subject of an allegory. An allegorical or imaginary being should not be allowed to act as an obstacle to devotion.

Those who believe God to be impersonal simply identify Him with some power or attribute in nature, though in fact He is above nature, her laws, and her rules. His holy wish is law and it would be sacrilege to confine His unlimited excellence by identifying Him with attributes which may exist in created objects such as time, space, etc. His excellence lies in His having mutually contradicting powers and attributes ruled by His supernatural Self.

"He is identical with His all-beautiful form, having such powers as omnipresence, omniscience, and omnipotence, the like of which cannot be found elsewhere.His holy and perfect personality exists eternally in the spiritual world, and at the same time exists in every created object and place in all its fullness. This idea excels all other ideas of the deity. Mahaprabhu1 rejects idolatry, yet considers the worship of Srimurti to be the only unexceptionable means of spiritual culture.

"It has been shown that God is personal and all-beautiful. Sages like Vyasadeva and others have seen that beauty in their soul's eyes and left us descriptions. Of course, words carry the grossness of matter.But truth is still perceivable in those descriptions. According to those descriptions, one delineates a Srimurti and sees the great God of our heart there with intense pleasure. Brethren! Is that wrong or sinful?

"Those who say that God has no form, either material or spiritual, and at the same time imagine a false form for worship, are certainly idolatrous. But those who see the spiritual form of the Deity in their soul's eyes, carry that impression as as far as possible to the mind, and then frame an emblem for the satisfaction of the material eye for continual study of the higher feeling, are by no means idolatrous. While seeing a Srimurti, do not even see the image itself, but see the spiritual model of the image and you are a pure theist. Idolatry and Srimurti worship are two different things! But my brethren, you simply confuse one with the other out of hastiness.

"To tell you the truth, Srimurti worship is the only true worship of the deity, without which you cannot sufficiently cultivate your religious feelings. The world attracts you through your senses, and as long as you do not see God in the objects of your senses, you live in an awkward position which scarcely helps you in procuring your spiritual elevation. Place a Srimurti in your house. Think that God Almighty is the guardian of the house. Offer food to Him and take it as His prasada (mercy). Flowers and scents should also be offered to Him and accepted as prasada. The eye, ear, nose, skin, and tongue all have a spiritual culture. You do it with a holy heart and God will know it and judge you by your sincerity. Satan will have nothing to do with you in that matter!

All sorts of worship are based on the principle of Srimurti. Look into the history of religion and you will come to this noble truth. The Semitic idea of a patriarchal God both in the pre-Christian period of Judaism and period of Christianity thereafter, and Mohammedanism, is nothing but a limited idea of Srimurti. The monarchic idea of a Jove amongst the Greeks and of an Indra amongst the Aryan karma-kandis is also a distant view of the same principle. The idea of a force and Jyotirmaya Brahma of the meditators, and a formless energy of the Shaktas is also a very faint view of the Srimurti.

"In fact, the principle of Srimurti is the truth itself differently exhibited in different people according to their different phases of thought. Even Jaimini and Comte, who are not prepared to accept a creating God, have prescribed focusing on certain aspects of the Srimurti, simply because they have been impelled by some inward action from the soul! And of course, we meet with people who have adopted the Cross, the Shalagram-shila, the Shivalingam, and other such emblems as indicators of the inward idea of Srimurti.

"Furthermore, if divine compassion, love, and justice could be portrayed by the pencil and expressed by the chisel, then why shouldn't the personal beauty of the Deity be portrayed in poetry or in picture or expressed by the chisel for the benefit of man? If words can impress thoughts, a watch can indicate time, and a sign can tell us a history, then why can't a picture or figure bring associations of higher thoughts and feelings related to the transcendental beauty of the Supreme Lord?"

1 The founder of GaudiyaVaishnavism considered to be the incarnation of Godhead for the present age.

## Sri Rangam

Pilgrimage to Visiting The Spiritual World

By Swami B G Narasingha & Swami B B Visnu

It was mid June when our party of two landed at Madras International Airport. The temperature was well over a hundred degrees when we stepped off the plane. It had been a long flight from San Francisco with stops in Hong Kong and Singapore, which left us feeling a little tired as we stood in line to clear immigration and customs formalities. We came out of the terminal building and caught a taxi to the Dasaprakash Hotel.

Madras is India's fourth largest city. As a seaport Madras is also famous as the gateway to the south and has been a crossroads for travelers in Asia since before the days of Christ. In ancient times South India was known as Malabar,, and Marco Polo, the 12th century traveler from Venice, praised it as being the "richest country in the world." Certainly India is no longer the richest country in the world, but she is still vastly wealthy in terms of her culture, art and spiritual tradition.

Inside the Dasaprakash Hotel, lobby revolving overhead fans created a cooling breeze, and the faint smell of incense burning behind the reception counter signaled that we were no longer in the Western world. The desk clerk, taking notice of our arrival, extended a respectful Indian greeting, "NAMASTE! NAMASTE!" Now we were officially in India.

After refreshing ourselves in our room we went down to the dining hall for a vegetarian dinner. In contrast to "dining out in America," where one has to look hard for a good vegetarian restaurant, India is just the opposite: there are over five hundred million vegetarians in India and their national pastime is eating, so vegetarian restaurants are readily available wherever one goes. After satisfying ourselves with a delicious meal we retired to our room for a good night's rest.

We remained in Madras two days before journeying to our final destination, the temple of Sri Rangam. One day's journey by train through two hundred miles of lush tropical countryside would bring us to the city of Trichi, short for Tiruchchirappalli, where we would then go by boat to an island in the Kaveri River. We weren't on the usual tourist program. In fact, we didn't consider ourselves tourists--we were pilgrims, on pilgrimage to the largest and possibly oldest temple in India.

On the morning of the third day we were up early and at the station by 6:30 to catch our train to Trichi. At the station we struggled through the crowds and haggled with porters. Once inside the train we put our baggage under the seat and waited. The train consisted of twenty second-class passenger cars and two first-class coaches, pulled by a turn of the century steam locomotive. Our seating was in the first-class coach. At 7:30 sharp the engineer blew the whistle, and the train inched away from the platform. We were on our way.

Rolling through the tropical countryside we sat back to enjoy the view and contemplate the wonders which awaited us at our destination. Back in San Francisco, the idea of traveling to an ancient land where time has practically stood still for thousands of years seemed like a distant dream. But that dream was fast becoming a reality.

In the fields outside our train window we watched men hard at work plowing the earth with oxen, while women and children were busily planting newly sprouted rice, the main staple of their diet. Although their means of livelihood seemed harsh compared to our Western mechanized method of farming, we noticed that the lack of tractors and other such farm equipment had solved the unemployment problem. No one was idle everyone was engaged in some work.

Religion and work go hand in hand in India. As we watched the rural community hard at work we were reminded of their faith in God. Most Indian people believe that "man proposes and God disposes." They believe in working hard for a living but with the understanding that the fruits of their labor are dependent on the mercy of God. In India a man and his family pray to God for the strength to work the fields, and in the evening when they return home they offer the results of their labor to God through worship. Their concept is that if God has given me the energy to work and provided for the fruits of my labor, then He is the ultimate proprietor of those fruits.

The train ride lasted about ten hours. When we pulled into the station at Trichi it was late afternoon. We had only to make our way to the bank of the Kaveri River and our destination would be in sight. Piling body and baggage into a rikshaw, we were an unusual spectacle for the local inhabitants as we passed through the crowed streets of the city.

At the banks of the Kaveri we got off our rikshaw and gazed across the river. Towering high above the groves of palm and coconut trees stood the Raj Gopuram, the tallest temple tower in Southeast Asia, at 236 feet. We anxiously boarded a small boat that would take us across the river. As the boatman rowed our boat on the swift flowing Kaveri, we could hear the faint sound of bells, musical instruments and temple drums coming from the island. It was time for the evening temple worship.

Reaching the shore of the island we walked up from the boat landing onto a dirt road lined with banana trees which led us to the temple gates. Once inside the first gate, we began to perceive the vastness of this great temple. Our first impression of Sri Rangam was that it was a place where the past still survives—a place where the spirituality of man is the central focus of life. The temple complex, spreading over 156 acres, constituted a city in itself, with seven concentric walls surroundeding and fortifying the city. These walls are called prakaras and are said to symbolize the seven yoga chakras. Taken as a whole, the temple construction corresponds to the cosmic body of the universe. Within the center of the city lies the soul of the universe, the deity of Narayana.

A total of twenty-one gopurams (gates) towered high above the walls, allowing visitors and residents entrance to the city. As we entered through the first three gopurams we came to a marketplace and stopped in front of a small shop. Seeing that we were new arrivals to Sri Rangam, the proprietor of the shop invited us into his store and offered us a glass of cold water. I asked for some directions and handed him a paper with a name written on it. "Ranga Raja Bhattar," said the shopkeeper as he read the paper out loud. "Head priest at Sri Rangam. He is my brother-in-law. Would you like to meet him?" "Yes!" we replied.

Within moments we were walking down the street which wound its way through the city. The next thing we knew we were at the house of Ranga Raja Bhattar, a simple two-story building with a colorfully painted porch. "Here we are," said the man, grinning from ear to ear. "This is the home of Ranga Raja Bhattar."

At this point our friend entered the house and left us standing at the doorway. Seconds later a large man about sixty-five years old appeared at the door accompanied by his wife and family members. It was Randa Raja Battar. He wasn't wearing a shirt, and a white string hung across his left shoulder. He was a brahmana or priest. He had a shaven head with a large tuft of uncut hair at the back of his head and on his forehead he wore tilaka (sacred clay) signifying that he was a servant of Vishnu and a devotee of the Indian saint, Ramanuja Acharya.

"Koti, koti dandavats", (hundreds and thousands of respects), he said, as he took us by the hand and invited us into his home. We were completely taken aback by the unexpected hospitality. There we were, two complete strangers, unannounced guests, being treated as though we were long lost family members coming home after a lengthy absence.

Mr. Bhattar, whose English was a little rough—though far better than my Tamil (the local language)—inquired where we were from and why we had come to Sri Rangam. I told him that we were on pilgrimage to the great temple of Sri Rangam and that we had come all the way from the United States.

"Wonderful," he said. "But are you Hindus?"

"No," we replied. "Does it matter?"

"It certainly does," he said. "If you are not Hindus you can not enter the sanctum."

This came as a major disappointment. We had come a long way, yet we would not be allowed to enter the sacred shrine. We would have to be content to see the sanctum from outside.

"Let me tell you the story of Sri Rangam," said Mr. Bhattar, as he sat back in his armchair. "At the dawn of creation," he began, "Brahma, the first living being in this universe, desired to see the form of God and thus he received the sacred gayatri mantra in the core of his heart. After he meditated on the gayatri mantra for one thousand celestial years, a hundred thousand years by earthly calculations, the majestic form of Godhead manifest before Brahma in the form of Sri Murti, the deity of Narayana.

"Narayana means the original person. We believe that God is ultimately a person, a divine person. Not like you or I but He is the original personality possessing a spiritual body made of the eternal elements of sat, cit and ananda--eternity, knowledge and bliss. Because He is the supremely worshipable Divinity He appears in this world as Sri Murti to accept the service of His devotees and to deliver the fallen souls.

"Brahma worshiped the deity of Narayana for a long time in the world of the demigods. Then Ikshvaku, the king of Ayodhya, went to the heavenly planets and brought the deity to the earth. Ikshvaku built a beautiful temple for the Lord and passed on the worship of the deity in the succession of his dynasty.

"During the time of Rama, an incarnation of Godhead who appeared in the dynasty of Ikshvaku, a war was fought with the demon king Ravana from Sri Lanka. When Ravana was killed by Rama, Vibhishana, the brother of Ravana, accompanied Rama back to His capital city. At Ayodhya, Rama presented the deity of Narayana to Vibhishana along with the instruction to return with the deity to Sri Lanka.

"Along the way Vibhishana stopped at Sri Rangam to observe a fast and some other religious rituals. But when he was ready to leave he found that the deity could not be moved. At that time King Chola Dharmavarman, who reigned over the country, consoled Vibhishana and promised to construct a suitable temple. When the temple was completed, Vibhishana departed for Sri Lanka.

"After many centuries had passed, the temple was flooded by the rising water of the Kaveri and buried under the sand. A dense forest grew over the area and the temple remained hidden for a long time. Then one day King Kili, a descendent of Dharmavarman, was resting under a tree in the forest and he heard a parrot repeating Puranic verses proclaiming that this was the site of the temple of Sri Rangam.

"Performing excavations at the place, King Kili discovered the remains of the ancient temple and the deity of Narayana within. The king immediately set about the task of constructing a new temple. Since that time, long, long ago, the temple of Sri Rangam has been maintained by the great kings of India such as Raja Krishnadeva Raya and others.

"According to our ancient scripture Sri Rangam is a holy place considered to be non-different from the spiritual world of Vaikuntha. Here a person receives the rare opportunity to see the transcendental form of Godhead and thus experience the fulfillment of his heart. Everyone who comes to Sri Rangam is blessed."

Mr. Bhattar fell silent for some time and appeared to be in a deep contemplative mood, when suddenly he spoke. "You have come here by the grace of God. You should not go away without seeing the deity and touring the sanctum."

"Is it possible?" we asked. "Can we enter the sanctum?"

"Yes," he replied. "I will take you to the sanctum in the morning. You can witness the ceremony of waking the deity and chanting the Vishnu Sahasranam, the thousand names of Vishnu. You may come with me. It is our rule that non-Hindus are not allowed to enter, but for you we are going to make an exception. I believe it is God's will. But you will have to wear a dhoti, our traditional temple dress. Even a Hindu can not wear pants and shirt in the sanctum."

Mrs. Bhattar, who had not said much until now, accommodated us in a spare bedroom and, after a glass of hot milk, we took rest.

We had just dozed off, or so it seemed, when there was a knock at the door. "It is time to go to the temple," said a voice from the outside. I looked at my watch. It was 3:15 A.M. After taking a quick shower we were each given a white dhoti and a cotton shawl to wear. Coming out of our room we joined Mr. Bhattar and his family and walked to the temple through the quiet streets. Every few houses a door opened and someone come out and joined us. By the time we reached the main gate of the temple our little group had become a major procession.

The doors of the sanctum, which were made of beautifully hand-crafted silver, were scheduled to open at 4:00 A.M. As we stood in the dim light the events began to unfold. First five brahmanas stepped forward and removed the huge padlocks and chains from the doors of the sanctum. Suddenly from around the corner came a mahout, leading a gorgeously decorated elephant. Everyone gave way as the elephant was led up to the door. The brahmanas began to chant Sanskrit hymns, and just as the shining silver doors were swung open, the elephant raised his trunk high above his head and gave a shrill scream that shattered the night atmosphere. Three times the elephant heralded the opening of the sanctum doors.

After completing his service, the elephant bowed down on his two front legs and was led away by the mahout. The barefoot brahmanas, followed by the others, entered the sanctum. Oil lamps were lit one by one as we proceeded down a long corridor. The smell of burning oil and incense filled the air.

We came to a full halt before another set of silver doors. The moments that followed were filled with suspense as we stood where few if any Westerners had ever been before. Slowly the doors began to open and we entered the final sanctum. There was only enough room in the sanctum for about twelve persons to stand at a time. We went in with the first group.

Mr. Bhattar emerged before us just when we began to feel a little bewildered by the whole experience and brought us to stand directly in front of the deity. "This is the Great Lord of Sri Rangam, Narayana," he said.

As we stood before the altar we beheld a marvelous sight. We saw the majestic form of Narayana, the transcendental form of Godhead. The deity was in a reclined position, being served by His attentive servants, the brahmanas. The immense image was glistening black and covered the entire width of the sanctum. The deity wore a gold crown bedecked with precious stones like diamonds and emeralds. A garland of pearls was strung around His neck and His hands and feet were covered in gold. He wore yellow garments and was decorated with fragrant flowers.

"Sit here," said Mr. Bhattar, as he gestured to two sitting places at the side. We sat and watched the proceedings with great wonder. An unending stream of people entered the sanctum one after another. They filed through the sanctum entrance and stood before the altar with folded hands, exhibiting intense feelings of awe and reverence for the deity. Some murmured prayers as they came and went, and others carried offerings of fruits, flowers, incense, cloth and other such items. All the offerings were given to the brahmanas who placed them before the deity of Narayana. Everyone was given three drops of sacred water to sip in the palms of their hands, and a golden object resembling a crown was raised and placed momentarily upon their heads. The gold crown symbolized the two lotus feet of Narayana, said to be the supreme benediction for the servitor.

The blissful glance that the imposing figure of Narayana cast on His visitors was too deep for the eyes to fathom and too vast for words to describe. This unique experience has to be felt to be properly appreciated - it was ecstatic.

As the brahmanas administered the blessings of Narayana, they chanted over and over again a special hymn: Om Tad Vishnu Paramam Padam... . "The lotus feet of Vishnu, Narayana, are the supreme object of all the demigods. His lotus feet are as effulgent as the sun.They are watching over us at all times."

This continued for some time until the last morning visitor left and the sanctum doors were again shut. Mr. Bhattar sat by our side and said, "Now the priests will recite the Vishnu Sahasranam, the thousand names of Vishnu."

The brahmanas stood in two straight rows before the deity and began to recite the hymn in perfect unison. The melody of each chanter harmonized perfectly with that of the other. The chanting continued unabated for about forty-five minutes and then complete silence dominated the chamber.

The hymn that they sang was a glorification of the thousand names of Godhead, corresponding to His various incarnations and pastimes. We rose from our seats and bowed heads in reverence; Mr. Bhattar escorted us through a side exit and into the courtyard.

The sun was rising when we came out of the sanctum. The flood of sunlight revealed the splendor of the shrine from beneath the shadows of darkness. The wonders for the eyes were never ceasing. Above the sanctum, we saw a great golden vimana (dome), covering the entire roof. The sight of so much opulence was mind-boggling.

As we walked around the courtyard we saw an extensive array of sculptured stone columns, colonnades, corridors, domes and passageways. In the middle of the courtyard stood a golden pillar with Garuda, the devoted bird-carrier of Vishnu, at the top. In a large pavilion with five hundred pillars, each with a different design, a group of musicians sat playing classical Indian ragas. The sounds of the drums, hand cymbals and shenai (wind instrument) created a pleasing, almost heavenly atmosphere. In another pavilion a brahmana sat and read the scriptures and another brahmana lit the sacred fire-all part of their morning rituals.

Several brahmanas came and placed fruits, flowers and a small basket of sweets in our hands. "This is the prasadam (mercy) of Narayana," they said. We accepted the articles respectfully and as we walked back to the home of Mr. Bhattar we felt grateful for the opportunity we had received. The moments we had spent in the sanctum before the deity of Narayana now seemed fixed in eternity.

As we returned to the home of Mr. Bhattar we paused to read an inscription engraved on a marble plaque beside the temple gate: "I bow to Narayana, who is the ocean of mercy, the shelter of all without any discrimination of higher or lower, the destroyer of the troubles of those who seek Him, the ocean of affection for those who rely on Him, the constant knower of the real inner truth about all living beings, and the friend of everyone."

Our pilgrimage to Sri Rangam was successful beyond our greatest expectations. We had seen and learned much more than we had anticipated. Indeed, we had acquired a genuinely transcendental experience that we would remember for a lifetime.

Swami B G Narasingha writes a regular spiritual travelog for Clarion Call. Swami B B Visnu is an associate editor for Clarion Call.

## Tantra

As Above So Below

By Jeffery Armstrong

In recent years, many books have been published on tantra and kundalini yoga. Tantra is naturally a very interesting subject to everyone since it deals directly with the significance of our sexual identity. Sex always sells, so many authors have jumped on the “New Age” tantra bandwagon. These books often end up to be a cross between Masters and Johnson and the *Kama Sutra.* The massage is in the message, that is, they are guides to states of higher sexual pleasure. No doubt, that is attractive and alluring, but it is also a distortion of tantra. Since tantra does include an understanding of sexual identity, physiology and energetics, you may study it to improve your sex life. Similarly, you may study hatha yoga in order to have a healthy body. But a healthy body is not the *goal* of yoga and good sex is *not* the aim of tantra.

Just what is tantra? No short answer will do, and here I intend to discuss it in the broadest of terms, rather than focusing only on the particular tantric technique involving sexual practice in the context of pursuing enlightenment. As we shall see, this there is more to tantra than this.

Studying other cultures, especially very ancient cultures, requires a great deal of patience and determination. It is as if you have entered into an elaborate conversation, going on between many great thinkers. Since you have come in at the middle of their discussion, before you can make an intelligent comment, you need to understand what has already been said. So, for anyone trying to understand the Vedic knowledge, which both yoga and tantra have arisen from, a great deal of background study is necessary. The discussion begins with how we know what we know.

According to the *Vedas*, there are three ways to acquire knowledge: direct perception by the physical body (the senses), inferences drawn by the mind based on the evidence of the senses, and hearing, which is also called descending knowledge. Put simply, our senses perceive the world and give us information. The mind, using the information of the senses develops a theory based on the information, or we may receive knowledge that has been given directly by an intelligence higher than our own. The Vedic knowledge is received through hearing. It is descending knowledge, received from self realized souls. Since our senses often fool us, and our mind is subject to creeping errors, those of Vedic culture decided to put their faith in descending knowledge given by the *rishis.*

Of course the three: body, mind/intellect, and descending knowledge or spirit (*shabda brahma)*, are all interrelated. All three unite to give information and experience which is necessary for the soul’s evolution. However, without the transcendental sound current, descending knowledge, it is not possible for the soul to evolve beyond the planes of sensual and intellectual experience—to achieve liberation. The sanskrit word *atma* indicates the source of consciousness which is eternal and joyful, in its original liberated state. And the entire edifice of Vedic thought is devoted to the liberation of the *atma* from all forms of limitation or bondage. “From darkness lead us to light, from ignorance lead us to knowledge, from death lead us to immortality.” That is the Vedic direction. To achieve that goal, many different paths and practices were prescribed or have evolved. Tantra is one of those paths. But tantra also has a broader application. Literally it means “that which expands.” In a sense you could say tantra is science. Just as science expands our knowledge, so tantra expands our experience. But it is science aimed ultimately at enlightening and liberating the *atma*, expanding the soul's range of experince beyond it's present self imposed limitations. And for this there are many tantric paths.

The generic tantric view is summarized in the saying: “*yat pinde, tat brahmande,*” or “As above so below.” To say the same thing more specifically, the universe corresponds to the individual. And on a higher level, the universe is a reflection of its source. Therefore it is said, “Matter is the dictionary of spirit.” Following this line of thinking, the forms, structures and beauty of the visible universe are viewed as hints or pointers whose existence is meaningful on many levels. In this sense, tantra is like an old word for what we now call psychology (maybe transpersonal psychology), the study of the mind. What we experience as mind, is actually somewhere between the visible world of matter and the invisible world of spirit. The students of tantra try to understand the interconnection between these different levels of reality, the physical body and the material world, and that of the *atma* and the world of consciousness. In order to do so they may avail themselves to, on the one end, hatha or astanga yoga for acquiring knowledge of the body and its energetics, and on the other to vedanta and meditation for understanding consciousness.

First let's look at the body, and in so doing the *atma* to some extent as well through the eyes of tantra. “Asta” means eight, “anga” means limbs. What is popularly known as hatha yoga is usually one or two of these eight limbs—*asanas* or postures and *pranayama* , or breath control. Tantric yoga and hatha yoga were originally the same system, thousands of years ago. They both follow the eight limbs, which are: *yama* (do’s) ; *niyama* (don’ts) ; *asana* (bodily postures); *pranayama* (breath control); *pratyahara* (sense withdrawal) ; *dharana* (concentration); *dhyana* (meditation) ; and *samadhi* (complete absorbtion). The basis of this physical approach to yoga is an elaborate yoga physiology which contains detailed information about the construction of the body and its energetic workings. Remember also, that the universe (*brahmanda*) and the human body (*pinda*) are identical except for size. Not only are they the same, but they are interrelated, such that changes in one are constantly reflected in the other. This concept also forms the basis for the science of astrology, which is, generically speaking, a tantric science as well. Similarly the meridians and acupuncture points used in Chinese and ayurvedic medicine, are in fact star maps laid out upon the human body. The 108 principle stars of the zodiac are considered points of release for certain cosmic radiations which we are constantly absorbing.

The first distinction drawn in yogic or tantric physiology is that of male and female, that is to say the world is dualistic and the interaction of the two primary energies *purusha* (male) and *prakriti* (female) gives rise to all other reality within the universe. Crossing cultures, one refers to these principles as *yang* (male) and *yin* (female); for the West in a binary mathematical model it is one and zero. These are simply impersonal or symbolic representations of the same reality. But for humans interested in self-realization and liberation, it is important that these two great realities are seen as personal. After all, we are persons. So in India the tantric scientists described the universe as a coming together of two realities, one male and one female, manifest in an endless multitude of forms. This is the secret behind the myriad of gods and goddesses depicted in the temple architecture of India. It is not that real Hindus are confused and worship many gods. The truth is, all manifestations of reality are seen as originally and continuously interconnected to various intelligent entities who are either male or female. As above, so below. The universe is alive, intelligent, and personal—we are not alone!

In yoga physiology the left hemisphere of the brain is considered male while the right is female. Remember, the use of male and female are not sexist terms, but rather scientific terms referring to the action of the energies. In tantra, space is a female energy, for it accommodates or contains, whereas time is a male energy representing extension. In the body then, there are two main channels for the life force. The *ida* is female or lunar, and starts at the base of the spine ending at the left nostril and connected to the right brain. The other solar nerve, *pingala*, is male, and starts in the same place ending at the right nostril, connecting to the left brain. Between these two is a third channel known as *shushumna*, the middle path, which flows straight up the spine. The familiar caduses of Mercury, used by the medical profession as their symbol, is a depiction of these three *nadis*, though aliopaths have long forgotten its signifigance.

Along the central pathway or *shushumna*, there are seven energy vortexes or *chakras*, starting at the base of the spine and ascending to the top of the head. Each center is a focal point of certain life forces. The *Vedas* describe that the physical universe we see is actually filled with many other less visible realms of existence. It describes the universe as having fourteen levels of reality called *lokas*. The first seven of these constitute the mineral plant and animal kingdom, up to the human level. On the human body these seven levels are situated on the legs up to the base of the spine. In that region, the first human center, *mooladhara*, is located, followed by *svadisdana*, *manipura, anhatta*, *vishudi*, *ajna* and finally *sahasrara*. Each of these centers is connected to a certain level of universal consciousness. If one truly opens a *chakra* and is conscious of its significance, one is also ascending to higher orders of universal intelligence.
