The*Vedas* speak of a mysterious tree which has its roots upward and its branches downward. If you go to a quiet pond and look at the reflection of a tree this metaphor will become clear. Our bodies are such reflections.

According to yoga and tantra, the vital force which animates all life is called *prana*. It is circulated throughout the body by means of 72,000 channels called *nadis. Nadis* are subtle pathways for energy flow. *Ida, pingala* and *shushumna* are the three principle *nadis*. A proper understanding of yoga physiology combined with certain physical and mental practices allow the yogi to gain mastery of certain bodily processes that are usually automatic. For example, the secret of the nose is that it is a switching device which connects the lungs, heart and brain. The left nostril is connected to *ida*, the right to *pingala*. By breathing through one nostril only, the corresponding energy can be activated. By means of this practice, the mind can be controlled mechanically. This is one simple example of a tantric or yogic practice. There are many such practices which the guru teaches the disciple. Some of them are very difficult and require years of guidance and practice.

In hatha yoga (ha means the Sun and tha means the Moon), the human body is seen as a living symbol of the secrets of the universe. Each person is either a manifestation of male or female energy, but since each body is also a universe unto itself, each of us contains with ourselves both male and female energies. When those energies work together harmoniously, we experience health, happiness and well being. It is for this reason that the by product of yoga is health. And that is why a correct understanding of tantric science leads to the highest possible sexual experience. But neither elevated sex or good health are the goal of yoga and tantra.

On the other hand, according to tantra, there is nothing inherently evil in sex. In a Western context, however, this concept seems to have lead to considerable abuse. The point is a practical one: sexual indulgence for sense pleasure is the very binding force that ties us to this limited plane of experience. Unlike Christianity and many other religions, sex is not seen as "sinful" nor is pleasure a source of guilt. In fact, according to the *Vedas* pleasure or *annanda* is one of the eternal features of *atma*. Therein the soul is described as *sat*—eternal, *chit*—full of knowledge, *vigraha*—possessed of a spiritual form and *annanda*— by nature full of ecstasy.So, in the view of the transcendentalists, the pleasure of sexual contact is a mirror or shadow of our true nature reflected into the realm of matter. Not to be judgemental, but shadow chasing is not a good idea. The goal of tantra is not union with the sexual partner of your choice, that can not liberate the soul. And it is liberation from the confines of material existence that both yoga and tantra ultimately advocate. After that our real life begins.

This first part of tantric science dealing with the body (hatha or astanga yoga), and also the *atma* thereby, is not religious or sectarian in any sense. It is a science that has been practiced at a high level in the East for thousands of years. The above mentioned scientific foundation is common to all systems of tantra and yoga. It is from this basic understanding of the material realms that teachers turn their attention to a particular concept of the ultimate reality, to be achieved through some meditative discipline. It does not necessarily follow, however, that if a teacher accurately describes the yoga physiology, bodily energetics, and the male/female relationship of the world, etc., that his or her philosophy regarding the ultimate reality is correct, or conclusive. Just because one accurately describes the wonders of the interconnectedness of this world, both gross and subtle, that is not sufficient reason to accept everything he or she says about life's goal. Many persons have exploited the basic knowledge of bodily energetics, etc. for their own ends, as have many material scientists. Partial knowledge can be a dangerous thing. Thus they have lead others *away* from life's goal and the knowledge of our spiritual origin. And it is life' s goal that is ultimately important. Knowing our origin is most important. Is our origin spiritual, or are we products of matter? Is it personal or impersonal? Answering these questions will determine much about the correct course of action for humanity.

The second half of tantra and of yoga is the meditation on which the aspirant’s mind is to be focused. This brings us to the end of knowledge and the goal of yoga. It is in this area that there is such a wide difference of opinion as to what is the ultimate goal of meditation. Here there is also much scope for misrepresentation. If one follows the do's and don’ts (*yamas* and *niyams*), masters the *asanas* (postures), learns to control the life force (*pranayama*), learns to withdraw the senses(*pratyahara*), concentrates the mind (*dharana*), then what is the correct meditation (*dhyana*) into which one should become fully absorbed (*samadhi*)?

In India this question has been answered variously by the differtent systems of thought. Even though many (the transcendentalists) agree that the goal of life is the liberation of the *atma* from the cycle of birth and death (*samsara*), still many vary in their view as to just how that liberation is to be achieved, and what the liberated condition entails. This is the larger philosophical discussion which has occupied India for thousands of years.

In India thare are five main phiosophical schools of thought (some have broken them into six) Each of them derives their understanding of God or life's goal in accordance with their particular belief as to the dynamics of the creation of the universe. Just as the universe is seen as a manifestation of male and female energies, so in a larger sense the universe itself may be envisioned as originating from male and female realities. So, if the creation comes from a creator, Godhead, that creator could be male (*purusha*) or *prakriti* (female), or both.

What is the nature of the ultimate creative force? Does everything including *prarkriti* (the female principle) come from *purusha* (the male principle) alone (Vedanta of Vyaas)? Is *purusha* dominant with *prakriti* playing a small role (yoga of Patanjali)? Do *purusha* and *prakriti* play equal roles (Vaiseshika of Kanada)? Is *prakriti*  dominant while *purusha* plays a small role (Nyaya of Gauttama)? Or is *prakriti* alone the sole principle in creation (Sankhya of the atheist Kapila)? All of these five basic visions of universal creation are tantric in one sense. Although they are not all schools of transcendental thought, they all accept the principal of "as above so below". It is only recently that tantra has been popularized to mean exclusively the worship of *shakti* — the female principle.

Focusing on this popular tantric tradition for a moment, rather than tantra in a generic sense, popular tantra in general, at its best, advocates the merging of the male and female aspects appearing microcosmically in our own bodies through an elaborate process involving various techniques, such that the principles of creation in the macrocosim affecting us are reversed, resulting in liberation. Shiva and Shakti unite, and the material conceptions of man and woman are transcended. Liberation here is *advaitic,* non-dual. In this conception individualism is extinguished along with all distinctions or variety. There are no forms and there is no Supreme Person. On the low end hightened sexuality is advocated as the goal. Returning to tantra in the generic sense, in the yogic tradition of vedanta we find various alternative conceptions of liberation, some of which, for example, advocate a relationship with a Supreme Person (Vishnu) beyond time and space, where individuality, and variety exist in spiritual harmony (Vaishnava tantra).

Thus tantra is a big word with many applications, and it is a great injustice to relegate it solely to its popularized present day usage. As we listen to the various tantric teachers, before we accept what we hear to be *the* truth about tantra, we would do well to draw back and find the place of any particular conclusion within the entire edifice of Vedic knowledge. We may be seeing only a small part of a much bigger picture.

In any sense of the term tantra is powerful knowledge. But it is a two-edged sword which can definitely be misused. That is the reason that some tantric science has been kept secret, suppressed and persecuted. In that sense tantra is neutral, like any scientific knowledge: it just is. But in the wrong hands it can be misused. Atomic knowledge did not have to be used to make bombs, but given the present state of human evolution it did. So the reader should beware that not all teachers of “tantra” have good intentions. For some it is the study of the true nature of the universe leading to liberation and love of Godhead, for others it is a chance to exploit others and have unlimited material power.

These are vast topics of spiritual understanding, too great to be described in one short article. But with these ideas in mind, it may be easier to read various tantric authors and understand the kind of tantra they are practising. For all tantrics, the basics of yoga physiology are the same. Everyone is looking at the same mountain. The crucial point for each aspirant is to understand where a teacher is directing your attention. Stilling the mind, controlling the breathing, understanding the male and female powers of the universe; all of these are preliminary steps. The real question is ultimately, "What is the final meaning and destination of the individual?" This vision quest is the real meaning of tantra. The *Vedas* declare the nature of *atma* to be joyful. Yoga is sometimes translated as union. Our real quest is not the abandoning of pleasure, but the search for its unlimited source.

This article is just a few thoughts gathered from an elaborate conversation between the great tantric thinkers. Great thoughts are like the seeds of a mighty tree. If you tend them with patience, weed them with determination, and water them with pure desire, they will grow into a great forest of understanding— a forest with its roots upward and branches downward.

## Terrorism

The Israelis and Arabs never seem to get out of news print. On the Arab side the Palastinians are perhaps most “at home” on the printed page, where for years they have been pursuing the wisdom in the sayings “Any publicity is good publicity” or “Bad publicity is better than no publicity.” Lately, the Palastinians, who are more famous as “terrorists” than “freedom fighters,” have gained ground in their struggle for world sympathy. At the same time the Israeli malitia while trying to keep the Palastinians in line within Isriael’s extended boarders have fallen in the popularity polls. Israel’s leathal and non leathal thrashings of these “homeless” peoples have been viewed largely as inappropriate.

In their search for their homeland we are moved to sympathize with the Palestinian people for in a sense we are all engaged in the same. Everyone wants a place to call their own. We must only raise objection to the direction in which they look- along with most persons of this world for that matter- as well as with their method of attainment. That method, however, may also be appreciated from the standpoint of the one-minded deternmination displayed, ie.,”do or die.” The inside of the affair is laudable, however, do to ignorance of the real home of the soul, their method is objectionable to us and for the most part counter productive for them.

The world is not soon to forget that it was the Palastinians who created the threat of terrorism. In their demand for freedom the Palastinian Liberation Organization (PLO) has made not only themselves known, but a method of warfare as well by which relatively small bands of rebels and even frustrated individuals can harass and intimidate the most powerful nations.

Although the original target of the PLO was the Israeli government, those who supported her were naturally added to the hit list. Thus the USA, Israeli supporter and world policeman, is usually right in the middle of the struggle. With the constant fear that the ongoing Israeli -Arab struggle may suddenly escalate at anytime into a global disaster the news of Middle Eastern developments are read abroad with a cautious eye. A permanent solution to the Middle East struggle is most desireable.

If we take a closer look at the very terrifying nature of the predicament we find ourselves in , which goes beyond this threat of an escalation of the Middle East conflict, we may find a solution. If the American, Israeli preoccupied Palestinian, for example, were to consider the true and observable evolutionary process ie., from subtle (conciousness) to gross (matter), he would be terrified to realize that his mental absorbtion on foriegn lands at the time of death might find him taking birth in those lands perhaps to continue the fight now against “his” own cause and country.

The subtle mental condition at the time of death determines the future embodiment of the living being. From conciousness matter evolves and takes a particular shape. As all material manifestions have their beginning in the subtle form of their very conception and only later appear in our speach, then action and finaly as the object itself, so our bodies are but a futher evolution of our concious thought pattern. Today an Arab, tomorrow an Israeli, it is quite possible. Unfortunately these subtle laws of nature are realitively unknown to even the so called learned men of the modern world, as is, and even more so, it’s lawmaker. Ironicaly much of the fighting is going on in His name.

I once explained the soul's transmigration to an elderly lady who aghast remarked, "Oh! That sounds horrible." I replied, "Yes, so why don't you do something about it!"Although the world is full of danger at every step, terrifying for the soul, acknowledging this fact may be the very beginning of our auspicious life. Failure is the pillar of success. The prostitute Pingala of the Bhagavatam whose utter dispair, upon not getting any costomers the entire night marked the beginning of her satisfaction of a superior quality, brings to mind the Sanskrit proverb, "Disappointment gives rise to the greatest satisfaction." As long as we try to hide from the inevitability of death our movements will not be able to save us. If it is terrorism, or nuclear war or a banana peel on the step which brings our death the lesson is death is sure, “as sure as death.” In order to make a solution to the very world of war we will have to build our house in that plane where there is no death. We must die here in order to live there. This is not the death of our gross body rather the demise of our exploitive mentality which brings upon us the fearful reaction of the world as we know it.

Another world is there and we must go there if we are at all to know peace. Arabs, Americans, Christians and Hindus, Muslims etc., will find common ground there and room for all. Beyond material designation lies our homeland in a friendly atmosphere of serving spirit. The call of Godhead strikes a chord within us which is of the same nature as that of the caller and thus we find we are “close to home” when we are in submissive aural reach of His message. Outside of that there is only terror and terrorism in so many forms.

Our critic will be quick to point out that what has been presented is a very simplistic out look. He may also remark that a religious fervor turning into fanaticism is at the root of terrorism. How can more religious fanaticsm do anything but cause more harm? Do we really think that the Arabs or Israelies upon reading this will lay down their weapons and embrace a third creed?

In reply it must be said that simple solutions are often the best. Simplicity is a divine quality. To be simple does not mean to be a simpleton. A simpleton or a fool will not see the logic of our reasoning. A more far reaching idea of terrorism has been alluded to above and that must be recognized. A common man may feed another hungry man. A third man will refuse to do so do to having his attention directed towards political reform, which he sees as more complete approach to solving the hunger crisis. Similarly a transendentalist looks still deeper than political adjustment to the further adjustment of man’s conciousness which is behind every thing. We have proposed that the numerous relative solutions offered by our critics are but phantasmagoria. Without self (soul) realization there is no question of peace for the embodied. Peace in prison, like honesty amongst thieves is only a shadow of the whole idea.

A trancendentalist is different from the religious fanatic. Ordinary church goers seeks to exploit dvinity for their own cause. They want to employ God in their service rather than serve Him, as in “give us our daily bread.” This is a sort of cheating process. It is not real religion. If we are engaged in such self deception how can we understand the truth? We may think, “My religion does not believe in reincarnation” and other such foolish ideas like “my religion says it’s all right to kill cows and eat them.” These ideas are clearly devoid of trancendental knowledge and experience.

The trancendentalist sees all living beings equally. He sees the ever changing nature of the world around him, and that he (the soul) alone remains constant. As long as we are attatched to this physical plane of experience we will remain here. That means a change of bodies is as sure as the change of seasons. If I am the constant observing factor amidst the ever changing material phenomana and if I choose to remain in this atmosphere I must change bodies at death.

The athiest seeks to improve the standard of sense gatification while scoffing at the ordinary thiest’s admonishments. Yet the trancendentalist sees the folly of both who in actuality are interested in different standards of the same thing. The only difference is that while one denies God the other asks His help. Both of them are concerned with this world.

We are not recomending another belief system. Today I may be a Catholic but tomorrow I may convert to Hinduism. Rather trancendental knowledge must be cultured. Knowledge about that part of ourselves that does not change will bring us to common ground beyond the world of birh and death.Still you may ask, it sounds good but do you really expect the whole world to embrace this?” In a word “no”, but what about you?

## To Err is Human

By Swami B.R. Sridhara

To err is human. Being imperfect, to err is inevitable for all. Still, no one wants to remain imperfect. There is an element within all that is animate that tends towards perfection. If it were not so, we would feel no want at all. Our tendency towards perfection is certainly very weak and limited; otherwise we could attain the goal at once. Our limited capacity and tendency for perfection makes room for the guide and guru.

The imperfect is not so if it is not in need of help from beyond itself. And the perfect—Godhead—is not perfect if he cannot assert himself or help others of his own accord. So the guidance to perfection or absolute truth is necessarily a function of the absolute himself, and the divine agent through whom this function manifests is the guru or divine guide.

For a seeker of the absolute truth, submission to the guru is unavoidable. A class of thinkers believes, however, that when scientific research is possible, why cannot higher spiritual knowledge also be evolved from within? Such people are ignorant of the most essential nature of absolute knowledge: that Godhead alone is the absolute subject, and all else, including ourselves, constitutionally stand only as an object to his omniscient vision. It is impossible for the eye to see the mind; it can have some connection with the mind only when the latter cares to mind it. In a similar way, our connection with absolute knowledge depends mainly on his sweet will. We must solely depend on his agent, or the spiritual master through whom he likes to distribute himself.

Our human society with its finest culture forms but an infinitesimal part of the dynamic absolute. How then, except by the direct and positive method of revelation, dare we hope to comprehend or evolve any conception of the supernatural knowledge of the unconditioned infinite? All intellectual giants prove themselves to be but pygmies before Godhead, the absolute omniscient omnipotence who reserves the right to give himself away through his own agents alone.

To our best knowledge and sincerity, however, we should see to it that we do not submit to a false agent. Here of course we can't help ourselves very much, because in our present state we are mainly guided by our previous *samskara* or acquired nature. "Birds of the same feather flock together." Yet although we are generally overpowered by habit, there is still the possibility of free choice to a certain extent, especially in the human species—otherwise correction becomes impossible, and punishment mere vengeance. Reality can assert itself. Light does not require darkness for its positive proof. The sun by itself can establish its supremacy over all other lights. Before an open and unbiased eye, the true guru or guide shines above all professors of phenomenon.

Sri guru manifests himself mainly in two ways: as the director from within and the preceptor from without. Both functions of the absolute help an individual soul—a disciple—to reach the absolute goal. In our fallen state we cannot catch the proper direction of the inner guide, so the merciful manifestation of the preceptor without is our sole help and hope. But at the same time it is only by the grace of the guru within that we can recognize the real preceptor without and submit to his holy feet.

A bona fide disciple must always remain fully awake to the fact that his highest spiritual fortune is but a gracious grant from the Absolute Lord, and not a matter of right to be demanded or fought out. Constitutionally, we are equipped only to be proper recipients of God's favor. In this connection it should be clearly understood that an individual soul can never be substantially the same as the absolute person. Not even in his liberated or fully realized condition can an individual soul be one with Godhead in all respects. The misconception of oneness has been introduced from the slothful nondiscrimination of the absolute personality from the luminous orb around his eternal, spiritual, and blissful home. In fact, an individual soul constitutes only a part of a particular energy of Godhead, and as such he is capable of being converted by both sides. He differs from the Absolute Person both in quality and in quantity, and is merely an entity dependent on the absolute. In other words, the absolute Godhead is the master, and the individual *jiva* (soul) is his constitutional subordinate or servant.

Such a relationship is constant and really wholesome for the *jiva.* The apprehension of slavery does not arise because of his free choice and immense positive gain; the freedom and individuality of the *jiva* are not only unharmed by surrender to the absolute good, but they really thrive in Him alone. Individual freedom and interest are the part and parcel of those who are of the absolute, and so they are quite at home there, as a fish is at home in water or an animal in a healthy atmosphere. But the freedom as well as all other qualities of Godhead are unlimited and transcendental, and so simply by their partial functions they harmonize all relative entities.

Sri guru is not exclusively the same as God, but he fully represents the essence of God's potency and embodies the most comprehensive and excellent service and favor of God. As he is the fittest servitor of Godhead, he is empowered by Godhead to reinstate all misguided souls to their best interest. So the guru is the divine messenger of immortal hope and joy in this mortal and miserable world. His advent is the most auspicious and happy event to the suffering animation, and can be compared to the rising of the morning star that can guide the traveler lost in the desert. Where a patriot or philanthropist fails in his frantic attempt to alleviate the deep-rooted pain of a suffering soul, a gentle touch of sri guru's merciful hand can wipe away the incessant tears from all weeping eyes. O the day when this poor soul realizes the causeless grace of sri gurudeva.

*This essay was originally published in 1934 in* The Harmonist.

## Vegetarian Jewish Society

CC Interview With MR. Pick: 3-24-88

Clarion Call: Mr. Pick, what inspired you to begin the Jewish Vegetarian Society?

Mr. Pick: Well, as a life-long vegetarian second generation and always active in the general vegetarian movement, I was always a bit sad about the way Jewish people would look upon their religion as being connected with the slaughter of animals. It actively started in 1964 when our daughter, who is a third generation vegetarian, was attending the Royal Academy of Music in London, and started singling out the Jewish vegetarian young men there, probably with an object in mind. She found quite a few, started forming the society, and was promptly told she couldn't do that in the academy. It was for music purposes, not for vegetarianism, so she handed it over to me, and from then on we started making a public event of it and it grew and grew.

At first we met hostility from the jewish people, but we've broken through, and leading rabbis in many parts of the world all confirm that to be truly kosher today, you need to be vegetarian, bearing in mind that the obscene and anti-Jewish activities of the factory farms in which animals are bred for so-called kosher purposes would alter the entire concept of Kashruths because of the treatment of these animals.

Clarion Call: Would you speak about some of the activities of the Jewish Vegetarian Society?

Mr. Pick: Well, it covers a very wide sphere now, as an international organization. We have about thirty rooms here, the headquarters for the production of our magazine which goes all over the world; we have naturopathic clinics here, there are lectures and social affairs in our meeting hall; we have a vegetarian restaurant on the premises and also a residential quarters for our long-term members.

Our activities have been based on many aspects, for example, there is the ethical aspect, the religious aspect, the compassionate aspect, the economic aspect, and we are active in all these spheres. Abroad as well we have various matters which we have to take up, for example, our society was the only one able to stop the advent of bull fighting in Israel. The Israeli government couldn't stop it under legislation, but we raised such an issued in many parts of the world that they eventually found the means of stopping this very serious matter of bull fighting in the holy land.

We also had a two-year campaign in England on the use of rennet from the stomachs of slaughtered cows, which is added to milk to make cheese and then stamped as "kosher." Since then we have heard that the Bethden in England will now only mark as kosher those cheeses which are made with vegetable rennet.

Then we handle a lot of general matters, for example, the Arts Council Public Concern ceased having vegetarian food in their various restaurants of the theaters, concert galleries, and so on, but we campaigned very strongly and now they're supplying vegetarian food in every area where they operate.

We also work with the Animal Welfare Society against the horrific cruelty that mankind is imposing on animals, we are very much concerned with the ecology; our activities are almost countless.

Clarion Call: You're saying that to be strictly or truly kosher, one must be vegetarian, yet somewhere in the Judaic scriptures there must be some mention about this "koshering" process, this supposedly more merciful process for slaughtering cattle.

Mr. Pick: Actually, the teachings of the Bible are very evident for anyone who doesn't wish to overlook them. There are two periods—the first period is in Genesis, where we have an absolute command: "The green herb of the field, the fruit of the tree, and the seed of each tree bearing seed: that shall be as meat to you." There is no getting around that. Adam, of course, was not permitted to eat flesh; animals were on an equal par with him in the Garden of Eden. He was the older brother, the guardian, he gave them names. And up to the time of Noah, it was a capital offense to kill an animal.

Then we come to the second period in Noah where God says: "Man and all life have become violent upon the Earth, and therefore I will destroy it." But then, just as the parent of a child who commits a murder would eventually try and save their own child, God says, "I've repented, I will not destroy the world; it will last forever, summer will follow spring, and I shall put a rainbow in the sky as My sign. And even as I gave you the green herb in the field and the fruits of the tree for food, now I give unto you the flesh of animals, with their blood thereof you shall not eat." So here is a new period— a concession to barbarism. And the very words used are "man is violent from his youth" and "If you lust after flesh." In the King James version it's been carefully retranslated to say, "If you desire flesh, you should eat it to your heart's content." But actually it is "If you lust after flesh, then eat it to your heart's content."Definitely the word in Hebrew is lust. And it goes on to say, "And your blood of your life will I demand both at the hand of man and at the hand of the animals."It was given with a curse. It was called a lust and given with a curse.

Regrettably, most Jewish people from that time on have taken a concession—an evil concession—as being almost a law, but it is not. You see, the sacrifices in bygone ages were something different, and my own personal opinion is that today, all the efforts for world peace and health are wasted because this curse is operating. Every time we destroy one of God's creatures or we mistreat them, we pay for it. This is the law of an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, applied in a universal matter. We pay for what we do, and the suffering that's going on—the illness, the cancer, the heart desease—we know that is directly linked. It is all part of this curse which is operating.

In the same way that we show a love for children, a love for old people, we've got to show a love for the weakest of all creatures that can't cry and can't plead for themselves. That's the Biblical aspect, and it is corroborated by Isaiah, who says the sword will be turned into a plowshare and the lion will lay down with the lamb, and "none shall hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain." We must remember that the covenant that God made with the world at the time of Noah was made with all creatures, not with man only, that they shall lie down in peace and not be afraid.

You see, we treat all animals as younger creatures on the great ladder of life evolving. If we believe in reincarnation, then we are stopping the evolutionary progress of the world by slaughtering the animals, because then they've got to come back again to fulfill their lives.

Clarion Call: Mrs. Friedman, you've written the official cookbook of the Jewish Vegetarian Society. I'd like to hear about how you came to write this book and how it was received, and how it is used.

Mrs. Friedman: The book was conceived because Jewish people have festivals throughout the year which are associated with particular types of food, and we thought there was a need for vegetarian alternatives or substitutes for some of the dishes which people have grown to love since childhood, and whereas many Jewish people might be happy to become vegetarians, they might worry about whether they would be able to observe the festivals properly.if they weren't able to use food that they've been accustomed to having at these special times. So bearing that in mind, we produced the book, but it relates not only to Jewish people, but to people from all over the world—from the Middle east, from America, from South Africa, from France, Germany, and Russia— and we've tried to reflect that in the selection of recipes. Have you glanced through the book?

Clarion Call: Yes, I was curious about the traditional meaning of Passover and its dietary restrictions.

Mrs. Friedman: Passover is a very special time of the year and requires particular care for the selection of food. It is not only a question of not eating leavened bread and eating unleavened bread, it's a question of the way one uses the other foods that are avaiable to us. We put quite a large Passover section in the cookbook.

Passover was the beginning of our freedom. Before Passover the Jewish people were slaves, and as soon as Passover came we "passed over" from being slaves to being free people. And every year, at the time of Passover, we relive that particular experience, and because we left Egypt in haste, we had no time to allow our bread to rise to become leavened, so we eat matzoh as a symbol of that. It's form of purification, if you like. And when we bake on Passover, instead of using regular flour, we use matzoh meal of potato flour.

People seem to be quite happy with the book's selection of recipes. It sold quite well over Passover and people found they could in fact enjoy the festival without having to have meat or fish. We devised an alternative to chopped herring which is so good that it's difficult to tell the difference, but you know, this book isn't just a question of finding substitutes which taste the same—although there are few like that—it's to show people that there are alternatives.

Clarion Call: There is a statement in your book that vegetarianism and Judaism are in complete harmony.

Mrs. Friedman: Yes, there is absolutely nothing in any Judaic writings which say that one must have meat, nothing at all. One can be the most completely orthodox Jewish person and celebrate all the festivals, including the Sabbath, without touching a bite of any meat or fish at all. So from that point of view, and from the point of view of closeness to the Creator and appreciation of this world in which we live—our blessings before and after we eat and for everything that happens to us everyday—Judaism is certainly very much in harmony with the vegetarian approach, which is a love and respect for all life.

Mr. Pick: There are always Biblical references to the animals and it is a teaching of Judaism that animals have an equal right on this planet along with us. We are the gardeners of the world, Adam was the gardner of the Garden of Eden, we were turned out because of our evil, and "the fiery sword was placed against the gates," but we hope to return one day to a pure state. Why should a good Jewish person not subscribe to this principle? The question of "Thou shalt not kill" is another point of contention. When I was a child—that was a long time ago, because I'm 75 now—the translations of that Commandment used to read "Thou shalt not kill." Today you look in the average prayer book and you find it says "Thou shalt not commit murder." That is not correct.

Now people have said, "You can't help killing when you live because you destroy bacterial life and unwittingly walk on insects." If I saw an insect I wouldn't walk on it actually, but people do, and at times cannot avoid killing. The answer of course lies in utilizing our good common sense: "Thou shalt not kill unnecessarily." I mean I can understand if a great many years ago people were perhaps living on an island and they fished and ate the fish, and if they didn't eat the fish they would die otherwise, because they didn't have the technology to help them like we have today. But today, when you consider that flesh foods, both fish and meat, are destroying people in their youth—that heart disease has come down to afflict those at the age of 20, when it used to happen to people in their 60's— when you consider that, and the wonderful production of food from various sources, and all the modern methods of transport—even if it was permitted to kill to live in those days, today it must certainly be contrary to the Jewish faith and contrary to the Ten Commandments to kill because it is no longer necessary. We just want people to be thoughtful; we don't want them to adopt vegetarianism without thinking, but just because our fathers and grandfathers and great-grandfathers did things in a certain way, we don't want people to follow those patterns today necessarily when times have changed and the opportunity is there for a greater understanding. Science has proved that vegetarianism is essential. Governments are recommending it, the British government is now going all out—in every hospital, you see all kinds of posters up encouraging it.

Clarion Call: You said that you were presently 75 years of age? If you would have asked me to guess, I would have said you were about 55.

Mr. Pick: I wish I were. It would give me some more years to do this valuable work. Thank goodness I'm still able to run a couple miles, go swimming three or four miles, and look after an acre of garden, among other things. I hope I'm blessed that I may be allowed to continue that, but we must always bear in mind that we are mortals dependent on God's grace.

Clarion Call: Do members of the Jewish Vegetarian Society who switch from a meat-centered diet to a vegetarian diet write to you, indicating that their health has improved because of that change?

Mr. Pick: Oh, we get letters like those every week. For instance, Mr. Harry Shuratz from Portsmouth, the oldest man in England, was a vegetarian for about 70 years. He lived on a very simple diet and just recently died at the age of 122. When he was 100 the police were begging him to stop cycling because they were worried about him having an accident. So you see, one can live quite well without the cruelty and the disease and the obscenity of the flesh industry.

Clarion Call: Has there been any difficulty with children maintaining a vegetarian diet when they are away from the direct infuence of the family? Say, under the pressure from their meat-eating peers at school?

Mrs. Friedman: Well, it is always a personal decision. I have three children; at home they are vegetarians. My oldest one is a vegatarian away from home as well, but I don't know what the other two are going to decide to do. They must make up their own minds.

Mr. Pick: I think it has a great deal to do with whether one or both of the parents are vegatarians. There are a lot of families where only one is a vegetarian, and then the children could go either way. But I think generally children at least need to be taught the ethics of vegetarianism, the love of creatures and their response to the great love the creatures give to us, and the lack of necessity for the horrible barbarism known as vivisection, which has made people think that all you have to do is ignore your health and there are immediate antibiotics to put you in good health again, instead of relying on a clean, toxin-free bloodstream, which is the best protection of all. If you teach them all these things, and if you give children animals as companions— a child and an animal are natural, beautiful little friends— I think they will remain vegetarians.

Thank goodness, with vegetarianism on the increase, many parents are beginning to wake up to the fact that their children are not going to die because they are vegetarians, and they're not going to be awkward either. In England, vegetarianism is increasing at the rate of 60% a year, and they reckon that by the turn of the century, the meat industry will be finished. We hope it will be like that in the U.S.A. too. It's not improbable, because of our 40 affiliated groups of members worldwide, 20 are in America.

We'd like the people of America—whatever their religion might be— if they are interested in our Jewish Vegetarian Movement, they can write to us, or they can write to our coordinator Charles Starler of Baltimore, and we'd be very happy to write them, very happy indeed to welcome them. And our cookbook which Rose has so beautifully prepared is available to anyone who'd like to write in for it. It is also being published in America by Thorson's Publications International Ltd. under the same litle.

Clarion Call: Thank you very much.

Clarion Call: What does it mean to keep kosher?

Mr. Pick: Well, the Jewish practice of Kashruths was instituted in order to stop the slaughter of animals. At one time it was thought that if you drank fresh blood from an animal you would become strong. People used to cut off animal's limbs and drink the blood. That is why from that time period you often see paintings with animals in the back on three legs.

Kashruths was intended to improve the situation by providing a more "humane" approach to meat eating. But obviously the vegetarian diet solves the whole problem. In my opinion there is no humane way to kill an animal, especially when it is for the purpose of eating his flesh which is unnecessary in the first place.

## Who Discovered America?

It very well may come to pass in the near future that those concerned with truth will wrestle primarily with history rather than science. The obvious reason for this is that, in the words of Dr. Wilfred Cantwell Smith, author of *Theology and the World's Religious History, "*Humanity is more important than things. The truth about humanity is of a higher order than the truth about things."

History tells an intriguing tale, one that ultimately may provide the greatest support for a spiritual worldview. But history has also been distorted. An example of this is the "common knowledge" that Columbus discovered America. Some say he didn't, nor were any other Europeans the first to touch America's shores. There is good reason to reexamine the history of the world and the Americas in particular. An unbiased look into the development of our planet's civilizations may help to bring about a change in values, a shift from material values to spiritual ones.

What if Europe was really in darkness in comparison to the Far East and India that Columbus set sail to find? What if the popular idea that the Tibetans and the American Indians have much in common in terms of their spiritual culture is largely a result of another historical scenario? What if Hindus and Hopis, Advaitins and Aztecs, Tibetan monks and Mayans were part of one world culture—a spiritual one? Perhaps the development of Western civilization and the Protestant ethic, which many of the West are now coming to abhor, have gotten in the way of the spiritual development of humanity. Perhaps many technological developments, while making physical contact with other cultures more possible, have distanced us from one another in a deeper sense. Another historical scenario: The spiritually sophisticated Asians were the first to set foot on Western shores, and Asia, not Europe, was the seat of culture. The central focus of that culture was genuine spiritual development, not the mere shadow of the same in the form of the politically-motivated Pauline Christianity and later the Protestant ethic, which licensed humankind's exploitation of nature.

This theory is found in the Vedic literature of India. The ancient *Puranas* (literally, histories) and the *Mahabharata* make mention of the Americas as lands rich with gold and silver. Argentina, which means “related to silver,” is thought to have been named after Arjuna (of silver hue), one of the heroes of that great epic. India's Puranic histories are, however, questionable to the rationalist. In the minds of the empiricists, they are more akin to myths. Yet myths have meaning, as the late Joseph Campbell has reminded us. The *Puranas* downplay in particular the mere recording of mundane events. The Puranic view is that even if its histories are only myths (which is not necessarily the case), the lessons to be learned from them are infinitely more valuable than what can be learned from recording the coming and going of humanity. In their view, only those human events that serve to promote transcendental knowledge are worth recording. Although empiricists are justified in dismissing them from their viewpoint, the so-called myths and their followers are also justified in dismissing the empiricist's insistence that empirical evidence is final.

Granted, India has shown some lacking in her ability to record her story. But that is due to her preoccupation with the transcendent, the suprahistorical, and not to any ineptitude on her part. According to Kana Mitra in her article "Theologizing Through History?" "We \[Hindus\] tend to forget about history, and the deemphasis of *nama-rupa*—name and form \[due to transcendent preoccupation\]—is one of the reasons for not putting down a name or date in many of our writings. Consequently present-day historians have a difficult time in determining the date and authorship of various works."

Fortunately, for dealing with the "I'll only believe it if I can see it" mentality of the empiricist, there is considerable hard evidence and academic support for the Vedic theory that most people are unaware of. Unbiased consideration of this remarkable evidence may move modern-day rationalists to give serious thought to the more realistic spiritual outlook of "Only if you believe it can you see it." After all, reality is a living thing and it may reserve the right not to show itself but to those to whom it so chooses. Otherwise, why are we in illusion, or *in search* of reality? If it is something we can *attain* by our own prowess, how did we get here (in doubt) in the first place?

Many historians have scrutinized historical evidence to find more insight into the marvelous cultures that populated the American continent before Christopher Columbus was born. Their thirst for research was based on the assumption that the great Mayan, Aztec, and Incan civilizations could not have appeared all of a sudden in the Western world. Rather, they must have received strong influence from ancient Eastern cultures, mainly from India.

Alexander von Humbolt (1769-1859), an eminent European scholar and anthropologist, was one of the first to postulate the Asiatic origin of the Indian civilizations of the Americas. His and other scholars' views formed the basis for the "diffusionist" argument, which was opposed by the "isolationist" viewpoint. Diffusionists believe that the world's civilizations are a result of social contact (civilized man meets uncivilized man). Isolationists believe that civilizations cropped up all over the earth without physical contact with one another.

It is readily accepted that some twenty thousand years ago primitive Asians crossed the Bering Strait into North America and gradually moved south all the way to Tierra del Fuego, Argentina. Diffusionists maintained that after this occurred civilized Asiatic people distributed themselves via the Pacific, thereby bringing civilization to the Americas. Isolationists insisted that after the nomadic tribes crossed the Bering Strait, a homogeneous race of "Indians of the Americas" was formed, and the American tribespeople then went about reinventing all culture, duplicating in two thousand years what originally took about six millenniums in the Old World.

Henry Charlton Bastian, author of *The Evolution of Life* (1907), presented the concept of physicochemical evolution, which gave strength to the isolationists. His theory advocated that the development of civilized man was a result of "a psychic unity of mankind," rather than social contact. Bastian's theory of *elementargedanke* influenced many anthropologists, and today, although the theory is not accepted, it is tacitly acknowledged as far as the conformities between America and Old World civilizations are concerned.This pseudo-evolutionist theory leaves much to be desired, and its unspoken acceptance casts doubt on the credibility of the anthropologists. After all, doesn’t it tax our credulity when we are asked to believe that a whole series of complicated techniques like casting by the lost wax method, the alloying of copper and tin, the coloring of gold by chemical processes, weaving, and tie-dyeing and batik were by some miracle invented twice, once in the Old World and again from scratch in the Americas? What mysterious psychological law would have caused Asians and Americans to both use the umbrella as a sign of royalty, to invent the same games, imagine similar cosmologies, and attribute the same colors to the different directions?

No archeologist today would attribute to prehistoric Europeans the independent invention of bronze casting, iron work, the wheel, weaving, pottery, writing, and so many other cultural elements that were derived from the Middle East. Similarly, the industrial developments in Britain were introduced from elsewhere within the European continent, not developed independently. What then would cause one to insist that what was not possible for the Europeans (duplicating culture independently) was possible for the American Indians? Especially when at the same time we are taught that the Europeans were of superior stock!

It was in 1949 that these opposing views met head-on at the Congress of the Americanists held in New York, which was sponsored by the American Museum of Natural History. At that time, the diffusionists presented an overwhelming mass of Asiatic-Pacific-American parallels. Nonetheless, much of the diffusionists' evidence continues to be ignored, and the isolationist view is more widely accepted. The reason for this may be more than empirical evidence or lack of the same. Indeed, it may be the faulty nature of the empirical approach, which depends on one’s imperfect senses and causes one to dismiss facts that do not conform with the prevailing worldview.

The Aryan civilization of India is a logical choice for the beginning of the diffusion of our planet's civilization. American historian Will Durant, in his book *Our Oriental Heritage*, described India as the most ancient civilization on earth, and he offered many examples of Indian culture throughout the world. He demonstrated that as early as the ninth century b.c.e. Indians were exploring the sea routes, reaching out and extending their cultural influence to Mesapotamia, Arabia, and Egypt.

Although modern-day historians and anthropologists might prefer to accept Egypt or Babylon as the most ancient civilization, due to various archeological findings, their theories are by no means conclusive. The popular theory in the academic community that the Aryans were an Indo-European stock, who spoke an unknown pre-Sanskrit language and only later invaded India subsequently occupying her, is also considerably lacking in supportive evidence. Indeed, there is very little evidence whatsoever for the postulated Aryan invasion of India. But perhaps it is easier for modern people to accept ancient Egypt and Babylon, whose ancient civilizations have no living representation and thereby do not pose any challenge to the status quo.

But India is alive and kicking. Prominent traces of ancient Vedic civilization can still be found today not only in India but outside her borders as well. The life science of ayurveda, yoga and meditation, and Sanskrit texts translated into modern languages are all prominent examples. If we recognize ancient India as a civilized spiritual giant, we will have to reckon with her modern-day representations. It is altogether possible that the Vedic theory, if thoroughly researched, poses a threat to many of the concepts of modern civilization and the current worldview, as can be seen by the fact that the Vedic literature and spiritual ideology loomed as the greatest threat to the British in their imperialistic conquest of India.

The Aryans' footprints are found throughout neighboring Southeast Asia. They were skilled navigators and pioneers of many cultural developments. According to several sources, these Aryans ruled in Java, Bali, Sumatra, Borneo, Philippines, Cambodia, Vietnam, Annan, Burma, and Thailand until the fourteenth century. Even today, the kings of Thailand bear the title *Rama* after the Indian *Ramraja (*the perfect kingdom said to have been governed by the incarnation of Godhead Ramachandra). And the story of *Ramayana* is depicted on the palace walls in Bangkok.

Cambodia, the ancient Kamboja, boasts the largest temple complex in the world, named Ankor, from the Sanskrit language meaning "the capital city." It was built in the ninth century c.e. in honor of the Hindu god Vishnu. The complex extends over an area more than twice the size of Manhattan and took thirty-seven years to complete. Its physical and spiritual grandeur is found elsewhere only in ancient Greece, Egypt, and among the Mayan and Aztec civilizations. Cambodia's principle river is today called Me Kong, which some scholars say is derived from India's Ma Ganga (Mother Ganges).

Vietnam, once called Champa, figures prominently as a stepping-stone in the story of India's cultural expansion to the Americas. Furthermore, the Hindu state of Java was founded by the king of Kalinga (Orissa) in the first century c.e. Java is said to be the ancient Yava-Dveepa mentioned in the *Ramayana* and other Sanskrit texts. The Indonesian national flag flies the symbol of Garuda, the bird carrier of Vishnu. Garuda is also the national symbol of that country.

In 1949, two scholars, Gordon Ekholm and Chaman Lal, systematically compared the Mayan, Aztec, Incan, and North American Indian civilizations with the Hindu-oriented countries of Southeast Asia and with India herself. According to them, the emigrant cultures of India took with them India’s system of time measurement, local gods, and customs. Ekholm and Lal found signs of Aryan civilization throughout the Americas in art (lotus flowers with knotted stems and half-dragon/half-fish motifs found commonly in paintings and carvings), architecture, calendars, astronomy, religious symbols, and even games such as our Parcheesi and Mexican *patolli,* which have their origins in India's *pachisi*.

Both the Hindus and the Americans used similar items in their worship rituals. They both maintained the concept of four *yuga* cycles, or cosmological seasons, extending over thousands of years, and conceived of twelve constellations with reference to the Sun as indicated by the Incan sun calendar. Royal insignias, systems of government, and practice of religious dance and temple worship all showed remarkable similarities, pointing strongly to the idea that the Americas were strongly influenced by the Aryans.

Another scholar, Ramon Mena, author of *Mexican Archeology*, called the Nahuatl, Zapoteca, and Mayan languages "of Hindu origin." He went on to say, "A deep mystery enfolds the tribes that inhabited the state of Chiapas in the district named Palenque. . . . Their writing, and the anthropological type, as well as their personal adornments . . . their system and style of construction clearly indicate the remotest antiquity. . . . \[they\] all speak of India and the Orient."Still another scholar, Ambassador Poindexter, in his two-volume 1930s treatise *The Arya-Incas,* called the Mayan civilization "unquestionably Hindu."

The Aztec culture in particular shows a striking resemblance to that of India. Aztecs divided their society into four divisions of both labor and spiritual status, as did the Hindus. In India, this system of government was known as *varnashrama,* or the division of society based on body types and mental dispositions resulting from past karma. As in Indian civilization, the Aztecs maintained a God-centered government in which people were employed in accordance with their natural karmic tendencies. The results of the labor of all the priests, administrators, mercantilists, and laborers were for the glorification of Godhead, who in turn was thought to provide for humankind.

Aztec boys were sent to school at the age of five, at which time they were put under the care of a priest and trained in various duties of temple life. The Aztec system of education bears a striking resemblance to the Indian system of *gurukula,* in which boys were sent to the care of a guru for spiritual and practical education. The Mayans and Incas had a similar approach to education, which was mainly a training for priestly service. Fanny Bandelier's translation of Sahagun's *History of Ancient Mexico* describes that the intellectually inclined boys were trained as "ministers to the idols."

Girls were educated in the domestic arts at home and did not mingle with young boys. Even as late as the 1930s, there was no courtship between Mexican Indian girls and boys, as is still the case in village life in India today. From conception to education, marriage, death, cremation, and even the observance of the *sati* rite, there are overwhelming parallels between Indian society and the Americas. Further evidence of cultural ties between the East and West is found in the statues of American gods who show a striking resemblance to the Hindu deities of Hanuman, Shiva, Indra, Vishnu and others. Such statues have been found throughout the Americas, and many of them can be seen today in museums in Central America.

The Mexican Indians and the Incas of Peru were primarily vegetarians. They were of high moral character and hospitable and generous as a habit. They practiced astrology, and mental telepathy was common among them. It was perhaps their peace-loving disposition that, like the Hindus, allowed them to be ruled by Europeans. Unfortunately, the American Indians did not survive their cultural exchange with Europe. The Europeans, through book burning and bayonet, successfully "converted" them, leaving very little trace of their noble civilization.

And what about Europe? When merchants sailing from India brought delicious spices, aromatic perfumes, incense, fine silk, precious stones set in delicate and rare jewelry, complex craftsmanship of ivory, and many other goods never seen before by Europeans, the riches and mystique of that land captivated them. The stories told by many navigators about that land of wonder, where the palaces were built of varieties of marble rather than rush stone, decorated with beautiful sculptures and wooden inlay, made the Queen of Spain so covetous that she provided Christopher Columbus with all necessities for his famous journey. Columbus had heard of India's riches through the writings of Marco Polo. Polo had written that India "was the richest and noblest country of the world."5

Europe, after Guttenburg's invention of the printing press, wasted no time in announcing the discovery of the New World. It was at this time that European historians began to present to the rest of the world that their land was the center of culture and civilization. In comparison to Indian society, however, the Europeans were rather crude. The ominous age of the Inquisition, with its persecution and fanaticism, the use of mechanical devices to insure the "chastity" of its women, the exploitation of the serfs, and self-destructive habits, such as indiscriminate eating and alcoholism within the higher classes, are all evidence of this. The original Palace of Versailles in Paris, although certainly a unique architectural creation requiring genius, was built without a single bathroom. Louis XIV and his court are said to have evacuated behind curtains, cleaning themselves with the same. The king was in the habit of substituting soap with Indian perfume and waited until his thirty-fifth birthday before he took his first complete bath.

When Europe was still uncivilized, Indian culture, as well as American culture, was highly advanced. When Europeans were still cave dwellers and nomads wandering from place to place subsisting through hunting, some American peoples were plowing fields and baking bread and dressing in cotton, the seeds for which came from India. The subtlety of Indian society, both eastern and western, marks its superiority to Europe. It was a subtlety of spiritual outlook that Europeans failed to appreciate.

The industrial revolution of Europe was prompted by India's cotton, which competed with European wool. Later when the popularity of cotton products imported from India increased, the Europeans began to manufacture cotton in mills. Thus it was even an Indian resource that prompted Europe's claim to fame—the beginning of modern technology.

Several ancient cultures of the Americas were more spiritually attuned than the Europeans. They also lived with great regard for nature. Many people today are searching out the spirituality of the Americas, a spirituality that was lacking in Europe and is now lacking throughout the world. The Christ's teachings were most certainly tainted with misunderstanding of that great savior's message of love. And he too is said to have been influenced by India's spirituality. His appearance in the world for that matter is mentioned in India's *Bavishya Purana* long before the virgin birth took place.

The theory that India, Mother India, is the earthly source of spirituality can be to some extent supported by the fact that India is still today the most religious country in the world, with a theology that dates back to antiquity. The idea that she is the source of civilization as well, although supporting evidence is available, will ultimately require that modern man reevaluate what constitutes civilization before it gains wider acceptance.
