## Women And Bhakti

A Historical Perspective  
By Steven Rosen

Two words should be defined for the uninitiated: Vaishnava and women. A Vaishnava is, literally, "a devotee of Vishnu," the Supreme Godhead of the Hindu pantheon. And Vasihnavism epitomizes the bhakti (devotional) tradition, delineating it most scientifically and thus distinguishing it from mere sentimental outpourings which fall short of realized knowledge of transcendence. In India, this term is quite common, and there are millions who follow the path of Vaishnavism. Ultimately, Vaishnava refers to the natural condition of the soul, since all living beings are constitutionally related to God in a mood of loving devotion.

Next, we may turn to the second word, which , although more familiar, is much more difficult to define, especially in our present context. The man/woman dichotomy relates primarily to the body, whereas the "Vaishanava" designation refers primarily to the natrure of the soul. In one sense, a Vaishnava is not really a man or a woman, and so reference to "women Vaishnavas" or "male Vaishnavas" is a priori absurd.

For the sake of common parlance, however, it is practical—if not downright necessary!—to acknowledge the bodily distinctions that exist within the material world. After all, a woman can serve God (i.e., act as a Vaishnava) by having children. Men cannot. So while women and men may be spiritually equal, they may also serve God in diverse ways. Worldly differences can thus be acknowledged and should be utilized in divine service. In this sense, then, we may rightly speak of "women Vaishnavas".

## Women and Spirituality

Before embarking on our survey of great women Vaishnavas, it will be useful to examine the role of women in religions with with which we may be more familiar. Of course, the Judeo-Christian tradition has come to be seen as grossly patriarchal, if not blatantly sexist. This tradition, as commonly understood, depicts women as "merely" having their place in the home and as persons who are not significant contributors to the literary activity or the inspirational merit of religious culture.

Conventional, mainstream spirituality will always suffer the great bane of bodily misconception and prejudice, for by its very nature it is external and superficial. But if we can, for a moment, leave this stereotypical view—acknowledging its relative validity—we can find another stream of thought in the Judaeo-Christian heritage. There is an alternative view, especially in the mystical tradition.

This view clearly hearkens back to the more ancient Vaishnava conception. Here, in both Eastern and Western tradition, we come across an understanding that fosters a genuine spiritual view of reality, one in which women, like men, are seen as pure spiritual-souls, part and parcel of Godhead. They are seen not simply the homemakers but as vital spiritual beings. Women mystics share the spotlight with their male counterparts. In fact, in parts of the Kabbalah, God Himself is seen to have both male and female manisfestations, masculine and feminine aspects.

It is true, too, that women were (and are!) often homemakers and wives, even in the mystical tradition. But these activities were (and are!) seen as exalted, direct manisfestations of divine service. In the esoteric biblical tradition, in fact, a man was often considered "spiritually bereft" if he did not have a good, God conscious wife. It was she who was seen as his liberator trhough her service in the home.

The Jewish commentary known as the Midrash assigned great spiritual significance to a woman's presence in the home: "One who has no wife remains without good, and without a helper, and without joy, and without blessing, and without atonement." A woman's potential spiritual influence in the home is further detailed in the Midrash as follows: "If a pious man marries a pious woman, she will make him pious. The woman's influence in the home is thus pervasive."

So, too, was the biblical woman's role as "mother" exalted to divine status. This was perhaps best expressed by a Talmudic rabbi, when, as he saw his mother approaching, said: "Let me arise and be respectful beofre the Shekinah ('Divine presence')." This was recorded by early rabbis to show the spiritual importance of the mother. In the Vaishnava traditions, too, the mother was seen as the child's first guru or spiritual guide.

Of course, in both the biblical and Vaishnava traditions, women mystics were never simply relegated to playing the role of wife or mother. There has also been among such women a venerable tradition of celibacy, equal to that of male spirituality. Women mystics were also ascetics and renunciants. St. Teresa of Avila, Catherine of Siena, Hildegard of Bingen, and Joan of Arc are glorified today as perhaps the greatest mystics in Western religious history. Similar Vaishnava women will be detailed later.

## Women in the Ministry of Jesus

Despite the equitable non sexist view of the mystics, mainstream Judaism did develop a highly patriarchal conception of reality. But if this was so within the Jewish tradition, it became considerably less so within the ministry of Jesus. As stated in Galatians (3.28), "There does not exist among you Jew or Greek, slave or freeman, male or female {italics added} . All are one in Christ Jesus." While the mainstream remained patriarchal—and this can be seen in much of Paul's writings and in the teachings of later Church Fathers— the above statement from Galatians simultaneouly brought forth a more liberal (and less sexist) tradition.

A close study of Jesus' followers gives additional emphasis to the importance of women in religious life. Indeed, there were many women who were counted among his most important disciples. Briefly, these include a woman who was a member of his physical family (his mother Mary), women who were friends but did not travel with him (the other Mary and Martha), and those women who devotedly followed Jesus in Galilee and to Jerusalam (Mary Magdalene and others).

That Jesus taught women and allowed them to follow him in discipleship stands as testimony to his great spiritual insight. It shows that he recognised sincerity where it manifests—in the heart, not in the gender. We need not detail the equality of women in Jesus' ministry here, but if one wishes to pursue this subject, there is a wealth of information in Luke and in the writings of John.

## Women in Vedic Culture

For a clear understanding of Vaishnava women and the activities that led them to greatness, one would do well to begin with ancient India's Vedic literature, the spiritual classics upon which Vaishnava dharma rests. In the earliest Vedic texts, we find a scenerario that is similar to the one in the Midrash , quoted earlier; namely, women were largely seen as "wife" or "mother." The emphasis was on her place in the home. The emphasis was again superficially patriarchal.

In similar fashion, too, her place in the home was given divine status. Her service was to manintain the spiritual environment of the home and to raise children as devotees of the highest order. This she could do only if her own spiritual practices were strong and if her meditations were profound. Guidelines are given in the scriptures that can assure perfection on this path.

It might be asked why the woman was given the "homemaker" service as opposed to the man. One answer offered by the Vedic texts is that since the child came from her body, she, as opposed to her husband, would take the service of raising the child in God consciousness most seriously. She could not bear to be away from her child—flesh of her flesh. It was unnatural. Rather, the husband had a less difficult time going out—away from the child—and making a living. The wife, in general, felt more comfortable at home. It was natural, pleasing, and according to her inclination. Both parties, playing their respective roles, served Godhead. In this sense, the roles are absolute—the roles they play are equal in that they are merely various ways to serve.

The Vedic epic known as Ramayana (Ayodhya-kanda 39.29) explains the social hierarchy that existed within the spiritual home: strinam bharta hi daivatam—that is to say, "The husband is the guru for the wife, even as the wife is guru for the child and the spiritual master is guru for the husband." In other wrds, in the Vedic household, everyone had a spiritual authority, and in this way social sanity was maintained.

Before we go any further it should be pointed out that there were many exceptions to this rule. But, in general, husband and wife lived happily under this injunction and progressed very nicely toward the ultimate goal of life: God realization. But exceptions there were, and as we delineate the great Vaishnava women throughout history, we will elucidate upon the ascetic tradition that made clear the spiritual equality between men and women.

"Be like Sitadevi"

Among the Goddesses delineated within the Vedic pantheon, the most important for Her representation of ideal womanhood is Sitadevi. She embodies all of the qualities to be found in the ideal Vedic wife. Although other Goddesses, such as Parvati and Lakshmidevi, and other heriones from the Vedic literature, such as Savitri and Damayanti, are also good examples, it is Sita who is particularly remembered as the ideal in conventional Vedic womanhood. Indeed, even today, one hears the Indian mother tell her daughter, "Be like Sitadevi...."

Sita's popularity as the perfect woman and exemplary wife was nicely articualted by sclolar Sudhir Kakkar, who wroter in his classic work The Inner World: A Psycho-Analytic Study of Childhood and Society in India (Oxford, Oxford University Press, 1978): "From earliest childhood, a Hindu has heard Sita's legend recounted on any number of sacral and secular occasions; seen the central episodes enacted in folk plays like the Rama-lila; heard Her qualities extolled in devotional songs; and absorbed the ideal feminine identity she incorporates through the many everyday metaphors and similes that are associated with Her name. Thus, 'She is as pure as Sita' denotes chastity in a woman, and 'She is a second Sita,' the appreciation of a woman's uncomplaining self-sacrifice. If, as Jerome Bruner remarks, 'In the...community there is a corpus of images and models that provide the pattern to which the individual may aspire, a range of metaphoric identity,' then this range , in the case of the Hindu woman, is condensed in one model. And She is Sita."

## Great Women Vaishnavas

Vedic culture gave rise to many great women. In addition to Sitadevi, there were the like of Draupadi, Kunti, and Gandhari. These women, however, are "pre-historical" personalities, many of them gracing the earth more than five thousand years ago. Since the period of their pastimes is now shrouded in antiquity, and since many of the stories surrounding their lives are often confused with mythlogical tales, it would be best (for our purposes) to restrict our survey to contemporary women Vaishnavas. Consequently, we will focus on women Vaishnavas from within the last five hundred years.

## Sachidevi

The first woman to distinguish herself as the superlative Vaishnava within our five hundred year time period is unquestionably Sachidevi, who appeared in Bengal in the mid fifteenth century. Playing the role as the perfect mother and wife, she was glorified as the mother of Shri Chaintanya and the wife of Jaganath Mishra. Briefly, Shri Chaitanya was the founder of Gaudiya Vaishnavism and was explained by his followersto be a combined manisfestation of Radha and Krishna, the divine couple. He was thus considered God incarnate and is one of the most important perosonalities in all of Vaishnavism. Jagannath Mishra, his father and the husband of Sachidevi, was a pious priest (brahmana) and a pure devotee of Godhead.

Sachidevi was the daughter of a well-known Bengali family who migrated from East Bengal (now Bangladesh) and settled in Navadvip. Her father, Nilambar Chakravarti, was a very influential man due to his knowledge of astrology and the Vedic scripturres.

After marrying Jagannath Mishra, Sachidevi went through great asterities as a mother. In fact, she lost eight female children during successive pregnancies, and she wept in anticipation for further offspring. Sachidevi's next child lived, a boy named Vishvarupa. Soon after, she gave birth to Shri Chaitanya. But while little Nimai (as Chaintanya was called in His youth) was still an infant, Vishvarupa renounced the world and became an ascetic. This brought untoled remorse to Mother Sachi, for now, as with her first eight daughters, Vishvarupa would no longer bring joy to the Mishra household. He would now wander the countryside—teaching and visiting temples—in a life of divine service.

Jaganath Mishra did noit survive the trauma of Vishvarupa's renunciation but died in separation from his first son. Sachi herself, however, managed to carry on, and she resolved to raise little Nimai to the best of her ability.

Due to the purity and intensity of her devotion, her aspirations for her last surviving child would be more than fdulfilled. As Nimai grew and the years passed, He developed exceptional features, profound schlorship, and a devotional attitude. His concealed divinity began to blossom, as the scriptures had predicted it would.

Shri Chaitanya, in fact, had asked for His mother's permission to lead the life of a renunciant in service to Godhead. Although it was difficult for her, she nonetheless relented, the only stipulation being that He make His headquarters in nearby Jagannath Puri (so that she would regularly hear news of his activities).

Although Shri Chaintanya's renunciation (sannyasa) is remembered as a pivotal event in the history of Gaudiya Vaishnavism, it is Sachidevi's renunciation that is glorified in the annals of Vaishnavas history as unbounded. For in allowing the avatara—her son—to live the life of an ascetic (away from home), she made the ultimate sacrifice: according to his desire, she agreed to serve him in separation. This high, esoteric relationship of service in sepearation was expereinced by Mother Sachi, and Vaishnavas throughout the world seek to emulate her uncompromising devotion.

## Vishnupriya

If Sachidevi was the perfect mother, Vishnupriya was the perfect wife. Lakshmidevi, Shri Chaitanya's first wife, died prematurely when she was bitten by a snake. Sachdevi then pleaded with her divine son to remarry. This he did and the bride was Vishnupriya, daughter of the aristocratic Sanatan Mishra (a well known politician of the time).

When Shri Chaitanya soon left to pursue the life of an ascetic, Vishnupriya made the same commitment and sacrifice as did Sachidevi. Vishnupriya, however, also had to take care of Sachi, who by then had turned in the direction of old age.

Vishnupriya spent as much time with the name of God as she did with her beloved mother-in -law. And her reputation as a prominent ascetic soon grew. It is said that she would set aside one grain of rice for every name of God she chanted in one day. When her utterances of God's name were completed at the end of the day she would boil the amount of rice so accumulated and take that as her meal.

As her devotion became known she was and is still today glorified for exemplifying the dual role of an ideal chaste wife and an ascetic of the mystical tradition.

## Jhanavadevi

Important women Vaishnavas soon took leading roles and even assumeed the position of guru, the exalted stage of teaching and guiding others on the path to spiritual perfection. One of the more prominent woman gurus was Jahnavadevi, wife of NItyananda Prabhu (Shri Cahitanya's intimate associate and plenary expansion).

When Nityananda Prabhu married the two daughters of Sarakhala Suryadasa Pandit, the entire Vaishnava community was overcome with ecstasy, for the two girls were extremely pious and were known as great Vaishnavas. The younger wife, Vasudha, gave birth to two children, a boy, Birachandra, and a girl, Gangadevi.

The young Vasudha soon passed away, however, and Jahnavadevi resolved to raise her sister's children. In addition, she adopted a boy named Ramachandra. So Jahanavadevi spent much of her youth taking care of the three children, making sure that they became great devotees and lovers of God.

Birachandra, especially, grew to be a great leader in the Vaishnava community, and when he accepted Jahnavadevi (his step-mother) as his guru, many prominent Vaishnavas did as well.

Her devotion to the famous Krishna diety, Gopinath, in Jaganath Puri, was so intense that this endeared her to the pious and impious alike, and by her personal example she showed how ot perform temple worship and how to devote one's life to spiritual pursuits. She even presided ever huge Vaishnavaa festivals and gave initiation to men and women alike. It was Jahanavadevi, too, who had the insight to keep close contact with the Goswamis of Vrindavan. In this way she sought to keep solidarity and unification between Gaudiya Vaishnavism in Bengal and in Vrindavan (Uttar Pradesh). The cohesive form of Gaudiya Vaishnavism that exist today is largely a result of her efforts.

One other phenomenon in the life of Jahnavadevi is pertinent to our discussion. Devotion to her mission and purpose became so strong that in her own lifetimne a deity was made of her, and this was to be placed alonside the Gopinath deity, who was the object of her veneration. A council was convened in Jaipur to decide the propriety of placing her diety next to Gopinath. The then King of Jaipur and the assembled Vaishnavas decided unanimousluy that the deity should be established, and it was, indeed, placed next to Gopinath within Jahnavadevi's lifetime. Such a distinguished honor is uncommon among Vaishnava males and females alike.

## Hemalata and Gangamata Goswami

In the next generation after Shri Chaitanya and Nityananda Prabhu (1600's or as late aws the 1700's), many great female Vaishnavas followed the example of Jahanavadevi, two of the most prominent being Hemlata and Gangamata Goswami.

Not much is known about Hemlata Thakurani. She was the eldest daughter of Shrinivasa Acharya and had many disciples, both male and female. She was a mystic of the highest order, and developed a profound sense of love of God.

Gangamata Goswami, on the the other hand, is written about quite a bit in the pages of Gaudiya Vaishnava history, especially in the historic records of the family of Nityananda Vamsa (form which she descends). Her guru was Haridas Pandit who, in turn was a disciple of Anantacharya (a follower of Jahnavadevi). In this way, her disciplic descent is traced to Nityananda Prabhu.

She was the daughter of King Naresh Narayana of Puntaya (in the district of Rajasahi). Unlike most great women Vaishnavas, even the mystics, Gangamata never married, and so she was given the title Goswami (literally, "controller of the senses") for her strict celibacy and profound wisdom. She did not take formal sannyasa (the renunced order), for she felt that the scriptures recommend this path solely for males. But, in spirit, she adopted this path, and thus the "Goswami" title was conferred upon her.

The deity of her heart was Madan Gopal, and she worshipped this form of Krishna with great devotion. In her youth, she studied in Vrindavan and then, after many years, she moved to Jagannath Puri (in the state of Orissa). While in Puri she lived in the ruins of what was formerly the house of the great scholar Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya. The Bhattacharya had been a prominent disciple of Shri Chaitanya, and although his house was now, almost two hundred years later, merely a run-down facsimile of its former self, Gangamata stayed there for the spiritual inspiration it bestowed.

At that house, she found the sacred Damodara Shila (a special deity), once worshipped by Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya himself. She worshipped this deity with the same intensity that she had worshipped Madam Gopal in Vrindavan. In this way, she humbly stayed at her holy hermitage, worshipped her deity, and became known as one of the greatest Vaishnava/mystics of her time.

Soon, Mukundadeva Maharaja, the then King of Puri, came to hear her recite Srimad Bhagavatam, the sacred scripture of the Vaishnavas. He was so taken by her purity and elaborate explanations of the devotional conclusions that he became her disciple, and encouraged much of Jaganath Puri to do the same. He financed a special temple to be built for her and she became one of the most prominent Vaishanavas of Orrissa.

## Conclusion

Due to lack of space we have only given some preliminary examples of great women Vaishnavas. Nonetheless, in our survey we have seen examples of a great Vaishnava mother, a wife, mystics, celibates, and gurus. In short, the Vaishnava tradition has established precedents for women to assert temselves and distinguish themselves as outstanding Vaishnavas, both in traditional roles more commonly ascribed to women and in very independent roles, that would perhaps be the envy of males.

Other women Vaishnavas who may be mentioned breifly include Kamala-devi. She was a disciple of Narottama Dasa Thakur and mother of the famous pandit Rupa Narayana Chakravarti. Govinda Dasi, too was an important Vaishnava woman—she was a disciple of Rasikananda Prabhu (an extremely important teacher in the history of Vaishnavism) and a prominent preacher of Gaudiaya Vaishnavism. Ichchhadevi should also be mentioned, since she was the famous wife of Rasikananda. She is credited with being the first Bengali wioman to translate the sacred scriptures from Sanskrit into the vernacular.

Writing, also, was not rare for great Vaishnava women, for unlike other village women in India, Vaishnava women have always (for the most part) been literate. The most prominent name in this regard is Chandravati (circa, eighteenth centruy), but we may also note Gangamayi, Gangamani, and Hati Vidyalankara (of the same time period). The list goes on and on, but the pioint is simple: great women Vaishnavas have existed throughout the ages, showing that the qualities of leadership, scholarship, intelligence, wisdom and devotion are an affair of the heart and mind, not the gender.
