## Words of Wisdom - Again Become A Mouse

Once upon a time there lived a little mouse in a great jungle in India. Being the smallest creature in the jungle, the mouse was constantly harassed by predators like the crows and hawks.

"If only I were a wolf," thought the mouse, "then I would be fearless and I could live a normal, happy life."

With this thought in mind the mouse approached the hermitage of a great sage who domiciled in that part of the jungle. Seeing the wary mouse, who shook and trembled with fright, the compassionate and merciful sage began to speak.

" O innocent creature of the jungle, why do you tremble so? Do you not find sufficient food to eat? Or have you taken ill with some unknown disease? Please reveal your mind and I shall try to comfort you."

"It is not disease or lack of food which troubles me, O wise and gracious sir," replied the mouse. "It is the dreadful thought of being eaten by my enemies that causes me to tremble."

"My dear little mouse," said the sage, "it is the insurmountable law of nature that one living being lives upon another. But since you have come to me for shelter I will certainly do my best to help you."

O great and powerful sage," said the mouse, "if you would kindly transform me into a wolf, then all my fears of being eaten by my enemies would be gone."

"It shall be as you have requested," said the sage, and by his mystic power the mouse was immediately transformed into a wolf.

Thrilled with his boon, the wolf ran into the jungle, singing as he went, "Now I shall live happily ever after."

But it was not long before the wolf was in distress. Although safe from predators like the crows and hawks, the wolf was now being harassed by bigger foes like jackals and tigers.

"I will never be happy," thought the wolf, "unless I can become the king of the jungle."

So with this thought in mind, the wolf approached the sage and begged to be transformed into a lion.

"O great and powerful sage, please turn me into a lion so I can live a happy life, free from the fear of being eaten by other animals."

"My dear unfortunate creature, replied the sage, "If you think that you will be happy by becoming a lion, then so be it."

By the power of the sage the wolf immediately became a lion, whose roar made all the other animals in the jungle flee in fear.

No sooner had the wolf become a lion than he began to look at the sage with his piercing eyes, and lick his lips, thinking, "I am hungry, and the flesh of this sage looks like it would be very tasty."

Just as the lion was about to pounce on the sage and devour him for a meal, the sage snapped his fingers and the lion once again became a mouse!

Moral

This analogy has been given in the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition to illustrate the point that if, after becoming advanced in spiritual knowledge by the grace of the guru and saintly persons, one then begins to think that he has become superior to his guardians and well-wishers and he becomes arrogant and mistreats others, he will immediately fall down from his exalted position and "Again Become A Mouse."

## Words of Wisdom - The Blind Men and the Elephant

by John Q. Saxe

It was six men of Indostan

To learning much inclined Who went to see an Elephant

(Though all of them were blind)

That each by observation

Might satisfy his mind.

The First approached the Elephant,

And happening to fall

Against his broad and sturdy side.

At once began to bawl:

"God bless me! but the Elephant

Is very like a wall!"

The Second, feeling of the tusk,

Cried,"Ho! what have we here

So very round and smooth and sharp?

To me tis very clear

This wonder of an Elephant

Is very like a spear!"

The Third approached the animal,

And happening to take

The squirming trunk within his hands.

Thus boldly up and spake:

"I see, quoth he, "The Elephant

Is very like a snake!"

The Fourth reached out an eager hand

And felt about the knee

"What most this wonderous beast is hi

Is mighty plain!" quoth he:

" 'Tis clear enough the Elephant

Is very like a tree!"

The Fifth who chanced to touch the ea

Said: "E'en the blindest man

Can tell what this resembles most:

Deny the fact who can.

This marvel of an Elephant

Is very like a fan!"

The Sixth no sooner had begun

About the beast to grope.

Than seizing on the swinging tail

That fell within his scope,

"I see," quoth he, "the Elephant

Is very like a rope!"

And so these men of Indostan Disputed loud and long. Each in his own opinion Exceeding stiff and strong, Though each was partly in the right. And all of were in the wrong!

Moral

So oft in theologic wars. The disputants, I ween. Rail on in utter ignorance Of what the others mean, And prate about an Elephant Mot one of them has seen!

## Words of Wisdom - The Blue Jackal

Adopted from "Panchatantra"

There was once a jackal named Howl who lived in the jungle near the outskirts of a village. Being driven by hunger, the jackal happened into the village one night. While searching for food the jackal was detected by the dogs of that village, who liegan 10 chase him and bite him with their sharp teeth. The jackal fled for his life, and in his attempt to escape fell into a val of indigo dye. Unable to find the intruder, the dogs returned home.

When the way was clear, the jackal, whose body was now completely blue, crawled from the vat and vanished into the jungle. The next day when ihe other animals in the jungle saw the blue jackal they wondered where this strange creature had come from. Thinking their lives to be in danger, all the animals, even the lions and tigers. began to run away in fear.

Opportunist that he was. Fierce Howl devised a scheme. Addressing the frightened animals in a grave voice he said. "Don't be alarmed, my dear subjects, i am Fierce Howl and 1 have been sent to you by Indra, the King of Heaven to rule the jungle and give you protection. I shall be your king, and as long as my powerful paws protect you nothing can harm you."

On hearing the words of Fierce Howl all the jungle creatures bowed their heads before him and said, "Dear Master, your wish is our command. What duties must we perform? How shall we .serve you? Please instruct us," Tn that moment Fierce Howl took full command of the jungle creatures and became their king. The lion was appointed his prime minister. The tiger was made keeper of the bedchamber. The elephant was given the duty of doorkeeper and animals of all description who lived in thai jungle were engaged in the service of the king. But to the jackals, who were of the king's own kind, he gave an admonishing and drove them from the kingdom. Thus Fierce Howl enjoyed the life of royalty for many days and nights. Then one day, as Fierce Howl sat in his court, a pack of jackals on a nearby hill began to howl. When the king heard the howl of his own kind he could not control himself. His heart throbbed, his body thrilled and tears of joy filled his eyes. Suddenly the king leaped to his feet and began to howl like the jackal that he was, "What is this?" cried the animals. "We have been deceived! He is not a king! He is simply a blue jackal!" Very much angered at having been cheated, the fierce animals like the tigers and lions immediately pounced upon the jackal and devoured his body for food.

Moral.

Whoever leaves his friends, Strange folk to cherish, Like foolish Fierce Howl, Will untimely perish.

A foolish and unqualified man may dress the part of a noble and wise leader, but when such a foolish person opens his mouth his ignorance and false position are revealed.

## WW-Uncommon Sense

## Beyond Pronunciation

Once two monks were crossing the river Ganges. One was a scholar, the other a simple practitioner. The scholar was intent upon teaching his fellow monk the correct pronunciation of the Sanskrit mantras from the morning's lesson. This led him only to exasperation, as his friend could not catch the meter, much less the proper intonation.

Losing his patience, the scholar began to philosophize on the importance of mastering the correct pronunciation, leaving aside the actual practice of repeating the mantras. Suddenly the river rose and the boat capsized. The scholar drowned, while the other walked to shore, still trying to catch the proper pronunciation.

## Hard of Hearing

Once, an elderly man who was hard of hearing called upon his good wife for service. "Wife! Please come into the den. I need your help." "I'll be there in a minute," she replied. "Wife! I'm calling you!" the man yelled, turning up the volume." Yes I hear you, I'll be there in a minute," came her reply. "Wife!" the man roared at the top of his lungs. "What's wrong with you, are you hard of hearing?"

One thinks others to be like oneself.

## Where is God?

A young boy asked his father, "How can I believe in a God who, while said to be everywhere, cannot be seen anywhere?" In response to the question the father asked him to put a lump of salt in a glass of water. The boy did so.

Some time later the boy's father asked him to bring him the lump of salt from the glass of water. When the boy could not retrieve it, he concluded that it was no longer there. Frustrated by this task the boy complained, "What about my question?" "First drink the water," replied his father.

## Humanity

Once, a young man tired of the ways of the world announced to his family members that he would work no more. "I want to be free from work and worry, and I want to meditate upon God without any interruption." Abruptly he left home and entered the forest, leaving all of his possessions behind.

After a week in the woods, humbled, he returned home. When he knocked on the door his brother asked who it was without opening the door. The young man identified himself, "It's me, your brother." "No, that can't be," came the reply, "I have no *human* brother. My only brother has gone to the forest and become a saint." Begging again the young man insisted, "No, it's me. Please let me in."

After leaving him in distress overnight, the young man’s brother opened the door the following morning, and seeing him there, informed him, "As long as you're still human you'll have to work again. As soon as you said 'I want,' I knew you were still human."

## Respect

An obscure Buddhist master was visited by the emperor. When his arrival was announced to the monk, he informed the emperor's attendant, "Tell him to come in and prostrate himself before me." Horrified, the attendant exclaimed, "What kind greeting is that for the *emperor?!*"

The monk replied, "When a person of poor reputation visits me I go to the gate and greet him. When an ordinary citizen comes I get up from my seat. But a great emperor cannot be treated like that—he deserves much more from me!"

## No Answer

A famous theoretical scientist who was the leader in his field was asked to address a body of students. This was to be his final speech. He pondered long and hard upon what he would say to the group who, in his estimation, were the future of the nation. All of his knowledge some day would have to be assimilated by them, he thought. As he came into the classroom he announced, "In my opinion there is no question that cannot be answered." One student abruptly asked, "Why are you so proud?" To this the man had no answer.

## This Too Shall Pass

Once, a powerful king, who was so wise that learned men flocked around him, became confused. Thus he called all the sages in his kingdom to assist him. When they arrived, in all gravity he explained to them, "I am impelled by intuition to acquire a magic ring which will entirely balance and stabilize my life. It must be such that when I am in distress, upon looking at it I will become happy, and when I glance at it in happiness I will become sad."

The wise men thus immersed themselves in contemplation, and after a long time came up with a solution. They had a craftsman create the simplest of rings upon which the inscription was written: "This too shall pass."

## Three Pieces of Advice

Once, a man after capturing a bird was informed by the feathered creature that in captivity he would be of no use to the man. "If you let me go," said the bird, "I will give you three pieces of advice: one when you release me, the second when I reach the window sill, and the third when I reach the branch of the tree outside."

The man agreed and proceeded to release the bird within the confines of the room. The bird then advised him, "If you lose something, even if you value it more than life itself, do not regret it."

The man then let the bird hop to the window sill, from where the bird further advised him, "Never believe in anything that is contrary to common sense without proof."

These two gems of advice were appreciated by the man, who opened the window, allowing the bird to fly to the tree outside. The bird then laughed. "You fool!" he said. "Within my stomach are two large jewels more valuable than anything you own. Now you have lost the chance to possess them."

Anguished to no end, the man was overwhelmed with regret for his apparent foolishness. It was all he could do to ask the bird for the third piece of advice. "When someone offers you good advice you should listen very carefully. Refer to the previous two advices," said the bird, "and see what a fool you *really* are."

## One String

There was once a musician who had a spiritual outlook on life. In his possession he had a wonderful stringed instrument consisting of many, many strings. The potential of this instrument to create music was extraordinary. But to everyone's bewilderment this fellow played only one string constantly, forever vibrating the same note.

One day his good wife asked him, "Why is it that although you have so many strings to play, you only play one note? So many other musicians are making so many wonderful sounds with their stringed instruments, and they do not have as wonderful an instrument as you."

"That is because *they*," replied the husband, "have not yet found their note."

## Secret Mantra

At the time of initiation, a famous guru, as was his regular practice, gave out a a secret mantra. On one occasion his best student came forward to receive the sacred initiation. "Do not repeat this mantra to anyone under any circumstances," said the guru. "It is very powerful, and it will fully enlighten you no matter how fallen you may be at present. But if you give it out to anyone, you will have to take birth thousands of times over before you can achieve liberation."

Bowing to his preceptor, the disciple went to the center of town and began to chant the mantra at the top of his lungs. Throngs of people gathered and listened as the young man told everyone about the power of the mantra. Grateful, they accepted it and went their way.

It so happened that the young disciple's guru happened by, and astonished at the actions of his prize student, he asked, "What are you doing? Did you not understand what I told you? You will have to suffer the reaction for giving out the mantra."

"Yes, I know," said the disciple. "I will have to take birth thousands of times more before I can achieve liberation. But if by doing that so many others can be liberated, then it is worth it." Upon hearing this the guru became *his* disciple.

## Honesty and Pride

Two young boys were sent to the local guru's ashrama for schooling. One came from high class family of brahmins, the other boy's father was unknown. As time passed the question of receiving the sacred thread (the symbol of the twice-born) arose. This ritual of initiation is reserved for the best of persons, who come from good families and exhibit godly qualities. This initiation certifies one as a priest, and qualifies the initiate to perform the temple rituals.

The guru called both boys before him. He asked the first boy about his family. "Who is your father?" said the guru. With obvious pride, glancing down at his fellow student, the boy replied, "I come from the best of families. Both my mother and father are very respectable brahmins." The second boy was then asked the same question, to which he replied "I don't know."

The first was denied the initiation because of his pride. The second received it because of his honesty.

## WW-Everything Is God's Arrangement

by Col. Raj Singh

One day, as the king of all the land south of the Himalayas sat in his court, an ambassador from Persia came and presented the king with a beautifully hand-crafted sword. While admiring the workmanship of the blade, the king accidently cut off the tip of his little finger. As the king was suffering this loss, the minister of the court stepped forward and addressed the throne. "Your Royal Highness, do not lament the loss of the tip of your finger, for everything is God's arrangement."

Hearing the words of his minister, the king became very angry, and said, "I think you cannot appreciate the loss of my finger because it is my finger that has been lost and not your own. You had better withdraw your statement lest you yourself may suffer the loss of more than just a finger."

"What I have spoken is true, your Majesty," replied the minister. "Everything is God's arrangement. Now you may act as your conscience directs." The king, his mind agitated and his anger out of control, ordered his soldiers to arrest the minister and take him to the prison.

It so happened that the next day a hunt was scheduled. On such occasions it was customary for the minister to accompany the king, but since the minister had been imprisoned, the king went alone.

While hunting in the forest, the king was attacked and captured by a band of savage cannibals. Struggling for his life, the king was dragged to the place where preparations for a human sacrifice were under way. The king was bathed in sacred oils and taken to the sacrificial altar.

Moments before the king was to be slain, the high priest of the sacrifice noticed that the tip of the king's finger was missing.

"This man is not fit to be sacrificed," said the priest. "The tip of his finger is missing, and therefore he is unacceptable." The other cannibals then carried the king into the forest and set him free.

The king remembered the words of his minister. Returning to the palace, the king went straight to the prison and released him. "What you have spoken is true," said the king. "Had I not cut off the tip of my finger, I would have made a suitable sacrifice and been eaten by cannibals. It was surely God's arrangement to save my life."

The king continued, "But I do not understand; why has God has allowed me to put you into prison? Was that also God's arrangement?

"Yes," said the minister. "Had you not put me into prison I would have accompanied you on the hunt and been captured along with yourself."

The king was still somewhat puzzled. "Yes...so?"

"So," replied the minister, "I'm not missing a finger."

Moral

Everything is God's arrangement.

## WW- SHELL NECK, SLIM, AND GRIM

Adopted from the Sanskrit Panchatantra\*

In a lake, in northern India, there once lived a turtle named Shell Neck whose friends were two ganders named Slim and Grim. It so happened that there came a ten year drought and the lake began to dry up. Seeing the situation the two ganders spoke to each other: "It will not be long before this lake is completely dry. We shall have to seek our home elsewhere. Before we go let us say good-by to our old friend, Shell Neck."

Slim and Grim came to Shell Neck and bid him a hardy fare-well. When all was said, the doomed turtle replied, "I am a water dweller. If you leave me here I will surely die. Indeed, if you are actually my friends you must take me with you."

Hearing Shell Neck's plea the two ganders said, " But what are we to do? You are a creature with legs and we are creatures with wings. How can we help you? How can you fly with us?"

"Yes, said Shell Neck, there is a way." And the turtle revealed his plan. "The two of you must take hold of the ends of this stick. Secure it tightly between your feet. I will bite the stick, in the middle, with my teeth. Then fly away and we will soon discover our new home."

The two friends objected,"It is a dangerous plan. If you engage yourself in the slightest conversation you will loose your grip, fall to the rocks below and be smashed to bits."

"Don't worry, said Shell Neck, I will take a vow. From this moment on I will not speak even a single." And so they began their journey. Slim and Grim flew high in the sky and Shell Neck held on to the stick with his teeth. As the strange trio flew above the villages many people began to point toward the sky and cry aloud: "What is this queer looking thing which is flying in the sky?"

Hearing the clamor of people below the turtle drew near his fate. "What are all those people yelling about." he asked. The moment he spoke the poor fool lost his hold and fell to the ground for dead.

The Moral of Our Story

"Friendly advice when given to a fool--falls upon deaf ears and one who can not control his words--draws death very near."

## WW-The Boatman &amp; The Scholar

by Col Raj Singh

An English scholar from Oxford chanced to visit India for the first time. Due to his vast learning and erudition he was overly proud of himself. This soon got him into trouble with the local folk and he was not one to ask for help.

One day as he approached the Ganges River he haughtily beckoned a local boatman to carry him across the swiftly moving water to his destination. As the boatman got underway, the scholar asked, "My dear boatman sir, I wonder if perhaps you have ever studied Quantum Mechanics? Are you familiar with Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle? Schroedinger's Equation? Have you studied Einstein's Theory of Relativity?

The surprised boatman, a simple working man with no education, replied, "No sir, I have never studied any of these subjects. I only know this boat and how to cross this river."

"Well then," the scholar replied. "One third of your life is lost!"

The boatman continued poling the boat along for some time, after which the scholar asked again, "I say, my dear boatman sir, are you familiar with Bohm's theory of the Holographic Paradigm? Perhaps you are familiar with the New Age phenomenon of Trance Channelling? Have you ever had an out of body experience?"

To these bewildering questions, the boatman replied simply, "No sir, I am not familiar with these subjects. I only know this river and how to work this boat."

"Aah, my dear boatman, another one third of your life is wasted," replied the scholar. The boatman continued pushing the boat toward the middle of the river with his long pole.

The appearance of ominous looking dark clouds overhead and a swell of waves in the river caused the scholar to remark, "My dear boatman sir, are you familiar with computer mappings of the earth globe and meterology? Do you know astrology—how the movements of the stars effect your good and bad fortune? Did you know that this planet has been visited by extra-terrestial beings?

The boatman replied, "No sir, I'm sorry that I don't know these things."

To this, the scholar steadying himself in the rough waters, once again replied, "Well then, my dear boatman, another third of your life is wasted."

Just then a large wave swamped the boat, at which time the boatman exclaimed, "I'm afraid that you will have to swim for the shore, as the boat is lost." The scholar shouted, "I don't know how to swim!"

"Well now," the boatman replied, "I guess your whole life is wasted!"

Moral

A lifetime spent in pursuit of knowledge without practical realization is a waste of time. It is better to spend one's time in the pursuit of self realization rather than collecting merely collecting information.

## WW-Uncommon Sense \[Several Stories\]

## Tears For the Mullah

Once there was a Mohammedan mullah who was very expert in reciting the holy Koran. His explanations were such that he himself was attracted to them. Indeed, everyone seemed to be in rapt attention whenever he spoke.

Somewhat enamored by his own prowess of speech, he began to notice one devoted listener in the audience—an old lady who always sat in the corner. Whenever the mullah spoke from the Koran, she would weep profusely, and he could not help but notice the tears constantly streaming down her cheeks. Intrigued, one day the mullah met the lady and asked her what she found in his lectures that so moved her.

Much to his embarrassment, she replied, "I used to have a goat with a beard that was just like yours. When the goat took her food, she would move her head on the grass just as you move your head when you read the Koran.That goat was very dear to me. Thus, whenever I come to your lectures, I cry."

## Say No More

A famous guru figure from the West was billed for a speaking engagement. Tickets sold for $15.00 each. The auditorium was packed and everyone waited in eager anticipation. Something very profound was about to happen.

When the speaker came onstage he received a standing ovation—*pranams* Western style. After a full ten minutes of applause the house quieted. Raising his hands with a shrug of his shoulders, the "guru" spoke: "What can I say?" The crowd went wild with applause and he walked off the stage. Unfortunately, no one was disappointed.

## Students Forever

Isaac Newton was so learned during his time that it is said that his contemporaries thought that he knew everything. The fact that he was truly a learned man, however, is illustrated in his reaction to their folly.

Newton said, "I know better than you, because I think that I am just collecting pebbles on the shore of the ocean of knowledge. If I am more learned than all of you, it is only because you think that I have come to the end of all knowledge, whereas *I know* that I have only touched its shore."

Thus we may not wish to think that we have learned everything at any time, but rather that we shall all remain students forever.

## Organized Truth

Once both God and the devil were walking down the road and something caught the Lord's eye. He knelt to pick it up, and Satan, captivated by its effulgence, asked, "What's that?" "This," answered the Lord, "is the Truth." "Here," replied the devil, "give that to me and I'll organize it for you."

## Beyond Formality

Once, young Alexander the Great and his father found a chariot whose harness rope was tied in a thick knot. Above the knot was the inscription, "Whoever can untie this Gordion knot will be a great king in the future." Upon learning of this, the young Alexander exclaimed, "I shall do it." Immediately he drew his sword and cut the knot. He did not keep the formality, yet he accomplished the task. Another man, a bystander, realizing the significance of Alexander's act, commented, "Yes, he will be a great king. It must be so." Sometimes formality must be disregarded; we must respect this principle. In spiritual culture we should always be attatched to the substance more than the form.

## Keep Chanting

Once a disciple who was engaged in chanting the names of God as a spiritual practice informed his guide that while chanting he perceived a mysterious blue light that came to surround him. Unmoved, his guru replied, "Keep chanting, it will go away."

## It's Not Cheap

Once, several very strict disciples somewhat sheepishly approached their spiritual master. Seeing that they had something on their minds that they were reluctant to express, the guru spoke up. "You want to say something, but you are apprehensive. What is it?" Reluctantly they replied, "Guru Maharaja, we have been serving you for the last ten years, applying ourselves diligently in accordance with the teachings you have given. But there is a doubt that has arisen within our hearts. You are always speaking about so many high things, and although it all sounds very nice, after ten years we are not experiencing those things. They are not manifesting in our hearts." With a sigh of relief that took them by surprise, the spiritual preceptor replied, "O, if you had said that after ten years all those high things were now within your grasp, then I would have been worried about you!" Spiritual life is not cheap.

## Knowing vs. Practicing

There was once a Buddhist *roshi* who practiced *zazen* in a tree. When the learned governor of the province heard about him, he went to search him out. When he arrived at the base of the tree in which the *roshi* was nesting in *zazen,* he questioned him thus: "My dear *roshi*, you look very insecure up there. Tell me, what is it that all the Buddhas taught?" To this the *roshi,* quoting the *Dharmapada,* replied, "Always do good, never do evil; keep your mind pure—thus all the Buddhas taught."

Insulted, the learned governor responded, "I knew that when I was three years old!"

"Yes, replied the roshi, "A three-year-old may know it, but even an 80-year-old can not put it into practice."

## One Rupee

During the Kumbha Mela many renowned sages, yogis, and devotees gathered, and it became an issue as to who was more spiritually advanced. The great thinkers put forward the best man from their group, and he displayed uncommon grasp of the scriptural aphorisms. Yet although he was also very renounced, wearing only a deerskin, he was passed over by the best of the yogis, who astounded everyone as he walked on the waters of mother Ganges.

When it came time to cast a vote, anyone and everyone was asked to speak up. While everyone praised the yogi, one simple devotee pilgrim remained silent to the extent that he became conspicuous. When asked his estimation of the value of the yogi's prowess, he replied, "One rupee, because for that I could cross the river by boat."

## Cost of Learning

Two young men set out to learn how to play the sitar. The first was already acquainted with the sitar to some extent, while the second really knew nothing about it, although he had a strong desire to learn.

The more learned of the two suggested that they become students of a famous teacher, and thus they submitted to him their request to become his students. The teacher interviewed each of them privately, beginning with the one who admittedly knew nothing about the subject. "Your lessons will be five dollars each," said the teacher.

Before the more learned of the two entered, he asked his friend what the teacher had told him. His friend answered, "He told me my lessons would be five dollars each." Confidently the more learned of the two came before the teacher. After a short interview in which the potential student informed the teacher of all that he knew about the sitar, the teacher told him, "Your lessons will cost ten dollars each." What do you mean ten dollars!" shouted the novice. "You only charged my friend five dollars and he knows nothing about music!" "Yes," replied the teacher, "First I have to unteach you everything you think you know before I can start."

## Quotes

"The more we desire to have that which is superfluous, the more we meet with difficulty."

—Moses Maimonides

## WW-Uncommen Sense (1)

## Obedience

Once, a yogi was attracting many people by his explanations of scripture. His style seemed spontaneous and people of all types were flocking to his *darshans*. Seeing what command the mystic had over his listeners, a well-known agnostic could not tolerate the fact that the yogi had been able to bring so many people under his control; he decided to crash the next gathering.

The next evening, the yogi was speaking to a full house; everyone sat respectfully rapt in attention. Suddenly the non-believer burst into the hall and proclaimed, "All of these people are obedient to you because they respect you; therefore they sit and listen. But I am not as foolish as they are. I have no respect for you. Let's see you make *me* obey you."

The yogi then asked the man to come forward. The man proudly pushed his way through the crowd to the front of the room. The yogi, smiling, gently asked him to come over to his left side. The man did so. Then the yogi changed his mind and said, "No, better you come around to my right side, we can talk better from there. Step over here." The man did this also, and smiling, the yogi said, "You see, you are obeying me, and I think you are a very gentle person. Now please sit down and listen."

## Cheaters and the Cheated

Seeing that many attractive men who had taken vows of renunciation were living along the banks of a sacred river, several young ladies made a plan to capture them for marriage (because those who practice celibacy generally have a lustrous complexion and a natural beauty about them, and their "seed" is considered to be very powerful, unlike that of the common stock). They wanted to cheat these gentlemen out of their vows and accumulated piety, but in this world we can only cheat ourselves: it seems that these men were actually not renunciates at all—they had merely gone to the holy place adopting the *dress* of renunciates in the hopes of being seduced by the cunning young ladies.

## The Light of Experience

There was once a man who had lived his entire life within a dark cave. One day someone from outside the cave came upon him and was astonished to learn that the cave dweller had spent his whole life more or less in the dark.

Taking the cave dweller by the hand, the man from outside said, "Come with me. I want to show you the sun." The man in the dark replied, "Wait, I will bring my lantern."No!" said the man from the light, "You won't need that!" But the cave dweller insisted that nothing could be seen without the light of the lantern. "All right," replied the man from outside, "If you want to take the lantern, you can, but it will not help you to see the sun."

When they reached the mouth of the cave the light of the lantern seemed to go out; in the presence of the sun it became useless. In the same way, it is said that when the light of Godhead chooses to reveal itself to us, our reasoning power will appear like that of the cave dweller's lantern in the light of the sun.

## Angry Buddha

Two Buddhist instructors were opposite in nature. One scrupulously keept the principles of discipline, while the other did not. When the disciplined instructor happened to visit his fellow instructor of poor reputation, the host offered him a drink of wine. (It is well known that a true Buddhist does not drink liquor). Thus the more disciplined of the two exclaimed, "I never drink!" Under the influence, the other replied, "Then you're not even human!" "You mean that because I do not drink I am not human?!" retorted the sober monk in outrage. "Then what am I?" "A Buddha," slurred the lush, "if it weren't for your anger."

## Three Days More

A young man left home and sought out a Buddhist monastery where he received the koan: "What is the sound of one hand clapping." After three years the student could not solve the riddle, and thus in tears one night he approached his master and requested permission to leave the monastery. The instructor advised him to wait one more week and meditate constantly on the koan. After one week the pupil was still unsuccessful, but the master asked him to try for another week. He did, but it was in vain.

Yet another week the student tried, and again decided he should leave, unsuccessful as he was. But the teacher advised him, "Remain for just three more days. If you fail, you may as well kill yourself." Finally understanding the necessity for self realization to be a matter of life and death, he solved the puzzle on the second day—the answer: there is no sound, it takes two hands.

## Dreamland

Once, a spiritual teacher of sorts, who had created a teaching by combining various disciplines, was questioned by his students about his regular afternoon nap. As it was, he never allowed his students to take the same liberty. Annoyed somewhat by their inquiry, he replied patiently with an air of confidence, "Every afternoon I go to Dreamland to meet old sages, just as Confucius did. "The students all knew that when Confucius slept he was said to have done so, meeting with sages, and then conveying their advice to the people.

Shortly thereafter on a very hot afternoon, some of the older students, disregarded the rules and took a nap. When the teacher came to know of this, he scolded them and demanded an explanation. In reply they offered, "We went to Dreamland as Confucius did to meet the sages." Their master then challenged them, "Oh? What was the message from those sages?" One of the students replied, "We asked the sages about your conversations with them, but they said you had never been there."

## Half a Hen

Once a man who lived by the sale of eggs reasoned thus: this chicken is supplying eggs from which I make my livelihood. From the hole on her underside comes my wealth. However, from the hole on the top she costs me everyday, and the price of chickenfeed is going up. One hole provides, the other takes away." He proceeded to cut off the chicken's head.

Once we *accept* a teacher, after scrutinizing his character, we should be careful to avoid the "Half hen philosophy" or pick and choose mentality. Otherwise we never really become a student at all, and thus what do we stand to learn?

## Visitors Only

The world of illusion has a hidden agenda. Along with all of the enjoyment we can eke out, there is a distress factor that we eventually will have to face for enjoyment at the cost of others.

Satan once invited a young man to visit him in Hell. "Don't worry," said the Devil, "You don't have to stay if you don't want to. I am merely a victim of bad publicity. It's actually quite pleasant down there."

After due consideration, the young man agreed to go. When he arrived, he was quite surprised to find many persons lounging in a relaxing atmosphere. Jacuzzis, saunas, lounge chairs, and cold drinks were ony a few of the amenities. Satan offered the man a towel and a chair, and no sooner had he sat down when an attractive young lady brought him refreshments. After some time he became adjusted to the atmosphere, and ventured to offer the devil a compliment.

"Say, Satan, this is great! More people should find out about your place." "Oh we're pretty well-known by now," replied the Devil. "Yes, but I mean people don't know how nice it is here. There's no work, no service to perform, everyone just enjoys—at least everyone I've met so far." "Would you like to stay/" asked Satan."I think I would!" said the young man, and he quickly signed the papers for permanent residence.

Suddenly, two of the Devil's assistants dragged him off and began to torture him. Aghast and exasperated, he called out to Satan. When the Devil arrived, the young man asked what was going on. "What about my quarters and servants" he cried. "Oh? replied the Devil, "that's only for the guests."

## A Moment of Ecstasy

It is said that it is very difficult to understand the minds of saintly persons.

Once a young lady disciple who had a background in art asked her guru if she could paint a picture of him. Her guru obliged her, and handed her a photograph of himself, asking her to copy it.

The guru went away for several months and when he returned he asked his disciple about the painting she had proposed. As it turned out she had not put the portrait to canvas. When her master asked her why not, she replied, "You looked so unhappy in that picture that I decided not to paint it." Unhappy? replied her guru, That was a moment of ecstasy!"

## WW-Uncommon Sense (2)

## Guru and the Cat

Once upon a time in a certain village in India there lived a guru. Every evening the guru would sit on his seat and deliver a lecture to the public from the *Bhagavad-gita*. It so happened that the guru had a cat, and just at the time of giving the lecture the cat would create a big disturbance. Being greatly annoyed with the cat, the guru decided to tie the cat to a tree before beginning his lecture. The guru tied the cat to the tree and then delivered his lecture without being disturbed. It worked very well and thus the guru regularly tied the cat to the tree before beginning his *Gita* discourse.

As time went by some members of the public joined the guru and became his disciples. Then after some years the guru died. His disciples continued their guru’s program by daily reciting the *Bhagavad-gita*. They also continued the ritual of tying the cat to the tree. When the cat died they bought another cat and thus the ritual of tying a cat to a tree continued generation after generation of disciples.

In the fifth generation that followed the guru, one of the renowned disciples wrote an elaborate treatise on the importance of tying a cat to a tree before beginning one’s studies of the *Bhagavad-gita.*

## All the Way Home

Two celibate disciples were once walking in the forest, returning to their master’s ashram. Upon reaching the riverside they met a young lady in distress. It seems that the river was exceptionally swift, swollen as it was from the recent rains. Unable to cross the river herself, she asked for the young men’s help.

Of the two, with caution, one volunteered to lend her a hand. Indeed, he carried her across the river, leaving her safely on the other side. This was all done to the astonishment of the other student, who subsequently took it upon himself to chastise his friend for his obvious deviation from the strict principles of *brahmacharya*, or celibate life. According to these principles the student should not even look at woman unless it is necessary in the course of one’s devotional service.

As they walked the distance to the ashram the one chastised the other. “How could you do that? She was so attractive. Her smile was charming, and her voice so soft. How could you hold her in your arms like that?”

“I may have held her for five minutes, but I cannot remember what she looked like,” said the friend. “But it seems that *you* have carried her all the way home!”

## One’s Nature

Once a camel was approached by a scorpion. The scorpion requested the camel to cary him across the river. The camel would have nothing to do with it, however, knowing that it is the nature of scorpions to sting without provocation.

The scorpion persisted, explaining his desperation to cross. “I promise I won’t sting you, and besides, if I did, how could I get across? Please let me sit on your hump, and do take me to the other side.”

The camel finally consented, and they engaged in light conversation as they forged the current. But upon reaching the other side, the scorpion proceeded to sting the camel. “Why did you do that?” exclaimed the camel with his dying breath. “Well,” replied the scorpion, “that’s my nature. You should have known that I can’t change that.”

## Tree House

There are eight objections to living in a house: 1) it is a lot of trouble to build; 2) it must be kept in repair; 3) someone might seize it; 4) too many people might want to live in it or visit it; 5) it makes the body tender; 6) it provides concealment for evil deeds; 7) it causes pride in ownership; and 8) it harbors bugs and lice.

There are ten advantages to residing under a tree: 1) it can be found with ease; 2) it can be found in any locality; 3) the sight of falling leaves is a reminder of the impermanence of life; 4) a tree arouses no covetous thoughts; 5) it affords no opportunity for evil deeds; 6) it is not received from anyone; 7) it is inhabited by good spirits; 8) it needs no fence; 9) it promotes health; and 10) it does not involve worldly attachments.

So say the Buddhists.

## Perfect Person

Two men sat together over dinner discussing relationships, life, and love. The elder of the two had never married, and the younger asked about this.

“How is it that you never married after all these years?”

“Well,” replied the older gentleman, “to tell you the truth, I spent my entire youth looking for the perfect woman. I met beautiful ones who were unintelligent, and intelligent ones who were not beautiful, and on and on and on. No one seemed just right. Finally, quite unexpectedly I found her—what I thought was the perfect woman.”

“What happened, why didn’t you marry her?” asked the younger man.

“Well,” came the reply, “It’s a sad thing. It seems she was looking for the perfect man.”

## No Risk No Gain

Once a young lady went bathing in a lake and almost drowned. When she called for help in desperation, several other swimmers came to her rescue. As she was helped out of the water, she took a solemn oath: “I swear never to go into the water again until I learn how to swim!”

## Somebody/Nobody

In a gathering of several people a discussion about values came to a halt when one man said, “Let’s face it, we are all trying to be somebody in life. To be somebody in the eyes of others is our most cherished value.”

Suddenly, out of the silence, an older, well-respected widow spoke up. “That is a common truth: Most people are trying hard to become somebody in the eyes of others. As you all know, I have indeed become somebody in all of your eyes. But it is now my understanding that it is more valuable to be nobody in the eyes of others, especially those who are so concerned with being somebody.”

## One Step

Regarding our spiritual progress, a Tibetan lama who crossed the Himalayas on foot during the Chinese occupation of his country was once asked how he had managed such a difficult journey. He replied: “One step at a time.”

## Beyond Knowledge

Once the great sage Narada was walking with Vidura. They came to the house of one of Narada’s many disciples, and found him engaged in worshiping his Krishna deity. Overwhelmed by ecstatic bliss, the simple disciple was peeling bananas to offer his Lord. However, in doing so, lost in divine rapture, he was offering the peel and throwing away the banana.

Narada remarked how extraordinary was the state of his disciple’s ecstasy. “More so,” said Vidura, “is the state of the Lord. He is known to be in full knowledge, but because he lives in a plane beyond knowledge, he’s accepting the peel!”

## WW- Uncommon Sense 3/4

## Philosopher’s Stone

A saintly person was known to live under a different tree every night. His possessions amounted to no more than a change of clothes and a lucky stone. His teeth he brushed with the twig of a nim tree, and the river served as his bathtub. He was always neat and clean, yet simple in dress.

One day a materialistic person, who was yet to make the fortune he yearned for, noticed the small stone in the possession of the saint. Knowing the saint to also be a learned philosopher, he quickly deduced that this must be the legendary philosopher’s stone, *chintamani*, or touchstone. Other than this stone, the materialist had no interest in the saint whatsoever. He had no interest to hear from the saint about spiritual matters, but the touchstone, that was something else. It is said that this mystical stone is most valuable, having the power to turn iron into gold.

The materialist, interpreting what the philosophers said about the touchstone in his own mind, decided to steal the stone. That very night while the saint rested, the materialist stealthily approached. Clumsy though he was, he was able to grab the stone and run, tripping along the way. While his heart beat rapidly, his mind reeled at the new possibilities that now lay before him. Finding a safe place, clutching the stone, he rested until daybreak.

When the materialist awoke he began to reflect upon the previous night. In retrospect it seemed to him that the saint was actually awake when he approached for the stone. If not, surely the saint must have heard him when he tripped and ran into the night. The more he thought about it, the more he became convinced. “He was awake!” thought the materialist. “He knew I was taking the stone, but he did not care.” These thoughts so much filled his mind that he could no longer think of using the stone to acquire gold. He had to know why the saint did not try to stop him from stealing the stone. “Didn’t he care about the stone? And if not, why? Did he have something else more valuable?”

By the force of his curiosity he returned to the saint. “Yesterday it was I who stole your touchstone,” he explained.

“Oh yes, I knew that,” replied the saint. “And now you are more interested in finding out from me what it is that I have that makes me so apparently disinterested in the stone. Why would I keep it, yet not protect it?”

“Yes, yes,” replied the materialist.

“The stone has done its work!” exclaimed the saint. “And now it is yours to keep until another thief comes along. You see, I was once just like you. Before I acquired the stone it was kept by a saint who has since passed on. I stole it from him, and now you have stolen it from me, and I shall pass on. Once the stone was in your possession, you lost interest in turning iron to gold, and thus you have become wealthy in another sense. You see, as long as one keeps this stone, the more it turns the iron of material desire into the gold of interest in that which is spiritual. It is, after all, a philosopher’s stone.”

## Where Do You Think You Are?

There was a man who died, and when he awoke he found himself in a beautiful place. He was surrounded by every conceivable comfort. Just then an attendant appeared before him and informed him, “You may have anything you want; just choose—food, entertainment, any sense pleasure at all.”

The man was delighted and he began sampling various delicacies and experiencing things that he had never even dreamed of on Earth. But after some time he became bored. He called the attendant and told him, “I’m tired of all this. I need something to do. What kind of constructive work can you give me?”

The attendant shook his head and replied, “I’m sorry sir. That’s one thing we cannot do for you. There is no work allowed here.”

“That’s a fine thing,” answered the man. “I may as well be in Hell.”

The attendant replied, “Where do you think you are?”

## Need No More

Common people pray to God when they are in need. When their need is met, they no longer feel the need to pray. But those who are not in need, yet feel the need to pray, need no more.

## Your Spirit

Once, much to the amazement of the villagers, the powerful Lord Shiva and his consort Parvati strolled through the village bazar. Stopping at a carpenters shop, they noticed two carved images of themselves. “Let’s put our spirits into these carved images,” said Shiva. Parvati agreed and suddenly the two dolls began to dance.

Many people gathered and and watched the now “living” dolls. Suddenly Shiva and Parvati withdrew their spirit from the images and the dolls fell inactive. Disappointed, the crowed asked them to enter the images once again. Shiva turned to the carpenter and said, “See if you can make them move.” Tying some loose string together, the carpenter joined the string to the joints of the two doll. Pulling the string, the dolls began to dance.

Amused, Shiva said, “You see, when you put *your* spirit into our images, you too can bring them to life.”

## Finding Something to Say

One day a man found a skull in the forest and said aloud, “What is this doing here?” To his astonishment, the skull answered, “I was waiting for someone to find me.”

“What! You can talk?’

“That’s not so remarkable,” said the skull. “It’s easy to speak, but much more difficult to.... Before the skull could finish, the man cut him off. Picking the skull up, he ran to his chief’s hut.

“I have something very valuable to show the chief!” he exclaimed.

“He’s busy now,” came the reply from the chiefs attendent.

“No, I must see him now. I have something very important to speak to him about. Moved by the man’s sense of urgency, the attendent agreed to let him in to see the chief. Standing before the chief, the man told the skull to talk. “Talk!” he ordered, but the skull remained silent.

“Get this man out of here!” yelled the chief. He has rudely disturbed me, and he should be punished.”

As the man was led away, the skull said, “That’s too bad.”

“What! Now you talk! Why didn’t you speak before the chief?” I started to explain that before you went to the chief, but you cut me off. You see, it is not so remarlable that I speak, that is not very difficult, that anyone can do. The difficult thing is thinking of something meaningful to say.“

## Smuggling

A mullah was regularly traveling across the Turkish border on a donkey carrying what appeared to be bags of sand. Absolutely convinced that he was actually smuggling, the border guard thoroughly searched him every time he passed. However, he could never find anything in the bags but sand.

Some time later, after the border guard had retired, he happened to meet the mullah again. Curious to know what it was that he was smuggling, the gaurd approached him in a friendly attitude. “I am convinced that you were smuggling something everytime you crossed the border, for no one would carry bags of sand in the desert. What was it you were smuggling?

“Donkeys” replied the wise mullah.

## Shadow/Substance

A traveller hired a donkey and a driver to take him to the next town. When thy stopped to rest, the sun was beating down, and the traveler sat in the donkey’s shadow, where there was room for only one person. “Get up, I want to sit there,” said the donkey’s owner. “You hired the donkey, not his shadow.”

“I hired both, argued the traveller. “When I hired the donkey that included his shadow.” But while the two men were arguing, the donkey ran off. They understood that in quarreling about the shadow, we often loose the substance.

## WW- The Ungrateful Man &amp; The Young Mendicant

## The Ungrateful Man

adopted from Mahabharat

Once upon a time in the land of Bharata-varsa there lived a poor village cobbler. One day the cobbler decided to leave his village in search of wealth and fortune. He traveled for many days until he reached a great forest. Entering the forest he found that his food supply had diminished and hunger pains soon gripped his stomach. After sometime the hungry cobbler wondered into a beautiful grove where he saw a magnificent crane.

Seeing the cobbler the crane said, "Dear sir, Please be comfortable. Where do you come from and why are you wondering alone in this forest?"

The crane was very beautiful. Indeed, he was no ordinary bird but the King of Cranes. Coming to sit by the side of the crane the cobbler said, "I am a poor cobbler from a far away place. I have wondered into this forest in search of wealth. But at present I haven't even enough food to fill my belly."

"I have plenty of food," said the crane, who then fed his guest to his full satisfaction. After the cobbler had eaten, the crane said, "I have a friend who is the king of many man-eaters, who lives in the far end of the forest. He is very favorable to me and if you go to him with my name he will satisfy all your desires. But you must go and return while the sun still shines because after dark the man-eaters might devour your flesh!"

The cobbler immediately set out to meet the king of the man-eaters and soon he came to a huge castle on top of a great mountain. Upon entering the castle the cobbler bowed before the man-eater king and told him that he had been sent by the King of Cranes.

"I am happy to receive you in my palace," said the king, "Your wish is my command."

Upon hearing of the poverty of the cobbler the king gave him many bags of jewels and gold coins. As the cobbler left the palace the king of the man-eaters requested him to give his respects to his friend, the king of cranes.

When the cobbler returned to the crane he told him all that had happened and the crane was very happy for his friend's good fortune. As the night progressed the cobbler felt a little hungry and he thought to himself, "It is only fitting that I celebrate my new fortune with a feast of crane meat."

Thinking in this way the cobbler killed the crane and cooked his tasty flesh on the fire. When this occoured all the birds in the forest began to cry in an outrage which made a tumultous sound. The cries of the birds could be heard all the way to the castle of the man-eater king who sent his soldiers to investigate.

Fearing his detection the cobbler fled leaving his jewels and gold behind. When the soldiers of the king arrived they found the remains of the king of cranes and the bags of gold. After a short pursuit the soldiers caught the cobbler and returned him to their king.

On hearing of the heinous actions of the cobbler the king ordered his death and the cobbler was immediately cut to bits. The King instructed his soldiers,"Take the flesh of this ungrateful man and feed it to the cannibals who live in this land."

When the body of the cobbler was given to the cannibals they said,"We are the lowest of all the human species because we will eat the flesh of any man or beast including our own people. However, we are not so low that we will eat the flesh of an ungrateful man." Hearing this the soldiers abandoned the body of the cobbler in the night and returned to their king.

MORAL

If one is ungrateful--being unable to appreciate the favors and help given by others--he is considered the most despicable--the lowest of the low.

Words of Wisdom

## The Young Mendicant

by Col. Raj Singh

There was once a young mendicant who lived on the banks of the sacred Ganges River. Being a member of the renounced order of life he kept only one loincloth to cover his body. Daily the young mendicant used to take his bath in the river and perform meditation and breathing exercises according to the Hatha Yoga system. After taking his bath he would but his loincloth in the sun to dry. One day while waiting for his cloth to dry the young mendicant had a thought,"It is certainly a great inconvenience for me to remain at this place while my loincloth is drying. If I had a second cloth I would save so much valuable time."

As the young mendicant thought in this way he was being observed by an elderly saintly person. Understanding the thoughts of the young mendicant the saint said, "My dear son, do not unnecessarily increase your material needs. It is better to tolerate small inconveniences and conserve one's time and energy for self-realization."

"What harm can there be in taking a second loincloth? replied the young mendicant, "It will hardly interfere with my spiritual practices."

Ignoring the advice of the saint, the young mendicant carried out his plan and got a second loincloth. The next day he bathed in the river and after placing his cloth in the sun to dry he put on his second cloth and happily went about his other activities.

The next day when the young mendicant went to bathe in the river he saw that a mouse had eaten a hole in his loincloth. "What shall I do now?, he thought, "I know! I will get a cat to keep watch over my cloth and protect it from the mice." And so he did. But the next day when he returned the cat was crying due to hunger.

"What shall I do now? thought the young mendicant, "I know! I will get a cow to supply milk for the cat." And so he did. But when the time for milking the cow arrived he did not know what to do and he sat down in a distressed mood.

Seeing the young mendicant with his cow a passer-by said, "Why don't you get a wife to milk the cow." And so he did. But after sometime a child was born, then two, then three, and the young mendicant had to buy a house. To buy the house he had to get a job and after sometime he had to get a second job to properly maintain his family.

Then one day the saintly person happened to see the young man and enquired, ?How is your advancement in self-realization?"

"Self-realization!, exclaimed the young man,"Why I'm to busy. I have to go to work. I have to take care of my wife and children. I have to milk the cow and feed the cat. There is no time for self-realization--no time! no time! no time!

MORAL

The bare necessities of life must be accepted, but one should not superfluously increase his necessities. Nor should they be unnecessarily decreased. One should simply accept what is necessary to help oneself advance in spiritual life.

## WW- The Young Man Under a Shade Tree

by Col. Raj Singh

There was once a young man who used to pass the time of day meditating under the shade of an old tree. One day some gentlemen from a neighboring town came along the road and saw the young man beneath the tree.

"Young man, they said, what are you doing there under that tree?"

"I'm just sitting here in the shade chanting the names of God", replied the young man.

Thinking that the young man was not properly engaged and therefore missing the opportunity of accumulating wealth and fortune, the gentlemen said, "Why are you wasting your time just sitting under that tree? You are in the prime of life. Why don't you get a job?"

"A job?, responded the young man , "Why should I get a job?"

"So you can save some money to buy yourself some land and build a house", they said.

"Well what would I do then?", asked the young man.

"Then you can get married and raise a family", they said.

"That's nice", replied the young man, "But what would I do then?"

"Then you can send your children to college and give them a good start in life", they said.

"Well what would I do then?", asked the young man.

"Then you can retire", they said.

"Retire?", remarked the young man, "But what would I do then?"

"Well", they said, "Then you can sit down here in the shade of this old tree and meditate or do what ever you like."

"That's interesting", replied the young man, "But that's what I'm doing now."

Moral

One should directly pursue the goal of life and not be distracted by unnecessary activities. Self-realization alone is the goal of life. That should be the ultimate aim of all endeavors.
